Upgrade DPIPixels code to remove need for shared banks.

When using latch chips, all latched outputs are now capable of
driving the full 1600 pixels per output.  Previously outputs
using the same GPIO pin but on different latches shared the
total number pixels for the pin.

This patch effectively doubles the number of pixels that a K8-Pi
can drive.  This applies to any cape using latch chips.  The
code can drive up to 4 latch chips with 20 outputs each supporting
up to 80 outputs with the full 800/1600 pixels per output.

Add checks before stopping and disabling services for Debian 13 (#2625)

These two checks are both required for the install script to run on Debian 13 (Trixie).

When Debian 13 is installed with only SSH and standard utilities, the following errors are present requiring these two checks for the script to proceed.

The unattended-upgrades package will not be installed, and the script will exit when it tries to stop a service that does not exist. The first check is to make sure this service exists before we attempt to stop it.

The beagle-flasher-init-shutdown service will not exist, and the script will exit when it tries to disable a service that does not exist. The second check is to make sure this service exists before we attempt to disable it.

Implement seamless migration to systemd-networkd

Added logic to seamlessly migrate from NetworkManager to systemd-networkd without dropping connectivity. Enhanced network configuration handling and ensured required packages are installed.

When installing on a base version of Debian 13 Trixie using the "--img" flag, the install fails as systemd-networkd is disabled by default and NetworkManager is in use. These changes will fix this by examining which service is in use, and cleanly migrating to systemd-networkd if necessary without losing connection.
Previously, the script would call commands to systemd-networkd with no regards to whether or not that was the running network daemon. If it was not, the script would fail.
This is a clean fix to move everything to systemd-networkd if NetworkManager is in use.

Fix fppd hang: wait(NULL) blocks on gst-ptp-helper child, remove invalid provide-clock prop

Two bugs prevented fppd from fully initializing after AES67 integration:

1. wait(NULL) → waitpid(pid, NULL, 0) in Plugins.cpp
   With SA_NOCLDWAIT set, wait(NULL) blocks until ALL children exit.
   Since gst-ptp-helper (spawned by gst_ptp_init) is a permanent child
   process, any wait(NULL) call would block forever — preventing fppd
   from reaching MainLoop() and starting the HTTP API server on port 32322.

2. Remove invalid 'provide-clock=false' from pipewiresrc/pipewiresink
   pipeline strings. This property doesn't exist on these elements
   (confirmed via gst-inspect-1.0). Pipeline clock selection is already
   handled correctly via gst_pipeline_use_clock(). Also fixes the config
   path separator (FPP_DIR_CONFIG already includes it).

Fix heap corruption crash: don't set PTP clock on playback pipeline

AttachInlineRTPBranches() was calling gst_pipeline_use_clock() to replace
the audio playback pipeline's clock with the PTP clock. When PTP is not
synced, gst_clock_get_time() returns GST_CLOCK_TIME_NONE (0xFFFFFFFFFFFF),
causing massive timestamp overflows inside GStreamer that corrupt the heap.

The PTP clock should only be used on standalone AES67 send/recv pipelines
created by CreateSendPipeline()/CreateRecvPipeline(). The playback
pipeline must keep its own system clock.

Replace gst-ptp-helper with ptp4l for proper AES67 PTP support

GStreamer's gst-ptp-helper is a PTP client only — it listens for PTP
Announce/Sync messages but never originates them.  This meant no PTP
packets were being sent on the network, making AES67 PTP non-functional.

Replace with ptp4l (from linuxptp package) which is a full IEEE 1588
PTP implementation that participates in BMCA and can act as grandmaster
or follower:

- Launch ptp4l as a managed subprocess with AES67-appropriate config
  (domain 0, 8 announce/sync per second, two-step, E2E delay)
- Hardware timestamping via /dev/ptp0 with automatic fallback to
  software timestamping
- Launch phc2sys to synchronize system clock to PTP hardware clock
- Remove gst_ptp_init()/gst_ptp_clock_new() — no longer needed
- Remove gst_pipeline_use_clock() from send/recv pipelines — system
  clock is now PTP-synced via phc2sys
- Update self-test: check ptp4l process status instead of GstPtpClock
- Properly terminate ptp4l and phc2sys on shutdown

Verified: PTP Announce, Sync, and Follow_Up packets now visible on wire.
Self-test: 22/22 pass. Audio playback works concurrently.

Fix AES67 send pipeline, error isolation, and VBR duration

Three runtime fixes:

1. AES67 send pipeline: Use stream-properties to register pipewiresrc
   with the correct PipeWire node.name instead of target-object. The
   filter-chain output uses node.target to find this node — the old
   target-object pointed at a node that didn't exist because nothing
   created it. Now the pipewiresrc registers AS the target node so the
   filter-chain connects to it automatically. RTP audio now flows.

2. Error isolation: BusSyncHandler now checks the source element name.
   Errors from AES67 inline RTP branch elements (aes67_*) are logged
   as warnings but do not stop media playback. This prevents the
   'all buffers have been removed' error on first track from killing
   playback and causing rapid track cycling.

3. VBR MP3 duration: Track maximum observed duration (m_maxDuration)
   across queries to handle GStreamer's fluctuating duration estimates
   for variable bit-rate files. Always update minutesTotal/secondsTotal
   from the latest max duration instead of caching only on first query.
   Prevents time-remaining from going negative or showing wrong values.

AES67: fix latency, distortion, and track transitions

- Force 48kHz output from GStreamer via capsfilter after audioresample
  in all three pipeline paths (video overlay, HDMI, audio-only). This
  prevents PipeWire from resampling 44.1kHz→48kHz internally, which
  caused both latency and audio distortion.

- Disable inline zero-hop RTP branches (tee→udpsink). Dual RTP streams
  with different SSRCs confused receivers, causing repeated/out-of-time
  audio. Single standalone pipewiresrc→udpsink pipeline only.

- Keep standalone AES67 send pipeline always running (no pause/resume).
  Pausing pipewiresrc with node.autoconnect=false prevented re-preroll.

- Add DetachAES67Branches() calls to Stop(), EOS handler, and error
  handler for proper cleanup if branches are re-enabled in the future.

- Add FlushPipeWireDelayBuffers() to zero filter-chain delay params
  between tracks, preventing stale audio carryover.

- PauseSendPipelines/ResumeSendPipelines are now no-ops.

Fix progress bar / time remaining always showing 0

Root cause: PlaylistEntryMedia::GetLengthInMS() cached m_duration on first
call. For GStreamer, TagLib's ParseMedia() fails for M4A files and
minutesTotal/secondsTotal are still 0 at that point (GStreamer discovers
duration asynchronously). So m_duration stayed 0, and GetElapsedMS()'s
guard 'if (f > m_duration)' set m_duration to the elapsed time. Once this
happened, GetLengthInMS() returned the cached (wrong) value permanently,
making seconds_remaining always report 0.

Fix in PlaylistEntryMedia::GetLengthInMS():
- Always try to refine m_duration from mediaOutputStatus.minutesTotal/
  secondsTotal, not just when m_duration is 0. Once GStreamer discovers
  the real duration and sets these values, the next call corrects
  m_duration since the real value is larger than the cached elapsed time.

Fix in GStreamerOut::Start():
- Pre-populate minutesTotal/secondsTotal from TagLib's ParseMedia() before
  the pipeline starts. This provides instant duration for formats TagLib
  supports (MP3, FLAC, OGG, WAV). For M4A/AAC where TagLib returns 0,
  the PlaylistEntryMedia fix handles it once GStreamer discovers the
  duration asynchronously.

Also in GStreamerOut::Process():
- Separate position and duration queries so position updates don't depend
  on a successful duration query (e.g., during format detection).
- Guard against negative remaining time when pos > effectiveDur.

  in /usr/share/wireplumber/scripts/linking/ to block default-target
  fallback for FPP combine-stream and filter-chain output nodes.

Fix: route media streams through input groups on output group save

SaveAndApplyPipeWireConfig() was unconditionally setting PipeWireSinkName
to the output group (fpp_group_*), overriding input group routing.  When
input groups with fppd_stream members exist, PipeWireSinkName must point
to the input group combine-stream (fpp_input_*) so audio flows:

  media stream → input group → output group

Now checks for active input groups before setting the target.  If input
groups own the stream slots, they take priority; otherwise falls back to
the output group (original behaviour for setups without input groups).

Fix: prevent fppd deadlock during save & apply

The save & apply flow (both output groups and input groups) was calling
file_get_contents('http://localhost:32322/command/Stop%20Now') without a
timeout.  If fppd's GStreamer teardown blocks (e.g. pipewiresink waiting
on a PipeWire connection that's about to be restarted), PHP hangs forever
and fppd's main thread deadlocks in a futex wait.

Fixes:
- Add StopFppdPlaybackSafe() helper with 3-second HTTP timeout
- Write PipeWireSinkName settings to file BEFORE PipeWire restart so
  fppd reads them from disk when creating new pipelines
- Use SetFppdSetting() wrapper that tolerates a non-responsive daemon
  (writes to file first, then best-effort SendCommand)
- Add timeouts to resume-playback file_get_contents calls
- Apply fixes to both SaveAndApplyPipeWireConfig (output groups) and
  SaveAndApplyInputGroups functions
fix labels on node types in visualiser

Fix: Stop() deadlock — clean up appsink/bus before state change

GStreamerOutput::Stop() was calling gst_element_set_state(NULL) without
first disconnecting appsink signal handlers or removing the bus sync
handler.  The streaming thread could be in the middle of an appsink
callback (OnNewSample) when Stop() tries to tear down the pipeline,
causing a deadlock due to malloc arena lock contention.

Close() had the correct cleanup (disconnect signals, set shutdown flag,
remove bus handler) but Stop() did not.  When 'Stop Now' is triggered
from the UI, the playlist calls Stop() directly — not Close() — so the
cleanup was skipped.

Fix: Move the critical pre-teardown cleanup into Stop() itself, and
simplify Close() to delegate to Stop() without duplicating the work.

Fix self-deadlock in StreamSlotManager: use recursive_mutex

StopAllSlots() held m_mutex and called Close(), which internally
called ClearSlot() that tried to acquire m_mutex again. Since
std::mutex is non-recursive, this caused a guaranteed deadlock on
every 'Stop Now' command. Same issue existed in ProcessBackgroundSlots().

Fix: change m_mutex from std::mutex to std::recursive_mutex so the
same thread can re-acquire the lock safely.

Also added logging around gst_element_set_state(NULL) in Stop() to
help diagnose any future pipeline teardown hangs.

Make PipeWire audio groups robust across reboots and USB changes

Three-part fix to ensure output group configs are always complete:

1. Robust card→sink resolution in GeneratePipeWireGroupsConfig():
   - Build sinkCardIdMap using /proc/asound/cardN/id for direct
     cardId→nodeName lookup (no card-number dependency)
   - Handle front:N, surround:N etc. ALSA paths (not just hw:N)
   - Support stored nodeTarget from previous successful Apply
   - Priority: stored nodeTarget > cardId map > cardNum map > skip

2. Persist resolved WirePlumber node names (nodeTarget) in JSON:
   - Stored during Apply so future regenerations work even when
     PipeWire hasn't enumerated all devices yet
   - WirePlumber names are deterministic (USB VID/PID/serial based),
     so stored names remain valid across reboots and USB re-plugs

3. Boot-time config regeneration via FPPINIT:
   - New script: scripts/regenerate_pipewire_groups
   - Called after PipeWire restart with --force flag
   - Re-resolves all card→sink mappings using current device state
   - Restarts PipeWire again only if config actually changed
   - Also regenerates input group config to keep in sync

USB hot-plug is handled natively by PipeWire's combine-stream
module — stream.rules are re-evaluated when new nodes appear,
so members auto-connect when devices are plugged in.

Fix graph: fppd_stream can target multiple input groups

The fppdStreamTargets map used a single value per stream name, so
when multiple input groups had the same fppd_stream_1 member, each
iteration overwrote the previous — only the last group appeared in
the graph. Changed to array-of-targets so all configured input groups
show correctly as virtual links and in the node subtitle.

pattern and correct AudioBackend check.

Fix PipeWireSinkName overwrite: first input group wins per stream slot

When multiple input groups claim the same fppd_stream (e.g. all 4 groups
have fppd_stream_1), the slotTargets map was overwriting on each iteration
so only the LAST group's node name was stored. This caused
PipeWireSinkName to be set to fpp_input_input_group_4 instead of
fpp_input_input_group_1, and since groups 2-4 had not been applied to
PipeWire, the pipewiresink target didn't exist — triggering the 5s stall
watchdog and skipping every track.

Fix: check isset() before assigning so the first input group claiming
each slot wins. Fixed in both ApplyPipeWireAudioGroups and
ApplyPipeWireInputGroupsConfig.

Fix input group volume/mute: match PipeWire loopback sub-nodes

PipeWire loopback modules don't create a bare parent node — they create
input.NAME and output.NAME sub-nodes only. The volume API was searching
for the bare name and failing. Now matches input.*/output.* prefixed
variants so channelmix.volume is correctly set on the loopback nodes.

Fix multi-channel output: generate custom ALSA adapters for >2ch members

When an output group member is configured with more than 2 channels (e.g.,
6ch ICUSBAUDIO7D), the default WirePlumber ALSA sink node only exposes 2
stereo ports. With stream.dont-remix = true, the extra channels (FC, LFE,
RL, RR etc.) were silently dropped.

Fix: GeneratePipeWireGroupsConfig() now generates custom ALSA adapter nodes
(context.objects) with the correct channel count and position layout. The
filter-chain playback targets this custom adapter instead of the default
stereo node, ensuring all physical outputs are driven.

Also adds missing channel position entries for 3, 5, and 7 channels to
both output group and input group config generators. Previously these
channel counts fell back to stereo positions, producing mismatched configs.

Updated Primary Audio Output tooltip to clarify that input mixing overrides
this setting when configured.

Fix: ShutdownPTP() on ApplyConfig so disabling PTP actually stops ptp4l

ApplyConfig() called StopAllPipelines() but never ShutdownPTP(). When the
user unchecked PTP in the AES67 config, the ptp4l and phc2sys child
processes kept running until fppd itself was restarted.

Fix: call ShutdownPTP() alongside StopAllPipelines() at the top of
ApplyConfig(). This also cleans up PTP when all instances are disabled
or the config file is removed.

Fix fppd_stream fan-out to multiple input groups via null-sink tee

When the same fppd_stream appears in multiple input groups, a single
GStreamer pipewiresink can only target ONE PipeWire node. Previously,
a loopback tried to capture directly from the fppd_stream node, but
since it's a Stream/Output/Audio (playback stream) — not a capturable
source — PipeWire fell back to the default ALSA source (e.g. CM106),
routing the wrong audio into the secondary input group.

Fix: introduce a null-audio-sink 'tee' node (fpp_tee_fppd_stream_N)
when a stream slot is claimed by 2+ input groups:

- context.objects creates the tee (support.null-audio-sink)
- PipeWireSinkName is set to the tee so fppd plays into it
- Each input group gets a loopback that captures the tee's monitor
  (stream.capture.sink = true) and plays into the group's combine-stream
- Single-group case unchanged: direct pipewiresink connection, no tee

Also updated:
- ApplyPipeWireInputGroups + ApplyPipeWireAudioGroups: redirect
  PipeWireSinkName to tee when fan-out detected
- SetInputGroupMemberVolume: handle fppd_stream loopback nodes
  (tee groups have loopbacks; primary-only groups don't)
- WirePlumber hook: block fallback for tee nodes and loopback sub-nodes
  (input.fpp_loopback_ig* / output.fpp_loopback_ig* patterns)
- Graph visualizer: classify + color tee nodes in Input Groups column
- Graph API: enrich tee nodes with fpp.tee properties, virtual fppd
  stream links point to tee when fan-out is active

Fix graph: preserve tee monitor ports so tee→input group links render

The monitor port blanket filter (p.name.startsWith('monitor_')) was
removing the tee node's monitor_FL/monitor_FR output ports.  These are
the only ports linking the tee to the loopback capture nodes (which get
absorbed into input group nodes).  Without them, the links had no
source endpoint and didn't render.

Fix: exempt fpp_tee_* nodes from the monitor port removal filter.

pipewire-graph: merge EQ routing hub nodes into EQ node

When an input group has EQ enabled, PipeWire creates a post-EQ
routing combine-stream (fpp_route_ig_N) with output.fpp_route_ig_*
sub-nodes.  These sub-nodes have mediaClass Stream/Output/Audio and
were falling through classifyColumn() to column 0 (Input Sources),
appearing as 'Input Group N (Routing) output' in the wrong column.

Fix: add merge rules 5 & 6 to mergeInternalNodes():
  5) output.fpp_route_ig_* sub-nodes → fpp_route_ig_* parent
  6) fpp_route_ig_* → fpp_fx_ig_* (EQ node)

This collapses the entire post-EQ routing chain into the EQ node,
so the graph cleanly shows: Input Group → EQ → Output Groups.

Also add fallback classifyColumn/nodeColor entries for fpp_route_ig_
in case the merge doesn't absorb them, and extend the duplicate-port
dedup to fpp_fx_ig_ nodes.

Fix video blank on first play and A/V sync with PipeWire

- Force GstSystemClock on pipeline instead of auto-selecting PipeWire clock.
  The PipeWire clock (from pipewiresink) is frozen at 0 on cold start until
  the graph processes its first audio quantum. With sync=TRUE, kmssink blocks
  forever in gst_clock_id_wait() because all frame PTS values are 'in the
  future' relative to clock time 0. GstSystemClock ticks from boot, so both
  audio and video sinks start gating immediately.

- Audio pipewiresink: sync=TRUE without ts-offset. Both pipewiresink and
  kmssink now sync against the same GstSystemClock, keeping A/V aligned.
  PipeWire filter-chain delay nodes handle inter-member alignment independently.

- Consumer kmssink: sync=TRUE, max-lateness=-1, skip-vsync=TRUE for direct
  HDMI output on connected displays not handled by the main pipeline.

- Skip disconnected HDMI connectors when building consumer kmssink branches
  (DRM connection check via ResolveDrmConnector).

- Position queries prefer consumer dkms_* sinks (sync=TRUE) over pipeline
  fallback for accurate playout position tracking.

- FlushPipeWireDelayBuffers() called at Start() entry for audio glitch fix.

- Add diagnostic logging: pipeline clock, rendered/dropped frame counts,
  element state, and wall-to-stream ratio at 5s intervals.

[ -n "${SDA1}" ] — quoting prevents the shell from expanding an empty variable to nothing, which would make the test always pass.

curl -fsSL — -f makes curl fail on HTTP errors instead of silently saving an error page as your network config. -sS and -L are standard good practice for scripted curl calls.

Avoid running crash-prone C++ global destructors at fppd shutdown on Linux too

main() tears down every subsystem explicitly, so the global/static singleton
destructors that run on a normal return are redundant. They are also crash-prone:
the single most common fppd crash on the dashboard is std::thread::~thread ->
std::terminate from __cxa_finalize, when a file-static std::thread in libfpp.so
(EVENT_PUBLISH_THREAD in Events.cpp, WarningHolder's notifyThread, ...) is still
joinable at process exit. The orderly shutdown joins these, but a late restart
during the drawn-out shutdown can leave one joinable again.

macOS already sidestepped the whole class of teardown crashes by calling _exit(0)
at the end of main(); the comment incorrectly assumed Linux was unaffected. Make
the _exit(0) shortcut unconditional so Linux skips the redundant, crash-prone
global-destructor pass as well.

Fixes the std::thread global-dtor terminate cluster (b2fcbed0c1, a6b073dc0e,
dd30ac1b13, 9f5d3c5023, 5067293cb1).

pinctrl: write AM335x pinmux via /dev/am335xpm when available

The AM335x control-module pinmux conf registers are hardware-protected and
only accept writes from kernel mode, so the existing /dev/mem pokes in
Ball::setMode were silently dropped -- the real muxing came solely from the
cape-universal pinmux-helper sysfs. Route register access through the new
am335xpm kernel driver (pread/pwrite) when /dev/am335xpm is present so the
kernel performs the privileged write; fall back to the legacy /dev/mem mapping
+ pinmux-helper otherwise.

- Ball: DomainAccess abstraction (pointer-poke vs fd) with readReg/writeReg;
  setMode skips the pinmux-helper sysfs when the fd path is active.
- AM335x: open /dev/am335xpm first (setDomainFd, base 0x800), else /dev/mem.
- Reads are unaffected (they always worked via mmap). K3/AM62 path unchanged.
- Covers both BBB and PocketBeagle1 (both call InitAM335xBalls).

rcn-ee keeps only the ~5 most recent dated builds online (rolling window), so
a hardcoded base-image date rots within weeks and breaks nightlies. Discover
the latest build at run time instead of pinning a date.

build-image-bb64.sh / build-image-bbb.sh:
- Add resolve_rcn_image_url(): parse the rcn-ee directory listing, pick the
  newest YYYY-MM-DD/ subdir, then the image whose filename starts with
  "<board>-debian-" (anchored so pocketbeagle2 beats pocketbeagle2-workshop
  and the .sha256sum sidecars are excluded). Default to latest; --base-image-date
  still pins a specific build, --base-image-url bypasses discovery entirely.

  is given, so discovered downloads stay integrity-verified.

CI: key BB base-image cache on resolved filename, not script hash

The BB builders now discover the latest rcn-ee image at run time, so the base
filename changes week to week while the script (and thus hashFiles(script))
stays constant. With the old key the cache only ever held the first-downloaded
image and every nightly re-fetched ~1GB.

Add a --print-base-image-url mode to build-image-bb64.sh / build-image-bbb.sh:
it runs the same listing discovery, prints the resolved URL on stdout (all
diagnostics routed to stderr), and exits before the root/--version checks so CI
can call it cheaply and unprivileged. The validate section is reordered
accordingly; the build machinery is unchanged.

build-images.yml resolves that URL in a new step and keys the download cache on
the image basename (Pi keeps its stable script-hash key since it pins its base
in-script). No restore-keys: an exact miss means a genuinely new base, which
should download fresh rather than restore a stale prior week's image. Result:
the ~6 of 7 nightly runs where rcn-ee hasn't published a new build get a cache
hit instead of re-downloading the base.

fpp-base-overlay: mux i2c2 persistently (cape RTC/GPIO-expanders need the bus)

Removing the bone-pinmux-helper also removed the persistent i2c2 boot mux its
"default" state provided -- which kept the whole cape i2c bus (not just the
EEPROM, but RTCs, GPIO expanders that often drive outputs, etc.) available.
CapeUtils only muxes i2c2 during EEPROM detection, which is fragile for those
peripherals. Mux i2c2 (UART1_CTSN/RTSN) in the overlay via pinctrl-0 on &i2c2 so
the bus is up from boot. am335xpm still bypasses the pinctrl-single claim, so a
cape that repurposes these pins can re-mux them. CapeUtils' i2c2 mux becomes a
no-op safety net (query reports "i2c").

Decouple jsoncpp and Drogon from the universal NOPCH include path

Under NOPCH/distcc builds (PCH disabled), every translation unit was
preprocessing the full Drogon framework and all of jsoncpp because both
were force-included via common headers -- even in files that use neither.
On a single-core BeagleBone, that preprocessing is the build bottleneck.

Drogon: split the HTTP type aliases (HttpRequestPtr/HttpResponsePtr) and
the drogon-free httpserver::webserver shim into a new lightweight
fpphttp_types.h. Declaration-only headers (Plugin.h, Commands.h,
httpAPI.h, Player.h, gpio.h, ...) include that instead of fpphttp.h; the
.cpp's that actually call Drogon include fpphttp.h directly. fpphttp.h's
public surface is unchanged for plugins. DEPRECATED.md documents the
httpserver:: compatibility shims for future removal.

jsoncpp: new fpp-json.h wrapper hides the Mac (<json/json.h>) vs
Pi/BBB/Debian (<jsoncpp/json/json.h>) include-path difference, replacing
the repeated __has_include dance. FPPWarning no longer derives from
Json::Value -- it stores its fields and serializes via toJsonValue() --
so Warnings.h (fan-in ~73) is now json-free. jsoncpp moved out of
fpp-pch.h's universal section into the NOPCH/PCH gate; the ~243 files
that use Json:: include fpp-json.h directly. Direct std includes added
where jsoncpp had been masking them (<map>/<vector>/<cstdint>/<unistd.h>).

Trims ~5.7% of NOPCH preprocessing and, more importantly, stops jsoncpp
from dragging the whole C++ standard library into every file -- a
prerequisite for per-file std-include reduction.

Verified: macOS PCH build links cleanly, and a NOPCH -fsyntax-only sweep
of all 167 macOS-compiled sources passes (0 failures). The 25 Pi/BBB-only
sources are unverifiable on macOS but a static scan shows no std-masking
gaps.

Forward-declare Json::Value in declaration-only headers

Follow-up to the jsoncpp decouple: the bulk sweep added the full
"fpp-json.h" include to every header that names Json::Value, but ~107 of
them use it only in declaration positions (method parameters/returns,
references) where an incomplete type suffices. Carrying the full include
made those headers re-propagate jsoncpp to all their includers, undercutting
the decoupling.

New fpp-json-fwd.h (the <iosfwd> idiom: `namespace Json { class Value; }`).
The 107 declaration-only headers now include it instead of "fpp-json.h".
The 11 headers that need the complete type -- a by-value Json::Value member
(Commands.h, ScheduleEntry.h, PlaylistEntryBase.h, ...) or a Json:: typedef
(Playlist.h's Json::UInt) -- keep the full include, as do the .cpp's that
define/call those methods.

Two transitive gaps the conversion exposed are fixed directly: MultiSync.h
now includes <map> for its std::map member (it had been getting it through
jsoncpp), and common.cpp includes "fpp-json.h" for MergeJsonValues().

Result: 39 of the 167 macOS-compiled sources no longer preprocess jsoncpp
at all (previously every TU did, via the universal PCH). Verified: macOS PCH
build links, and a NOPCH -fsyntax-only sweep of all 167 sources passes.

fpphttp_types.h: undef trantor LOG_WARN/INFO/DEBUG for plugin compat

Plugins that include <drogon/...> directly (e.g. fpp-osc, fpp-arcade,

not), so the cleanup stopped happening for those plugins. Restore the undefs
here. They are no-ops for FPP itself (LOG_* are enum values, not macros, when
FPP includes this header).

the gpiod line as an open-drain output with pull-up: setValue(0) drives
low, setValue(1) releases (high-Z, pulled up), and getValue() reads the
actual line level so a released line reflects what a peer is driving. This
lets a plugin bit-bang an I2C-style bus with no per-bit direction flipping.

- GPIODCapabilities: open-drain request + getValue reads the live line.
- BBBUtils (BBB/K3): "gpio_od" muxes the pad once to gpio_pu (keeps the
  receiver / RXACTIVE / INPUT_EN on so the released line stays readable)
  and leaves the drive to gpiod -- avoiding configPin's per-call line
  release/re-request and the /usr/bin/pinctrl fork on every flip.
- PiGPIOUtils (Pi/RP1): handle "gpio_od" instead of letting it fall into
  the generic "gpioX -> pinctrl set; return 0" short-circuit, which set
  the pad function but never created the gpiod request (so get/setValue
  no-op'd). Set the function via pinctrl, then create the open-drain
  request.

Validated on a Pi 5 (RP1): bit-banged read of the on-board PCF8523 RTC
over GPIO2/3 returns the correct time, confirming open-drain drive +
read-back work on real silicon. Used by the rewritten fpp-edmrds plugin.

Defer playlist presets/callbacks until transitions complete; flatten start cascades

TriggerPreset and PluginManager::playlistCallback run arbitrary code
inline (preset commands, native plugins, forking script plugins).
They previously fired from inside Play/Start/StopNow/SetIdle/Process
while m_playlistMutex was held and playlist state was mid-transition.
The recursive mutex masked the re-entrancy instead of making it safe:

- A PLAYLIST_STARTED preset that starts another playlist re-entered
  Play() on the same stack; chained presets (A starts B, B starts A)
  recursed without bound until stack overflow.
- Presets observed and mutated half-updated state (a PLAYLIST_STOPPED
  preset starting a playlist mid-SetIdle left the trailing idle
  publishes lying about the actual state).
- The mutex stayed held across fork/waitpid script-plugin runs.

New invariant: a state transition completes before any preset or
playlist callback runs. Notification sites queue snapshot-capturing
closures; every public transition method holds a thread-local
PlaylistTransitionGuard, and the outermost guard drains the queue
iteratively after the mutex is released. A Play() triggered by a
drained notification executes inline at depth 1 and appends its own
notifications to the same queue, so preset chains flatten into
iteration; runaway loops stop after MAX_NOTIFICATION_CASCADE events
with a loud LogErr + WarningHolder warning instead of a crash.
"query_next" deliberately stays synchronous — it is the decision-point
hook plugins use to insert the next item before the
SwitchToInsertedPlaylist checks run.

Re-entrant Play() calls (depth > 1, e.g. a "Start Playlist" command
entry executing inside its own StartPlaying frame) are recorded and
replayed by the same drain, generalizing the old PlaylistEntryCommand/
PlaylistEntryScript dynamic_cast special-case to every re-entrant
caller. The pending-start record moved from per-Playlist members to
file scope since the active Playlist instance can be swapped or queued
for cleanup between defer and replay; draining at guard exit (not just
in Process) also covers requests deferred while going idle, where
Process stops running. SwitchToInsertedPlaylist uses the new internal
PlayImpl so inserted child playlists still start inline within the
parent's transition.

Verified on hardware: a PLAYLIST_STARTED preset that endlessly restarts
another playlist now converges after the cascade cap with a warning
(previously unbounded recursion), and a command entry starting another
playlist defers and replays correctly.

Fix nested-playlist teardown when a command entry starts a new playlist

Three interacting bugs, all reachable when "Start Playlist At Item" (or
Stop Now) runs from a command entry inside an inserted-playlist stack:

1. StartPlaylistAtCommand pre-stops the current playlist with an INLINE
   Player::StopNow(1). Executed from an entry's own StartPlaying frame
   (e.g. three playlists deep), that StopNow tore the stack out from
   under the live SwitchToInsertedPlaylist/Start frames: SetIdle
   switched the global playlist pointer and condemned intermediate
   levels to PL_CLEANUPS while they were still referenced. Re-entrant
   StopNow is now deferred exactly like re-entrant Play (public
   StopNow/private StopNowImpl split); queue order preserves
   stop-before-start relative to a deferred start. Internal
   orchestration (PlayImpl's stop-before-load, Process's
   invalid-section bail-out) uses StopNowImpl inline.

2. PlayImpl loaded the new playlist into `this` even when its own
   StopNow had just unwound `this` to the parent (global pointer moved,
   `this` condemned to PL_CLEANUPS): the new playlist started on an
   object the player never processes and the next Process tick deletes
   — the historical "started a playlist from inside nested playlists
   and it blipped and vanished while the outer playlist resumed" bug,
   which predates the deferral work and also hit plain external "Start
   Playlist" during nested playback. PlayImpl now delegates to the
   newly-active playlist after its StopNow, repeating per level until
   the stack is flat and the root (global) object performs the load.

3. SetIdle could hand the global playlist pointer to a parent already
   condemned to PL_CLEANUPS (resurrecting an object the unconditional
   cleanup drain then deletes). It now walks up past condemned parents;
   if the whole chain is condemned, the exiting playlist becomes the
   resident idle object (never self-condemned while global) and drops
   its dangling parent pointer.

Verified on hardware: outer playlist inserts middle, middle inserts
inner, inner's last item is "Start Playlist At Item" — previously
crashed in Playlist::Load on the condemned object (fppd restart), now
the stack unwinds level by level and the new playlist plays at the
root. Plain single-playlist start/stop regression clean.

Add per-destination UDP output pacing, DSCP marking, and local-drop diagnostics

Bursting a full frame at line rate overruns switch buffers on the 1G->100M
speed mismatch to most pixel controllers, and with no acks in the protocols
the drops are silent until lights visibly glitch. Install the fq qdisc on
show ethernet interfaces at boot (flow_limit sized so fq never drops paced
frames at enqueue; only stock qdiscs are replaced; only interfaces with a
routable IPv4 so dedicated ColorLight NICs are untouched) and cap each
unicast destination socket with SO_MAX_PACING_RATE so the kernel clocks
frames out at a rate the controller port can absorb.

The pacing decision is per destination via a route lookup, re-evaluated on
address changes and undone if a route fails over to a non-fq egress;
multicast/broadcast sockets stay on the legacy drain path. The rate is
configured on the UDP outputs page (pacingRate in co-universes.json,
hot-reloadable, default 90Mbps for 100Mbps controller ports). Paced
destinations always use the batched non-blocking send path, so the Sending
mode selector collapses to Single/Multi-Threaded while pacing is enabled.

Also:
- Mark show traffic DSCP EF / SO_PRIORITY so managed switches and wifi WMM
  queues prioritize it
- Run the channel output thread (FIFO 10) and UDP send workers (FIFO 5) at
  real-time priority so frames don't bunch (and double the burst) under load
- Disable Energy Efficient Ethernet on ethernet NICs at boot
- Fix threaded-send races: per-destination sendLock (frame-thread paths
  try_lock and defer so a stuck worker can never stall the frame loop),
  WorkItems own copies of their mmsghdrs, SendSocketInfo held via
  shared_ptr, atomic errCount, and a generation counter so late completions
  of a timed-out frame don't skew the next frame's accounting
- Bound each send with a wall-clock budget so a destination slower than the
  pacing rate degrades to a logged frame drop instead of a permanent straggler
- Surface local packet drops (interface tx_dropped plus qdisc drop counters,
  the only place fq enqueue drops are visible) as a UI warning, sampled once
  a minute on a detached thread

CI: make nightly release replacement non-destructive and fix disk exhaustion

The nightly build failed with "No space left on device" in the
nightly_release job and, because that job deleted the existing release
before recreating it, the crash left the repo with NO nightly release at
all (both the release and its tag were wiped).

Two fixes:

1. Non-destructive replacement. Instead of `gh release delete` followed by
   `gh release create`, force-move the nightly tag, create the release only
   if missing (else edit in place), and upload assets with --clobber. The
   release is never in a deleted state, so a partial/failed run can only
   ever leave the previous night's assets, never zero. This also self-heals
   the currently-missing nightly on the next run.

2. Disk headroom. The four platforms' artifacts total ~11 GB; the flatten
   step copied them into a second directory (~21 GB peak) on a ~14 GB
   runner. Switch cp -> mv so artifacts aren't duplicated, and add the same
   "Free disk space" SDK strip the build jobs use. Applied to both the
   nightly_release and tag release jobs.

CI: retry mold link on qemu signal crashes; make nightly resilient to a failed platform

Nightly build 28919049221 failed because mold (the linker) took a
SIGSEGV *inside the qemu-arm emulator* while linking a plugin .so in the
armhf/Pi chroot -- a nondeterministic qemu-user emulation crash, not a
real link error (the equally-emulated BBB build passed in the same run).
Because one build leg failed, nightly_release was skipped, so no nightly
was published that day.

Two fixes:

1. Retry the link in the mold wrapper (src/makefiles/common/mold-wrapper/
   ld.mold). A crash shows up as death-by-signal (exit status >= 128);
   a legitimate link error (undefined symbol, etc.) exits with a small
   code. Retry only the former, up to 3 attempts, so transient qemu
   crashes self-heal in ~1s while real errors still fail fast. Native
   builds never crash, so the loop runs once and is a no-op there.

2. Make the nightly_release job resilient to a single-platform failure.
   It now runs when some build legs failed (!cancelled() + prep success)
   and publishes whatever platforms built; a platform missing from this
   run keeps its asset from the previous nightly (the publish step is
   non-destructive / --clobber, never a delete) and the coverage is
   logged so a partial nightly is never silent. Versioned/tag RELEASES
   stay all-or-nothing -- the separate `release` job keeps its default
   success() gate and only runs when every platform succeeds.

Add shared-memory ring support for streaming PRU output data on AM62x

On the AM62x, PRU reads from DDR (XFR2VBUS or LBBO) have a 1.1-1.8us
round trip with much larger spikes, which cannot sustain the data rates
the PRU output drivers need (and the PRUSS-M has no second XFR2VBUS read
port to overlap them).  Reads from the 32KB PRU shared RAM take ~20
cycles and are fully predictable, so an ARM real-time thread streams the
output data into a ring there instead and the PRU never touches DDR.

- pru/SMEMRing.hp: ring layout and the data-RAM config handshake, shared
  between PRU assembly (via cpp) and C++, including a 16K/16K split for
  when both PRUs stream (the split keeps clear of the FalconV5 listener
  capture area in the lower shared RAM)
- BBBPruSMEMRing in BBBPruUtils: the ARM-side producer, with counter and
  pointer flow-control conventions selectable per firmware
- BBBPru::run now writes the remoteproc firmware name explicitly before
  starting a core; the sysfs setting is sticky, so firmware loaded on the
  core by anything else would otherwise get re-booted in place of ours

BBShiftPanel: 16 output support, much higher refresh, SMEM ring data path

Support for the 16 output PocketScroller (two banks of 8 outputs, 12
bytes shifted per pixel clock) plus a set of optimizations that raise
the refresh rate and remove the visible flicker:

- The panel clock edges are now emitted in the middle of shifting the
  next pixel instead of via a NOP-padded toggle, cutting the pixel cost
  from 46 to 40 cycles (16 out) and 28 to 22 (8 out) while increasing
  every edge and setup margin (the 16 output hardware regenerates the
  control signals per group of four outputs, so margins were already
  better than the original single-buffer 8 output cape).
- The bit plane schedule (formerly the hand-tuned BIT_ORDERS tables) is
  now computed, and bits whose on-time is a multiple of the stride shift
  time are split into multiple shorter pulses spread evenly across the
  frame.  Same total light, but the dominant flicker component moves to
  ~4x the frame rate (e.g. ~420Hz at 104Hz refresh).  Brightness timing
  defaults now account for the doubled shift length of 16 output slots.
- Frame data streams through the shared-memory ring (SMEMRing.hp)
  instead of XFR2VBUS from DDR; measured on a 64 panel 8-bit load this
  took the refresh from 77.5Hz (with ~3.5ms/frame of DDR stalls) to a
  stall-free 104.5Hz.  Frame buffers moved to normal cached memory, so
  the prep threads no longer write uncached DDR and the per-frame msync
  and cache flush are gone.  Ring wait and frame counters are exported
  in the PRU data RAM for diagnostics.
- The FM6363C/PWM path uses the ring as well, and its 16 output DATA
  loop (never finished when 16 outputs were added) now outputs 16 pixel
  blocks so a full frame is consumed.  Real FM6363C hardware still needs
  a verification pass; the command, register, GCLK handshake and data
  flows were verified against the ring accounting.
- Fixed a teardown race that crashed fppd when saving the config while
  outputting: processTasks now always drains (queued tasks reference the
  calling frame's stack), and StoppingOutput/StartingOutput gate
  PrepData/SendData so a reload cannot race in-flight calls.

BBShiftString: use the SMEM ring for pixel data on AM62x

The AM62x XFR2VBUS latency spikes could stretch the WS281x low time far
enough to latch a partial frame; the shared-memory ring (SMEMRing.hp)
reads are ~20 cycles and fully predictable.  AM335x keeps the direct
LBBO path: XFR2VBUS does not exist there, DDR reads are fast, and the
single core has no room for a pump thread.

- The ring lives in the upper half of the shared RAM (SMEM_RING_SPLIT1
  for PRU1), clear of the FalconV5 listener capture area used on PRU0.
- The pump streams the frame data and any FalconV5 packet data in
  exactly the order the firmware consumes blocks, and writes the start
  command once the PRU has taken the previous one, preserving the
  latest-frame-wins drop behavior under overrun.
- Frame flipping buffers moved from the PRU DDR region to normal cached
  memory; the per-frame msync and cache flush are gone on AM62x.

BBShiftPanel: round bit-pulse splitting to nearest instead of free-only

Splitting a bit plane was only done when the pieces stayed at least as
long as the stride shift time (zero frame-time cost).  On longer chains
that leaves the second MSB unsplit, carrying a quarter of the light as a
single pulse at the frame rate (e.g. 57-86Hz), which is the remaining
visible flicker component.  Rounding the piece count to nearest allows
pieces slightly shorter than the shift time: bounded dead time of at
most half a shift per bit (~3% frame rate) in exchange for moving that
light to twice or more the frequency.  Verified on a 96 panel 8-bit
load: 77.3Hz measured vs 75 estimated, second MSB now two pulses at
~150Hz instead of one at 75Hz.

with random byte reads instead, and unmapped channels drop out of the
map entirely.

Configurations whose estimated refresh rate lands below 60Hz (e.g. 10
panel chains at 12-bit compute to ~38Hz, which is chain data bandwidth,
not fixable by scheduling) now raise a UI warning suggesting a lower
color depth or fewer panels per output.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

BBBMatrix: 4.6x faster PrepData via precomputed LUTs and NEON accumulate

The per-pixel work in PrepData was 6 data-dependent branches ORing single
pins into DDR per bit plane, plus a virtual interleave map call per pixel
and a full frame memset per frame.  On the single-core AM335x this capped
the Octo capes at ~18 P5 panels before the ARM pegged at 100%.

Rework it around precomputed tables built once at Init:
- per output, a 64-entry LUT of the 4 GPIO bank words for every 6-pin
  combination
- gamma values bit-spread so byte b holds bit-plane b, letting one shift/OR
  chain produce the pin-combination index for all planes of a pixel pair
- interleave handler results captured into flat row/column maps
- panels grouped by chain position so all outputs sharing gpio words
  accumulate in a register (NEON vorrq) and store without read-modify-write,
  which also makes the frame fully overwritten each frame - no memset needed

If an interleave map turns out not to be a clean bijection onto the chain
block, buildPrepTables detects it and PrepData falls back to the historical
memset + OR behavior.

Verified byte-identical to the old algorithm across depths 8/11, output by
row/bit, identity/zigzag/folded interleaves, and ragged chain lengths.
Measured on AM335x (BBB, 18 P5 panels, depth 8): 23.2ms -> 5.1ms per frame,
depth 11: 34.1ms -> 7.4ms, uneven 5-chain: 42.0ms -> 5.5ms.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

BBShiftString: tile the interleave+bitflip in PrepData, ~1.4x faster

The per-string interleave wrote one byte every 64 bytes across the whole
frame, so once the frame outgrows the cache every line gets re-fetched for
every string.  At K128 scale (64 strings per PRU) that made the interleave
pass the dominant ARM cost.

Interleave and bit-flip in 4KB tiles that stay in L1 instead: gather 64
positions from all strings with a NEON 8x8 byte transpose, then bit-flip
the tile straight into formattedData.  Strings that are unmapped, shorter
than the longest string, or exhausted supply zeros exactly as the old
zeroed interleave buffer did, and the interleave buffer itself is gone
(saves frameSize bytes of RAM per PRU).

Measured per PRU (64 strings x 800px), current vs tiled: AM335x 7.5ms ->
5.6ms, AM62x 3.5ms -> 2.4ms; byte-identical output verified for full,
ragged, and partial string lengths.  Verified live on a K16-Pro (BB64):
ring streaming, PRU consuming, test patterns clean.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

BBShiftString: fuse brightness/gamma into the tile fill, 2.6x total on AM335x

The K128 runs 128 strings on the single-core AM335x, so prepData is on the
critical path with no second core to lean on.  Two changes on top of the
tiling:

- prepareOutput's full-size per-string staging buffer is gone: the
  brightness/gamma application renders directly into the 64-position tile
  column, walking each string's virtual strings with a cursor that carries
  across tiles.  Test mode still uses the tester-provided buffers.
- virtual strings whose channel map is a plain run (chMap[i+3] ==
  chMap[i]+3 for the whole map - everything except grouping/nulls) skip the
  per-channel map indirection entirely, which was 4 bytes of map read per
  output byte (~614KB/frame per PRU at 800px).  Detected once at Init;
  anything irregular falls back to the mapped walk per virtual string.

Also only copy/flush the bytes the PRU will consume in sendData on AM335x
instead of the full allocated frame.

Measured per PRU (64 strings x 800px): AM335x 7.8ms -> 3.0ms, AM62x 3.3ms
-> 2.2ms; K128 both PRUs on AM335x ~15.6ms -> ~6.0ms per frame.  Verified
byte-identical against the old semantics across multi-virtual-string,
mixed affine/grouped, zero-length-span, truncated, overlong, and unmapped
configs; verified live on a K16-Pro with overlay-model data and test
patterns.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Survive wedged V4L2 decoder: supervised pipeline teardown + fppd self-restart

The 2026-07-03 soak (3 rigs, 15-sec clips, ~5700 pipeline cycles) proved
the CMA/DRM leak fixes hold (CmaFree flat all 25h) but reproduced the
issue #2695 decoder wedge with memory healthy: at ~24h a pipeline never
prerolled (CmaFree=402MB), the preroll watchdog correctly forced a stop,
and then gst_element_set_state(NULL) on the wedged pipeline hung the
playlist thread for 2h25m until it died with SIGBUS. Both old (~400 long
cycles) and new (~5700 short cycles) soaks failed near the 24-hour mark,
so the wedge appears time-correlated (kernel/firmware suspect), not
cycle- or memory-correlated — FPP can only detect and recover.

Recovery, two layers:

1. Supervised teardown: Stop() now drives the pipeline to NULL on a
   reaper thread with a 10s deadline. On timeout the pipeline is
   deliberately abandoned — the reaper keeps the ref and the pipeline
   leaks (~40 fds) — so the playlist thread survives and the show can
   continue. Close() then must NOT release the abandoned pipeline's DRM
   planes or shared DRM fd refs (its kmssinks still own them in the
   kernel; handing them to the next pipeline would conflict). A late-
   completing teardown is logged so "late" and "never" are
   distinguishable in soak logs.

2. Escalating self-heal: consecutive wedge events (preroll-watchdog
   fires, abandoned teardowns) are counted; at the limit (setting
   GStreamerWedgeRestartLimit, default 3, 0=disabled) fppd restarts
   itself via ShutdownFPPD(true), which re-opens the V4L2 device and
   bounds the abandoned-pipeline leakage. The counter resets whenever a
   pipeline reports a valid playback position.

Verified: normal play/stop cycles show no added teardown latency.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Escalate to system reboot when fppd restarts don't recover a wedged decoder

Issue #2727's dmesg proved the #2695 wedge lives in the VideoCore
firmware, not the driver: bcm2835_mmal_vchiq stops getting replies
("timed out waiting for sync completion", "received invalid message
context"), the codec driver can't disable ports (-ETIME) or flush
buffers, and fppd's teardown blocks forever in VIDIOC_STREAMOFF. No
userspace restart resets wedged firmware — only a reboot does — so a
wedge that survives the fppd-restart rung would otherwise loop
restart/wedge/restart until someone reboots by hand (mid-show, that
means dead video for the night).

The wedge escalation now has a second rung: each wedge-triggered
restart is recorded in /run/fppd/gstreamer_wedge_restarts (tmpfs —
survives fppd restarts, cleared by reboot, matching the firmware-state
lifetime exactly). When GStreamerWedgeRebootLimit (default 2, 0 =
disabled) wedge-triggered restarts occur within a 2-hour window, fppd
syncs and reboots the system instead of restarting again. First
incident: fppd restart, ~1-2 min video dropout. Firmware-level wedge:
one restart attempt, then a reboot, ~2-4 min outage total, unattended.

On platforms without /run/fppd or a reboot command (macOS, Docker) the
count can't persist / the reboot fails, and the logic degrades to the
restart rung by construction. The escalation decision is latched so
wedge events racing in during shutdown can't double-record or
double-trigger.

Kernel side is tracked upstream: the rigs run 6.18.34+rpt-rpi-v8 and
raspberrypi/linux#7174 reports a 6.18.y regression where H264 playback
kills kernel<->firmware comms on Pi4 (6.12.y unaffected).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

CI: auto-retry failed Build Images jobs once

The nightly image build has three independent transient failure modes that
are not code defects:

  1. qemu-user mis-emulating concurrent atomics in the armhf chroot, which
     SIGSEGVs a build tool. The mold linker case already self-heals in
     src/makefiles/common/mold-wrapper/ld.mold, but a segfault in cc1plus
     does not.
  2. GitHub failing to allocate a hosted runner. On 2026-07-09, during the
     "Delays starting Actions runs" incident, all four platforms built
     successfully and then nightly_release sat unassigned for 15 minutes
     before GitHub cancelled it: "The job was not acquired by Runner of type
     hosted even after multiple attempts."
  3. Transient artifact upload/download failures.

Add a workflow_run companion that calls `gh run rerun --failed` exactly once
on a failed run. Because --failed re-runs only the failed jobs and reuses the
successful ones' artifacts, recovering a dead publish costs ~5 minutes rather
than a ~55 minute rebuild.

Guarding on run_attempt < 2 makes this loop-safe: attempt 2's completion
event fails the check, so any run is retried at most once. Cancelled runs are
never retried, so a human cancel (or the concurrency group superseding a run)
still sticks.

Fix pinmux on am335x with latest fpp kernels

BBBMatrix: split the GPIO output across both PRUs on AM335x, ~1.35x pixel clock

Measured on AM335x, the two PRUs get fully independent GPIO write
throughput (simultaneous writes show zero slowdown, even to the same
bank), while a pixel spends most of its ~507ns in serialized posted
writes.  The copy PRU was only prefetching (~70% idle), so in dual-PRU
mode it now writes up to two of the data GPIO banks itself:

- The copy PRU prefetches the pair from DDR, writes its banks
  (CPY_OWNS_GPIOx, chosen by BBBMatrix.cpp), then publishes the pixel's
  bank words + sequence via scratchpad bank 11.  The output PRU writes
  its banks + clock and acknowledges via bank 10.  A pixel's banks are
  only written after the previous pixel was clocked, and the copy PRU's
  writes always precede its publish - so data never changes under a
  pending clock edge and always lands before the clock write.
- The scratchpad banks are PACKED (transfers land at bank offset 0
  regardless of start register), so each bank carries exactly one record.
- The copy PRU detects a frame restarted while it was blind in an LBBO
  (acknowledge outside the lockstep window) and resyncs from the frame
  base; it also clears the control record at startup since the
  scratchpad survives restarts (a stale exit sentinel killed it).
- Row tails stay quiet: the last pixel's release is deferred past the
  latch (and the ByRow blank row, whose copy-owned banks the output PRU
  clears directly).

GPIO0 (multi-microsecond L4_WKUP write-landing jitter) and the controls
bank stay on the output PRU in the existing write order, so their timing
behavior is unchanged.  Single-PRU configs (K8-B-Scroller style) keep
the existing code; the cape JSON can set noSplitOutput and the
BBBMatrixNoSplitOutput setting disables it for A/B testing.

Validated on an AM335x with pins unmuxed: Octoscroller (by depth and by
row + blank row) and OctoPlus (pru=1, r30 latch/oe) pin configs, every
GPIO DATAOUT sample matching the expected pattern over 60s soaks
including ~4700 same-address frame restarts; classic non-split and
SINGLEPRU variants still build and stream.  Simulated pixel loop
measured 370ns vs 507ns (real panel verification pending).

BBBMatrix split: restore change detection on the copy PRU for by-depth

banks and the pin state persists across frames, so the same change
detection + set-all/clear-all fast paths as OUTPUT_GPIO are valid; by-row
keeps the unconditional write since the blank row clears the pins behind

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Shared allocator for the PRU reserved DDR region

Outputs that share the 4MB reserved region used hardcoded offsets that
could silently overlap.  On the K8-B-Scroller (BBB48String strings +
BBBMatrix panels + BBBSerial together), the strings' two buffers occupy
at least 72KB from the bottom while the panels' cape dataOffset starts
them at 64KB - the overlapping tail corrupted both ways (string-end
pixels stomped by panel frames, panel sparkles from string writes,
matching long-observed behavior).  BBBSerial's top-of-region area was
likewise inside the panels' frame range.

BBBPru::ddrAlloc/ddrRelease is a named, page-aligned, first-fit
allocator over the region: strings and serial request their exact
footprints, and BBBMatrix (whose config loads last on a full start)
takes up to 4 frame slots of what remains - 3 is the tear-free flip
threshold, and leaving the rest of the region free lets other outputs
grow across partial config reloads, where initialization order is
arbitrary.  The cape dataOffset is kept as a floor.  A request that no
longer fits fails with a UI warning instead of silent corruption.

Verified on an OctoPlus (panels, 4 slots at 0x0-0x308000, output
unchanged) and a K16A-B (BBShiftString at 0x0-0x9C000, frame flipping
intact); armv7 + aarch64 + macOS builds clean.

BBShiftPanel: FM6353 / ICN2153 PWM panel support

The FM6353 is the older sibling of the FM6363C and speaks the same wire
protocol: five 16-bit config registers selected by LAT hold length
(4/6/8/10/2 clocks) with a 14-clock pre-active before each, and per-frame
stop-GCLK / registers / restart / data - exactly the command sequence the
PWM firmware already runs, so the PRU1 firmware is unchanged.  Register
values come from DMD_STM32 (board707/DMD_STM32, the reference
implementation for this chip), with the scan row count patched into
register 1 like the FM6363C does.

What did change is the GCLK program: the pulse counts (FM6353 rows switch
every 138 GCLK pulses vs 74/78 on the FM6363C) and the row select are now
configuration read from PRU DRAM bytes 0-3 instead of hardcoded, and a
direct binary row select mode joins the DP32020A-style shift register
pattern - FM6353 boards commonly drive the row mux directly.  For PWM
panel types the Panel Addressing Type dropdown now selects the row
transport: Direct Row Select = binary on SEL0-4, Standard = the shift
register.  Unconfigured bytes fall back to the FM6363C values so the
firmware pairs safely with an older libfpp.

Verified on fpppanels: FM6353 register block content (0x0F70 scan config
for 16 rows), 138/138 GCLK config, direct/shift row mode plumbing, and
per-frame command consumption; FM6363C regression-checked on the new
GCLK firmware (78/74).  Real FM6353 silicon not yet tested.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

BBShiftPanel: FM6373 / DP32019B PWM panel support

The FM6373 family (FM6373, ICN2055, ICN1065, DP3264, SM16380SH per
DMD_STM32's taxonomy) is a second generation of the SPWM protocol.  The
frame data format is unchanged from the FM6363C, but everything around it
differs:

- Registers: instead of five fixed words selected by LAT hold length, the
  upload is vsync + 11/14-clock LAT bursts, then five words all latched
  with LE high for the last 5 clocks: the 0x00AA/0x01AA write-enable pair,
  ONE word of a 47-entry {address, value} config sequence, and the
  0x0055/0x0155 commit pair.  Both reference implementations rotate the
  sequence one word per frame as a continuous refresh; setupPWMRegisters
  clocks the whole sequence through at init so the panel starts fully
  configured, then SendData rotates.  The rotating slot rewrite is
  race-free because it happens after the previous DATA command was
  dispatched: the PRU executes commands serially and the data upload
  never reads the register slots.  Sequence values are the kingdo9
  per-color DP32019B capture; register 0x02 (scan rows) is patched at
  runtime like DMD_STM32 does.

- GCLK: no free-running pulse packets.  The chip PWMs off the constant
  DCLK; the GCLK program only advances the display row with a single
  short OE pulse per row period (~20us, about 128 DCLKs at the data
  clock rate), free-running between frames so the panel keeps scanning
  at low FPP frame rates, plus a wider opener pulse after each restart.
  Direct binary row select only (what the DP32019B boards use).

The chip family flag shares the 0x1DF8 config word with the shift
firmware's row addressing config.  The five per-register upload blocks
in the FM6363C path could not simply be duplicated - that blew the
16-output firmware past the AM62x 12KB PRU IMEM (remoteproc "bad phdr
da 0x0 mem 0x3548") - so the FM6373 path loops one register-offset-based
block sender over the five slots.

Verified on fpppanels with real frame flow (fppd test mode): firmware
fits and boots, 47-word init completes, per-frame REGISTERS|STARTGCLK
consumed, rotating slot content changes every frame, FM6353 and standard
shift configs regression-checked.  Real FM6373 silicon not yet tested.
Note: fppd's test mode API needs "mode" as a string (e.g. "RGBFill") -
numeric mode values are silently ignored.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

BBShiftPanel/BBShiftString: groundwork for a shared panels+strings cape

Software support for a future PocketBeagle2 cape that runs panels on
PRU1 and pixel strings on PRU0 of the same PRUSS (the PB2 equivalent of
the K8-B-Scroller).  On the AM62x every PRU-capable header pin can be
muxed to either PRU, so the cape frees pins for the string side simply
by not listing them - no PRU or prep code changes on the panel side.

BBShiftPanel:
- Mux only the union of the cape's named control pins and the data pins
  its outputs reference (full historical set for capes without a
  controls section), and release exactly that set on Close.  Data pins
  a combo cape leaves unreferenced stay unmuxed for the string driver -
  the PRU still writes all 8 data bits of r30, writes to unmuxed bits
  just never reach a pin.  The OE handoff to PRU0 in dual-PRU mode
  follows the cape's "oe" control instead of a hardcoded P1-36.
- "sharedPRUSS": true in the cape (or output) config forces single-PRU
  mode and the SPLIT1 half of the shared-memory ring, and rejects the
  PWM panel types (they need PRU0 for GCLK) with a warning.

BBShiftString:
- The cape can override the per-PRU pin sets by name: pruPinConfig =
  {"pru": n, "dataPins": [names], "clockPin": name, "latchPin": name}.
  Cape configs and eeproms only ever carry header pin names; the
  mapping to r30 bits happens against the platform pin table
  (BBBPinCapabilities::pruPin), the same portability contract that let
  PocketBeagle1 capes work unchanged on the PocketBeagle2.
- Data pins need no firmware change: the stringMap index is the r30
  bit lane, so named pins resolve to their bit before the map is
  filled (identity for the default pin sets); bits outside r30.b0 are
  rejected with a warning (would need a -DDATA_BYTE firmware build).
- Clock/latch are runtime: the firmware's toggles take their bit
  numbers from a register loaded from PINCFG_OFFSET (published by the
  ARM after the firmware load, 0xA5 marker, reread while idle,
  compiled defaults otherwise).  PRU SET/CLR with a register bit
  operand is the same one cycle, so ws2811 timing is unchanged.
- "sharedPRUSS" skips clearing memory the panel driver owns and
  refuses FalconV5 with a warning: the listener is itself a PRU0
  program and its capture area overlaps the panel ring half.
- The PocketBeagle2 pin table already carries both PRUs' r30 bits for
  every string pin (P2-17 clock = PRU1 bit 19, P2-18 latch = bit 16),
  including the PRU0 side a combo cape will use - the freed data pins
  land on PRU0 bits 8-15 (r30.b1), so that firmware build is the one
  remaining piece once hardware exists.

BBBPru::run() gains a clearSharedMems flag so that in shared mode a
Save/restart of one output cannot wipe the other's ring or command
state: neither driver clears the 32KB shared RAM or the other PRU's

Split Falcon smart receiver handling into V4 and V5 protocols

Falcon V4 is send-only: the receiver chain config packet goes out (about
30 pixels of frame-time cost) but no queries are scheduled, no listen
windows open, and the PRU0 listener firmware is never loaded.  It works
on every BBShiftString cape, including a future shared panels+strings
cape.  Falcon V5 remains the full bidirectional protocol and requires
the cape's falconV5ListenerConfig; a V5 selection on a cape without
listeners (or with a shared PRUSS) falls back to V4 handling with a log
message, which matches what those setups effectively got before.

differentialType encoding: 10-15 stay Falcon V5 (existing configs keep
their behavior), 16-21 are Falcon V4.  The UI offers "Falcon v4" on any
BBShiftString cape and "Falcon v5" only with listener support (replacing
the old combined "Falcon v4/v5" entry), and the max-FPS estimate charges
30 pixels for v4 remotes vs 90 for v5.  Send-only chains are excluded
from the query scheduler and skip the numbering/fuse packets; the config
packet resend cadence is unchanged.

Testing this on the AM62x exposed two latent bugs in the SMEM-ring path
- the bidirectional protocol had never run on that architecture (no
receivers ever configured on a PocketBeagle2 test box):

- The dynamic (query/toggle/count) packet infos never set their len, so
  the pump streamed 0 packet bytes while the command flags promised a
  packet; the PRU starved forever in its ring wait on the first query
  frame.  The AM335x path reads packets by DDR address and never
  noticed.
- The FalconV5 listener startup (PRUControl) cleared the entire shared
  RAM after the string PRU's ring was already attached and live, wiping
  the ring counters (the same failure class the sharedPRUSS work
  guards against; it now passes clearSharedMems=false).

Verified on fppk16pro (K16-Pro): V4 streams the config packet every
12th frame with PRU0 left offline; V5 runs the full cycle - config,
number packets, per-frame queries with listen windows - with the
listener firmware on PRU0, sustained with no wedge (first time the
bidirectional path has run on the AM62x ring); plain no-receiver
configs regression clean.  Real receiver hardware still untested on
this box.

BBB48String: Falcon V4 smart receiver support

Send the Falcon V4 (send-only) config packet on BBB48String capes so the
Falcon differential receivers become an option on the direct-GPIO string
outputs (some receivers have trouble with the v2 protocol).  Selecting
"Falcon v4" on 4 consecutive ports forms a receiver chain; the config
packet content comes from the same FalconV5Support send-only chains the
BBShiftString V4 path uses.

The packet rides as 57 extra byte-slots appended to the frame data in
the existing byte-lane format (bytes pre-reversed so the UART LSB goes
out first) and command bit 16 tells the firmware it is there.  The
firmware grows a FALCONV4 section that reuses READ_DATA and the
DO_OUTPUT zeros-mask computation but drives UART framing instead of
ws2811 cells: a low/high lead-in, then per byte a low start bit, 8 data
bits and a high stop bit, each ~1130ns (the same wire timing as
BBShiftString's Falcon path).  Only the chain's first-port lines toggle
- the FALCON_MASK_GPIOn defines are generated per configuration by the
runtime firmware compile - so every other output sits at its post-frame
low.  Cost is ~30 pixels of frame budget every twelfth frame.

Falcon chains are refused on GPIO0 pins (the multi-microsecond write
landing jitter that causes ws2811 white flashes would corrupt the
~1.1us UART cells) and on inverted outputs, with warnings.  V5
selections fall back to V4 with a log message - these capes have no
listener hardware.  Note WAITNS cannot wait 1130ns (its compare
immediate is 8 bits, ~1020ns max at 250MHz); the section uses
WAITNS_LOOP like BBShiftString does.

Verified on fppgarage (K4-PB, AM62x): firmware compiles with the falcon
section, and PC sampling shows it executing at a 0.109% duty cycle vs
0.108% predicted for a 645us packet every 12th frame at 20fps - the
cadence and total wire time are both right.  The configured pixels are
unaffected (the packet addresses pixels past the string end).  AM335x
build compile-checked on fppmaster.  Real receiver hardware and a logic
analyzer capture of the packet timing still pending.

BBShiftPanel: scan-ratio aware brightness cap and a bigger stride table

Two row-count blind spots in the stride scheduling, exposed by the 1/32
scan P2.5 128x64 panels:

- The MSB on-time ramp bounds (0x8800..0xE800) were tuned for 16 scan

  (and at 1/8 scan they may grow).  1/16 scan behavior is unchanged.

  budget at 12 bit color, leaving the MSB flashing at the raw frame
  rate.  1/16 scan configs also gain headroom (24 -> 48 slots) for
  splitting more mid bits on short chains.

with the MSB split 4 ways: measured 74Hz frame rate (model predicted
71.6) with the dominant pulse at ~296Hz, vs 66Hz/66Hz unsplit before.

BBShiftPanel: OE PRU prefetches the ring data in the two-PRU shift mode

The OE PRU is mostly idle between brightness commands, so in the two-PRU
shift configuration it now owns consumption of the ARM shared-memory
ring: it keeps one 48-byte (four/eight pixel) block fetched ahead and
publishes [sequence, block] through scratchpad bank 11; the main PRU's
LOAD_DATA becomes a single XIN plus an acknowledgement on bank 10,
replacing the shared-RAM read and ring bookkeeping.  The sequence/ack
pair makes the single scratchpad block safe (the same publish-with-
sequence pattern the AM335x split-GPIO matrix uses), and blocks are
only fetched during the OE-on window when more than 64 cycles remain so
short bit planes keep their exact timing.

Finishing touches on the original draft: the display-off refill is
hoisted out of the extraWait loop (whose 3-cycle iterations are what
calibrate that delay), the published sequence is cleared at startup so
the main PRU can never consume a stale block from a previous run (the
scratchpad survives firmware reloads), the ring-wait statistics now
count the prefetch waits, and the 8-output variant is wired up alongside
the 16-output one.  Not used for the PWM panels (the other PRU runs the
GCLK program) or single-PRU configurations (no other PRU available,
e.g. a shared panels+strings cape).

Measured on fpppanels (16 outputs, 4-panel chains, 12 bit): 83.2Hz vs
80.0 baseline (+4%), zero prefetch-wait spins - the OE PRU always stays
a block ahead.  This config is half on-time-bound; fully shift-bound
chains gain ~8%.  The scheduler's cycles-per-pixel constants are
recalibrated from the measurement (48 -> 42 for 16 outputs, 26 -> 25
for 8) so the refresh estimate lands on the measured value (83 est /
83.0 measured).

feat(time): Switch NTP daemon from ntpsec to chrony (#2736)

ntpsec sources its client queries from UDP source port 123, which some
consumer routers / ISP gateways (e.g. newer Comcast gateways) drop as
suspected NTP reflection/amplification -- so time never syncs on those
networks (#2736). chrony sources from ephemeral ports and syncs cleanly,
and is a better fit for FPP's frequently-powered-off, often-RTC-less
hardware (fast step-on-boot, RTC discipline via rtcsync).

Preserves FPP's long-standing behavior of running an always-on NTP server
that other controllers point at via the "Override default NTP Server"
setting: chrony.conf uses "allow all" (users are on arbitrary IP ranges,
so no subnet restriction) and "local stratum 10" so a controller keeps
serving from its own clock/RTC when there is no reachable upstream.

- SD/FPP_Install.sh: install chrony (was ntpsec), configure_ntp writes the
  managed /etc/chrony/chrony.conf, purge ntpsec, mask systemd-timesyncd,
  tmpfiles for /run/chrony-dhcp; bump FPPCFGVER 106 -> 116.
- www/common/settings.php: SetNTPServer/RestartNTPD rewrite chrony.conf and
  restart chrony (default minsources 1 replaces the ntpd minsane toggle).
- src/boot/FPPINIT_Network.cpp: boot SNTP reads chrony.conf; DHCP-source
  reconcile replaces the /etc/default/ntpsec -g/IGNORE_DHCP handling.
- etc/networkd-dispatcher/routable.d/{ntpd -> chrony}: nudge chrony
  (online/burst/makestep) on reconnect without dropping the daemon, and
  populate /run/chrony-dhcp when UseNTPFromDHCP is enabled.
- scripts/healthCheck, healthCheckSSE, www/troubleshoot-commands.json:
  status via chronyc tracking/sources instead of ntpq.
- upgrade/116: migrate existing installs (purge ntpsec, install+configure
  chrony, preserve custom ntpServer, replace the routable.d hook).

Validated on real hardware (Debian 13, chrony 4.6.1, pcf85363 RTC),
including the ntpsec->chrony upgrade path and a reboot: fast sync, serves
off-subnet clients, serves at stratum 10 with no upstream, rtcsync keeps
the RTC in step, chrony starts after fpp_postnetwork.

feat(channeloutput): drop rpi_ws281x, migrate Pi string configs to DPIPixels

The rpi_ws281x library is poorly maintained upstream: support for each new
Pi model lands only after a long delay, and PRs adding hardware support have
sat unmerged for 6-9 months.  DPI drives the same GPIO pins, already works on
every Pi model we support, and does not conflict with the onboard audio, so
remove the RPIWS281X driver entirely and move its capes to DPIPixels.

Existing configs keep working without user intervention:

 - ChannelOutputSetup remaps the RPIWS281X output type to DPIPixels, so a
   config that has not been migrated yet still loads.
 - DPIPixelsOutput::LoadStringConfig() resolves the string config: the known
   capes map to their DPIPixels variant, an unknown cape falls back to a
   "-DPIPixels" variant if its EEPROM ships one, and finally to the config as
   named.  A third-party cape with a physically burned EEPROM only has an
   RPIWS281X config, which uses the same pin format, so it is consumed as-is
   and any pin DPI cannot drive is skipped with a warning rather than failing
   the whole cape.
 - setupChannelOutputs() migrates co-pixelStrings.json on disk at boot, and
   co-pixelStrings.php applies the same mapping so a Save writes the migrated
   output back out.  RPIWS281X capes are no longer offered in the UI.

The rPi-28D is special cased.  Its third RPIWS281X output is ws2801 over SPI,
which DPI cannot drive, so it maps to the 4 output variant that drives CN1's
clock and data pins as WS281x and its ws2801 protocol is rewritten to ws2811.

DPIPixels now grants two unlicensed outputs on every Pi rather than only on
the Pi 5.  RPIWS281X was never license gated, so without this a migrated PiHat
on a Pi 3/4 would drop from 1600 pixels per port to 50 and the UI would refuse
to save.

Also:
 - Add the post-migration keys to CONFIG_EEPROM_UPGRADE_MAP.  That map is what
   installs the virtual EEPROM, and it was keyed only on the RPIWS281X type, so
   once a config was migrated the EEPROM could never be reinstalled.
 - Guard GetDPIPinBitPosition() returning -1, which indexed outputToStringMap
   out of bounds.  Previously unreachable, but RPIWS281X configs can name pins
   that are not DPI capable.
 - Only RGBMatrix now blacklists snd_bcm2835; pixel strings no longer disable
   the onboard audio.

fix(epoll): don't invoke a callback for a descriptor removed mid-batch

epoll_wait() returns a batch of up to 40 events.  A callback invoked for one
event is free to remove descriptors belonging to later events in the same
batch: Bridge_Initialize() drops its sockets when the output ranges change,
and avahi's fpp_watch_free() removes a watch's descriptor and deletes the
watch.  waitForEvents() looked the callback up with callbacks[fd], and
std::map::operator[] default-constructs an empty std::function for a key that
is no longer there, so invoking it threw std::bad_function_call and aborted
fppd.  Reloading a channel output config while an E1.31 bridge was receiving
was enough to hit it.

Look the callback up with find() and drop events for descriptors that are no
longer registered; they are stale, the descriptor is not being watched any
more.  Copy the callback out of the map before invoking it as well, so a
callback that removes its own descriptor does not destroy the std::function
while it is still running.

feat(BBShiftPanel): park the PRUs while the output is idle

A shift panel only holds an image for as long as the pump thread keeps
re-shifting it, so a panel nobody is outputting to is simply dark.  The
pump did not know that: when the channel output thread went idle it kept
streaming the last (blank) frame forever.  On a 64 panel PocketScroller-16
that is 768KB/frame at 62.8Hz - 49.4MB/s of black, and 58% of a core for
as long as fppd runs.

StoppingOutput() already fires on exactly that transition, and the channel
output thread only stops once forceOutput() reports nothing at all wants to
output (sequences, overlays, effects, testing, bridging), so there is
nothing to show at that point.  Park instead: the pump stops on a frame
boundary and clears the command word, each PRU reads that at the end of the
frame it is in and parks in its command wait loop with the display off, and
both cores are then halted.

Halting is what makes the park safe to hold.  The PRU cycle counter
saturates after 2^32 cycles (~17s at 250MHz) and the hardware clears CTR_EN
when it does; RESET_PRU_CLOCK does not recover from that, and the OE PRU's
GET_PRU_CLOCK spin loops then never exit, wedging the panels until fppd
restarts.  Nothing resets the counter while a core idles in its wait loop,
so a running park would trip this every time.  A halted core does not count.

The pump only parks on a frame boundary and the ring is far smaller than a
frame, so the PRU consumes exactly what was produced and the two stay
aligned in the byte stream across the pause.  If either the park or the
drain does not complete, the refresh is left running rather than halting the
cores at an unknown point - a frozen mid-scan output would hold a row lit.

BBShiftString is unaffected: its pump is event driven and strings latch
their data, so there is no refresh to sustain.  PWM panels drive themselves
from their own registers and their pump already idles between commands.

Measured on a 64 panel PocketScroller-16: idle 58% -> ~1% of a core, both
cores halted, ring drained on an exact frame boundary, cycle counter frozen
across a 90s park, and a resume after a 30s+ park back to a sustained 83Hz.

fix(testmode): do not let a malformed request abort fppd

POST /api/testmode forwards its body to fppd untouched, and the test
patterns read it with jsoncpp accessors that throw on a type mismatch - a
color sent as "#202020" rather than an int was enough.  Nothing in the
command dispatch catches Json::Exception, so it unwound out of MainLoop and
std::terminate aborted fppd.

Catch it at ChannelTester::SetupTest() so every pattern is covered, present
and future, and clean up behind a pattern that threw part way through
Init(): Testing() only checks that the pointer is set, so a half configured
pattern would otherwise be handed to OverlayTestData with its channel data
unallocated.  That mirrors what the Init() failure path already does.

The controller had two bugs of its own.  It passed an array to
json_decode(), which takes a string, so every call raised a TypeError - and
it did so after SendCommand(), which is how the bad payload reached fppd in
the first place.  Return the array directly and reject a body that is not a
JSON object up front.
