feat(status): push fppd status over a WebSocket instead of polling

Every web page polled api/system/status on a timer (default 5s). That PHP
endpoint fetches /fppd/status and augments it with slow-moving host data
(advancedView cpu/mem, wifi, interfaces, reboot/restart flags, plugin
indicators). On a BeagleBone that augmentation is ~180ms of PHP per request
(measured: BBB 180ms / PocketBeagle2 97ms / Pi5 15ms, vs 0.7ms for the raw
fppd status), paid continuously by every open tab -- a real load on the
devices least able to afford it.

Split the fast-moving half off. fppd now serves a WebSocket at /fppdws
(drogon WebSocketController) and pushes its /fppd/status payload whenever it
changes, at most once a second, and nothing when no client is connected. The
push runs on drogon's own event loop, not the epoll-gated fppd main loop
which doesn't tick reliably during playback. Warnings are already part of the
status payload, so a WarningListener triggers an immediate push on change.

Client (fpp.js): when the socket is delivering status, the PHP poll drops to
30s (gblSystemAugRefreshSeconds) and fetches only the host augmentation via a
new ?systemonly=1 param, merging it onto the pushed base without clobbering
the live status. If the socket never connects or drops -- an odd reverse
proxy, or fppd itself being down -- everything falls back to the full poll,
which is also the only path that can report "fppd Not Running" and surface a
crash report. Warnings are unioned from two independent sources kept separate
so a cleared fppd warning disappears at once instead of lingering in a stale
PHP copy: fppd's live warnings (WebSocket) and PHP's crash/down warnings
(which must survive an fppd crash, so they stay in PHP).

Apache reverse-proxies /fppdws same-origin (ProxyPass ws://), so no CORS and
it works under HTTPS. mod_proxy_http tunnels the upgrade natively on Apache
>= 2.4.47 (all supported FPP OS images); proxy_wstunnel is enabled as well for
defense. upgrade/120 recopies the config and enables the module on existing
systems.

Verified end to end on a Pi5 in headless Chrome: socket connects through
Apache, status merges live with the augmentation without clobbering, the
clock advances via continuous pushes, warnings union correctly (fppd + crash),
and the poll falls back cleanly with the crash warning still surfaced when the
socket is unavailable.

feat(DPIPixels): variable, per-sequence frame rate without reboot

DPIPixels was locked to a fixed 20fps or 40fps framebuffer mode chosen by
the DPI_FPS setting, and switching between them required rewriting config.txt
and rebooting.  A string too long for 40fps dropped all the way to 20fps.

The Pi5/RP1 DPI (drm-rp1-dpi) accepts a custom modeset at runtime via the
same drmModeSetCrtc path KMSFrameBuffer already uses.  Since each WS bit is a
fixed 48 framebuffer pixels at the fixed 38.4MHz clock, the frame rate is just
pixel_clock / (htotal * vtotal): keeping the clock and resolution fixed and
varying only the vertical blanking (vtotal) changes the rate with no reboot,
no framebuffer reallocation, and no change to the WS bit timing.

- FrameBuffer: add SupportsVariableRefresh/GetMaxRefreshRate/SetRefreshRate
  virtuals (base no-ops) and a "VariableRefresh" config flag.
- KMSFrameBuffer: when VariableRefresh is set, keep the connector's horizontal
  timing and pixel clock but drive its own vertical, sized to a requested
  vactive.  SetRefreshRate(fps) reprograms only vtotal via drmModeSetCrtc on
  the output thread (under mediaOutputLock, same pattern as SyncDisplay).
- DPIPixels: size the framebuffer height once to the longest string
  (ceil(channels/5) rows + a blank reset tail), compute the max supportable
  fps, and each frame set the DPI rate to min(sequenceRate, maxFps) - only
  re-modesetting when it actually changes.  The old FrameBufferIsConfigured
  20/40fps + urlPut(DPI_FPS)/rebootFlag cliff is removed.
- FPPINIT: always write vactive=997 (the tallest envelope / lowest 20fps rate)
  as the boot mode so every runtime mode is a subset; drop the DPI_FPS branch.
- upgrade/121: strip the now-deprecated DPI_FPS setting; bump FPPCFGVER to 121.

Validated on a Pi5: a 900ch string runs at 40/50/100fps (measured vblank
39.999/49.998/99.997) and clamps a 125fps sequence to the 104fps ceiling, all
at a fixed 38.4MHz clock with the framebuffer unchanged; verified end-to-end
after a reboot into the 997 boot mode.

fix(video): resolve the DRM card by connector name, not the saved path

pipewire-video-consumers.json stores the cardPath that was current when the
video output group was configured, and GetHdmiConsumers handed that stored
path straight to the kmssink attach path. DRM card numbering is not stable:
a Pi5 was observed moving its HDMI connectors from card2 to card1 across a
plain reboot (connector IDs stayed the same). After such a renumber the saved
path points at the wrong device.

ResolveDrmConnector(), falling back to the stored values only if the connector
can't be found now, and log when a correction happens. The lookup is done
before the skipConnectorIds test because the caller builds that skip list from
live lookups, so it has to be compared against a live id.

consumer config, playback now logs

  VideoOutputManager: HDMI-A-1 moved /dev/dri/card2 -> /dev/dri/card1 since
  config was saved; using current path

and proceeds to open the shared DRM fd and assign an overlay plane on card1.

fix(video): convert format before kmssink so software-decoded video plays

The HDMI video paths linked the decoder straight to kmssink with no
videoconvert, on the assumption that "kmssink accepts HW decoder's native
NV12/DMA output" and that skipping the converter avoids ~100% CPU on a Pi4.

That assumption only holds when the decode actually happened in hardware.
A Pi5 has no hardware H.264 decoder at all, so every H.264 file goes through
avdec_h264 in software and comes out as I420, which will not negotiate against
the DRM plane. The result was that HDMI video output failed completely --
qtdemux aborted the stream with "not-negotiated (-4)", nothing ever reached
the plane, and playback stalled with fppd sitting at 0% CPU.

Insert a videoconvert ahead of kmssink on all three paths (the tee'd primary
sink, the per-consumer direct sinks, and the plain direct sink). videoconvert
negotiates to passthrough when the formats already match, so a hardware
decoder's NV12/DMA still reaches kmssink without a CPU-side copy and the Pi4
behavior is unchanged; it only does work when a conversion is genuinely
required, which is exactly the case that used to fail.

Confirmed with a reduced test on a Pi5 driving a real monitor:
  decodebin ! kmssink                -> not-negotiated (-4)
  decodebin ! videoconvert ! kmssink -> plays
and in fppd itself, playing an H.264 file to HDMI-A-1 now decodes (~1.2 cores,
matching a 1080p software decode), commits a framebuffer to its overlay plane
(plane-4 crtc-2 fb=685, previously crtc=(null) fb=0), runs to completion, and
releases the plane, the shared DRM fd and CMA on teardown.

feat(media): let Play Media target a video output, so non-primary slots can drive a display

GStreamerPlayData hardcoded an empty videoOut when constructing its
GStreamerOutput, so media started via the Play Media command was always
audio-only. Stream slots 2-5 are reachable only through that command, which
meant a non-primary slot could never produce video at all -- the sequence's
own media entry (which does carry videoOut) was the only way to get a picture.

it is the empty string and behavior is exactly as before; set to a connector
such as "HDMI-A-2" it lets that slot drive its own display. The content list

with two displays: two different files playing concurrently, one per connector,
each landing on its own DRM overlay plane and CRTC --
  plane-4 crtc-2 fb=685   (slot 1 -> HDMI-A-1)
  plane-5 crtc-3 fb=687   (slot 2 -> HDMI-A-2)
at ~2.5-3.4 cores for two 1080p software-decoded H.264 streams. Teardown is
clean on both natural end-of-stream and an explicit Stop All Media (exercised

fix(media): make non-primary stream slots report and stay in step

Stream slots 2-5 existed but were only half wired up.  Three defects, all
found while running companion media on a Pi5:

ProcessBackgroundSlots() was gated on SlotState::isBackground, which
nothing in the tree ever sets, so it was dead code and nothing called
Process() on slots 2-5.  Their position never advanced and the UI and
status API showed a frozen value for the whole track.  Pump every active
non-primary slot instead.  Teardown is deliberately not done there: media
started by "Play Media" is owned by runningCommandMedia and freed off the
GStreamer bus when Stopped() fires, so the delete the old branch did would
have been a double free.

ClearSlot() reset the status state but not the timings, and
GetAllSlotsStatus() reports those for any slot holding an active output,
so a freshly started stream read as though it were already minutes in
until its first Process() landed (observed: a new stream reporting
118.48s).

A slot can now opt into following the show's media clock, via a "sync"
argument on "Play Media" and a hook in Playlist::Process().  Measuring
first showed this must be a repair path rather than a control loop: two
slots started together on one box share the pipeline clock and hold
0.000s offset across a whole track with no correction at all, while
driving AdjustSpeed() at the main loop's ~100Hz pushed exactly-locked
streams to 0.9-2.5s apart, oscillating, never converging.  That is
because these pipelines refuse GST_SEEK_FLAG_INSTANT_RATE_CHANGE, so
ApplyRate() falls back to a *flush* seek, which moves the position enough
to feed the next correction; at 100Hz it also reset the decoder
continuously and took fppd down inside libmpg123 (longjmp /
__fortify_fail on mp3).

So sync is checked twice a second and only seeks past MAX_DRIFT_SEC,
which on one box never happens -- it is there for a genuinely displaced
stream (primary seeked or restarted, or MultiSync rate-adjusting the
primary on a remote).  Checks are suppressed for SYNC_SETTLE_MS after a
slot starts, because a fresh pipeline reports a settling position for
about a second and so does the primary it is compared against: on resume
the primary was seen reporting 0.486s having just been handed
Start(6040), and correcting against that produced a pair of pointless,
audible seeks.

Adds GStreamerOutput::SeekTo() and StreamSlotManager::SeekSlot() for the
correction, the latter alongside the existing SetSlotVolume() so callers
do not need to reach into GStreamer.

Verified on a Pi5: sync on, drift stays within the 10ms status sampling
resolution across start/pause/resume/stop, with zero rate fallbacks and
zero corrective seeks.

fix(media): let any stream drive a PixelOverlay model, not just the primary

The overlay push ran off the single static m_currentInstance, which slot 1
claims whenever it is playing (GStreamerOut.cpp:1827).  A non-primary
stream pointed at a model would resolve the model, register a listener and
log "video overlay: model=... size=...", decode frames -- and then have
them go nowhere, because ProcessVideoOverlay() only ever read
m_currentInstance.  The model simply never updated, with nothing in the
log to say why.

Track every output driving a model instead, and push each one's frames to
its own model.  m_currentInstance still selects the WLED audio tap, which
genuinely is a single-source thing.

Deregistration happens before m_videoOverlayModelLock is taken in Close(),
since ProcessVideoOverlay() walks the registry and then takes that lock --
the other order would be a lock inversion.

Verified on a Pi5: two different videos to two different models at once
(CenterWindowMatrix and TuneToMatrix), both updating independently with
distinct content at every sample, ~145% CPU, stable.  The pre-existing
single-video case still works.

feat(playlist): companion media that lives and dies with a media entry

A media entry can now declare extra media that starts and stops with it,
on its own stream slot:

  { "type": "media", "mediaName": "show.mp3",
    "extraMedia": [
      { "mediaName": "spanish.mp3", "slot": 2, "sync": true },
      { "mediaName": "lobby.mp4",   "slot": 3, "videoOut": "HDMI-A-2" }
    ] }

The stream slots this rides on already existed; what was missing was any
way to tie one to a show.  Running a second audio feed or a second display
alongside a playlist meant firing "Play Media" from a start-of-entry
command and remembering to fire "Stop Media Slot" from a matching stop
hook -- and anything that ended the entry another way (media finishing on
its own, Stop Now, a playlist change, a pause) left the companion playing.
Declaring it on the entry gives it the entry's lifetime instead, including
the natural-finish path in Process() and Pause()/Resume().  Because
pausing a media entry rebuilds the output rather than pausing the
pipeline, companions are restarted the same way, at the entry's offset.

Start and stop delegate to the existing Play Media / Stop Media Slot
commands rather than reimplementing slot setup, keeping one code path for
"play something on a slot", and are dispatched outside the media output
lock since they run commands.

"both" entries get this for free: PlaylistEntryBoth builds a
PlaylistEntryMedia from the same config and delegates the lifecycle to it,
so a sequence with audio picks companions up with no extra code.

For the UI, "Extra Media", "Extra Media Slot" and "Extra Media Video Out"
are declared args on the media and both entry types.  They are flat fields
rather than an editor for the array because of how the playlist editor
round-trips an entry: psiDetailsForEntry emits field_<name> per *declared*
arg and GetPlaylistEntry reads those back, so anything the schema does not
declare is silently dropped on save.  A declared field is the only shape
that survives.  One companion covers both things this was asked for -- a
second soundtrack on its own output device, and a second video on the
other HDMI -- and the array stays as the escape hatch for more than one.

The slot is the output route: which audio device a companion lands on is
configured per slot in the PipeWire audio groups, which write
PipeWireSinkName_<slot>.  Choosing the slot on the entry and leaving the
device with the group config keeps routing in one place instead of
repeating it on every entry.  The editor writes the slot as a string and
hand-authored playlists may use an int; jsoncpp's asInt() throws on a
string, so both are handled, and an out-of-range slot warns and falls
back to 2.

Known limitation: an extraMedia array with more than one companion still
does not survive being edited in the UI.  That needs a repeatable-row
widget in PrintArgInputs / psiDetailsForEntry / GetPlaylistEntry, a change
to the shared renderer the command editor also uses.

Verified on a Pi5 across media and both entries: companion starts with the
entry and holds its timeline, two videos run one per HDMI connector at
different resolutions with a constant sub-frame offset and no drift, a
companion drives a PixelOverlay model, audio companions land on a separate
sink (confirmed with pw-link), and both slots tear down across repeated
start/pause/resume/stop cycles with CMA flat.

fix(net): serialize NetworkMonitor callback map access

NetworkMonitor::callbacks (a std::map) was read and mutated from two
threads with no lock: callCallbacks() iterates and invokes it on the
netlink/EPoll dispatch thread, while registerCallback()/removeCallback()
insert and erase it on the main thread (channel-output Init/Close,
MultiSync setup). A netlink NEW_ADDR/DEL_ADDR event landing during a
register or erase corrupts the red-black tree, which surfaces later as
heap corruption at an unrelated free() - e.g. an fppd SIGSEGV on shutdown
freeing a UDPOutputData object. It reproduced in the wild during
"systemctl restart fppd", whose ExecStartPre (fppinit bootPre)
reconfigures networkd and generates address-change events.

Add a mutex guarding all three accessors. It is held across dispatch so
removeCallback() blocks until any in-flight callback returns, letting the
caller safely tear down the state the callback captured (the callbacks
capture 'this'). Deadlock-safe: no callback re-enters register/remove,
and no caller holds another lock before acquiring this one. Confirmed
with ThreadSanitizer: the unlocked pattern reports a data race, the
locked version is clean.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat(udpout): per-controller UDP output pacing override

The fq/SO_MAX_PACING_RATE pacing rate was a single global setting applied
to every unicast destination. A show mixing gigabit FPP instances with
100Mbps (or slower, ESP32-class) pixel controllers wants different caps
per controller, not one compromise value.

Add an advanced-mode "Pacing" column to the universe outputs table. Each
unicast row selects Default (the global rate), Disabled (line rate), or a
specific Mbps cap. The value persists as a per-universe "pacingRate" in
co-universes.json (omitted when Default, so existing configs are
untouched and keep falling back to the global rate).

UDPOutput::Init builds an IP->bytes/sec map from the overrides;
findOrCreateSocket looks up each destination and applies its rate, else
the global one. Overrides arm the pacing machinery (fq install included)
even when the global rate is Disabled, so a lone ESP32 can be capped with
everything else unpaced. Sharing a socket per destination IP, the most
conservative (lowest) rate wins when universes to the same controller
disagree. A pacingDrainRate member (smallest positive rate) feeds the
pre-sync drain-sleep estimate so the global-disabled case can't divide by
zero. The max-fps hint under the global selector now accounts for
per-destination rates. 30Mbps added as a step to both selectors.

Verified live: strace confirms sockets get SO_MAX_PACING_RATE 11250000
(90Mbps default) and 3750000 (30Mbps override) while a Disabled override
gets none.

fix(e131bridge): size input socket receive buffers to universe count

The three bridge input sockets (E1.31/DDP/ArtNet) each requested a flat
512KB SO_RCVBUF, which the kernel silently clamps to net.core.rmem_max
(384KB). A show pushing several hundred universes delivers a full frame
as one back-to-back burst, and if the main loop stalls a frame or two
draining output, the undersized buffer tail-drops packets.

Scale the request to InputUniverseCount (~4KB/universe, 512KB floor,
16MB cap) and try SO_RCVBUFFORCE first so root bypasses rmem_max; raise
the boot-time rmem_max ceiling to 8MB for the fallback path. Move the
live `sudo sysctl igmp_max_memberships` out of the bridge reload path
into FPPINIT_Network where the other socket tuning already lives.

fix(multisync): bound sync send so an unreachable remote can't stall output

SendControlPacketViaMsgs() retried sendmmsg in a loop whose giveup was dead
code: the inner "int oc" at the top of the loop body shadowed the outer one
(-Wshadow confirms), so "oc = -1" on budget exhaustion assigned the inner
variable and the "while (oc >= 0 ...)" condition never changed. Worse, that
branch also skips the 250us sleep, so past the budget it spun hot on
sendmmsg while holding m_socketLock - on the channel output thread, ahead of
the frame's channel data.

Reachable whenever a destination fails persistently and is not the first in
the list (sendmmsg partially succeeds, so the loop is entered). Measured
against a destination with an unreachable route: the old loop never
terminated - 20/20 iterations had to be cut off by an external 500ms
watchdog - which in the shipped code means the output thread stops for good
and the show stops with it.

Restructure into a single loop with no duplicated initial send (removing the
shadowing entirely), and:

- Skip a destination that will not take the packet instead of retrying it
  forever or abandoning the whole batch, so one bad remote neither stalls the
  thread nor desyncs the healthy remotes behind it in the list.
- Cut the retry budget from 10ms to 2ms for the whole call. A remote that has
  dropped off the LAN leaves its neighbour entry unresolved and the kernel
  answers sends with EAGAIN (not EHOSTUNREACH) while it is gone - measured at
  ~97% of sends under load - so a long retry turns one dead remote into a
  per-frame stall for every controller. Dropping a sync packet is far cheaper;
  the next frame sends another.

Same test, fixed loop: 27us median, unreachable destination skipped, healthy
destination still delivered.

refactor(commands): move disallowMultisync off the Command vtable

d7b5ecb51 added a virtual disallowMultisync() to Command, which external
event/channel-output plugins subclass and compile separately against these
headers. Inserting a virtual shifted the Command vtable, so on a pre-built
plugin's object FPP dispatched Command::getDescription()'s internal
disallowMultisync() call into the wrong slot - it landed on the plugin's
run() and crashed fppd on the first /api/commands request.

The flag is pure UI metadata (it only tells the frontend to hide the
Multisync option; the runtime multisync decision is driven entirely by the
incoming JSON). Emit it by overriding the existing getDescription() virtual
via a new FPP-internal LocalOnlyCommand base instead, and reparent IfCommand
onto it. Command's vtable is restored to the layout plugins were built
against, and a comment records the ABI rule: no new virtuals on Command.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(commands): isolate per-command failures in /commands endpoint

getDescriptions() looped describeCommand() with no per-command guard, so a
single command that threw while being described took out the entire
/commands response - and the command UI that depends on it. This is exactly
what a stale external plugin does: its Command/CommandArg layout no longer
matches these headers, getDescription() reads a std::string field at the
wrong offset, and jsoncpp rejects the garbage length ("length too big for
prefixing").

Wrap each command's description in try/catch, logging and skipping the
offender (keyed by the map's own safe string) so every healthy command
still lists. Complements the vtable/ABI rules in Commands.h - together they
degrade an ABI-incompatible plugin from "crash/500 the whole daemon" to
"that one command is missing." Cannot catch a hard memory fault (e.g. a
cross-ABI destructor free()); only the ABI rules prevent those.

fix(plugins): reject plugins that never defined an API version symbol

The "compiled against an older FPP API" branch in loadSHLIBPlugin was
unreachable. dlsym() on a handle searches the object and its DT_NEEDED
dependencies; every plugin links -lfpp, and libfpp.so also defines the weak
fpp_plugin_api_version (Plugin.h emits it into every TU that includes it).
So a plugin predating the version mechanism resolved straight through to
FPP's own copy and reported a version that trivially matched.

Confirm the symbol actually lives in the plugin by comparing the shared
object it resolved from against the one createPlugin() resolved from -
that entry point is never defined by libfpp, so it identifies the plugin.

Note this cannot be fixed by having core stop exporting the symbol: in-tree
channel outputs (libfpp-co-*.so) load through this same path from
ChannelOutputSetup, and suppressing the definition core-side would reject
every one of them.

Verified on Debian 13/aarch64 - rebuilt plugin accepted, stale-version
plugin rejected on version, symbol-less plugin now rejected as expected
(previously accepted), in-tree channel output still accepted.

fix(aes67): serialize ApplyConfig so it can't assign over a live SAP thread

ApplyConfig() joins m_sapAnnounceThread/m_sapRecvThread at the top and
re-creates them ~70 lines later, after LoadConfig() and pipeline creation.
Nothing serialized that window, and the function has three independent
callers: the boot sequence (fppd.cpp), AES67ApplyCommand::run on a command
thread, and m_rebuildThread from the SAP watchdog.

Two overlapping calls both pass the joins, then both reach
"m_sapAnnounceThread = std::thread(...)". Assigning over a still-joinable
std::thread is an unconditional std::terminate(), which is what the crash
reports show: std::thread::operator= (std_thread.h:195) under
AES67Manager::ApplyConfig, reached from AES67ApplyCommand::run.

Adds m_applyMutex, held across ApplyConfig(), Cleanup() and Shutdown().
Shutdown() takes it only after joining m_rebuildThread, since that thread
calls ApplyConfig() and holding the lock across the join would deadlock.

Note the sibling OpusRTPManager has the same shape; its existing guard only
covers self-join re-entrancy, not concurrent callers, so it is likely
exposed to this too.

fix(http): drain in-flight compat requests before a plugin is unloaded

The libhttpserver compat shim routes requests through a shared_ptr slot
holding an atomic http_resource*, and unregister_resource() nulls that slot.
That makes a *newly arriving* request safe, but not one already running: the
handler loads the pointer, and PluginManager::Cleanup() then dlclose()s the
.so as soon as unregisterApis() returns, unmapping the object and its vtable
before the handler makes its virtual render_*() call.

Crash reports show both halves of that window -- a fault on the slot load
(fpphttp_compat.cpp:97) and on the dispatch itself (fpphttp_compat.cpp:105),
under drogon's HttpControllersRouter on a trantor I/O thread.

Adds s_dispatchMutex, held shared across each handler's render_*() call and
taken exclusively by clearSlot() after the slot is nulled, so
unregister_resource() cannot return while a request is still inside the
plugin. Nulling first means new requests bail at the null check instead of
queueing behind the drain. Applies to both the exact-path and the family
regex handler.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix: stop using "does /boot/firmware exist" to locate the boot partition

Every shell copy of the boot-dir probe tested for the /boot/firmware
*directory*.  Current BeagleBone Black images ship that directory
(ID.txt, START.HTM, sysconf.txt) while keeping the real boot files --
uEnv.txt, kernels, dtbs -- in /boot on the root filesystem, so the probe
picked /boot/firmware on every BBB that has it.

upgradeOS-part1.sh is where that actually broke an fppos upgrade.  Its
FPPBOOTDIR feeds the bind mount that exposes the old boot partition to
the chroot, because `mount -o bind /` is not recursive.  On a BBB it was
binding /boot/firmware onto itself and never covering the real boot
files.  What that line needs is not "where do the boot files live" but
"is there a separate boot mount, and where" -- two different questions
that only happen to share an answer on the Pi.  Probe mounts with
findmnt instead, and skip the bind entirely when there is no separate
boot partition (the BBB case, where the bind of / already covers /boot).

The same directory test also gated the "downgrading to an OS without
/boot/firmware" branch, which a BBB could fall into by accident; key it
off the boot mount so only a system genuinely booting from
/boot/firmware can reach it.

scripts/common, Pi-FlashUSB.sh and rpi-clone keep the "directory holding
the boot config" meaning but now probe for config.txt / uEnv.txt /
extlinux/extlinux.conf, newest layout first, matching
findBootConfigFile() in CapeUtils.cpp.

Verified on hardware -- Pi5, PocketBeagle2 (BeagleBone 64), and BBB on
both Debian 12 and 13:

  fpppi5        Raspberry Pi   FPPBOOTDIR=/boot/firmware  BOOTMOUNT=/boot/firmware
  fppk16pro     BeagleBone 64  FPPBOOTDIR=/boot/firmware  BOOTMOUNT=/boot/firmware
  fppgaragedoor BBB Debian 13  FPPBOOTDIR=/boot           BOOTMOUNT=""
  fppcarport    BBB Debian 12  FPPBOOTDIR=/boot           BOOTMOUNT=""

fppgaragedoor is the box the old test got wrong (it returned
/boot/firmware there).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat(BBShiftPanel): allow several LED panel matrices to share one cape

The PRUSS shifts a single frame out of every output on the cape -- one buffer
whose byte lanes are the data pins, one stride schedule, one shared memory
ring, one pair of PRU cores -- so a matrix could not previously be anything
but the sole owner of the hardware. Now that the driver can feed far more
panels than most people hang off one board, the useful configuration is
several independent displays on one cape: a two sided display, or a column
either side of a door, which until now needed a controller each.

Split the driver into BBShiftPanelManager, which owns everything that defines
the shared frame, and BBShiftPanelOutput, which owns only one matrix's mapping
into it. The lane a pixel lands in is fixed by which cape output its panel is
on, so members driving different outputs scatter into disjoint bytes with no
coordination at all, and a single bit-plane pass converts the combined result.

Per frame: every member scatters into the shared intermediate, the last one to
arrive runs the ISPC bit-plane pass, and the first SendData publishes. Keeping
the expensive pass in PrepData leaves the other outputs' wire sends unblocked;
a member that is stopping still counts toward the frame boundary, or output
would stall permanently.

Registering a member recomputes the shared geometry and re-maps every member,
so adding a matrix with a longer chain widens the frame for the ones already
registered. Members must agree on everything that shapes the frame (panel
size, scan, interleave, type, addressing, color depth, output order) and may
not claim an output another member already drives; either is refused with a
warning naming the reason rather than silently producing a garbled display.

Gamma stays per matrix for free -- it is applied in each member's own scatter.
Brightness is per matrix too: the OE on-time is a property of the cape, so it
runs at the highest any member asked for and the others scale their own gamma
table down to reach it. Taking the max keeps every ratio at or below 1.0, so
it is always a reduction and never clips, and it does not depend on
registration order. The worker pool, which used to be spawned per output, is
now shared, as are the pin mux, the idle park and the PRU teardown.

Verified byte-identical on a 16-output cape driving 64 panels: one matrix
before and after the split, and 2, 3 (unequal 6/5/5 splits) and 4 matrices all
produce exactly the frame the single 16-output matrix produces. Refresh, duty
and idle park are unchanged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat(ui): support multiple cape-driven LED panel matrices

Raise the one-matrix limit for cape outputs and split the settings into two
boxes: Matrix Settings (layout, start channel, start corner, gamma, brightness)
and a new Panel Settings box describing the panels themselves (size, scan,
color depth, addressing, panel type, color order, interleave). Since a cape
shifts one frame out of all of its outputs, the panel settings belong to the
cape rather than to any one matrix on it, so that whole box is hidden on the
second and later matrices, which inherit those values and show a note pointing
at the matrix that owns them.

A new matrix inherits the panel geometry at creation rather than being mirrored
afterwards, so the size select and the auto layout work off real values instead
of the page defaults, and it starts past every matrix already configured
instead of silently overlaying another one's channels. Auto Layout now numbers
its rows from the first output no other matrix is using -- laying out a second
matrix used to re-claim the first one's outputs, so neither would start -- and
warns if the remaining outputs cannot fit the requested rows. Two matrices
claiming the same output are flagged as the layout is edited and block the
save; fppd refuses the second matrix outright in that case.

Detecting a cape matrix deliberately does not use the per-matrix connection
dropdown: it reports the legacy LEDscapeMatrix value for Hat/Cap/Cape even on
a cape with a different driver, and a newly added matrix has no subType at all
until it is saved. It can be trusted to rule the cape out, not to confirm it.
The Add dialog also never stamped a subType for cape matrices, which is fixed
here.

Also fixes two pre-existing problems in the same area: outputByRowClicked()
referenced an undeclared panelMatrixID, so "Blank between rows" only appeared
when another function had happened to leak a global of that name, and its
initial state was only ever set from a handler emitted on some sub-platforms.

fix(plugins): freeze the Command/CommandArg ABI behind a pimpl, bump to v5

CommandArg gained a std::string section two days after FPP_PLUGIN_API_VERSION
was bumped to 4 for exactly this hazard, and the version was not bumped again.
section was inserted between help and children, so it both grew
sizeof(CommandArg) and shifted children/toggleStyle/toggleLabel. A plugin built
against the version-4 headers still reports 4, passes the load-time gate, then
push_backs onto Command::args with its own smaller std::list node while
Command::~Command destroys those nodes with the larger one - running ~string
past the end of the plugin's allocation. Crash reports show this faulting in
Json::Value::Value under Command::getDescription() on builds that already have
the version-4 gate.

Bumping the number again would only hold until the next time somebody forgets,
so the layout is no longer something a human has to remember:

- Command and CommandArg each hold a unique_ptr to an out-of-line struct
  (Command::Data, CommandArg::Ext) defined in Commands.cpp. New state goes
  there, where plugins only ever see a pointer, so neither sizeof can move.
  Note sizeof(std::list) does not depend on its element type, so Command::args
  stays put however much Ext grows.
- Every field added since API version 3 - advanced, help, children,
  toggleStyle, toggleLabel, section - moved into Ext. All six landed within
  the past week and v5 forces a rebuild regardless, so the frozen block is now
  exactly the long-lived version 3 member set. Setter signatures are unchanged
  and no call site needed editing. sizeof(CommandArg) drops 288 -> 208, more
  on libstdc++ where std::map is larger.
- Both sizes are published as weak, default-visibility fingerprint symbols the
  loader compares against its own, reusing the dladdr provenance check already
  used for the version symbol. A plugin that never includes Commands.h does
  not define them and is not checked, so this cannot reject a plugin that
  registers no commands.

getDescription() output is byte-for-byte identical, verified by diffing a
command that exercises every field against a build of the previous tree. The
reject path was exercised on aarch64 under LTO and --gc-sections: a mismatched
CommandArg and a mismatched Command are both refused, a matching plugin loads,
and a commands-free plugin skips the check.

fix(videoinput): quote config values spliced into gst_parse_launch descriptions

StartSource() built its pipeline description by concatenating config strings
straight in - the RTSP/uri location, the v4l2 device path, the videotestsrc
pattern, the multicast group and the intervideosink channel name. That
description is a grammar, not a format string, so a value containing whitespace
silently reshapes it: a URI of "rtsp://cam/live stream" parses as an element
named "stream", and one carrying credentials with a space fails the same way. A
backslash was worse than a parse error - it was swallowed, so the URI reached
the element subtly wrong.

Everything now goes through GstQuote(), which wraps the value in quotes and
escapes backslashes and quotes inside them. Quoting a value that needed no
escaping yields the identical string, so this is safe to apply to all of them
unconditionally. Control characters have no representation in the grammar and
never belong in a URI or device path, so StartSource() rejects them once up
front with a warning rather than trying to encode them.

Verified against libgstreamer by parsing both forms and reading the property
back off the element: plain URIs are byte-identical either way, while space and
backslash cases go from "no element" / silently mangled to exact round-trip.

StartSourceWithAudio() had its own local escaper that handled quotes but not
backslashes, and hand-quoted its uri= properties; it now uses the same helper.

This does not reproduce the reported gst_value_deserialize <-
gst_caps_from_string fault seen on two devices - several malformed-caps
payloads were tried against gstreamer 1.26 without crashing it, so the link to
those crashes is inferred from the stack, not confirmed. It does remove the
malformed descriptions that are the precondition for it, and fixes the
misparsing in its own right.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(fseq): don't divide by a zero channel count from an ESEQ header

FSEQFile's read constructor computed the ESEQ frame count as
(fileSize - headerSize) / channelCount with the divisor taken straight from
the file, and openFSEQFile() validates only the 'ESEQ' magic and that the
header is fully present. A corrupt or truncated effect file with a zero
channel count therefore divided by zero. On 32-bit ARM that traps in
__aeabi_ldiv0 and kills fppd - the reported crash came in via StartEffect ->
FSEQFile::openFSEQFile, matching an ESEQ header (which reports major version
2, hence the V2FSEQFile frame in the stack). On 64-bit it does not trap and
silently produces a garbage frame count instead, which is its own problem.

Guarded, reporting an empty sequence and logging the header values so a bad
file is identifiable. Confirmed on a 32-bit ARM target that the previous
expression dies with SIGFPE for a zero channel count and the guarded one
returns zero frames.

The guard also covers fileSize < headerSize, which would underflow the
unsigned subtraction into a huge frame count. That is not reachable through
openFSEQFile today - it already rejects a short header - but it is the same
expression and costs nothing to hold.

Merge pull request #2785 from jessica12ryan/MoreBackupFixes

fix(backups): MQTT local broker not starting after backup restore, and stale version info from backed-up fpp-info.json

fix(config): reject wrong-shaped JSON at load instead of aborting fppd

LoadJsonFromFile() returned true for any valid JSON document, so a config
file that parsed cleanly but held the wrong kind of value - an array where
an object was expected, or the reverse - was handed straight back to a
caller that immediately indexed it. Every jsoncpp accessor those callers
reach for next (operator[], isMember(), getMemberNames(), get()) throws
Json::LogicError on that mismatch, and nothing in fppd catches it, so a
single malformed config file aborted the daemon at startup and again on
every reload after that.

Crash reports show it as a loop through whichever subsystem reloads next:
one device aborted in LoadInputUniversesFromFile, BridgeReloadDMXInputs,
Variables::load, ReloadChannelOutputsForFile and GPIOManager::SetupGPIOInput
in turn - five distinct stacks from one bad set of files, not five bugs.

A backup restore is one way to get there. The restore path round-trips each
config file through a decode-to-map and re-encode, which does not preserve
JSON shape: an empty object comes back as an empty array, and an array whose
keys are no longer sequential comes back as an object. That is worth fixing
on its own, but no config file, however it got that way, should be able to
kill fppd.

Add a shape-checked loader that takes the root the caller requires, and
route all 39 call sites through it. A mismatch now logs the file, what it
holds and what was expected, then yields an empty value of the expected
shape, so callers that ignore the return value iterate over nothing instead
of aborting. Well-formed configs are unaffected.

The check is a new overload rather than a defaulted argument on the existing
entry points: adding a parameter would change their mangled names and break
already-built plugins that link against them. All three previous symbols are
unchanged. The expected shape is an FPP enum rather than a Json::ValueType
so common.h can keep using the Json::Value forward declaration instead of
pulling jsoncpp into every includer.

Verified against jsoncpp that each reported stack throws for the wrong root
type and stops throwing after the change, and that a well-formed object
still loads and returns true with its data intact. Built on Pi, BB64 and
macOS - the first two matter because BBBMatrix.cpp and FPPOLEDUtils.cpp are
not part of the macOS build, so their .o files there are stale leftovers.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(config): treat a null JSON root as empty, and shape-check CapeUtils too

Follow-up to 8d3e0b418, which was too strict. A null root is not a shape
mismatch: jsoncpp treats null as an empty value of whatever type it is first
used as and never throws on it, and FPP writes null itself - Variables::save()
stores a default-constructed Json::Value, so a stock variables.json with

fix(playlist): guard empty sections after a mid-play reload

SwitchToMainPlaylist()/SwitchToLeadOut() indexed m_mainPlaylist[0] /
m_leadOut[0] while trusting the caller to have checked the section size,
and two call sites in Process() made that check unsound:

  - "else if (m_leadOut.size()) { ReloadIfNeeded(); SwitchToLeadOut(); }"
    tests the size before the reload that can empty it.
  - the repeat-loop path calls ReloadIfNeeded() and then starts
    m_mainPlaylist[0] with no size check at all.

ReloadIfNeeded() -> ReloadPlaylist() -> Load() -> Cleanup() pops every
entry into PL_ENTRY_CLEANUPS and reloads from the file, so a playlist
edited while it is playing can come back without that section. pop_back()
does not release the vector's capacity, so [0] returns the stale pointer
to an entry that is queued for deletion: the vtable is still mapped, the
virtual call dispatches, and the fault lands inside StartPlaying() rather
than at an obviously bogus address.

Enforce the invariant where the section is actually indexed instead of at
each call site - both SwitchTo* functions now go idle on an empty section,
matching every other "no more playlist entries" branch - and route the
repeat-loop restart through SwitchToMainPlaylist() so it picks up the same
guard.

feat(crash): capture the context that makes a crash stack actionable

Crash reports carried a stack and almost nothing else, so triage repeatedly
stalled on questions the daemon could have answered at fault time. Four
additions, all written to a new /tmp/fppd_crash_context.log that the report
bundler ships alongside the stack:

Log ring buffer. The line that explains a crash is routinely one nobody
kept: the trigger is logged at LogDebug, production runs at info, so it is
filtered out before it is ever formatted. A fixed 256-slot ring now retains
those lines in memory without writing them anywhere. It is lock-free and
allocation-free on purpose - the normal log path takes a mutex, and a crash
handler that blocks on a lock the faulting thread already holds hangs the
process instead of producing a report, which is exactly the heap-corruption
case that most needs the trace.

Per-facility opt-out for the ring. ChannelOut/ChannelData are excluded:
HexDump() emits at LogInfo rather than debug, and one channel output calls
it ungated on every frame, so a level-based filter alone would not have
caught it. Such a facility would both burn CPU formatting into the ring and
evict the whole history within a frame or two. LOG_EXCESSIVE is dropped
everywhere as a second filter.

Playlist state. Plain scalars refreshed at the points where the section or
position changes, read without the playlist mutex for the same reason as
above. The three section sizes are the useful part: a section that a caller
believed was non-empty is the shape of a whole class of bug here.

Fault registers and a recoverable fallback. The handler received the signal
ucontext and ignored it; it now records pc/sp/lr and the argument registers,
which is the only evidence that survives when the unwinder cannot walk the
stack at all - a crash inside a hand-written-assembly libc routine reports a
single frame and no caller, because that code carries no unwind tables no
matter how this daemon is compiled. The link register still holds the return
address into the caller. Alongside it, dumpstack_gdb() now reports why it
failed (fork failure under memory pressure, no output, watchdog timeout,
ptrace refused) instead of leaving a symbol-only stack indistinguishable
between causes that call for different remedies, and the fallback writes the
reason, the raw frame addresses and the module map with write() only, before
attempting backtrace_symbols() - which allocates, and so may never return in
precisely the crash that produced the fallback.

Verified on aarch64 and 32-bit ARM hardware; the ring's filtering is covered
by assertions that mutually control (an always-empty ring and an
always-capturing ring each fail a different subset).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

perf(log): cache the formatted date, drop per-line integer conversions

Every log line rebuilt "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS" from scratch: a localtime_r
plus seven width-qualified integer conversions inside a twelve-specifier
snprintf. That is invisible on a desktop and is not on the small ARM boards
FPP actually runs on. Measured on an AM335x: localtime_r ~5us and the prefix
snprintf ~12us, against ~1.7us to render the caller's actual message -- the
timestamp cost several times more than the thing being logged.

The seconds field changes once per second, so cache it keyed on the second it
describes, and emit the milliseconds directly (always exactly three digits)
rather than through a format string. Integer conversion, not string copying,
is the expensive part of snprintf, so the remaining call has none of the
padded numeric fields left.

thread_local rather than a shared cache: this is on every log call from every
thread, so a lock or atomic would cost more than it saves, while an unguarded
shared buffer would corrupt timestamps. Cost is one time_t and 20 bytes per
thread. A DST change is picked up at the next second boundary, since the key
is the second itself.

Measured on an AM335x, min-of-7 to filter contention:
  cache hit  (several lines within one second)  14885ns -> 4536ns  (3.3x)
  cache miss (first line of a new second)       15072ns -> 14664ns (neutral)

So the worst case is unchanged and bursts get 3.3x cheaper -- which is the
case that matters most now that the crash ring formats debug-level lines that
were previously discarded before they were ever rendered.

Output verified byte-identical against the previous implementation across
77220 prefixes spanning multiple epochs, every millisecond value, and DST
boundaries; the comparison was confirmed able to fail by perturbing a single
digit of the new formatter.

fix(crash): gate the log ring by share level; freeze it during the handler

Two defects in the crash-context work from 45ac03e43, both found by building
a real crash report on hardware and reading what came out.

PRIVACY: the context file was copied into the report outside the share-level
gates, so the retained log ring shipped even at "Stack Traces Only". A sample
report from a normal LAN carried 14 IPv4 addresses, 12 IPv6 addresses and the
names of discovered devices -- a user who deliberately narrowed sharing to
stack traces was sending their network topology. Log content had never
travelled below level 3 before this; fppd.log has always been gated there.

The fix splits the two kinds of data rather than gating them together,
because they are not the same thing: the playlist state and fault registers
are bare scalars that identify nothing and are exactly what makes a stack
actionable, so they still ship at every level, while the ring is log content
and now goes where logs/fppd.log goes, with the same scrubbing applied.
Keeping them in one file is what caused this, so they are now separate files
with the reasoning recorded at both ends.

The ring is also frozen when the handler starts. Everything the handler logs
-- the signal line, the gdb stack -- was being pushed into the ring, evicting
the pre-crash history that is the only reason the ring exists, to duplicate
content already in the stack file.

Verified on aarch64 hardware by generating real reports at each level:
  level 1: context present, ring absent, 0 network identifiers, 5KB
  level 3: context + ring + fppd.log, 216 lines of genuine pre-crash history
           ending at the fault, 0 handler self-log lines (was 3)

feat(crash): keep crash reports locally without sending them

ShareCrashData conflated two independent choices -- whether a crash report
exists at all, and whether it leaves the machine. Selecting "Disabled" got
you neither, so the users most likely to want to inspect a crash themselves
were the ones left with nothing to inspect. The web UI had assumed otherwise
for a long time: the warning for that setting tells the user to "submit to
FPP developers or delete" reports that were never being written.

Report generation is now independent of sending. The levels become a ladder:

  -1  Disabled - do not create a report
   0  Keep locally, do not send      (a full report, sent nowhere)
   1  Send stack traces only
   2  Send, include settings
   3  Send, include settings and configurations

At 0 the report is generated at full detail, since its purpose is for someone
to read or submit by hand, and the upload is skipped. -1 is the option that
means what "Disabled" used to say, and exists because 0 no longer does.

Note for anyone reading this on upgrade: an existing "0" now writes a report
where it previously wrote none. It still sends nothing, but the file lands in
the media crashes folder, which the web UI file manager exposes -- choose -1
if that is not wanted.

Also corrects the UI warning to test <= 0 rather than == 0. Reports written
while sending was enabled stay on disk after switching to 0 or -1, and
telling the user those are queued for upload is wrong in both cases.

feat(crash): resolve fallback stack addresses to file:line on the device

When fppd cannot get a stack out of gdb it now records raw frame addresses
and /proc/self/maps, which is recoverable but not readable. This resolves
them with addr2line at report time, turning the degraded pile from "no
actionable stack" into function names with line numbers.

Resolving on the device rather than centrally is a correctness requirement,
not a convenience. FPP builds from source on the device and supports in-place
git pull + make upgrades, so a locally rebuilt binary and an image-built one
at the same commit produce identical build strings - and across the fleet
that same commit spans different Debian releases and gcc versions, so the
code layout differs. An archive keyed on the build string cannot tell those
apart, and feeding addresses to the wrong binary yields confidently wrong
line numbers, which is worse than none. On the device there is nothing to
guess: the binary that faulted is the one being read.

Details that decide whether the numbers are right:
  - Frame 0 is the faulting PC and is exact. Every frame above it is a return
    address, so the lookup steps back one byte; resolving verbatim reports the
    line after the call, and for a call in tail position often the following
    function entirely.
  - ET_EXEC addresses are absolute and must not have the load base removed.
    The type is read from the ELF header directly rather than parsed out of
    readelf's output, which is locale and version dependent.
  - The load base is the lowest mapping of the file, not the first executable
    one.
  - One batched addr2line per module. Inline expansion (-i) is deliberately
    not used: it emits a variable number of lines per address with no
    separator, so a batch cannot be split unambiguously.

Never allowed to fail the report: no-ops when gdb succeeded, when the helper
or addr2line is missing, or on a malformed log, and runs under a timeout.
Output is a separate file so existing parsers of fppd_crash.log are untouched.

Verified on aarch64 by forcing gdb to fail and crashing a real fppd: 11 of 12
frames resolved, e.g. EPollManager::waitForEvents at EPollManager.cpp:232 and
MainLoop at fppd.cpp:1814. Each cited line was independently confirmed to sit
inside the function addr2line named by walking the source to the enclosing
definition. Negative control: removing the load-base subtraction drops
resolution from 11/12 to 0/12, so the check can fail. ELF type detection
checked against purpose-built -no-pie and -pie binaries, and on a missing file
and a non-ELF file.

Don't let libgpiod v1 exceptions escape GPIODCapabilities get/setValue

GPIODCapabilities::setValue()/getValue() have separate libgpiod v1 and v2
branches, and only the v2 branch was exception-safe: it checks the request
handle and wraps the call in try/catch + LogWarn.  The v1 branch called
line.set_value()/line.get_value() bare.

libgpiod v1's line::set_value() routes through line_bulk::set_values() and
throws -- std::system_error on a failed ioctl, std::logic_error on an empty or
unrequested line handle.  configPin() and requestEventFile() only raise a
warning when a line request fails, and leave the line unrequested, so the
first setValue() on such a pin threw out of a call site that has no handler
anywhere up the stack: __cxa_throw -> std::terminate -> abort, taking fppd
down at startup.  Reported on a Debian 12 (libgpiodcxx.so.1) board, which is
every 32-bit BeagleBone build.

Apply the v2 branch's contract to the v1 branch rather than guarding the
callers: a GPIO read/write failure degrades to a logged warning, and getValue()
returns 0, exactly as the v2 path already does.

fix(pb2): detect the PocketBeagle 2 Industrial, and stop keying capes off the model

The device-tree model reads "BeagleBoard.org PocketBeagle2" on the industrial
board as well as the base one, so the "Industrial" substring test never matched
and every industrial board was treated as a base PocketBeagle 2.

Detect it from the hardware instead. Only the industrial has eMMC populated, so
config.php keys the logo off /dev/mmcblk0, the same way the storage UI already
identifies the eMMC. BB64-AutoFlash.sh needs a stronger answer, since it runs
precisely when the EEPROM is suspect: it now reads the board ID at EEPROM offset
46 ("PB2I" vs "PB20"), which survives the valid-header/blank-serial failure mode,
and falls back to probing for eMMC only when the header itself is blank. That
path matters beyond cosmetics -- u-boot's SPL applies the 1GB DDRSS timings only
when the EEPROM identifies the industrial variant, so stamping a base-board
EEPROM onto one leaves it running on half its RAM.

Separately, 'Variant' is the board model on every other platform (Pi 4,
BeagleBone Green Wireless), so it now names the model here too: "PocketBeagle 2"
and "PocketBeagle 2 Industrial". The code that was matching it for exact equality
was really asking "am I a PocketBeagle 2 family board" and now asks that
directly, via the SubPlatform substring idiom already used elsewhere.

one entry in the vendor cape catalogs -- so it gets its own key, CapeVariant,
defaulting to Variant. That fixes a pre-existing bug alongside the new one: the
Beagle branch of the cape filter matches only on the variant and deliberately
skips Platform (the PocketBeagle shares the BeagleBone Black platform but takes
different capes), and the catalogs list only "BeagleBone Black", so the Green,

empty cape list. They now map to the BeagleBone Black compatibility class. The

than a guess at its pinout. Raspberry Pi needs no CapeVariant -- that branch
already falls back to Platform, which is the string the catalogs use.

Finally, MultiSync::ModelStringToType() matched on "PocketBeagle2" and is fed a
remote's Variant for HTTP-discovered controllers, so the spaced spelling fell
through to the PocketBeagle test and reported a PocketBeagle 2 as a PocketBeagle

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat(video): give each video output a region, so one video can span two displays

A single decoded video could previously only be shown whole on every output.
Splitting a double-wide file (e.g. 3840x1080) across two HDMI ports meant
decoding it twice and cropping outside FPP, which no board has the headroom
for.

Each HDMI member of a video output group now carries a region -- whole video,
one of the four halves, or a custom rectangle -- selected in the video output
groups UI.  Give two displays opposite halves and they show two halves of one
decode.

The region is stored as fractions of the source rather than pixels, so the
same configuration splits any resolution and adapts if the resolution changes
mid-stream; the pixel crop is resolved from the negotiated caps by a pad probe
on the CAPS event.  Resolving it there rather than after PLAYING matters: the
first frame is already cropped, instead of flashing a full uncropped frame
across both displays on every track change.

The videocrop element is placed immediately upstream of kmssink, after any
videoconvert.  kmssink advertises GstVideoCropMeta, so videocrop then crops by
metadata -- the region becomes the DRM plane's source rectangle and the
display hardware applies it during scanout, at no per-frame cost.  Any element
between the two silently downgrades that to a full per-frame copy.

Crop offsets and extents are forced even because NV12/I420 subsample chroma
2x2, and an odd source rectangle would split a chroma pair across the seam
between the two halves.  A missing videocrop element falls back to the whole
frame with a warning rather than failing the pipeline.

Verified on a Pi 5 against the DRM plane state rather than logs: for a
3840x1080 source on a 1920x1080 display, the halves, quadrant-style custom
regions and the out-of-range clamp all produce the expected plane source
rectangle, while the framebuffer stays 3840x1080 throughout -- confirming no
pixels are copied.  The uncropped control renders 3840x1080+0+0 letterboxed,
so the check distinguishes cropped from uncropped.

Note this applies to video output groups only.  Simple mode has a single
video output, and changing the VideoOutput setting there regenerates the
group config.

fix(ddp): DDP input heap buffer overflow and out-of-bounds read in channel bridging

fix(plugins): fingerprint the FPPLogger layout, which is plugin ABI

The VB_* macros expand to a member of the single FPPLogger::INSTANCE, so a
plugin bakes in "INSTANCE + N * sizeof(FPPLoggerInstance)" at compile time and
passes that address to libfpp's _LogWrite() as an FPPLoggerInstance&. Adding
the crashRingCapture bool grew that class from 28 to 32 bytes on 32-bit ARM,
which moved every facility after the first: plugins built against the older
header resolved VB_PLUGIN 52 bytes short of where libfpp put it and landed 12
bytes into the previous facility, inside the SSO buffer of its std::string
name. facility.name.c_str() then handed strlen() a pointer assembled from raw
character bytes and fppd died on the plugin's first log line -- a boot loop,
since plugins load during startup.

Confirmed rather than inferred: the fault registers in a report gave the
faulting pointer as 0x6c6f72, and reproducing both layouts on 32-bit ARM
produces exactly that value -- the tail of the name "Control", read at
_M_local_buf[4]. The stack showed only bare libc because the fault is inside
__vfprintf_internal, which gdb cannot unwind past.

Publishes sizeof(FPPLoggerInstance) and the byte span from the first facility
to the last as weak fingerprint symbols, compared at dlopen the same way the
Command/CommandArg sizes already are. The span is measured rather than
sizeof()'d because both ways this breaks -- growing the instance and
inserting a facility -- move the later VB_* macros, and only the first shows
up in a sizeof. They live in Plugin.h, not log.h: log.h normally arrives
through the PCH, and a weak definition nothing in the translation unit
references is not emitted from there, so plugins exported nothing to compare.

FPP_PLUGIN_API_VERSION is deliberately not bumped. A bump is the only thing
that reaches binaries already built, but it would equally refuse the ones
since rebuilt correctly; the gate here covers recurrence instead. The layout
rule is recorded on the class so the next member added to it is a decision
rather than an accident.

Verified on ELF hardware: a plugin reporting the pre-change span is refused,
one reporting the current span loads, and one exporting no fingerprint is
skipped, which is the documented escape hatch and the reason the version
bump is what a field-wide break needs.

fix(sequence): bounds-check the FSEQ variable-header parser

ProcessVariableHeaders walked an FC/FE block straight out of a file with no
bounds checking at all: it read the version byte and the entry count off a
vector that may be empty, took both the entry count and each range count from
the file without a size check, and built the IP-list and command strings with
a bare std::string((const char*)data). A truncated or malformed block ran
strlen() off the end of the buffer and killed fppd inside OpenSequenceFile --
before a single frame played, so the sequence never started and the crash
repeated on every attempt to play it.

Rewritten around an explicit end pointer with bounds-checked u32/string
reads, which also drops the unaligned uint32_t* casts. A header that does not
parse now logs a warning and is dropped, keeping whatever it had already
yielded; nothing here is worth failing a show over.

Verified under ASan against the old implementation on the same inputs:
identical output on well-formed blocks with and without an IP list, and all
seven malformed shapes survive -- empty, version-only, truncated count,
truncated mid-range, unterminated tail, absurd counts, and no NUL anywhere.
The control goes red: the old parser SEGVs on the first of those, at the same
read the crash reports die on.

fix(effects): don't leak the FSEQFile when the effect limit is reached

StartEffect takes ownership of the FSEQFile it is handed -- the effect-ID
failure path below deletes it, and so does StopEffect -- but the
"maximum number of effects already running" early return did not, leaking the
whole file and its mapping. That fires exactly when a controller is already
at the ceiling and something keeps retrying, so the leak compounds under the
one condition that produced it: one report leaked 48 of them while a caller
restarted the same effect several times a second, alongside the read-ahead
thread each concurrent effect already owns, until thread creation failed and
the uncaught std::system_error took fppd down.

This is one contributing leak, not the whole story: an 8MB-stack read-ahead
thread per concurrent effect is heavy on 32-bit, and a std::thread constructor
throwing anywhere in that path is still fatal.

The struct FPP writes at the start of the PRU data ram declared address_dma
as uintptr_t.  FalconSerial.asm reads that block with a fixed
"LBCO &r0, CONST_PRUDRAM, 0, 8" and stores to fixed offsets 4 and 8, so the
layout has to be address@0 / command@4 / response@8.  On a 64 bit build the
pointer is 8 bytes wide, pushing command to 8 and response to 12: the PRU
never sees a start command, and the ARM reads the PRU's response as its own
command field and spins in RawSendData forever.  Every other PRU output
(BBB48String, BBBMatrix, BBShiftString, BBShiftPanel) already declares this
field as uint32_t; BBBSerial was missed.  Static asserts now pin the three
offsets the firmware hard-codes.

This is one prerequisite for a 64 bit serial output, not the whole of it -
the PRU program is still linked against the wrong core's command file and
is not built with the right platform defines.

Three related problems in the same file:

 - BBBPru::run() clears the PRU data ram, so writing address_dma/command/
   response before calling it accomplishes nothing.  Measured on a 32 bit
   build: immediately after startup address_dma reads 0 and the PRU clocks
   frames out of physical address 0 - correctly framed DMX with every slot
   zero.  It recovers only because RawSendData force-writes the address on
   frame 1.  Initialize after run(), the way the other PRU outputs do.

 - Close() stopped the PRU, deleted the BBBPru (unmapping both the PRU data
   ram and the shared DDR region) and released the DDR allocation while the
   ThreadedChannelOutput worker was still running and still dereferencing
   m_serialData and m_ddrArea.  Stop the thread first; the second
   StopOutputThread() from ThreadedChannelOutput::Close() is a no-op.

 - The "wait for the previous draw" spin was unbounded, so a PRU that never
   answers pegs a core indefinitely with nothing shown in the UI.  Bound it
   and raise a warning instead.

feat(plugins): plugin API 6 - routes a plugin can hand back, and a shutdown contract

Bumps FPP_PLUGIN_API_VERSION to 6, so every plugin binary needs rebuilding. This
is the API half of making a plugin unloadable; the runtime load/unload that uses
it follows separately.

Drogon has no route removal API, so a plugin calling
drogon::app().registerHandler() directly leaves a function pointer into its own
.so in the router forever. That makes the plugin impossible to unload, and
impossible to replace in place: a newly loaded build cannot take over a path the
retired one still owns. (Nor can it be loaded over the top of the old one --
dlopen() of a rebuilt binary at the same path hands back the already-loaded
object, because glibc matches by name before it ever looks at the inode.)

FPPPlugins::registerPluginApi()/unregisterPluginApi() fix that. The drogon route
for a path is created once, ever, and belongs to libfpp; it dispatches through a
slot that any generation of a plugin can arm. Unregistering disarms the slot --
the path answers 410 Gone rather than dispatching into freed memory -- and does
not return until no request is executing inside the handler AND the handler
object itself has been destroyed. That object's code and captured state live in
the plugin's .so, so destroying it before returning is what a later dlclose()
depends on: destroy while still mapped, then unmap.

FPPPlugins::Plugin::shutdown() is the teardown point, and is what moves the ABI
version: a new virtual shifts every later vtable slot. FPP calls it once routes
are disarmed and before the plugin is destroyed - a destructor is too late,
because a thread calling in during destruction reads an object already half
gone. It returns a readiness predicate rather than void, so shutdown() can be
"ask everything to stop" with the real teardown in the destructor once it has;
FPP polls that predicate before destroying the plugin. Anything ending
asynchronously - a media pipeline unwinding, or a drogon loop that may still run
a queued handler - is expressible either as a readiness check or as a deadline.

CurlManager can now cancel by owner. Every add* takes a trailing owner argument
(FPP's own callers leave it empty); a plugin passes its name, and its in-flight
requests can be dropped as a group - removing the transfers from the multi
handle and destroying their callbacks WITHOUT running them, which is what
releases the plugin-owned callable. A request's header list is now owned by the
callback rather than freed inside it, so it is released whether the request
completes or is cancelled, and in both cases after curl_easy_cleanup() rather
than while the easy handle still referenced it.

FPP_PLUGIN_SUPPORTS_UNLOAD is how a plugin declares it is safe to unmap,
documenting what it is asserting - including the case that is easy to miss: a
drogon client queues the plugin's handlers onto a trantor loop whenever a
network event arrives, stopping the client does not close that window, and
trantor offers no way to see or cancel what is queued, so only elapsed time
helps there. Measured: unmapping a plugin with a live WebSocket immediately
after stopping it took a SIGSEGV inside doRunInLoopFuncs().

Fixed on the way, and independently a landmine:
EPollManager::removeFileDescriptor() only erased the callback when epoll_ctl()
succeeded. A caller that had already closed its descriptor - which removes it
from the epoll set by itself - made the EPOLL_CTL_DEL fail with EBADF and left a
std::function behind for a descriptor nobody owned. The next addFileDescriptor()
to reuse that descriptor number then destroyed it by assigning over it. When the
callback belonged to an unloaded plugin that meant running a destructor in an
unmapped library; even without plugins it is a stale callable nobody can reach.

Removes the libhttpserver compatibility shims at the same time, since the bump
forces the rebuild that made them worth keeping. They existed so plugin source
written against libhttpserver could recompile unchanged after FPP moved to
drogon. Of the 58 plugins in fpp-data's pluginList.json, 41 have no C or C++ at
all, 9 have C++ but register no HTTP API, and every one that does register uses
drogon directly; the three that matched a source scan were two false positives
and one plugin whose libhttpserver path is selected only when the Plugin.h it
compiles against lacks the no-arg registerApis(), i.e. FPP 8/9, where real
libhttpserver exists. That check covered the non-default branches and pinned
shas pluginList.json points FPP 10 at, and the plugins whose repos hold no
source but fetch a binary. Gone with them: the deprecated
registerApis(webserver*) virtuals (another vtable shift, free while 6 is
unreleased), the per-route "recompile against the new API" warning, and the
SRC_HTTPSERVER_HPP_ define that neutralised <httpserver.hpp> to protect the
shims. The modern HttpRequestPtr/HttpResponsePtr/HttpCallback aliases and the
inline helpers stay - those are the current API. HTTP_RESPONSE_CONST also stays,
an empty define kept deliberately for plugin source compatibility.

Verified with a harness that registers a handler, serves it, unregisters, then
registers a second handler on the same path while drogon is running: 200 while
armed on both the exact path and a family subpath, 410 on both once disarmed,
and 200 from the replacement handler after re-arming - with the first handler's
captured state observed destroyed before unregisterPluginApi() returned. Every
listed plugin that registers an HTTP API builds against these headers, and a
plugin written to the old libhttpserver API compiles cleanly against the
pre-removal headers and fails against these.

feat(plugins): load and unload plugins at runtime

Installing a plugin now takes effect and uninstalling one stops having effect
without restarting fppd - which on a running show means not interrupting it.
POST /api/fppd/plugin/<name>/load and .../unload, called by the plugin manager
either side of the install and uninstall scripts. Built on the plugin API 6
contract from the previous commit.

Unloading disarms the plugin's HTTP routes, calls shutdown() so the plugin stops
its own threads and timers while it is still a whole object, cancels the
CurlManager requests it tagged with its name, withdraws the epoll descriptors it
registered, takes back the commands FPP registered on its behalf, drops it from
every registry that would call into it, and destroys it. The plugin is detached
immediately; destruction waits for the readiness predicate shutdown() returned,
polled about once a second and capped at 60s, so a plugin whose machinery
unwinds asynchronously finishes properly and anything arriving late finds a
quiesced object rather than freed memory.

dlclose() happens only for a plugin that declared FPP_PLUGIN_SUPPORTS_UNLOAD.
Otherwise the mapping is kept until fppd restarts - a few hundred KB, against a
crash class that would land in the middle of a show. Either way the plugin
object is gone, so it stops doing anything.

Reloading after an upgrade silently ran the OLD code: dlopen() matches an
already-loaded object by name before it looks at the file, so reopening the same
path returned the copy still mapped while the new build sat on disk unused - an
upgrade that reports success and changes nothing. loadSHLIBPlugin() now notices
the file behind a known path was replaced, hard-links it to a private name to
open, and unlinks that name immediately; the mapping keeps the inode alive, so
nothing accumulates.

Unloading is refused for a plugin that actually produced a ChannelOutput: that
object is owned by the output system and may be mid-show, and nothing here can
take it back. Keyed on having produced one rather than on implementing
ChannelOutputPlugin, which every plugin deriving from the FPPPlugin convenience
class does whether or not it ever returns an output.

Script plugins go through the same path and mostly just leave the internal
lists, with two things worth naming. Their destructor runs the "shutdown"
lifecycle callback, so the script is told - which is why destruction is deferred
rather than skipped. And FPP now takes back the commands it registered from the
plugin's commands/descriptions.json: CommandManager::removeCommand() only
unregisters, so these are deleted too. Before this an uninstalled plugin left
its commands listed, pointing at scripts no longer on disk.

A plugin with no callbacks script is not a failed load. Plenty are web UI only
and have nothing for fppd to run; treating that as an error told the user to
restart FPPD to enable something that needs neither.

Verified on hardware through the REST endpoints: a plugin's endpoint answers
200, unload takes it to 410, load returns it to 200, and cycles leave the pid
and RSS steady; a build swapped between an unload and a load is the one actually
running afterwards; an opted-in plugin reporting ready after 4s is detached
immediately and unmapped 4.0s later, and five unload/load cycles of a plugin
holding a live WebSocket leave the library unmapped each time with fppd alive;
uninstalling a script plugin removes its directory, withdraws its command and
fires its shutdown lifecycle callback; and installing a UI-only plugin reports a
plain OK with no restart warning.

fix(plugins): withdraw a plugin's commands when it unloads

A Command subclass declared in a plugin has its vtable, and usually a
back-pointer to the plugin, in that plugin's .so. CommandManager::addCommand()
carries no owner, and nothing took those back at unload: only the commands FPP
registers itself from a script plugin's commands/descriptions.json were tracked.
Every C++ plugin that calls addCommand() - most of them - left its commands
listed and runnable after being unloaded.

That is not cosmetic. Running one afterwards dispatches through a Command whose
plugin has been destroyed, so it reads freed memory: measured with a plugin
whose three commands survived an unload, invoking one returned success, wrote
its config file through the dangling plugin pointer, and did not crash - silent
corruption rather than a fault. Once a plugin declares
FPP_PLUGIN_SUPPORTS_UNLOAD the same call lands in an unmapped library.

The contract, documented in Plugin.h, is that the plugin cleans up after
itself: it withdraws AND deletes its own commands in shutdown(). Note
removeCommand() only UNREGISTERS - CommandManager owns whatever is left in its
registry and deletes it at shutdown - so a plugin taking one back owns it again
and must delete it.

FPP keeps a backstop for a plugin that forgets. PluginManager records what
appears in the command registry while a plugin is loading - by diffing around
its constructor, registerApis() and addControlCallbacks(), the same way
addControlCallbacks() already deduces a plugin's epoll descriptors, since
addCommand() cannot gain an owner argument without breaking every plugin that
calls it - and deletes anything still there at unload. It is deliberately a net
and not the mechanism: it only reaches the load window, so a command registered
later from a request handler or a thread is the plugin's alone, and when it
fires for a plugin with a library it logs a warning naming the plugin and the
commands rather than quietly covering for it.

The net cannot double-free: it deletes a command only if the registry still
holds that exact name AND pointer, so one the plugin already withdrew is
skipped, and one something else has since re-registered under the same name is
left to its new owner. For the same reason a name that already existed before
the plugin ran is never attributed to it, so a plugin whose command name
collides with an existing one cannot get the original deleted out from under
its owner.

Verified on hardware, in both directions: with plugins doing their own cleanup,
seven commands across five plugins are withdrawn on unload, all five libraries
unmap, and no warning is logged; with one plugin's cleanup deliberately
disabled, the net still withdraws its three commands and the library still
unmaps, and the warning names the plugin and all three. fppd survives five
unload/load cycles of each with steady RSS. Before the change the same check
went red - the commands stayed listed and remained runnable.

fix(plugins): build plugins -fno-gnu-unique so dlclose can actually unmap them

glibc permanently marks a shared object NODELETE if it is the first to define an
STB_GNU_UNIQUE symbol: dlclose() then returns success and unmaps nothing, for
the life of the process. GCC emits STB_GNU_UNIQUE for a static local in an
inline function - which includes every method a plugin defines inside its class
body. One "static const std::string" in a formatting helper is therefore enough
to make a whole plugin impossible to unmap, and nothing reports it: the unload
still succeeds, the routes still go to 410, the commands still come back, the
plugin object is still destroyed. Only the address space is never returned, so
FPP_PLUGIN_SUPPORTS_UNLOAD silently means less than it says.

Measured on a plugin with seven of them - three static locals, their guard
variables, and a static char lookup table. It never unmapped, through any
number of unload/load cycles, while four other plugins on the same box unmapped
every time. dlopen(RTLD_NOLOAD) after the dlclose confirmed the object was still
resident, and an extra dlclose did not shift it, so it was NODELETE rather than
an outstanding reference. Rebuilding it with this flag, source unchanged, made
it unmap on the first unload. The plugins that were already unmapping have one
unique symbol each, std::piecewise_construct, which libstdc++ defines first -
which is why they were never marked.

Check a plugin with:  nm -D lib<plugin>.so | awk '$2=="u"'

The trade is the point of the flag: statics in inline functions are no longer
unified between a plugin and libfpp. That sharing is exactly what glibc refuses
to unload a library to protect, so it cannot be kept alongside unloading - and
a plugin is the wrong place to be relying on it.

Applied in the existing plugin-only block in setup.mk, so it reaches every
plugin that includes it - including ones built from source FPP does not
control - without each author having to know about any of this. Not applied to
FPP's own build, which is never dlclose()d, nor for clang, where Mach-O has no
STB_GNU_UNIQUE and the flag is rejected.
