fix(plugins): unload a plugin by the directory it was installed from

A plugin's own name - what it passes to FPPPlugins::Plugin's constructor - is
not required to match the directory it was installed from, and nothing makes an
author keep the two in step. Everything outside fppd speaks directory names: the
Plugin Manager, the install and uninstall scripts, and the load/unload REST
endpoints. unloadPlugin() matched on the plugin's own name, so for any plugin
where the two differed it found nothing, took the "not loaded, so the caller's
goal already holds" path, and reported success.

Nothing was unloaded. The routes stayed armed, the registrations stayed in
place, and the library stayed mapped - and because the Plugin Manager treats
that success as "fppd has let go", an uninstall then deleted the plugin's files
out from under a plugin that was still running. That is the crash the runtime
unload path exists to avoid, arrived at by a different route.

One shipped plugin was in exactly that state - fpp-LoRa called itself "LoRa" -
and it is being renamed to match, but that fixes one plugin, not the class: an
out-of-tree plugin can still call itself anything.

So the identity used for all of it is now the directory name. mPluginDirNames
maps a live plugin back to where it was installed from, dirNameFor() reads it
(falling back to the plugin's own name for anything not loaded through
loadUserPlugin(), where the two are the same by construction), and
findPluginByDir() resolves the name the outside world uses. mPluginLibraries,
mPluginControlFds, mPluginCommands, mPluginsWithOutputs, isPluginLoaded() and
unloadPlugin() are all keyed on it. This also settles an inconsistency in the
command tracking, which was keyed by directory name on the load path and by
plugin name on the register/addControlCallbacks paths, so the two did not meet
for a plugin whose names differed.

multiSyncData() deliberately still matches on the plugin's own name: that is
the identifier a plugin puts in the MultiSync packets it sends, not an
installation identity. findPlugin() also still matches on it - its only caller
looks up channel output libraries by a synthesized name that never corresponds
to an installed directory, and those are not unloaded through this path.

Verified on hardware: before the change, unloading the mismatched plugin
returned Status OK, logged nothing at all, and left the library mapped; after
it, all fourteen C++ plugins unload and reload by directory name, twelve of them
unmapping, with fppd surviving throughout.

fix(artnet): let e131bridge own the shared ArtNet socket's epoll registration

ArtNet fixes the port it listens on, so the bridge and anything else that speaks
ArtNet - a plugin adding trigger or timecode support - necessarily receive on
one socket. Each interested party was registering that descriptor with
EPollManager itself, which does not work for a shared one. EPollManager holds a
single callback per descriptor, so the second registration silently replaced the
first, and the first removal took the descriptor out of the epoll set for
everyone: unloading a plugin that had registered it stopped the bridge receiving
ArtNet until something happened to register it again.

The registration now belongs to this file and nowhere else, driven by whether
any opcode handler currently wants packets. Add/RemoveArtNetOpcodeHandler() -
which the bridge and plugins already both call - keep it in step, so there is no
new API for a plugin to learn and the caller that used to hand the descriptor
around simply stops doing so.

Two things follow from keeping it here. The callback is always FPP's own, never
a plugin's, so an unloaded plugin cannot leave the loop dispatching into an
unmapped library - which a reference count on the descriptor would not have
fixed by itself, since the callback it kept alive might be the departing one's.
And BridgeShutdownUDP() now gives back only the bridge's own handlers on a
reload and lets the registration re-evaluate, so a plugin keeps receiving ArtNet
across a bridge reload rather than going deaf until something re-registers.

The socket is created on demand when a handler wants it and there is none, which
is what the callers registering it themselves were doing implicitly by calling
CreateArtNetSocket(). Without that a plugin's triggers would silently stop
working on any player whose own configuration has no ArtNet input.

Verified end to end on hardware, on a player with no ArtNet input universes
configured: a plugin enabling ArtNet triggers receives a real ArtTrigger packet
and runs the command it carries. With this change reverted and the same plugin
in place, the identical packet is ignored.

feat(api): let plugins document their HTTP routes on the API page

Plugin routes all landed under "Undocumented - see plugin documentation" on the
API page. There was nowhere for a plugin to say what its routes do: fppd can
list every route Drogon has registered, but Drogon's registry does not record
who registered one, so nothing on the FPP side can attribute a path to a plugin,
let alone describe it.

A plugin can now ship an apiDocs.json at the top of its directory, and
MergePluginApiDocs() folds it into the generated spec before the undocumented
sweep runs, so anything described there drops out of that sweep instead of being
reported. Ownership is simply which directory the file came from, which is the
attribution Drogon cannot give us. The documentation then ships and versions
with the plugin, needs no rebuild to change, and covers a plugin that is
installed but not currently serving.

The file is an OpenAPI fragment - a "paths" object, keyed by the path the plugin
registered with FPPPlugins::registerPluginApi() - so it composes with the rest
of the spec untranslated. Whether that path is reachable directly or through the
generic /api/plugin-apis/ passthrough is worked out here, so a plugin does not
have to know. Subpaths of a family=true registration can be documented too, even
though only the parent is registered with Drogon and fppd therefore never
reports them; without this they could not be documented at all.

A plugin cannot claim a core path: an operation FPP already documents is never
overwritten. A plugin shipping a broken file gets logged and skipped rather than
taking the whole API page down with it, the same way the PHP endpoint scan
handles a conflicting api.php.

Also documents the plugin load/unload endpoint added with runtime plugin
loading, which was itself in the undocumented bucket. Drogon registers it with
positional {1}/{2} placeholders, so it is described under readable parameter
names and the raw form is skipped - the sweep's "already documented?" checks
compare paths literally and cannot match one against the other.

Verified on a running player: the six shipped plugins that serve HTTP routes
document eleven operations between them, and the only entries left in the
undocumented bucket belong to a plugin that has not shipped a file yet.
Malformed and structurally wrong plugin files were both confirmed to leave the
spec serving 200 with the offending plugin's routes falling back to the
undocumented stub.

fix(BBShiftPanel): prime the SMEM ring before starting a PWM frame

6543a19b1 moved the self-PWM panel types onto the shared-memory ring along
with the shift panels.  The ring delivers every byte - the produced and
consumed counters stay exact and aligned to the PRU's 48 byte load, which
is what that commit verified - but it delivers them late.  Measured on
FM6363C hardware, the PRU entered RINGWAIT about seven times per frame for
40-50us each.

That is harmless for a shift panel, where the same PRU drives both the data
and the row address.  A self-PWM panel is different: it refreshes from its
own engine while its row scan free runs, so a gap in the shift out lets the
scan walk away from the data.  Roughly 300us of gaps per frame against a
~13.8us row period is more than a full pass of drift, which is why the
image slid vertically by a different amount every frame while every
byte-level check came back clean.

The ring was empty at the start of every frame (produced == consumed there),
so the dominant term was the pump's wakeup latency: it polled the frame
sequence on a 500us sleep, and the DATA command went out before any bytes
had been written.  So wake the pump from PrepDataPWM rather than having it
poll, hold the DATA command until the pump reports the ring full, and back
off in 20us steps instead of 150us once it is running.

The stall count is unchanged afterwards but every RINGWAIT entry now
resolves on the first reload of the producer counter, so the wait drops
from ~300us per frame to nothing measurable.  Checked on 8 and 16 output
capes driving an 80x40 1/10 scan panel.  The shift path is untouched and
was re-checked with 64x32 1/16 scan panels on a 16 output cape.

fix(BBB): stop clobbering the PRU sleep firmware when installing PRU programs

/lib/firmware/<prefix>-pruN-fw ships as a symlink to the -fw.sleep parking
firmware that the image boots the PRUs with.  BBBPru::run() copied the PRU
program to that path with CopyFileContents, whose creat() follows the
symlink - so the first time any PRU output started, the sleep firmware
itself was overwritten with the output program.  Every board that has ever
run a PRU output boots its PRUs into the last output program instead of the
parking firmware.  For most outputs that is a benign wait-for-command loop,
but FalconSerial free-runs a frame every ~190ms without waiting for a first
command, so a board that ever ran the serial output blasts garbage serial
data from boot on whatever pins end up muxed to the PRU.

Install the program under its own -fw.fpp name and atomically repoint the
-fw symlink at it, and have stop() point the link back at the sleep
firmware so a clean shutdown restores the boot behavior.  Boards whose
.sleep file was already overwritten need it restored out-of-band; the fix
only prevents future corruption.

Verified on an AM335x board: the .sleep hash survives an fppd start/stop
cycle, the -fw link tracks program vs sleep, and serial output data is
unaffected.

with mutex_ held.  The callbacks do arbitrary heavyweight work (reloading
channel outputs, constructing/destroying plugins), and if one of them
crashes, the process exit path runs the plugin destructors on that same
thread - Plugin::~Plugin calls FileMonitor::RemoveFile, which blocks on
mutex_ forever.  The observed result is a crash that turns into a hung
zombie fppd that systemd still reports as active, instead of a crash-exit
the watchdog can restart.

Collect the callbacks under mutex_ and invoke them after releasing it.  A
separate callbackMutex_ preserves the (previously incidental) serialization
of callback execution between the init path and the inotify event loop;
the exit path never takes it, so a crash mid-callback can no longer
deadlock teardown.  This also makes AddFile/RemoveFile callable from
within a callback.

FalconV5: derive the listener's shared RAM reservation from one constant

The PRU listener's store cap and the ARM's copy-out clamp were two
independent magic numbers (12000 and 4096*3) for the same quantity: how
much of the PRU shared RAM the listener is allowed to fill.  Replace both
with SMEM_RING_LISTENER_BYTES and document what actually sizes it.

That size is driven by the capture rate, not the FalconV5 bit rate.  The
listener stores one byte holding all eight listener pins every
FALCONV5_PERIOD - 166ns on the AM62x, not the 1130ns bit period - so it
captures at ~6MB/s, and the window BBShiftString leaves it enabled is
~2.1ms.  That is ~12.6KB, which makes 12KB a floor rather than a generous
cap; shrinking it truncates the tail of a capture.

Also add SMEM_RING_V5_BASE/SMEM_RING_V5_SIZE for the layout where one PRU
outputs strings while the other runs the listener.  The listener captures
from the base of shared RAM upwards, so the ring cannot simply move to the
top half - it takes the 20416 bytes above the reservation instead of a
16320 byte split half.

Fix an 8 byte stack overflow at the clamp boundary while here:
processListenerData copies (len + 8) bytes, and the PRU keeps incrementing
length after it stops storing, so the buffer needs the reservation plus 8.

BBShiftString: 16 strings per data pin on AM62x

A cape can declare "stringsPerPin": 16 to drive 128 strings from one PRU's
eight data pins using a 16 deep shift register chain.  Absent, or 8, keeps
the existing behaviour byte for byte.  16 selects a separate SHIFT16
firmware image rather than a runtime switch, because the shift loop count,
the T0 high time and the command table record layout all differ.

AM62x only.  At the AM335x 200MHz the three shift phases of a 16 deep chain
total 1045ns against a 1120ns bit budget with no room left for the data
block read, and two PRUs already reach 128 strings there.

Firmware (SHIFT16):
 - 16 clocks per shift phase instead of 8
 - output masks move to scratchpad banks 11 and 12 with r21-r24 as a
   transient window.  16 deep needs 32 bytes of masks and r2-r29 are all
   spoken for; XIN/XOUT costs one cycle regardless of length, so this buys
   the space for two cycles per phase and no registers at all.  Bank 10 is
   the FalconV5 listener handshake, and a shared panels+strings cape forces
   the panel driver into SINGLEPRU, whose build has no XIN/XOUT compiled in.
 - T0_TIME 220 -> 300.  A 16 deep shift takes 260ns so the 8 deep deadline
   has already passed by the time the data is out; 300ns lands T0H at
   ~312ns, inside WS2811/SK6812/WS2815 tolerance and closer to nominal than
   8 deep manages for WS2812B.
 - a second block load per pixel byte, since a 64 byte block only carries
   four of the eight bits
 - SPP bit 0 cleared at startup.  Both the mask transfers and the listener
   handshake assume register aligned XIN/XOUT, and a panel driver sharing
   the PRUSS enables a PRUSS wide shift by r0.b0.
 - ring-empty events counted into SMEM_RING_STATS_OFFSET, since a 16 deep
   chain drains the ring at twice the byte rate

ARM side: NUM_STRINGS_PER_PIN becomes MAX_STRINGS_PER_PIN for buffer sizing
plus a runtime m_stringsPerPin.  prepData and bitFlipData are templated on
the depth and dispatched once per frame so the 8 deep codegen is unchanged;
bitFlipData gains an 8x16 transpose.  Command table records go 18 -> 34
bytes and gained the bounds check they never had - 128 strings can overflow
commandTable[3578] and the staging buffer.

Measured on a 16 port cape with 8 deep chains running the 16 deep firmware:
bit period 1198 -> 1221ns, frame bytes exactly doubled, and with a FalconV5
listener on the other PRU no ring starvation at all with the frame six
times the ring size under a load average of 7 on four cores.  Output is
visually identical to the 8 deep baseline on real pixels.

fix: don't destroy channel outputs while the output thread is walking them

ReloadChannelOutputsForFile() unlinked the outputs belonging to a config file
and then deleted them behind a sleep_for(100ms), on the theory that the channel
output thread would have finished a cycle by then.  That is not a barrier.  The
output thread holds outputThreadLock across PrepareChannelData() and
SendChannelData(), and a cycle that runs longer than 100ms - which happens
whenever the send side backs up - simply runs past the sleep.  The walk can
then be inside inst->output->PrepData() when the instance is freed, and
inst = inst->next reads the freed node as well.

Take outputThreadLock across the unlink/stop/close/delete instead, and in
addChannelOutput(), so list mutation is serialized against the walk uniformly.
Only the teardown is covered: Init() of the replacement outputs can run for a
long time (matrix PRU compiles, firmware loads) and holding the lock across it
would stall output for that whole time, whereas a half-populated list is
harmless.

outputThreadLock is now declared in channeloutputthread.h along with the
invariant and the two ways it must not be used.  StartChannelOutputThread()
waits on a flag the new thread sets only after taking the lock, and the output
thread holds the lock across Sequence::SendSequenceData(), which runs
FSEQ-triggered commands - so nothing reachable from a command may take it.
That rules out locking HasUniverseOutputs()/GetOutputTypes(), which still walk
unguarded from API threads; closing those properly wants a read side that
cannot block the writer, so they carry a comment rather than a lock.

BBShiftPanel had the panel-side half of the same race.  StartPRU() left
m_pumpSeq/m_pumpedSeq/m_pumpPrimed at their previous values, so after a
teardownHardware() and restart the new pump thread believed a frame from the
old configuration was still owed; and the PWM branch of runPumpThread() used
m_frontBuffer without the null check the shift branch already had, which is
what turned the race into a fault on a near-null address.

Measured on an AM62x box driving a live panel output, with a detector that
raises a flag around the list walk and checks it immediately before the
teardown destroys anything: the old sleep gave 2 violations in 26 teardowns,
the lock 0 in 123.  The control only trips once an output cycle exceeds 100ms,
which is why this presented as an intermittent, single-device crash.

fix: BBShiftString rendered frames at the wrong offset on AM62x

The command word tells the firmware how many pixel bytes to render but
not where the frame begins - it just reads on from wherever it stopped.
The pump issued the next command as soon as the firmware had taken the
previous one, and the firmware takes it at frame start rather than frame
end, so a command could go out while a whole frame was still unread in
the ring.  Whatever was buffered at that moment became a permanent skew:
every later frame rendered that many bytes into the previous one.

Only issue a command once the ring has drained, the one moment the read
pointer provably sits on that frame's first byte.  Streaming ahead within
a frame is unaffected, and any skew is now absorbed rather than carried
forever.

The read pointer is also published after the wrap instead of before, so
the value the ARM sees is always a real ring address; publishing the
one-past-the-end value made an empty ring compare as occupied.  drained()
keeps a modulo compare as a backstop.  Counter-mode consumers are
unchanged.

Finally, clear the command word after the 0x1 "firmware started" marker.
Nothing reads that marker, and the wait loop read it back as a one byte
frame, consuming a ring block the ARM never wrote.

Measured on a 16 port cape with 50 pixels per port by decoding the ring
back to per-port bytes: a single lit pixel on channel 1 rendered 102
bytes late (pixel 35 of 50) and the ring never emptied; afterwards the
offset is 0 and the ring is empty 97% of the time.  Full length strings
hid this because the skew is a fixed byte count - a few percent of a long
frame, and invisible under a uniform test pattern.

fix(capes): map renamed kernel modules so cape audio isn't lost to snd-dummy

Cape EEPROMs list the kernel modules the board needs, but an EEPROM is
programmed once and stays in the field forever, so an older one can name a
module the running kernel no longer has. The pcm5102a codec is the case that
bites: the driver is now snd_soc_pcm5102a, so "modprobe pcm5102a" fails
silently at cape detect. The codec then only autoloads later via its DT
modalias, which is late enough that setupAudio has already found no soundcard
and loaded snd-dummy -- leaving Dummy as card 0 and the real cape audio at
card 1.

This only surfaced recently: the codec used to be built into the kernel on
the older images, where the failed modprobe cost nothing.

Add a legacy-name map consulted at modprobe time. Names are resolved with
"modprobe -n -q" first and the map is only used when the EEPROM's name does
not resolve on this kernel, so a kernel that still has the old name keeps
using it. Names that resolve to nothing now log instead of disappearing into
2>/dev/null.

pcm5102a is the only real rename across every shipped EEPROM; the other names
in use (gpio_pcf857x, lm75, rtc-pcf8523, rtc-pcf85363) all still resolve, and
modprobe already treats '-' and '_' as equivalent.

Also fold both modprobe loops into one helper. The second loop, which reloads
modules after pinctrl is applied, had no isMember("modules") guard, so on a
cape with pinctrl but no modules the lookup inserted a null member that was
then serialized into tmp/cape-info.json.

fix(audio): don't load snd-dummy while a real sound card is still binding

Loading snd-dummy is a one-way door: it takes the next free card number, so a
real card that binds a moment later lands behind it and the default selection
resolves to Dummy. setupAudio took a single "aplay -l" snapshot and committed
to snd-dummy on the spot, which loses the race against a codec whose driver is
still being autoloaded -- observed on a BeagleBone with an audio cape, where
Dummy took card 0 and the cape's card landed at card 1.

Before committing to snd-dummy, give hardware that is physically present a
bounded chance to finish binding: up to 5s polling /proc/asound/cards, then
fall through to snd-dummy as before. Poll /proc/asound/cards rather than
re-running aplay -- it is pure kernel state, visible the instant the card
registers, with no dependency on the /dev/snd node.

Gated on evidence that a card is actually coming, so the wait is never paid
speculatively:
  - the device tree declares a sound card, or
  - a USB audio device is plugged in (class 01, excluding MIDIStreaming --
    a MIDI-only device yields a card with no playback device and could never
    satisfy the probe)
A board with neither -- no audio cape and no USB audio, the common case --
does two directory scans and falls straight through, unchanged.

Read the USB state from sysfs rather than lsusb: only "lsusb -v" reports
interface class and it costs ~200ms on an AM335x board since it walks and
wakes every device, against a handful of open() calls here.

Once the card registers, settle udev before re-probing. "aplay -l" reads
/dev/snd/controlC*, which udev creates ~115ms after registration (measured),
and that node is the one part of this udev genuinely owns. Note this is also
why "udevadm trigger --subsystem-match=sound --settle" cannot fix the original
race on its own: trigger only re-emits uevents for devices already in sysfs,
so with the driver unbound it drains an empty queue and returns success having
changed nothing.

The aplay parse moves into a lambda so the re-probe cannot drift from the
initial one.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(audio): load the CPU DAI and machine driver so the cape card can bind

The previous commit waited up to 5s for a declared-but-unbound sound card, but
on a BeagleBone with an audio cape it still timed out and took snd-dummy. The
wait was sound; its premise was not.

An ASoC card cannot bind until *every* component it references is present: the
codec, the CPU DAI, and the machine driver. A cape EEPROM only names the codec,
and the other two are device-tree platform devices whose drivers udev autoloads
from their modalias. Module load times on a failing boot:

  snd_soc_pcm5102a       +22s   (cape detect modprobes it -- early, as intended)
  snd_soc_davinci_mcasp  +59s
  snd_soc_simple_card    +59s   (10s AFTER snd-dummy was loaded)

So the codec was up the whole time and the card still could not bind, because
udev's coldplug does not reach the other two until tens of seconds into boot on
a slow single-core board. No amount of waiting would have helped.

Do udev's job for the audio devices instead of waiting on it: walk the platform
bus and modprobe the modalias of any still-unbound device whose compatible looks
audio-related. Driving it off the kernel's own modalias means no module, SoC or
codec name is hardcoded, so this covers any cape/codec/CPU-DAI combination.

Verified on a BeagleBone with a 16-port cape. Before: Dummy at card 0, cape
audio at card 1. After: cape audio at card 0 and snd-dummy never loaded, with
the card binding immediately once the drivers were present ("registered after
0.0s"), which also confirms an ASoC card binds synchronously as its last
component registers.

The modalias is single-quoted for the shell -- it embeds the DT compatible and
contains parentheses, which are shell metacharacters. A modalias containing a
quote is skipped rather than trusted.

fix(logging): restore journal visibility for fppinit, fpprtc and fppoled

Two separate regressions left the non-fppd services writing to only one
place, and between them most of what FPP prints at boot stopped showing up
where people look for it.

fppinit never linked the logger, so the stdout suppression was not its
problem: consolidating init logging replaced `tee -a fppd.log` with a bash
line-prefixer on the far side of the dup2. tee wrote both places; the
replacement only appended to the file, so fppinit's output -- and that of
everything it forks, which is the point of the dup2 -- stopped reaching
journald entirely. `systemctl status fppinit` went quiet, as did a hand-run
`fppinit setupAudio` in a terminal.

teeOutput() is a real tee again: it dup()s the console before dup2 takes fd
1 over and the writer emits to both, prefixed into fppd.log and raw to the
console (journald stamps and tags its own lines already). It moves to
common_mini.cpp so fpprtc can use it too -- which RTC and driver were found
is exactly what a "clock is wrong after a power cycle" report needs, and it
was going only to a RAM-only journal that dies at reboot.

fppoled *was* hit by the stdout suppression: it was global, so every binary
linking log.o lost its journal copy once a line reached fppd.log, not just
fppd. Make it opt-in (SetSuppressDuplicateStdOut) and have only fppd ask --
it is the one with a firehose to deduplicate. The small services are a
handful of lines a boot and `journalctl -u <service>` is where they are
looked for.

fppoled needed the other half too: it had 3 Log* calls against ~35 printfs,
so unsuppressing alone would have left it contributing almost nothing to
fppd.log. Convert those printfs to Log*, building the two lines that were
assembled across several printf calls into one string first, since a log
line is one record with its own prefix.

Also create fppd.log as fpp:fpp 0664 when teeOutput gets there first, so a
root-run service does not lock out fppd and the PHP-side writers that share
the file.

fix(audio): don't pick a PCM format the card can't hold at the target rate

Format detection took the widest format in the ALSA FORMAT: list and used it
unconditionally:

    if (strpos($fmtLine, 'S32_LE') !== false) { $fmt = 'S32LE'; }

On a fixed-bit-clock I2S card the bit clock is the constant, not the rate, so
widening the sample size halves the achievable rate.  A BeagleBone cape with
McASP driving a PCM5102A advertises "FORMAT: S16_LE S32_LE" and
"RATE: [22050 44100]", but 32 bits/frame x 44100 == 64 bits/frame x 22050 --
S32_LE exists and 44100 exists, yet S32_LE at 44100 does not.

`aplay --dump-hw-params` cannot express that.  It reports the unrefined
capability space and ignores both -f and -r (verified: constraining either one
returns the identical FORMAT and RATE lines), so nothing in its output hints
that the pair is invalid.  Only actually opening the device reveals it.

The result was not a subtle quality issue.  PipeWire requested the impossible
pair, failed adapter creation ("no format found (def:267)", where 267 is
SPA_AUDIO_FORMAT_S32_LE), aborted context creation and exited 234.  systemd
restarted it every few seconds forever: 129 format failures in a single boot
and NRestarts=2418 on a board that had been up a couple of hours, burning CPU
indefinitely on a single-core SBC that could never produce sound.  The
RuntimeDirectory=pipewire-fpp teardown on each exit also took the pulse
service's runtime dir with it, so fpp-pipewire-pulse crash-looped alongside it
with a confusing "chown: cannot access /run/pipewire-fpp/pulse" -- a symptom of
this bug, not a separate one.

Verify a candidate by opening the device: feeding 8KB of zeros reports the
negotiated rate and exits in ~250ms without emitting audible sound.  Candidates
are tried widest-first and fall back through the narrower ones to the
universally-safe S16LE default.

Two deliberate choices:

  * Unverifiable (device busy, probe timed out, aplay missing) declines to
    widen.  A needlessly narrow format costs bit depth; a wrongly wide one
    costs a permanent crash loop.
  * In C++ the pick moved after alsaPath resolves, so the probe opens the
    device that will actually be configured (hw: vs sysdefault:) rather than
    assuming hw:.

All four sites are fixed -- both PHP generators in pipewire.php and both C++
generators in FPPINIT_Audio.cpp -- since the 97-conf is regenerated through the
PHP path at boot and the C++ path on the first-boot fast path.

Verified on a BBB cape (McASP + PCM5102A): regeneration now emits S16LE,
NRestarts=0, zero format errors, and the sink runs at s16le 2ch 44100Hz across
a reboot.

BBShiftString: opt-in ring starvation counter in the PRU firmware

Whether the ARM pump keeps the shared memory ring fed cannot be measured
from userspace once the output duty cycle gets high: at 780 pixels and a
25ms frame the PRU outputs 93% of wall clock, and a sampling process's
own scheduling jitter runs to about a millisecond - the same size as the
stalls being looked for.  Polling the read pointer produced two different
confident-looking answers, both wrong, before the firmware was asked
instead.

The counter itself already existed but only in the 16 deep build.  Move
it behind RING_STALL_STATS, off by default and documented at the top of
the file next to SLOW_WAITNS, so it can be switched on for a test build
on any cape depth.  When data is ready it costs the same two instructions
as the plain wait loop, so the overhead only lands on the path where the
firmware is already starving; with the define off the wait loop assembles
back to exactly the LBBO/QBEQ pair it was.

Note this turns the counter off by default for 16 deep builds, where it
was previously always on.

To convert polls to time, freeze the pump for a known wall time and
divide - that calibrated one poll at 48.1ns on an AM62x. At 780 pixels
and 40fps the firmware waits 672 polls per frame, so even if all of a
frame's waiting fell in one contiguous stall it is 32us against the ~50us
WS281x latch threshold.

fix(boot): stop a duplicate WirePlumber ALSA sink from hanging boot, and cut ~11s off postNetwork

WirePlumber's ALSA monitor enumerates every card independently of the static
fpp_alsa_* adapters PipeWire loads from 95-fpp-alsa-sink.conf, so a card FPP
already owns also gets a monitor-created node.  Both want the same PCM, and the
monitor's node -- backed by a real device object, unlike a bare context.objects
adapter -- wins the default-sink election.  Every untargeted stream then lands
on a node whose snd_pcm_open() returns EBUSY: the node parks in error and the
stream neither starts nor ends, so the client blocks in poll() forever.

That made a board unbootable, not merely silent.  fpp-announce-ip.service was
Type=oneshot with no timeout, so the wedged pw-play held multi-user.target and
graphical.target in "start waiting" with no upper bound; an affected board sat
at 13 minutes of "boot" and climbing until the process was killed by hand.

- Generate 50-fpp-suppress-alsa-dupes.conf, disabling the ALSA monitor's device
  for every card that already has a static adapter.  Keyed on
  api.alsa.card.name: alsa.id and alsa.card_name show up in pw-dump but are
  attached to the device only after monitor.alsa.rules are evaluated, so a rule
  keyed on those silently never matches -- confirmed on hardware, where the
  duplicate still appeared.
- Make the announcement genuinely fire-and-forget, as its own comment already
  claimed: Type=simple so it cannot hold a target, RuntimeMaxSec as a backstop,
  and timeouts around flite and pw-play so nothing about announcing an IP
  address can wedge a boot service again.

The same investigation found postNetwork re-deriving work it had already done:

- "inactive" from `systemctl is-active fpp-pipewire` is a cold start, not a
  crashed stack.  The PipeWire units ship disabled and postNetwork is what
  starts them, so that test was false on every normal boot and the
  skip-restart fast path was dead code on exactly the boards it was written
  for.  Every boot paid a full three-service restart, a hardcoded 3s settle and
  a forced PHP regeneration to re-derive a config the cheap C++ validation had
  already proven byte-identical and card-complete seconds earlier.
- Port RestorePipeWireGroupVolumes() to C++.  Forking php plus common.php plus
  the API controller to emit a handful of pactl calls measured 6s uncontended
  and 12s under boot load on a single-core board, all of it on the critical
  path to fppd.  The PHP remains the implementation behind the UI's interactive
  applies; both sides are commented to be kept in sync.
- On single-core boards only, order exim4, exim4-base, chrony and shellinabox
  behind fppd, apache2 and php-fpm.  Those three decide when the box is
  actually usable and they lose the fight for the one core: php-fpm starts in
  2.3s cold on an idle board but took 20.9s at boot, and being last up it alone
  sets that moment.  Gated on $FPPPLATFORM rather than nproc, because
  FPP_Install.sh runs inside a chroot during image builds where nproc reports
  the build host's core count and the gate would silently never fire.
  Multi-core Pi and BeagleBone 64 emit byte-identical drop-ins to before.

Measured on a single-core AM335x board with a cape-attached I2S DAC: boot never
completed -> 1m30s total; postNetwork 23.9s -> 16.1s; fppd 62.9s -> 56.5s;
apache2 76.6s -> 57.8s; php-fpm 80.1s -> 72.9s.  The C++ volume restore was
A/B'd against the PHP with non-default levels and produced identical results,
with a control confirming the check could have failed.

perf(boot): stop DHCP from dragging systemd-hostnamed and polkit into the boot

systemd-networkd sets the transient hostname from the DHCP lease unless told
otherwise, and the DHCP server echoes the hostname the client sent, so the
option is always present.  The moment the lease lands networkd calls
org.freedesktop.hostname1, which D-Bus-activates systemd-hostnamed, which
activates polkit to authorize the call -- to set a hostname FPP had already
written to /etc/hostname itself.

Nothing else on an FPP box uses polkit: it is a static unit, reachable only by
D-Bus activation, and there is not a single reference to it in the tree.  It was
being started, and paid for, purely as a side effect of this one call.  On a
single-core AM335x board the pair cost 4.3s (hostnamed) plus 16.8s (polkitd) --
about 21s of a 90s boot, landing squarely in the window that decides when fppd
and the web UI come up.

Set UseHostname=false on the DHCPv4 sections FPP generates and on the shipped
ether default.  Verified on a 4-core BeagleBone 64: hostname1 D-Bus activations
1 -> 0, and systemd-hostnamed and polkit go from 1.809s and 1.745s to never
starting at all, with the hostname and address unchanged.

Note that hand-editing /etc/systemd/network/10-*.network to test this does not
work -- setupNetwork() regenerates those files on every boot, so the change has
to come from the generator.

fix(audio): judge the PCM format probe by aplay's exit status, not its banner

formatHoldsRate() decided a candidate format worked by matching "Playing raw
data" in aplay's output.  aplay prints that banner from header(), which runs
before set_params() negotiates anything, so it shows up even when the card then
rejects the request outright:

    Playing raw data '-' : Signed 24 bit Little Endian in 3bytes, ...
    aplay: set_params:1387: Sample format non available

A format the device cannot produce therefore read as success.

The two failure shapes are different and both have to be caught: an unusable
format makes aplay exit non-zero, while a rate the driver quietly refines to a
reachable one only warns ("rate is not accurate") and still exits 0.  Keying on
the exit status covers the first; the existing "not accurate" check still
covers the second.

execAndReturn() hands back only stdout, so the C++ probe appends
`; echo "fpp-audio-probe-rc:$?"` and parses that tag back out -- $? after the
pipeline is aplay's own status.  The PHP probe moves from shell_exec() to
exec(), which reports the status directly.  A missing status still declines to
widen, preserving the original bias: a needlessly narrow format costs bit
depth, a wrongly wide one costs a permanent PipeWire crash loop.

Verified against real hardware on both an AM335x cape (advertising
"S16_LE S32_LE" / "[22050 44100]") and an AM62x cape ("S16_LE S32_LE" /
"[88200 176400]").  S24_3LE was accepted by the old check and is rejected by
the new one on both, while every pair that legitimately opens -- S16_LE@44100
and S32_LE@22050 on the former, S32_LE@88200 on the latter -- still passes.
The false positive was masked in practice because bestFormatForRate() only
probes formats the card already advertises in its FORMAT list.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

perf(boot): defer rsyslog off the boot path, and stop shipping atd and ufw enabled

rsyslog duplicates the journal into /var/log/syslog, and on an SD/eMMC-backed
board those writes compete for the device with the reads the boot itself needs.
It was starting at 26.5s, squarely inside the fppinit/networkd window, for a log
nothing reads during boot -- journald is the primary and is persistent here, and
syslog.target has no dependents.

Deferring it loses nothing, which is worth spelling out because it looks risky:
syslog.socket is DefaultDependencies=no and Before=sockets.target, so it exists
from the very start of boot with an 8M ReceiveBuffer, and rsyslog is TriggeredBy=
it.  journald forwards into that socket whether or not rsyslog is running and
rsyslog drains the backlog when it starts.  A whole boot's journal on a BBB is
~95KB, about 1.2% of the buffer.  Verified on hardware: with rsyslog held back to
77s, /var/log/syslog still contains the boot's first kernel line, and it captured
85.8% of the journal's lines against 64.6% and 65.6% on the two preceding
early-start boots -- the shortfall is journald declining to forward everything,
and it did not widen.

Also stop shipping two services enabled that this appliance never uses:

- atd runs one-shot jobs queued with at(1).  FPP queues none; scheduling goes
  through fppd's own scheduler and cron, so the daemon starts, finds an empty
  spool and idles.
- ufw ships enabled but unconfigured, so it starts, applies no rules (`ufw
  status` reports inactive) and exits.  Nothing in the tree references it, and an
  admin who wants a firewall runs `ufw enable`, which enables the unit anyway.

Both were confirmed to have no reverse dependencies before disabling.

perf(boot): let the IP announcement yield to fppd, apache and php-fpm

Being Type=simple, the announcement starts the instant fpp_postnetwork finishes
-- which is precisely when fppd, apache2 and php-fpm are all coming up and
fighting over one core on an AM335x board.  Measured there, the flite render
spends 3.6s of CPU in that window; apache2 spends 1.1s over the same span.  So a
spoken IP address that nothing waits on was taking CPU from the three services
that decide when the box is usable.

announcing an IP is to say it promptly, and niceness only costs latency when
something else actually wants the core, so a multi-core Pi or BeagleBone 64 is
unaffected.

perf(boot): stop scanning /proc twice a boot for a removed AES67 implementation

setupAudio unconditionally ran two `pkill -f` scans to clean up daemons from the
legacy Python AES67 approach, which fppd's AES67Manager replaced.  Each is a
/bin/sh plus a walk of every /proc/*/cmdline, they run on the critical path to

perf(php): stop loading twelve PHP extensions FPP never uses

Each was verified rather than guessed: every shared extension's real functions
and classes were enumerated with ReflectionExtension and matched against all 205
of FPP's PHP files.  None of these twelve is referenced anywhere.

This is a memory and attack-surface change, not a boot-time one.  Cold PHP
startup on a single-core AM335x board goes from 1.08s to 0.84s, but php-fpm loads
extensions once in the master and then forks its workers, so that is ~0.24s of
boot, once -- about 1% of the 26.7s php-fpm actually takes there, which is
contention, not module loading.  The real gain is ~1.6MB per worker: 9.7MB across
the six workers that board runs, up to ~40MB at pm.max_children=25, on a device
with 480MB of RAM.  Dropping ffi also takes the Foreign Function Interface out of
a web-facing PHP.

sqlite3, pdo and pdo_sqlite are equally unreferenced by FPP core and were
measured safe, but stay enabled on purpose: a third-party plugin under
/media/plugins could reasonably keep its own data in SQLite, and a source scan of
this repo cannot see those plugins.

Verified with the twelve disabled: every UI page and API endpoint tested returns
200 and php-fpm logs no errors.

fix(network): re-enumerate a USB network adapter that came up dead

Some USB WiFi adapters lose their register interface during init and never
recover on their own.  Observed with a Realtek 8822bu on an AM335x musb-hdrc
controller: the driver binds, wlan0 duly appears and reports Link UP, but every
register access returns -EPROTO -- 65,956 of them on one boot against exactly 1
on a healthy boot.  The radio never associates.  The board itself is fine; it
reaches graphical.target in the usual time and keeps running the show.  It is
simply unreachable, and stays that way until somebody walks out to it and
re-plugs the adapter, which fixes it instantly.

Nothing between the kernel and wpa_supplicant retries at the USB level, so make
FPP do it.  waitForInterfacesUp() already detects this exact state -- it is what
logs "No network interfaces with link detected" -- so before giving up there,
unbind and rebind any USB-attached adapter that has no carrier.  That is the same
full re-enumeration as a physical re-plug; measured on hardware it brought wlan0
back with its original address in about 15 seconds.

Deliberately narrow:

- Runs only on the no-interface-came-up path, and only once, so a healthy boot
  never executes any of it.
- Skips adapters that have carrier -- one of those is working even if DHCP has
  not finished, and resetting it would cause the outage it is meant to prevent.
- Skips anything not behind USB, so an unplugged onboard eth0 is not a target.
- Does nothing when no USB network adapter is present, so a standalone board with
  no network at all does not pay for a second wait.  A board that does have a USB
  adapter but no reachable AP will spend roughly 12s extra before giving up.

The unbind/bind recovery and the interface selection are both verified on
hardware.  The end-to-end path is not: the -EPROTO fault cannot be induced on
demand, so what is tested is each link -- detection state, target resolution, and
that a re-enumeration restores the link -- not the composition.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(bbb): stop rtw88 USB WiFi adapters trying to switch to USB 3 mode

rtw88_usb switches the chip into USB 3 mode during probe by default.  No
BeagleBone USB host can do USB 3 -- AM335x musb-hdrc and AM62x both enumerate at
480Mbps and expose no SuperSpeed port -- so the attempt cannot succeed and is
pure risk.

The switch is a register write (0xc4) that forces the device to re-enumerate, and
on AM335x it intermittently leaves the adapter wedged: every register access then
returns -EPROTO or -ETIMEDOUT, the radio never associates, and the board boots and
runs perfectly well while being completely unreachable.  Observed twice in roughly
fourteen boots on one board, logging 65,956 driver errors on one occasion against
exactly 1 on a healthy boot.  Every boot logged at least one failed 0xc4 write,
so the adapter was always riding the edge.

What makes it nasty is that re-probing re-attempts the same switch.  Unplugging
and replugging the adapter does not reliably recover it, and neither does
unbinding and rebinding it in software -- the cure re-triggers the cause.  The
only reliable recovery was a power cycle.

Disabling it costs nothing even on a Beagle that does have SuperSpeed: the
kernel's own parameter help offers N as the way to stop USB 3 signalling
interfering with the 2.4GHz band, and a WiFi adapter has no need for more than
USB 2 high-speed at FPP's traffic levels.

Measured on a BBB across a reboot: failed 0xc4 writes 1 -> 0, USB
re-enumerations 2 -> 1, total rtw88 errors -> 0 -- the first boot in a long
session of them with a completely clean radio bring-up.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(network): don't let the USB adapter recovery feed itself into a reset loop

The re-enumeration added in c33c76e64 was reachable from every caller of
waitForInterfacesUp(), including `fppinit checkForTether`, which
networkd-dispatcher runs on carrier changes.  A re-enumeration *is* a carrier
change.  On the first boot where the adapter actually wedged, the recovery fired
11 times: once from postNetwork as intended, then ten more from the dispatcher,
about every seven seconds, for as long as the box stayed up.

That is worse than not having it.  The adapter got reset every few seconds, so it
never had time to associate -- and it very likely defeated the operator, who
physically unplugged and replugged the adapter twice with no effect and had to
power cycle the board.  Each replug would have been followed by another reset
within seconds.

Two guards, because one is not enough:

- Recovery is now opt-in via a new argument, and only the postNetwork boot path
  passes it.  The tether callers are dispatcher-driven by construction and must
  never enable it.
- A /run marker enforces one re-enumeration per boot even so.  Every fppinit
  invocation is a separate process and they cannot share the in-process flag, so
  the structural guard alone would still allow a loop if a future caller opted in
  by mistake.  The marker is written before the reset, not after, so a crash
  mid-reset cannot re-arm it.

Verified on hardware: two consecutive `fppinit checkForTether wlan0` runs now
produce zero re-enumerations and never create the marker, with the interface
untouched.

fix(network): actually call disableWLANPowerManagement()

The function has existed since it was written and has never run. There is exactly
one reference to it in the tree -- its own definition -- and `git log -S` shows

- getifaddrs() returns one entry per address family, so a single adapter appears

fix(panels): refuse an interleave that maps outside the gpio frame

PanelInterleaveHandler::createHandler() falls back to NoInterleaveHandler
for any interleave type it does not recognize, including "Off".  That
identity map is only valid when the panel scans half its rows.  On a panel
that scans fewer - a 64x64 1/16 or a 64x32 1/8, say - the rows never fold
into the extra columns, so the mapped y runs up to panelHeight/2 while the
frame holds only panelScan rows, and BBBMatrix::PrepData writes roughly
twice the allocation, faulting on the first frame the output produces.

The contract belongs to the map, not to each caller, so it is checked once
where the handler is built: mapFitsFrame() walks the range the callers
actually map - y in [0, panelHeight/2), all x - and requires every result
to land inside the panelScan rows and panelWidth * panelHeight /
(panelScan * 2) columns the frame is sized for.  A handler that does not
fit is refused, which BBBMatrix::Init already turns into a disabled output
and a warning; that warning now names the geometry and says to set the
interleave.  This covers every handler type, not just the fallback, and
both callers.

Verified under ASan with a harness replaying PrepData's addressing against
the real handler: the reported geometries overflow the frame by exactly
the amount the indexes predict, and after the change they are refused
while every scan*2 == height panel and every valid folding interleave
(8, 32, 16z, 8c, 8s, RPi*) still fills a frame cleanly.

Note for BBShiftPanel: it sizes its frame from the map rather than from
panelScan, so it never overflowed - it drove the wrong row count instead.
It now gets the same refusal, which is a behavior change for a panel whose
configured scan does not match its wiring.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(fseq): don't abort fppd when the read ahead thread can't be created

Every open compressed FSEQ starts its own read ahead thread, and each FSEQ
overlay effect opens one.  A box triggering effects several times a second
keeps dozens of them open at once, and once the process runs out of threads
or (on 32 bit) address space, std::thread's constructor throws
std::system_error.  Nothing catches it, so the daemon aborts.  One report
had 92 live read threads at the point pthread_create finally failed.

Two things kept that count climbing:

 - prepareRead() assigned over m_readThread unconditionally.  Only the last
   thread is ever joined, in the destructor, so an earlier one was leaked
   and left spinning for the life of the daemon.  It now reuses the running
   thread, which is all the newly queued blocks need.

 - Thread creation is wrapped.  The read ahead is an optimization, so on
   failure it logs and leaves m_readThread null, and getBlock() services
   the queue inline on the calling thread instead of waiting for a thread
   that does not exist.  The block read moved to readQueuedBlock() so both
   paths run identical code.

Verified on a multi block zstd sequence: reading every frame produces the
same hash before the change, after it, and with thread creation forced to
fail, and the inline path completes in the same time rather than stalling
on the condition variable.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(bbb): make the rtw88 USB-3-mode-switch option actually apply

The option was installed correctly and silently did nothing on BeagleBone 64.
Two separate reasons, both of which fail without any warning:

Module naming. The rtw88 USB core is rtw88_usb on some kernels and rtw_usb on
others -- 7.1.6-fpp16 has the former, the 6.18.x arm64-k3 builds the latter --
and modprobe ignores options for a module that is not present. Both spellings are
now listed; the absent one is ignored harmlessly.

File ordering. modprobe concatenates options from every file in /etc/modprobe.d in
filename order and the last value wins. The out-of-kernel lwfinger/rtw88 driver
ships /etc/modprobe.d/rtw88.conf setting the opposite, switch_usb_mode=y. BB64
uses that driver and keeps that file; only the BBB image removes it
(build-image-bbb.sh). So "fpp-rtw88-usb.conf" sorted first and was overridden on
every boot. Renamed to zz-fpp-rtw88-usb.conf so it sorts last, and the old name is
removed on upgrade.

Neither failure is visible from the config: the file is present and correct, and
the parameter still reads Y. Only reading it back from
/sys/module/*/parameters/switch_usb_mode catches it. Verified after the fix on two
BB64 boards: parameter reads N, failed 0xc4 writes 1 -> 0 per boot, and the
spurious extra enumeration is gone.

Worth recording what those boards showed while the option was inert, because it is
a clean control for the radio-wedge investigation: 40 boots across two BB64 boards
with switch_usb_mode=Y logged the failed 0xc4 write on every boot, and the extra
enumeration with it, and never once wedged -- while AM335x boards with identical
driver behaviour wedge between 1-in-12 and 3-in-4. The mode switch is a real defect
worth disabling, and is confirmed not to be the cause of the wedge.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(network): reboot instead of re-enumerating a wedged USB network adapter

A USB WiFi adapter can enumerate, bind and bring up its netdev, and then have
the USB link fail at the protocol layer: every register access returns -EPROTO,
the radio never associates, and the board runs perfectly while being completely
unreachable. Measured at roughly 5% of boots on one adapter/controller pairing.

The re-enumeration recovery this replaces does not work. On a captured failure
it fired, re-enumerated the device four times, and the descriptor reads failed
on every one. Disabling and re-enabling the root-hub port leaves the device
"not attached"; unbinding the host controller brings the controller back but
not the device; even a physical replug is unreliable. A reboot is the only
recovery that has ever worked, so do that instead.

Rebooting a show controller is not something to do on a guess, so all of these
must hold: a USB-attached interface with no carrier, no usable address on any
other interface, tethering not configured, and this boot's kernel log carrying
-EPROTO/-ETIMEDOUT against that adapter's own USB port id. Anchoring on the
port id is what separates a wedged adapter from an out-of-range access point on
a box that also has a flaky USB device. Replayed against three captured wedges
(2405/1411/2274 matching lines, two at port 1-1 and one behind a hub at 1-1.2)
and clean boots (0 each), with a control anchored to the wrong port id on a
real wedge log (0) to confirm the anchor constrains anything.

Two things about how the reboot is issued, both learned on hardware:

It must not be synchronous. /usr/sbin/reboot is a symlink to systemctl, which
asks logind over D-Bus to set a wall message, and early in boot that activation
can time out -- measured blocking for 37+ seconds until systemd killed
fpp_postnetwork on its start timeout. fppd's start depends on that service, so
the reboot did not happen AND fppd never started, which is worse than the wedge.

It must not be graceful. A wedged USB stack is exactly what prevents a clean
shutdown from finishing: tasks block in uninterruptible sleep on the dead
device, where neither SIGTERM nor SIGKILL reaches them. Measured, an ordinary
reboot.target began stopping units 8s after the decision and then sat for 37
minutes -- the controller logging "musb-hdrc: VBUS_ERROR in a_wait_bcon" as the
USB stack churned -- leaving the board unreachable for the whole outage this is
meant to end. So sync() and then force the reboot, backgrounded so it cannot
stall this service, with a sysrq fallback if systemctl itself cannot run.

Capped at two attempts within an hour, tracked in /var/tmp so it survives the
reboot it is counting, and cleared once the network comes up, so a permanently
broken adapter cannot boot loop. Off switch: AutoRebootOnUSBNetworkFailure.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(outputs): keep ports enabled and started across a config reload

A controller that had its config uploaded while it was already outputting
went on receiving data with every port powered off, and stayed that way
until output stopped and started again.

Reloading a string config tears the channel outputs down and builds them
again, which re-registers every port with OutputMonitor.  AddOutputPin()
drove each enable pin to the disabled state as it went, because the only
thing that ever turned them on was the AutoEnableOutputs() the channel
output thread makes when it starts -- and that had already happened.
Whether the ports came back was purely a matter of whether the upload
landed before or after output started.

OutputMonitor now tracks whether outputs are meant to be on and brings a
port up in the state it is already in.  The receivers[0].isOn bookkeeping
goes with it: that flag is what decides whether an eFuse trip is reported,
so leaving it false would have swallowed a real trip on a reloaded port.

The same teardown/rebuild skipped StartingOutput() on the outputs it
created, even though it hands StoppingOutput() to the ones it removes, so
a reloaded output ran in the stopped state for the rest of its life -- a
shift panel driver leaves its PRUs parked and the panels dark, PCA9685
never comes out of sleep.  The point where an output is published to the
list now makes that call, under the same lock the output thread uses for
its own StartingOutput(), so the two cannot race.

Also drop a port from the eFuse retry list when it is unregistered:
reset() clears the pin pointers processRetries() dereferences, which is a
null deref once eFuseRetryCount is non-zero.

Verified on a 16-port cape: ports stay enabled across a reload that lands
mid-output, and still follow output start/stop otherwise.

fix(network): run one wpa_supplicant, not two

The wpasupplicant package enables both the generic wpa_supplicant.service and
the per-interface wpa_supplicant@<iface>.service, so every board boots two
supplicant daemons. FPP only ever drives the per-interface one, so the generic
instance is a second daemon doing nothing on a board with 480MB and one core.

Disabled WITHOUT --now deliberately: the generic unit declares
RuntimeDirectory=wpa_supplicant, so stopping it makes systemd delete
/run/wpa_supplicant -- including the control socket the RUNNING per-interface
instance created there, which would break wpa_cli and the network status page
until the next reboot. Taking effect at the next boot avoids that entirely.

Two callers only ever needed "associated, and to what", which nl80211 answers
directly, so they move to iw: station_connected_ssid() in wifi_scan.sh and the
managed-mode branch of network_interface_in_use(). That drops their dependency
on a wpa_supplicant control socket altogether.

network_wifi_status() keeps using wpa_cli on purpose. That endpoint exists to
report WHY a connection is failing, and it branches on the intermediate states
(4WAY_HANDSHAKE, INACTIVE, ...) that have no nl80211 equivalent -- iw can only
say associated or not, so converting it would have quietly downgraded "wrong
password" and "connecting..." into a bare "not connected". It gains iw/ip
fallbacks instead, so the page degrades to basic connected/SSID/IP rather than
going blank if the socket is ever unreachable.

Verified on a wifi-only board with the generic unit disabled across a reboot:
the per-interface config declares its own ctrl_interface, so that instance
creates /run/wpa_supplicant itself and wpa_cli keeps working -- wpa_state, ssid
and ip_address all still reported, wifi scan output byte-identical to the
pre-change baseline, and the status API unchanged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat(BBShiftPanel): add DP3364S PWM panel support

The DP3364S is a 16 channel self-PWM constant current driver with an
internal GCLK PLL, addressed the same way as the chips already
supported here: 16 bit words on SDI/CLK with the instruction selected
by the LE pulse width.  The data phase needed no changes at all - the
existing 16 latched bursts per row are already the chip's documented
data instruction sequence (16 words per chip, channel 15 down to 0).

What is new:

- OUTPUT_REGISTERS_DP3364 in the PWM firmware: VSYNC (LE 3), PRE_ACT
  (LE 14), then WR_CFG - one {addr, data} word through the chain with
  LE over its last 5 clocks.  Simpler than the FM6373 upload, which
  needs write-enable and commit words where this chip uses PRE_ACT.

- DP3364_SCAN in the GCLK firmware.  The chip makes its own grayscale
  clock, so this side only advances the row and strobes ROW (which
  replaces OE) once per row, W12 at the top of a group and W4 for the
  rest.  Unlike the FM6373 path the row transport honors the
  addressing dropdown, because a panel above 32 scan rows cannot be
  addressed by the 5 SEL lines at all and needs the token shifter.

- The 15 config registers, rotated one per frame, which is how the
  datasheet says to refresh them.  Register 0x02 is patched with the
  scan count and 0x08 - the documented linear current multiplier -
  becomes the brightness control, scaling down from the captured
  value so the per-color trim does not move with brightness.

Row period and ROW pulse width come from the datasheet's line time
formula rather than being hardcoded, so they track the registers.

The register values were captured from a working 1/64 scan panel by a
third party; the vendor datasheet specifies the access protocol but
not the register map.  Untested on hardware - no panel available.  The
three values to check first on a scope are the W4/W12 widths (emitted
as times, since ROW and DCLK come from different PRUs with no phase
relationship), the row period, and the output current.

feat(BBShiftPanel): add ICND1065L, SM16380SH and ICND2153 PWM panels

All three reuse register grammars this driver already implements, so the
additions are register tables plus a small amount of parameterization.

ICND1065L and SM16380SH take the FM6373 upload: bare LAT bursts, then N
16-bit slots each latched over their last 5 clocks, with slot 3 rotating
through the config sequence one word per frame.  That path is now driven
from a per-chip descriptor rather than hardcoding the FM6373, because the
two differ from it in two ways - SM16380SH skips the middle 11 clock LAT
burst and carries a sixth slot (0xF003) ahead of the commit pair.  The
slot count and burst length are passed to the firmware in the chip config
word, and the register buffer grew to six slots with a static_assert that
it still clears the config offset.

ICND2153 takes the FM6353 {4,6,8,10,2} grammar with its own payload, and
unlike the FM6353 it does carry per-color current words.  It is a
separate panel type rather than being folded into FM6353: the two share
the grammar but not the values, so existing configs keep what they have.

fix(BBShiftPanel): keep the PWM firmware inside the PRU's 12KB IMEM

The 16 output PWM firmware had grown to 0x320c bytes of .text against a
12KB instruction memory, so the kernel refused to load it:

    remoteproc1: bad phdr da 0x0 mem 0x320c
    remoteproc1: Failed to load program segments: -22
    BBShiftPanel: Unable to start PRU(s). May require a reboot.

Nothing caught it at build time because AM62x_PRU0.cmd and
AM62x_PRU1.cmd declared PRU_IMEM as 0x4000 when the hardware has
0x3000, so clpru linked a firmware that could never be loaded and the
failure only appeared when fppd started.  Both files now declare the
real size, which turns this into a link error.

The overflow itself is removed by dropping OUTPUT_REGISTERS_DP3364: it
was the FM6373 upload with a single register slot and no middle LAT
burst, which the firmware can already express, so the DP3364S now
selects that path through the chip config word instead of carrying a
duplicate copy of it.  In the 16 output build every LAT burst expands
inline, so the duplicate was expensive - .text drops from 0x320c to
0x2b50, leaving 1200 bytes spare.

Verified on a PocketBeagle2 with a real FM6363C panel: all sixteen
AM62x PRU firmwares link under the corrected limit, both PRUs boot, and
the panel's geometry dump is unchanged from before this series (rows
10, length 160, 16 slots, addressing mode 51).  Restoring the oversize
firmware now fails the link with "program will not fit into available
memory", so the guard is known to bite.

feat(www): version-gate vendor panel settings so new options can't break FPP 9

The vendor panel data is fetched live from fpp-data master by every FPP
install, so anything added there reaches FPP 9 players immediately.
Unknown *keys* are safe - both versions walk the settings object through
an if/else chain with no final else - but unknown *values* are not.

and .val() then returns null. For panelType that saves parseInt(null),
i.e. null, into the config. For the panel size it is worse: the null
lands in ledPanelsSize, which is then split("x") unconditionally in
three places, so a size an older UI has no option for throws rather than
degrading. The panel types and full height sizes added for the PWM
chips are exactly that kind of value.

gathered from the bare subType plus every "-vN" tier up to this player's
major version, applied in ascending order so a later tier refines an
earlier one. Describing a panel that needs FPP 10 options is therefore a

whatever is left - possibly nothing - without breaking.

`settings["all"] !== undefined || details`. details is always a truthy

fix(media): keep pipewiresink's clock for audio-only, so the file starts at 0

Playing an audio file lost the first 240-280 ms of it -- the clip was audible
but started partway in, from the status page and from a playlist alike.

Start() forces the pipeline clock to GstSystemClock for every pipeline.  That
was added for video: the PipeWire clock reads 0 until the graph processes its
first quantum, and kmssink's sync=TRUE then blocks forever because every frame
PTS looks like the future.  For an audio-only pipeline the same override is all
cost and no benefit -- there is no kmssink to wedge, and a wall clock that is
already running is exactly what truncates the head.  base_time is latched when
the pipeline reaches PLAYING, but pipewiresink prerolls before its PipeWire
stream is actually streaming, so everything rendered in that gap is already late
and never reaches the graph.  pipewiresink's own clock does not advance until
the stream runs, so with it no buffer is ever late.

Measured on a BeagleBone with an I2S cape by capturing the ALSA sink monitor
while playing a 10 s linear chirp, which makes the recording self-timestamping
-- the frequency of the first audible audio says which source timestamp it came
from.  Isolating the two things Start() does that a bare gst-launch of the same
pipeline does not:

  sink's own clock, plain volume       39 ms lost
  sink's own clock, 0 + 50 ms ramp     37 ms
  forced system clock, plain volume   759 ms
  forced system clock, 0 + ramp       587 ms

so the startup volume ramp contributes nothing and the clock is the whole
effect.  A native pw-play of the same file loses 0 ms, ruling out PipeWire, the
filter chain and the card.  Through the real Play Media path the fix takes
238/277 ms of loss down to 15/23/22 ms over three runs -- one PipeWire quantum,
the floor.

Video and HDMI pipelines keep the override, so an A/V file's audio still starts
late; fixing that needs the kmssink wedge re-tested against current GStreamer
and PipeWire rather than worked around from the clock.

Fixes #2817

fix(www): send the test-stop with keepalive so unload can't drop it

The Current Monitor and PWM pages start a test on the player and rely on

feat(crash): record installed plugin versions in the crash report

fpp-info.json carries FPP's own build string with its git hash, which is
what lets the crash bucketer ancestry-check a fix commit against the
build a report came from -- crashes on pre-fix builds are stale binaries
and stay resolved. A fix that lands in a plugin repo gets no such gate:
nothing else in the bundle says which plugin build the device is running,
so a plugin bucket can only be aged out by date, and a device still on
the old plugin binary looks like a regression.

Plugins are git checkouts, so the information is already on the box. Add
a plugins.json next to fpp-info.json recording each installed plugin's
commit, describe output, branch and origin remote.

Included at every crash level, alongside fpp-info.json rather than behind
the settings/config levels: the crashing plugin's .so path already
appears in the stack at every level, and these are public repo commits,
so nothing here is more identifying than fpp-info.json already is.

Three failure modes are handled explicitly, each verified against a
fixture on real hardware:

  - Ownership. The plugin trees are owned by 'fpp' and this runs as root,
    so a bare git call fails with "detected dubious ownership" and prints
    NOTHING -- which downstream reads as "no plugins installed" rather
    than "the probe failed". With safe.directory the hashes resolve; the
    control, with that flag removed, now emits an explicit "error" per
    plugin instead of an empty string.
  - Dirty or pinned trees. pluginInfo.json pins a sha per FPP version, so
    a tree can sit on an older commit than its repo head, and a user can
    edit in place. describe output is recorded including any -dirty
    suffix, plus a separate boolean, so a modified tree is not silently
    reported as that commit.
  - Credentials. A remote cloned over https can carry user:password in
    the URL, so any userinfo is stripped before the remote is recorded.
    Verified with a token-bearing remote: neither the user nor the token
    appears in the output.

Also checked: valid JSON in every case including a box with no plugins
installed (where the glob does not expand), and a full end-to-end run of
the script producing a bundle whose plugins.json parses.

This is only the reporting half. The dashboard still date-checks plugin
resolves; it can move to true plugin ancestry once enough reports carry
this file.

fix(CapeUtils): stop the i2c1 EEPROM probe stranding the pins it borrows

The i2c1 fallback in findCapeEEPROM() borrows the i2c1 pads to look for the
cape EEPROM, and on the BeagleBone Black those pads are P9_17/P9_18 -- pins
capes routinely use as plain GPIO, including for OLED navigation buttons. It
handed them back with ConfigurePin(pin, "default"), which no longer restores
anything: the pinctrl tool has no "default" mode, and it printed "Unknown mode"
while still exiting 0, so ConfigurePin took that as success and skipped its
sysfs fallback. The pads stayed muxed to i2c1 for the rest of the boot, and any
GPIO event request already open on them stopped delivering edges -- buttons dead
until the owning process was restarted. Reported as FPP issue #2828.

Four changes, each closing one step of that chain:

- pinctrl exits non-zero on an unknown pin or mode (and on a missing argument),
  so no caller can mistake a rejected mode for an applied one. "default" is
  deliberately left unknown rather than aliased: there is no portable meaning
  for it. On the Pi a pin's default is a per-pin, per-model reset mode; here
  "reset" is bare mode-7 input with no pull, and BBBPinCapabilities maps
  "default" to a bias-less "gpio" -- handing a pulled-up button pin any of
  those makes it float instead of restoring it.

- ConfigureI2C1BusPins captures each pin's actual mode before borrowing it and
  writes that exact string back, mirroring what the i2c2 path already does. If
  the capture fails it says so and leaves the pin alone rather than guessing.

- PinCurrentMode reads the bracketed mode from "pinctrl -l" instead of the last
  token of "-q". "-q" prints every mode name matching the register value, so a
  pad muxed for i2c came back as the "i2c_scl" alias rather than "i2c" -- which
  also means the existing i2c2 save/restore was re-muxing on every call and
  would have restored the wrong alias.

- The probes that decide whether to fall back now retry briefly. The pads for a
  bus are re-muxed microseconds earlier and the lines still have to charge
  through their pull-ups, so a single missed probe was enough to send detection
  to i2c1 and take the button pins with it.

Also: CapeInfo is built lazily once per process, not once per boot, so fppd
re-runs this entire probe when a channel output first asks for its config --
long after the OLED process has muxed and claimed its pins, with no interlock
covering it at all. Only the first run has to search for the bus now; later ones
take it from the location the first one recorded and never go near i2c1.

fppoled logs whether its cape-detection wait completed or timed out. The wait is
the only thing ordering it after cape detection, and giving up silently is what
makes the resulting race look like unrelated flaky buttons.

Verified on a BBB with an am335xpm kernel: with the stock tool, setting a pin to
i2c and asking for "default" back leaves it on i2c and reports success; with
this, the pin returns to its exact prior mode. Cape detection finds the EEPROM
on i2c2 with no fallback and the pins untouched, and a later fppd start logs
that it reused the recorded bus instead of probing again.

fix(pinctrl): survive an unmappable /dev/mem, and add the missing P8_26

Two gaps found while working on the i2c1 pinmux restore.

mmap() failure was stored as-is. MAP_FAILED is (void*)-1, not nullptr, so it
sailed straight past readReg()'s null check and segfaulted on the first query
of any pin whenever /dev/mem could not be mapped -- and the fallback path only
runs on kernels without /dev/am335xpm, exactly where that is most likely.
Register access now no-ops instead, which is what the null check intended.

P8_26 was commented out along with P8_20-P8_25. Those six are the eMMC pins and
must stay out, but P8_26 is GPMC_CSN0 (gpio1_29) and is free to use; it was just
swept into the same block. Without it, anything asking FPP to configure P8_26 --
a plugin GPIO, a cape pin -- produced only "Unknown pin: P8_26" and no mux
change. Confirmed against the kernel's own pinctrl debug view: the ball's
0x87c offset is register 44e1087c, and the tool now reads back the same value
the kernel reports for it. The eMMC pins stay commented, with a note saying why
so they don't get "fixed" later.

fix(audio): stop trusting a PipeWire ALSA config the hardware rejects

95-fpp-alsa-sink.conf lives in /etc and survives every upgrade, and the
"adapters already match present cards" fast path re-validates only which cards
it names -- never how it described them. So an install keeps a conf that FPP's
own code would no longer generate, forever, and fixing a probe rule only ever
helps boxes flashed after the fix. A conf that picked S32LE for a fixed-bit-clock
I2S cape therefore outlives the fix for that very bug: PipeWire fails adapter
creation, aborts context creation and exits, systemd restarts it every few
seconds, and the box boots clean with no audio -- thousands of restarts on an
install that already has the fix. Reported as FPP issue #2811.

Four changes, all in the path that derives an ALSA adapter from a card:

- The generated conf carries a generation number, and a missing or older one is
  reason enough to re-probe. That puts every future change to the probe rules
  behind one chokepoint instead of adding another one-off validator beside the
  channel-count check, which is the same bug wearing a different face. Costs one
  extra probe on the first boot after an upgrade; the fast path is untouched
  once the tag matches.

- A board with a real sound card that finishes with no sink in the graph now
  discards its derived config and re-runs the setup once against freshly probed
  hardware. Every config check above it was satisfied -- the conf is internally
  consistent and names only present cards; it is simply one the hardware
  rejects, and only the graph can see that. Bounded to a single retry, and only
  a box that is already silent pays the timeout. Just the derived files go: the
  groups JSON is the user's own config and is what the regeneration reads.

- A busy device's format is taken from /proc rather than re-probed. PipeWire
  holds the selected output on every postNetwork run, so the probe hit the same
  EBUSY that forced the /proc fallback in the first place and, by its own
  bias-to-safe rule, rewrote a working S32 card as S16LE. On a board whose card
  set never matches the cached conf that fired on every single boot. /proc
  reports what the hardware is running right now, which is the thing the probe
  exists to establish.

- A wider format is judged against the rate the S16LE fallback actually
  achieves, not against the rate that was requested. A card can be unable to
  deliver the requested rate in any format: an AM62x PCM5102A cape clocks no
  lower than 88200, so a 44100 request is refined upward for S16_LE and S32_LE
  alike, and treating refinement as rejection threw away S32 for a card that
  pays nothing to provide it. An AM335x cape refines S32_LE from 44100 down to
  22050 while S16_LE holds 44100 exactly, and must still land on S16LE -- taking
  S32 there is what starts the crash loop above. Both are one rule once the
  comparison is against what the fallback achieves: widen only when it is free.

Verified on three clock architectures, with the failure reproduced first each
time. A fixed-bit-clock AM335x PCM5102A cape: S32 halves the rate, still picks
S16LE. An AM62x PCM5102A cape with an 88200 floor: every format refines, now
picks S32LE where it used to pick S16LE. A flexible pcm512x I2S DAC: nothing
refines, picks S32LE, and is no longer demoted to S16LE on the busy boot path.
A conf poisoned to fail the way the reported one did reproduces the exact
signature (mod.adapter "can't get format", "failed to create context",
status=234) and is recovered automatically instead of surviving reboots.
