fix(fseq): bound the compressed block search and the frame index

The v2 compressed readers locate a frame by walking m_frameOffsets forward
until the next block starts after it:

    while (frame >= m_file->m_frameOffsets[block + 1].first) { block++; }

Nothing bounds that walk.  It terminates only because the table ends with a
sentinel entry at getNumFrames() + 2, which is not a bound at all: the frame
number reaching prepareRead() comes from a MultiSync sync packet or a playlist
start position, so a remote whose copy of the sequence is shorter than the
master's walks straight off the end of the vector.  That is a crash inside
V2CompressedHandler::prepareRead(), reported from the field, and reproduced
here under ASan as a container-overflow read at exactly that line.

Once a block is chosen, the ZSTD handler computes fidx = frame - blockStart
and then guards it with "if (fidx < 0)" - a test that can never be true,
since fidx is uint32_t, as the comment above it half admits.  When the block
table says a block starts after the frame being asked for, fidx underflows to
~4 billion, m_framesPerBlock underflows with it, and the code asks malloc for
a ~4GB decompression buffer.  On 64 bit that quietly succeeds and the frame is
read out of the wrong place; on a 32 bit player the allocation fails, the
result is never checked, and zstd writes to a null buffer or memcpy reads
about 4GB past it - which is the degenerate "memcpy <- ???" stack this shows
up as, with no unwind information surviving the bad read.

So:

- findBlockForFrame() bounds the search by the size of the table rather than
  by the sentinel, and all three walks (prepareRead and both getFrame
  implementations) use it.
- The block table's start frames are held in order where the table is built,
  at load, since they are file data and every reader downstream computes
  frame - blockStart from them.  The writer's own finalize() has a standing
  comment about seeing files whose block table was never filled in.
- The dead "fidx < 0" check is replaced with the bounds check the bulk reader
  already does: the frame's byte range must fit the decompressed block.  The
  buffer's real capacity is now tracked, because m_outBuffer.size is zstd's
  per-frame output limit and moves with every frame, so it cannot answer
  whether the frame fits.  A failed allocation is checked.
- The ZLIB handler gets the same treatment, plus its own 32 bit
  "int outsize = numFrames * channelCount" overflow.

Well formed files are unaffected: re-encoding a real 5.6MB zstd sequence
through fsequtils gives byte identical output before and after, as does
hashing every frame of a generated file, in order and out of order, for both
zstd and zlib.  The two crashes above are reproduced as ASan failures before
the change and become a logged error and a blank frame after it, with the
load-time repair and the per-frame bounds check each verified to hold on
their own with the other disabled.

Note one deliberate behaviour change: the decompression buffer now only ever
grows.  It used to be freed and reallocated whenever a block needed more than
the base 8MB/32MB, which could also shrink it; blocks within a file are sized
uniformly, so this trades a little peak memory for not churning the allocator
per block.

feat(pixelstrings): per-port pixel protocols - TM18xx and 16 bit parts

The per-port protocol was saved by the UI but never read, and the
inverted-output support added for a backwards-wired differential line
was unreachable from any config.  Wire the two together and build out
what those protocols actually need.

Inverted protocols (TM18xx).  A port's protocol now selects the idle
level, composing by xor with the cape's "inverted" flag so a TM18xx
string on a reversed pair cancels out.  TM1814 also needs its C1/C2
constant current words ahead of the pixel data - without them the part
sits at its 6.5mA floor - so PixelString gains a protocol preamble
carried at the head of the output buffer and counted in the wire
length.

Falcon smart receivers are refused on an inverted chain head, and on
any chain carrying an inverted protocol; the config packet path cannot
survive either.  That leaves the one shipped use of a cape declared
inversion working, since it only ever lands on a non-head line.

T0 moves 220ns -> 320ns.  Every port on a PRU shares that latch, and
320 is inside both the TM18xx 310-410ns window and the far looser
ws281x one; 220 was under spec for TM18xx and WS2812B alike and only
worked because the silicon is forgiving.  The 16 deep firmware no
longer needs a separate value.

Shared brightness tables.  A table is a pure function of (brightness,
gamma), and many ports are commonly configured alike - a megatree goes
from one table per virtual string to one for the whole thing.
Inversion therefore swaps to a complemented table instead of flipping
in place, which would corrupt every other port sharing it.

16 bit parts (ucs8903/8904/7604).  Sequence data is always 8 bit per
channel, so the extra range comes from evaluating the same
brightness/gamma curve to 65535 rather than 255 - at gamma 2.2 the low
inputs otherwise all round to the same output.  Only the wire length
grows; the PRU is unchanged.  Refused alongside v1/v2 smart receivers,
whose fixed width markers would mean two widths in one stream.

Drivers that cannot honour a protocol now say so rather than emitting
something wrong: BBB48String undoes the inversion, drops the preamble
and un-widens, and warns.

m_outputChannels becomes m_outputBytes, which is what it has always
meant and now visibly differs from the channel count.  That surfaced
two bugs: the licensed-output clamps rebuilt the wire length from the
virtual strings and dropped the preamble, and BBB48String refused an
inverted protocol while keeping the preamble, offsetting every pixel
on the port.

The Protocol column is now shown whenever a cape offers a choice
rather than being hidden by platform, and the frame rate estimate
accounts for bit depth and preamble bytes.

fix(www): stop the port page reporting status and current it can't measure

Capes whose local outputs carry only an enable line - no eFuse, no current
sensor - rendered a port grid full of "undefined ma", "NaN ma" totals, and a
permanent green eFuse check.  The green check was the worst of the three: a
status that can never go red is worse than no status at all.

appendTo() emitted "status" unconditionally, defaulting to true whenever the
port had no fuse pin to read.  It now emits the key only when there is a fuse
pin, so the absence of a reading is reported as absence.  Ports with eFuses
are unaffected - their rendering is byte-identical before and after.

The page reads the fields the same way: each line is printed only when the
port reports it, totals skip ports with no current reading, and the totals

feat(pixelstrings): take the bit cell at runtime, and drive the slower parts

T0, T1 and the end of the bit cell were compiled into the firmware, so
the 400kHz and longer-cell parts could not be offered at all: driving
them with the ws281x cell does not shift an edge, it puts the pulse
outside the window the part decodes.  Supporting them by shipping a
firmware image per timing would have meant twelve of them, so the
firmware now reads the three waits from its data RAM instead.

This is a refactor of where the constant comes from, not a timing
change.  Measured with the PRU's own cycle counter, compile-time and
runtime land the zero-bit edge on exactly the same cycle: 91 on the
AM62x, 75 on the AM335x.  The overhead the ARM subtracts accounts for
LBCO being two cycles slower than the LDI it replaces, and the two
cancel.

The values live in the unused buffer words of the PRU data RAM struct,
which matters: LBCO's offset field is 8 bit, so anything it reads per
bit has to be in the low 256 bytes.  That is also why the clock/latch
config is read through a register - fine once per frame, too expensive
three times per bit.  The firmware waits for the ARM to publish before
its first frame, as it already does for the ring config, because
loading the firmware clears these memories.

Each protocol now carries its own exact cell rather than being sorted
into invented classes, and the controller takes its timing from the
ports in use.  Those instants are shared by every port on the PRU, so
there is no such thing as a per-port bit cell - which is why the UI
picks the timing once and then filters what each port may be set to,
rather than letting an unworkable combination be selected and
complaining afterwards.  The protocols are partitioned across the
groups, so a mix cannot be expressed.

A config that arrives already mixed - from a controller upload, which
has no way to know about this constraint - is not silently accepted:
the driver names the offending ports in a warning that reaches the web
UI, and says in the log that they will not work.  There is no safe
common value to fall back to.

Also:
- the frame rate estimate scales with the bit period, or a 400kHz
  group would be reported at over twice the rate it can reach
- numeric table inputs honour their size attribute, which browsers
  ignore for type=number, so a column holding a 0-9 null count no
  longer renders as wide as one holding a channel number
- start channel is sized for eight digits, ahead of the channel
  count growing past 8388608

fix(upgrade): keep the device identity across an OS upgrade on Beagle images

The Beagle rootfs carries /etc/bbb.io/ssh_regenerate, a first-boot marker that
makes bbbio-set-sysconf run bb-regenerate-ssh-host-keys: rm /etc/ssh/ssh_host_*
followed by ssh-keygen -A. The root rsync copies that marker out of the image
and onto the live system, so it fired on the first boot AFTER part2 had already
restored the saved host keys - the restore was undone about a minute later and
every client got "REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED".

The same service applies user_name=/user_password= from the boot partition's
sysconf.txt, which the image ships for first-boot user creation, so an upgrade
also reset the fpp user's password back to the image default. Acting on either
one costs an extra "Rebooting after setting up sysconf.txt options" reboot.

An in-place upgrade is not a fresh flash, so clear both markers on the target
after the restores. Also fix the neighboring guard that was meant to disable
first-boot key regeneration: it required ssh_host_dsa_key, which Debian has not
shipped in years, so it never fired. It now gates on the key types OpenSSH
actually has, only removes the legacy unit when it exists, and warns in the
upgrade log if the host keys were not restored.

feat(overlays): bulk pixel data REST endpoints

Writing pixels to an overlay model over HTTP meant one request per pixel
via PUT .../pixel. The only bulk path was the shared memory buffer, which
needs shm_open/mmap and only works from a process on the player itself.

Add:

  PUT /api/overlays/model/{model}/data      write a frame, or a rect of one
  GET /api/overlays/model/{model}/data/raw  read it back as raw bytes

The PUT body may be raw pixel bytes, an encoded image (PNG/JPEG/GIF/BMP/
TIFF/WebP, decoded with GraphicsMagick), or JSON carrying base64 -- so a
shell script can post a PNG with curl --data-binary and no image has to
exist on the player first. Query args cover placement (x/y/w/h), pixel
format (rgb/rgbw/mono), blend, image scaling, whether to target the
channel data or the shared overlay buffer, auto-enable and effect
eviction. See docs/PixelOverlayBulkData.md.

Measured on a 4-core ARM board through the normal Apache path, against a
128x96 model: a full frame is one request at 1380 frames/s, against 12288
per-pixel requests at 0.165 frames/s. The binary read-back runs 1694 req/s
at 34% CPU where the JSON array form manages 32 req/s at 98%, since JSON
spends 4-6 wire bytes per payload byte.

Details worth knowing:

- The blend argument is ?blend=, not ?state=. PUT .../state sets the
  enable state of the model, which is a different thing; one name for
  both would be a trap.
- A region hanging off an edge is clipped to what is visible rather than
  rejected. Only a fully-outside region is an error. That is what lets a
  caller move an image around by reposting it at changing offsets.
- Body kind is decided by length first and magic bytes second. Raw pixel
  data can begin with any byte sequence -- FF D8 FF is an ordinary
  reddish pixel, not necessarily a JPEG -- so image sniffing is consulted
  only once a body has already failed to match the raw geometry.
- On the image path w/h are the scaling box and, unlike the raw path,
  have no body length to check them against. They are clamped to the
  model: a larger box cannot draw more, since the excess is clipped, but
  GraphicsMagick would allocate for it first. Unclamped, a 4x4 PNG with
  a 9999x9999 box took peak RSS from 51MB to 1579MB, which on a 512MB
  board is an out-of-memory kill from one small request.
- The handler releases the models lock before decoding or blitting. The
  Text branch already did this; holding that lock across a GraphicsMagick
  decode, on an endpoint meant to be called at frame rates, widens a
  pre-existing window where the channel output thread is blocked on it.

Two adjacent fixes needed to make the above work:

- render_PUT() looked models up with a raw map find while render_GET()
  used getModelLocked(), so every PUT verb 404'd on a lazily materialized
  xLights submodel that GET could resolve. Both now use getModelLocked().
- GET .../data/raw on an unknown model would have inherited the behaviour
  of the legacy paths: 200 plus the four-byte body null. A binary
  endpoint must not hand back a JSON literal a caller will read as
  pixels, so that one path returns 404. The legacy JSON paths are
  unchanged.

fix(overlays): deadlock between the output thread and the HTTP API

A Sub overlay model could wedge every overlay HTTP route permanently.

Two lock orders existed on the same pair:

  HTTP handlers   modelsLock, then activeModelsLock
                  render_PUT/render_GET take modelsLock for the model
                  lookup; any state change then reaches
                  modelStateChanged(), which takes activeModelsLock.

  Output thread   activeModelsLock, then modelsLock
                  doOverlays() holds activeModelsLock across the whole
                  pass, and PixelOverlayModelSub::doOverlay() called
                  foundParent() -> getModel() -> modelsLock.

When both land in the window the two threads block on each other. The
symptom is unpleasant to diagnose: fppd keeps running, the main loop and
MultiSync stay healthy and /api/fppd/status still answers 200, but every
/api/overlays and /api/models request hangs forever and overlays stop
updating, so a health check sees nothing wrong.

foundParent() caches, so normally the output thread takes modelsLock
exactly once per Sub model -- a narrow race, which is presumably why this
was never reported. It stops being a race entirely if the parent cannot
be resolved: nothing gets cached, so getModel() runs on every frame and
the window is permanently open. A submodel left pointing at a renamed or
deleted parent is exactly that shape, and with a few concurrent state
changes it wedges in about twelve seconds, repeatably.

Fix by removing the edge rather than reordering around it. Resolve the
parent in setState(), before the base class publishes the model into the
manager's active list and therefore before the output thread can reach
it. setState() already runs under modelsLock on every path that gets
there, so this is a recursive re-acquire, not a new one. doOverlay() then
uses the cached pointer and never resolves.

The alternative -- taking modelsLock before activeModelsLock in
doOverlays() -- would have put modelsLock on the per-frame output path,
where any slow HTTP handler (the Image effect decodes with GraphicsMagick
under that lock) would stall output directly. Trading a rare deadlock for
routine jitter is a poor deal on a show controller.

Grid submodels are untouched: they scatter straight to the parent output
channels, never dereference the parent pointer, and so need no resolution.

An unresolvable parent is now inert instead of fatal, and is reported once
per state change rather than once per output frame (~40/s).

Verified on a 4-core ARM board: the orphan-parent repro wedges the API in
12s before this change, with gdb showing one thread in modelStateChanged
holding modelsLock and the channel output thread in getModel holding
activeModelsLock; after it, three consecutive 30s rounds survive. A
separate functional test confirms submodel data still composites into the
parent at its offset -- deliberately broken first to confirm it fails when
resolution is wrong, since a silently inert submodel would make the
deadlock repro pass for the wrong reason.

feat(flash): one flash implementation for Pi, BeagleBone and BeagleBone 64

Replaces the vendored rpi-clone on the Pi path and BBB-FlashMMC.sh on the
Beagle path with a shared SD/flash_storage.sh. Every platform runs the same
phases -- preflight, partition, format, mount, copy, fixup, verify -- and the
platforms differ as lookup tables (partition layout, labels, which file carries
root=), not as logic. Both auto-flash scripts use it too.

The bug this fixes: rpi-clone decided what to copy from the live mount table,
so an unmounted /boot/firmware silently dropped the boot partition from the
copy and the flash still printed "complete". The initialize-vs-sync test was
gated on the same flag, so a blank target got a raw dd that worked by accident
while re-flashing an already-flashed target left its old boot partition in
place. flash_storage.sh names the boot filesystem instead of inferring it,
refuses to start if it is not mounted, and verifies the destination carries
what that platform needs to boot before reporting success.

Failure is the default outcome and only reaching verify changes it. Three shell
behaviours made that harder than it sounds:

  - set -e does not propagate a failed arithmetic expansion out of the function
    it happened in; bash unwinds every frame, including a checker function, and
    resumes at the next top-level command with the function reporting success.
    Each phase records its own name as its last action and a top-level phase_ok
    verifies it.
  - scripts/common uses `[ -f x ] && y` at top level, so it must be sourced
    before set -e.
  - udevadm settle returns success while partition device nodes are still
    missing, so partitioning polls for the nodes it just created.

A failed flash no longer powers a board down, so it cannot be mistaken for a
finished one: previously the rsync ended in `|| true`, so running out of space
was swallowed and the board still wrote fstab and powered off. It also blinks
every user LED, and sweeps them while working. Those are globbed rather than
indexed because BeagleBone Black exposes usr0-usr3 and PocketBeagle2 exposes
usr1-usr4 -- the old cylon_leds() tested for usr0 first, so it silently did
nothing at all on a PocketBeagle2, and it only ran when powering down, which
the auto-flash path never does.

Platform detection matches both "BeagleBone Black" and "BeagleBone 64", the two
values /etc/fpp/platform actually holds; matching only the first refused to run
on a PocketBeagle2 at all.

On the Pi, program_usb_boot_mode is a Pi 4 / CM4 OTP fuse and is no longer
written on a Pi 5 where it does nothing, and a USB target gets
usb_max_current_enabled=1 -- a Pi 5 caps total USB current at 600mA unless it
detects a 5A supply, which is not enough to boot from many drives.

The BeagleBone btrfs layout is a single partition. u-boot 2022.04 reads btrfs,
so the 96MB ext4 /boot it used to carry earned nothing on a 3.7GB eMMC. But
u-boot cannot *decompress* btrfs: it traverses the filesystem and returns
correct file lengths, then hands back corrupt content with
"ZSTD_decompressStream error 7", which is not a missing feature -- the zstd and
btrfs symbols are all linked in. So everything u-boot reads is marked
NOCOMPRESS before the copy and the flag is inherited by the files rsync
creates: /boot and also /lib/firmware, which uEnv.txt points at for the cape
overlays and which is not under /boot. That path is resolved with readlink -f
against the source, because /lib is a symlink to usr/lib on a usrmerge system
and pre-creating "lib/firmware" is silently replaced when rsync reproduces the
symlink. The mount consequently uses plain `compress`, since compress-force
overrides NOCOMPRESS.

uEnv.txt gets "mmcrootfstype=btrfs rootwait fixrtc", not a bare "btrfs":
u-boot's mmcrootfstype carries the root flags with the filesystem name, so
overriding it with just the name drops rootwait and the kernel panics ~30ms
before the eMMC enumerates. Preflight refuses --btrfs outright on a kernel that
cannot mount it, since these images ship no initramfs by design and a btrfs
built as a module is never available at mount-root time.

Flash-time compression is zstd:1 rather than the default 3. Measured on an
AM335x over ~814MB of real binaries: level 1 = 134s/358MB, level 3 =
273s/347MB, level -3 = 123s/431MB. Half the time for 3% more space, on a single
core that is entirely the bottleneck.

Media directories are marked NOCOMPRESS: nearly everything a player writes
after the flash is already-compressed mp3, fseq and video, and the installed
fstab uses plain `compress`, which honours the flag -- measured 190MiB landing
as 190.74MiB with it versus 6.08MiB without.

Verified booting on hardware: Pi to USB, BeagleBone Black to eMMC as both ext4
and single-partition btrfs, PocketBeagle2 to eMMC, and the full init= factory
auto-flash path. The three-partition eMMC layout is not exercised by any
hardware to hand.

fix(mdns): stop the Avahi warning sticking, and firing on a clean shutdown

The "Abnormal Conditions" banner appeared on every reboot and shutdown, and
once raised it never went away.

Two separate causes:

fppd is an Avahi client but nothing ordered it against avahi-daemon, so systemd
was free to stop avahi first. fppd is still running at that point, sees the
client drop, and reports it -- during an ordinary clean shutdown. Ordering fppd
after avahi-daemon makes systemd stop it first, since units are stopped in the
reverse of the start order. Wants rather than Requires: no mDNS is a degraded
FPP, not a broken one. The client-failure warning is additionally suppressed
once runMainFPPDLoop is clear, for the case where fppd is already on its way
down.

Nothing ever removed the warning. WarningHolder matches on the id and the exact
message text, and there was no matching RemoveWarning anywhere, so a single
transient -- avahi restarting, or simply not being up yet when fppd started --
left the banner on screen for the rest of the session. Observed on a running
player: the warning was present with avahi-daemon healthy, and stopping and
restarting avahi changed nothing either way.

The client callback now clears each warning on the path that proves it is no
longer true: the client-failure one when the client reaches S_RUNNING, and each
browse warning when that browser is created successfully. The three message
strings are named constants, because add and remove having to match by text is
exactly how one of these becomes permanent again.

fix(upgrade): let the boot-partition sync actually delete, and keep user files

The boot filesystem rsync passed -x. rsync's --one-file-system also stops
its deletion recursion on the RECEIVING side, so on any board where the
boot files sit on their own filesystem the --delete was a silent no-op:
files were still copied in, but nothing was ever removed. Stale boot files
have therefore accumulated across every OS upgrade.

That is how a Pi 5 ended up unusable. The firmware picks its kernel by
filename and prefers kernel_2712.img over kernel8.img. The images ship only
the 4K-page kernel8.img and strip every other module tree, so a
kernel_2712.img left behind by raspi-firmware's postinst hook (from images
predating KERNEL=none in /etc/default/raspi-firmware) made the box boot a
stock 16K-page kernel with no /lib/modules at all. The symptoms landed
nowhere near the cause: no ipv6 module, so apache aborted on
"Listen [::]:80" and took the whole web UI down, and no zram module, so
dev-zram0.device timed out and added 90s to boot -- 20s became 3m03s.

Dropping -x is safe on the send side: /boot inside the mounted image has no
submounts. But it is not safe on its own, because two things on the boot
partition belong to the user and are not in the image -- fppinit's
handleBootPartition() runs <bootDir>/fpp_boot.sh on every boot and copies
<bootDir>/fpp/ into the media directory. BOOT_KEEP excludes both, which
rsync also honours as a receiver-side protect rule since we do not pass
--delete-excluded. Both bootDir spellings are listed because fppinit picks
/boot/firmware whenever that directory merely exists.

The Beagle branch gets the same treatment. Three layouts are now in the
field -- no /boot/firmware, an empty stub directory, or a real small FAT
mount -- so it assumes none of them. There the kernel stays in /boot on the
rootfs even when the FAT exists, so --delete-during is kept; deleting on
that FAT is safe because build-image-bbb.sh keeps it mounted through
mksquashfs and its contents are inside the image. On the layouts without a
separate partition -x suppressed nothing, so that branch had already been
deleting the user's fpp_boot.sh and fpp/ on every upgrade.

Verified on hardware against a real vfat target for both branches: the
stale kernel and obsolete files are removed, the user's files survive, and
a control run without the excludes destroys them.

fix(apache): pick the port 80 listener at start time so no-IPv6 boxes still serve

ports.conf was written with an unconditional "Listen [::]:80". That is the
right listener when the kernel has IPv6 -- with net.ipv6.bindv6only=0 one
socket serves both families -- and a hard failure when it does not:

  AH00078: alloc_listener: failed to get a socket for ::
  AH00526: Syntax error on line 5 of /etc/apache2/ports.conf
  Listen setup failed

apache then refuses to start at all, so the entire web UI is gone and the
player is reachable only over ssh. Any box booted with ipv6.disable=1 lands
here, as does any box whose kernel is missing the ipv6 module.

Decide at start time instead. apachectl sources envvars on every
start/restart/configtest, so the probe re-runs on each start and a box that
gains or loses IPv6 later corrects itself with no reinstall.

upgrade/130 applies the same change to existing installs, and deliberately
restarts apache rather than calling gracefullyReloadApacheConf. A graceful
reload cannot carry this change and actively breaks the server: the define
comes from the master process's command line, which apachectl builds from
envvars at start, so a master started before the upgrade re-reads the new
ports.conf without FPP_HAVE_IPV6, takes the "Listen 80" branch, and cannot
change listening sockets on a graceful restart. Reproduced on hardware --
it leaves apache failed with nothing on port 80 until the next reboot.

Verified on a Pi 5 booted with ipv6.disable=1: apache starts and serves on
0.0.0.0:80, while the old unconditional config on the same box fails to
start. With IPv6 present it binds the dual-stack wildcard as before.

fix(image): refuse the stock 16K-page 2712 kernel packages on Pi

KERNEL=none stops raspi-firmware from copying a stock kernel into
/boot/firmware, but nothing stopped apt from installing one in the first
place. A Pi 5 boots by filename and prefers kernel_2712.img over
kernel8.img, so a single apt run that pulls a newer
linux-image-*-rpi-2712 puts a 16K-page stock kernel back on the boot
partition -- and the images strip that kernel's module tree, so the box
then boots with no modules at all (dead apache, 90s zram timeout at boot).

Pin those packages to priority -1. Nothing depends on them: the metapackage
has no reverse-depends beyond itself, so refusing them outright is safe.
Verified with a control -- without the pin apt installs the package, with
it the candidate becomes (none).

upgrade/131 brings existing installs up to the same state: it writes the
pin, sets KERNEL=none on images that predate it, and removes a
kernel_2712.img already sitting on the boot partition (only ever with
kernel8.img present to fall back to), flagging a reboot when the running
kernel is the one with no modules. It is gated on the absence of a stock
2712 module tree, so a manual FPP_Install.sh on top of stock Raspberry Pi
OS -- where that kernel and its modules are legitimate -- is left alone.
Both branches of that gate were exercised on hardware.

fix(image): drop the gpu_mem settings from config.txt

Nothing in FPP has drawn on the firmware GPU memory split for years. The
comment justifying these still referenced omxplayer, which is long gone --
that comment was the last mention of it in the tree. Video now goes through
GStreamer, and the display, DPI and virtual-matrix buffers all come from the
vc4-KMS CMA pool, which the installer already sizes to 256MB on the overlay
line just above. There is no MMAL/OpenMAX path left to feed.

What the settings were actually doing:

  pi5   256  no effect at all -- the firmware does not implement a GPU
             memory split on this SoC, and vcgencmd reports the key as
             unknown on a running board
  pi4   256  ~180MB carved out of usable RAM, 3.4x the documented maximum
             of 76 for this model, where the 3D block has its own MMU and
             allocates from Linux instead
  pi3   128  ~52MB above the 76 default
  pi02  128  64MB above the default, on a board with only 512MB total
  pi2    64  actually BELOW the 76 default for a 1GB board
  pi1    64  equals the default -- no-op
  pi0    64  equals the default -- no-op

So the entries were a mix of no-ops and waste, with the worst on the two
most memory-constrained cases. Removing them restores the firmware defaults
(64 below 1GB, 76 at 1GB and up) rather than substituting fresh guesses. The
model blocks that held nothing else go with them; the ones that carried real
settings keep them.

Verified on a Pi 5: with the entries gone the board boots clean, CMA is
unchanged at 256MB, and the web UI and daemon come up normally.

fix(commands): refuse a command invoked without its required first argument

A Command that declares arguments reads args[0] to get its subject - the
playlist name, the media file, the volume. Most check that it is there
first; eight index it bare, and operator[](0) on an empty vector hands
run() a reference to nothing. Four crash buckets are that read: "Play
Media" faulting inside GStreamerOutput's constructor, "Insert Playlist
Immediate" inside Playlist::Play (twice, via GET and via POST), and
"Start Playlist At Random Item" surfacing later as a free() fault.

Two ways to reach zero arguments: a bare GET /api/command/<name>, or a
POST whose body is not JSON - LoadJsonFromString() logged the parse
failure, returned an empty value, and the command ran anyway.

Enforce the contract once, in a new invokeCommand() that every dispatch
site now goes through, rather than in each run(): that covers GET, POST,
MQTT, presets, GPIO bindings, playlist entries and MultiSync at once,
and covers plugin commands, which cannot be audited here. A command that
genuinely works with no arguments says so by declaring its first
argument optional - "Stop Gracefully" is the one that did not, and its
declaration is corrected to match what run() has always done. POST also
now answers 400 for an unparseable body instead of running the command
with nothing.

Two commands need their own guard because no dispatcher can see their
shortfall:

- "Test Start" declares two arguments but reads up to five; the rest
  come from its "subcommand" argument, whose shape is published per test
  pattern by the testing endpoint. An under-supplied call indexed args[3]
  off the end. Its interval is parsed with atoi() now too, since an empty
  value is reachable from the API and std::stoi() throws where nothing
  catches it.
- "Check Pixel Count" indexed a captured argument vector inside a timer
  a second after the call returned; it resolves all three against their
  declared defaults up front instead.

Verified against the built library with a harness driving the real
dispatch path. Both controls go red: with the dispatch check stubbed
out the zero-argument call is a SIGSEGV, and with the "Test Start" guard
stubbed out and that translation unit rebuilt under libc++ hardening,
the reported two-argument call trips "vector[] index out of bounds".
With the guards in and the bounds detector still active, every valid
call - including the four-argument "Test Start" that "Check Pixel Count"
itself issues - still runs clean.

fix(settings): stop reporting success when a settings write fails

WriteSettingToFile() opened the settings file with @fopen($f, "c+") and never
checked the result.  When the web user cannot write the file, the open returns
false and PHP 8 throws "TypeError: flock(): Argument #1 must be of type
resource, false given" -- but the API response is still HTTP 200, so the
browser's success handler runs and jGrowl reports "setting saved" for a value
that was never written.  The setting then reverts on the next page load, with
nothing in the UI to say why.

The way in is a stray root write.  Apache/PHP run as fpp, and FPP's own writers
put ownership back (PutFileContents -> SetFilePerms chowns to fpp; sed -i
preserves the owner), but anything running as root that replaces the file with
a fresh inode leaves it root:root.  Boot re-runs "chown -R fpp:fpp" over the
media directory, so the broken state lasts only until the next reboot -- which
is exactly long enough to look like a bug in whichever setting was being saved.

- WriteSettingToFile() returns bool, checks both the open and the write, and
  logs which setting was lost.
- On an unwritable file it re-asserts fpp ownership via sudo and retries once.
  Boot already asserts that same ownership, so the correct owner is not a
  guess, and one stray root write no longer disables saving for the rest of the
  uptime.
- PutSetting() returns 500 with a JSON error instead of {"status":"OK"}, and
  skips the apply/restart path so the running system cannot diverge from disk.

Existing callers ignore the new return value and are unaffected.

fix(audio): run the PipeWire graph at the cards' configured sample rate

90-fpp.conf pins default.clock.rate to 48000, but the ALSA sink adapters are
created with audio.rate set from the AudioFormat setting -- 44100 by default.
Whenever those differ the sink adapter resamples on every graph cycle, and it
does so for as long as the graph runs, not just while media is playing.  The
graph never reaches idle (the filter-chain playback link is not passive), so an
FPP box that is playing nothing has been paying for a permanent 48000 -> 44100
conversion.

Emit default.clock.rate into the generated 95-fpp-alsa-sink.conf, set to the
same pipewireSampleRate the adapters already use.  That file sorts after
90-fpp.conf, so it wins; allowed-rates stays in 90-fpp.conf, which already
lists every rate the AudioFormat switch can select.

Measured on a single-core AM335x board, sink work per graph cycle and the
pipewire process share of the core:

  44100-only I2S cape   478us -> 171us   idle 4.7% -> 2.5%, playing 5.6% -> 3.6%
  USB audio card        538us -> 107us   idle 4.7% -> 2.6%

Also make a sample-rate change invalidate the cached conf.  The skip-probe path
compared only the set of cards present, so changing AudioFormat kept the old
conf -- which pins both the graph rate and every adapter's audio.rate to the
previous value.  Bump the generation tag so existing installs re-probe once.

Not covered: capes whose clock refines the requested rate upward (an AM62x
PCM5102A cape asks for 44100 and lands on 88200).  FPP writes the requested
rate, not the negotiated one, so those still resample; forcing the negotiated
rate by hand there measured 779us -> 160us, so it is worth a follow-up.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat(audio): let the PipeWire graph suspend the sound card when idle

The audio group chain is combine-stream -> filter-chain -> ALSA sink.  None of
those links were passive, so the sink never reached idle and PipeWire clocked
the card and recomputed the whole chain every quantum forever -- on a player
sitting idle with nothing queued.  Measured at 4-5% of a core on single-core
boards, and it is the reason the graph clock can never be renegotiated either.

Mark the filter-chain playback link and the combine-stream output streams
passive so only a real stream starts the graph.  With this the ALSA PCM goes to
'closed' when nothing is playing and the pipewire process drops to 0% of the
core, coming back automatically on the next playback.

Verified on a single-core AM335x board with an I2S cape.  Audio content was
checked against a silence control (idle capture reads bit-exact zero, so the
check can fail): a 6.000s source plays back as 5.95-5.97s of audible signal
both with and without this change, and the delay from the play command to first
audio does not measurably grow.  Nothing is lost coming out of suspend.

Exposed as PipeWirePassiveSinks, an Advanced-level checkbox on the Audio
settings page, defaulting to on, so it can be turned off if a card does not
resume cleanly.  Both generators honour it -- the Simple-mode C++ path and
GeneratePipeWireGroupsConfig() in pipewire.php -- and the boot-time cache check
now compares the conf's passive state against the setting.  Without that the
cached conf and the file PipeWire loaded stay consistent with each other while
disagreeing with the setting, and toggling it would silently do nothing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(audio): clock the graph at the rate the card really runs, not the one asked for

The graph rate was set from the configured AudioFormat, but that is a request,
not an outcome.  A fixed-bit-clock I2S cape can refine it upward: an AM62x
PCM5102A cape clocks no lower than 88200, so a 44100 request lands on 88200 and
the graph, pinned to 44100, resampled for the life of the process -- the exact
problem the previous commit set out to remove, still present on those boards.

Take the rate from the device instead.  When it is already open (the normal
case in postNetwork, where PipeWire holds the selected card) /proc reports the
negotiated rate for free; otherwise achievedRateForFormat() asks it directly.
Only the selected output card is consulted: there is one graph clock, and every
other card is resampled to it either way.  aplay --dump-hw-params cannot answer
this -- it reports the unrefined capability space and ignores -r -- which is why
the existing probe already opens the device to learn the achieved rate.

Measured in the sink node, per graph cycle, on the 88200 cape: 779us -> 97us,
and playback 6.2% -> 3.6% of a single core.  A 6.000s tone still plays back as
5.968s of audible signal against a silence control that reads bit-exact zero.

Emitting the conf moved after the card loop, since the rate is only known once
the card has been probed; the generation tag stays the first line because the
cache check matches it as a prefix.  Bumped, as the probe can now produce a
different conf for unchanged hardware.

allowed-rates is left alone: a clock rate outside that list is honoured anyway
(verified with 88200 against the stock [ 44100 48000 96000 ]).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(audio): stop the master volume from overwriting the output group's volume

PipeWireSinkName points at the primary output group, and setVolume() wrote the
master straight to it -- the same node the group volume control and
RestorePipeWireGroupVolumes() write.  Master and that group's slider were one
knob, so whoever wrote last won.  At boot that is always fppd: the group volume
is restored from fppinit, which runs before fppd starts, and fppd then
overwrites it.  A group left louder than the master therefore came back quieter
after every reboot, with the UI still showing the value the user had chosen.

Point the master at the output sinks instead (fpp_alsa_* for local cards,
aes67_* so a network-streaming box still has a working master).  Those sit
downstream of every group, so master, group and member volumes now multiply
instead of overwriting each other, which is what the UI has always implied.
Loudness is unchanged for the ordinary single-group case.

Verified on a cape with no hardware mixer at all: master 70 puts 0.343 on the
card sink and leaves the group at 1.0; setting the group to 50% then restarting
fppd leaves both untouched, where before the restart reset the group.  Mute and
unmute-from-zero still land 0.0 and 0.343.  Software volume on these adapters
was confirmed to reach the device by looping a sink through snd-aloop and
capturing what ALSA received: 100% -> unity, 50% -> 0.125, 25% -> 0.0156.

Also here, all from the same investigation:

  * Skip amixer entirely when the card exposes no playback mixer control.  A
    bare I2S DAC has none -- "Audio Output Mixer Device" is legitimately empty
    on the settings page for those capes -- and FPP was shelling out to amixer
    with an empty control name on every single volume change, to no effect.

  * Give ALSA mode the same cubic taper the PipeWire path gets from pactl's
    percentage, so the same number does not mean a different loudness just
    because the backend changed.  Only the taper can be matched: amixer's
    percentage is of the control's own raw range, and cards describe that range
    uselessly often enough (a USB DAC here spans 0.00 to -0.12 dB across all 31
    steps) that there is no portable dB to aim at.

  * Grow the command buffer.  The sink-enumeration command runs past the old
    256 bytes and snprintf silently truncated it, leaving the volume unset.

  * Note the perceptual scale on the status page slider: the 0-100 is not a
    percentage of amplitude (70 is about -9 dB, 50 about -18 dB).

fix(mdns): rebuild the Avahi client when the daemon goes away

The "mDNS/Avahi client failure" banner was still appearing on every reboot, and
the earlier attempt at this fixed neither half of it.

An Avahi client does not reconnect.  Once avahi-daemon goes away the client is
finished for good, and the service advertisement and both browsers die with it.
Nothing rebuilt it, so a plain "systemctl restart avahi-daemon" left the player
advertising nothing and discovering nothing until fppd itself was restarted --
confirmed on a BeagleBone: after the restart the box no longer appeared in
avahi-browse -tp _fppd._udp, and never came back.

That is also why the warning stuck.  The remove ran on AVAHI_CLIENT_S_RUNNING,
which a dead client never reaches again, so the one path that could clear the
banner was unreachable from the moment it was raised.

The client failure callback now hands the rebuild to a timerfd on the main loop
-- freeing the client from inside its own callback would be freeing the object
we are executing in -- which frees the dead client, builds a new one and
re-registers the service and both browsers.  Retries back off 2s to 30s and keep
going for as long as fppd does, so a real outage is picked up the moment it ends.
The same path covers avahi-daemon not being up yet when fppd starts, which used
to leave mDNS off for the whole session.

The warning is now only raised once the daemon has stayed gone for 30s, and is
cleared on reconnect.  Ordering fppd after avahi-daemon turned out to protect
nothing: avahi-daemon does not wait for its own SIGTERM, it exits the instant the
system bus goes away, and dbus.service had no ordering against fppd.  The stop
job for fppd started, dbus went down 2s later, avahi followed it out, and fppd
saw the client drop half a second before it was told to shut down -- so the
"don't warn while shutting down" guard could not fire.  fppd.service is ordered
after dbus.service as well, which is correct in its own right for a D-Bus client
and puts the shutdown in the right order: fppd, then avahi-daemon, then dbus.

Verified on hardware: an avahi-daemon restart reconnects in 2.0s and
re-advertises with no warning; a 90s outage raises the warning at 30s and clears
it on recovery; a reboot from the UI raises nothing at all.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(audio): pin the hardware mixer to unity, and drop the mixer-device setting

In PipeWire mode the hardware mixer's only job is to get out of the way at
unity, so the software volume is the sole attenuator.  FPP did that by setting
the single control named by AudioMixerDevice to 100%, which is wrong whenever a
control's range runs above 0 dB.  A PCM512x cape's "Main Digital" spans 0..255
with 0 dB at 207 and +24 dB at 255, so pinning it to 100% put the card 24 dB
into clipping -- measured, not inferred.  That is what a user got for picking
the one control on that card that genuinely is the volume.

The setting could not steer them away from it either: it is auto-populated with
`amixer scontrols | head -1`, the alphabetically first control, which on that
cape is "Main Analogue" -- a two-step switch (Limits: Playback 0 - 1) that
cannot express a volume at all.  And pinning only the selected control left any
other volume control sitting wherever the driver had left it.

Pin every playback volume control on the card to 0 dB instead, selected by the
pvolume capability so the switches and tuning enums those cards also expose
(Deemphasis, DSP Program, Auto Mute, Overclock, Volume Ramp...) are never
written.  On the cape above that picks exactly 2 of 19 controls and lands both
at 0.00 dB.  Controls with no dB scale fall back to 100%, the top of a plain
range.  bcm2835 keeps its old max behaviour deliberately: its mixer reaches
+4 dB and FPP wants that headroom above the software stage.

With the pin no longer reading it, AudioMixerDevice has no remaining function --
ALSA mode is retired, so there is no configuration where it controls volume --
so remove it from the settings page.  The key itself is left defined and any
stored value untouched; nothing reads it now.

Also default MediaBackend to pipewire-simple in isPipeWireBackend() and in
setVolume().  Both compared against "" and so treated a box with no MediaBackend
key as the retired ALSA backend, quietly selecting a path the UI cannot even
select and FPPINIT migrates away from at boot.

Verified on a card with no mixer at all (list comes back empty, nothing is
shelled out, software volume still tracks 40 -> 0.064 and 70 -> 0.343) and on
the PCM512x cape (old logic measured +24.00 dB, new logic 0.00 dB).

fix(audio): restore group volumes from the config that describes the running graph

Both volume-restore paths read pipewire-audio-groups.json unconditionally, but
that is the Advanced-mode config.  Simple mode's groups live in
pipewire-audio-groups-simple.json, and the two describe different groups under
different names: Simple mode's single group is "Default" (node
fpp_group_default, which is what buildSimplePipeWireGroupsConf emits), while a
leftover advanced config on the same box named its group "Main Output".

So on a Simple-mode box carrying an advanced config from an earlier setup, every
restore pactl'd fpp_group_main_output -- a node that does not exist.  pactl says
"No such entity", the exec output is discarded, and the restore silently did
nothing: whatever volume the running group had was left as-is, and the volume
stored for it was never applied.

Select the file by MediaBackend, the same way runAudioSetup() already picks
between the two when validating the cached conf.  Fixed in both implementations,
which are documented as needing to stay in sync.

Verified on a Simple-mode box: knocking fpp_group_default down to 50% and
re-running setupAudio now restores it to the 100% the simple config specifies,
where before it stayed at 50%.  Control for the old path: pactl against

fix(audio): restart fppd when the PipeWire daemon is restarted under it

fppd cannot survive the PipeWire daemon restarting underneath it.  The GStreamer
PipeWire plugin caches its connection to the daemon process-wide, so once that
connection dies every later pipewiresink reuses the dead one: the pipeline
reports PLAYING, nothing is ever posted on the bus, and playback is silent until
the process restarts.  Confirmed by wedging a box this way and then running the
same pipeline from a separate process, which played fine -- the daemon and the
graph were healthy, only fppd's own connection was dead.

RestartPipeWireStack() already knew this and restarts fppd, but the other paths
that restart the stack did not: the audio-settings apply, the clear-groups path
in ApplyPipeWireAudioGroups(), resetConfig, and setupAudio itself.  Applying
audio settings therefore silently killed audio until the next fppd restart.

Restart fppd from those paths too.  In setupAudio it is gated on fppd actually
running, which at boot it is not -- setupAudio runs in postNetwork, before fppd
starts -- so a normal boot does not take it, and an unchanged config does not
restart the stack at all and so does not trigger it either.  In the settings
apply it has to be the last step in the backgrounded script: restarting fppd
before the daemons it depends on would just leave the new process wedged again.

Also make the failure loud.  set_state() returning ASYNC only means "in
progress"; when a sink never prerolls the pipeline sits in PAUSED forever with
no bus error, and nothing noticed.  Process()'s preroll watchdog covers this for
playlist media, but a standalone Play Media never runs Process() -- only
PlaylistEntryMedia calls it -- so that case was invisible.  Wait out the
transition and log an error plus a UI warning naming the cause.

Verified: an audio config change with fppd live now logs "PipeWire was restarted
under a running fppd" and bounces it (pid changes, audio works after), and a
wedged fppd now reports "pipeline never reached PLAYING within 15000ms
(state=2)" where it previously printed nothing at all.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

perf(media): stop resampling the same audio twice on a 44.1 kHz graph

The GStreamer pipeline pinned audio/x-raw,rate=48000 before the tee to
save PipeWire the conversion.  That stopped being true once the graph
clock started following the card: on a 44.1 kHz output -- an I2S cape or
most USB cards -- audioresample converted 44100 up to 48000 and
PipeWire's client adapter converted it straight back down.  Nothing
needed 48000; the AES67 inline branches that would have are a no-op stub
and AES67's own 48 kHz pipeline is standalone off pipewiresrc.

Whoever converts, someone pays; the only question is who.  Measured on a
single-core AM335x feeding a 44100 Hz graph, 30 s of stereo, gstreamer +
pipewire + wireplumber summed as a percentage of the one core:

  source     pinned 48000   unpinned   pinned to graph rate
  44.1 kHz      25.2%         18.0%           18.0%
  48 kHz        20.9%         20.6%           24.0%
  88.2 kHz        --          41.0%           34.5%
  96 kHz        42.8%         41.2%           37.0%

PipeWire's resampler is roughly three times cheaper than audioresample,
so leaving the rate alone wins whenever the two are close -- including
48 kHz into 44.1 kHz, where converting costs more than the 9% fewer
samples it saves.  That flips once the source runs at twice the graph
rate or more, where carrying the extra samples through volume, the tee,
the sample tap and the sink outweighs the slower resampler.

So: pin nothing unless the source is at least twice the graph rate, in
which case pin the graph rate.  No graph FPP configures runs below
44100, so nothing at or under 48000 can reach that threshold and the
graph query is skipped entirely for the rates essentially all media
uses.  The rate comes from the live daemon (pw-metadata, ~40 ms, cached
per run) because a cape can refine the configured rate upward, falling
back to default.clock.rate in the generated conf.

End to end through fppd on a 44.1 kHz mp3: 25.9% of the core to 19.0%.
A 60 s tone still plays in 60 s at both 44.1 and 48 kHz.

The stream format is unchanged and was never the problem -- the sink
path already negotiates S16LE; the F32LE capsfilter is only on the mono
sample tap, and pinning S16 against F32 measured within noise.

fix(media): report the position the DAC is playing, not the one queued

gst_element_query_position() on pipewiresink returns what the sink has
handed to the PipeWire graph, not what has left the card, and pipewiresink
adds nothing of its own to the GStreamer LATENCY query: it answers
min = upstream + processing-deadline + render-delay with render-delay at 0,
identically no matter which node it targets, so it never asks PipeWire how
far the data still has to travel.  Everything queued downstream was
invisible to mediaSeconds, and the sequence -- which
CalculateNewChannelOutputDelay() servos to exactly that number -- ran ahead
of the sound by the whole downstream depth.

Measured by encoding the sequence's frame index into the channel data,
capturing it off the wire with kernel timestamps, and anchoring the audio
against a sample-accurate reference: the lights led the sound by 22 ms on
an AM62x board with an I2S cape, 56 ms on a Pi 5 with an I2S cape, and
160 ms on an AM335x board with a full-speed USB dongle.  It tracks the ALSA
queue depth, so it is a per-platform constant rather than anything a user
could reasonably be asked to dial in.

Back the reported position up by the card's own delay figure, which
/proc/asound/cardN/pcmMp/sub0/status gives in frames and which needs
neither a new library nor a patched GStreamer plugin.  It matched the
measured offset to within 3 ms on the platforms where both could be
cross-checked.  PipeWire's declared SPA_PARAM_Latency was tried and is
worse: it is the nominal quantum + headroom + period, which under-reports
the live queue by 30 ms on the USB case.

After the change the same three boards measure 4 ms, 16 ms and -2 ms.  The
residual is the +-1 frame dead band in CalculateNewChannelOutputDelay(),
which the servo is free to wander inside.

The card is resolved from the adapter FPP generated rather than from the
AudioOutput setting, since that is the card the running graph actually
feeds.  The value is cached with a 250 ms refresh because the queue barely
moves during a track while Process() runs at frame rate, and a closed
device keeps the last good value so the position does not snap at track
gaps.  Only applied when the position came from the audio sink; with a
kmssink present the position is video playout, a different path.

mediaOffset is deliberately untouched and still applies on top in
setMediaElapsed(), so it remains purely a user knob.

fix(multisync): stop unchecked unicast remotes re-checking themselves

fix(sequence): stop the RT output thread livelocking on the sequence pointer

Sequence::m_seqFile is an AtomicSharedPtr, which resolved to the C++20
std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<T>> specialization wherever the standard
library had one.  libstdc++ implements that with an internal spinlock
whose backoff calls sched_yield(), and that is fatal here: the channel
output thread runs at real-time priority and reads m_seqFile several
times per frame, while the frame reader thread writes and reads it at
normal priority.  When the normal-priority thread holds the spinlock and
is preempted, the real-time thread spins on sched_yield() -- which only
ever yields to threads of equal or higher priority, so the lock holder
can never be scheduled to release it.  Nothing breaks the cycle until
kernel RT throttling (sched_rt_runtime_us, ~95%) forcibly deschedules
the spinner.

On a single-core AM335x board that froze every non-RT thread on the
system for ~1.0 s in roughly a third of one-minute playbacks, at random
times: a second of frozen output, after which the sequence was left
permanently ~600 ms out of step with the audio.  An ftrace of the output
thread across one freeze showed 115,000+ sched_yield() calls and almost
no other syscalls, with that thread on-CPU for 0.936 s of a 0.97 s
freeze.  Multi-core boards never showed it -- the lock holder simply runs
on another CPU -- which is what made it look like a platform quirk
rather than a scheduling bug.

Drop the native specialization and always use the mutex implementation
that was already present for Apple's libc++, which blocks on a futex
instead of spinning, so the real-time thread sleeps and the lock holder
runs.  Give that mutex PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT as well: blocking alone still
allows unbounded inversion, since the normal-priority holder can be
preempted by any other normal-priority thread while the real-time thread
waits behind it, and there are a dozen of those.

Freezes went from 5 in 16 runs to 0 in 10.  Frame timing is unchanged
(p50 20.06 ms, p95 21.0 ms, p99 27.9 ms against a 20 ms frame), and the
cost is one uncontended lock per load(), a handful of times per frame.
The priority-inheritance half measured no different from a plain mutex on
an idle board; it is there for contention under load, which that test
cannot produce.

Demoting the output thread off real-time priority was measured as an
alternative and rejected: it costs p95 21.0 -> 22.9 ms and takes frames
over 40 ms from 1 to 4 per minute, on an idle board at that.

than pipewiresink's write pointer.

c0d35f97f added a check that re-probes the audio hardware when AudioFormat
changes, by comparing the conf's default.clock.rate against the configured rate.
The card-set comparison beside it cannot see that change -- the same cards are
still present, just at a different rate -- so the check is needed.

plain search finds the wrong one on any card with a mic.

fix(audio): restart fppd from every path that restarts the stack, and only once

fppd cannot survive the PipeWire daemon restarting under it -- the GStreamer
PipeWire plugin caches its connection process-wide, so every later pipewiresink
reuses a dead one and playback is silently nothing -- so f60c3651b restarts fppd
when that happens.  The gate it used, pipewireRestarted, is set in only two of
the four places runAudioSetup() brings the stack up or down.

Missed:

  - the post-regen restart, taken when regenerate_pipewire_groups reports a
    changed group config, did not set the flag
  - pipewireColdStarted was not considered at all, though a stack that was down
    while fppd was up leaves fppd's cached connection just as dead, and starting
    the daemons underneath it does not revive it

Both leave fppd holding a dead connection: the pipeline reports PLAYING, nothing
is posted on the bus, playback is silent and nothing is logged -- the exact
failure f60c3651b set out to eliminate, still reachable.

In the other direction, the settings-apply path restarted fppd twice.
settings.php backgrounds `fppinit setupAudio` and then restarts the three
daemons itself before restarting fppd last; setupAudio's own restart therefore
fired first, landing *before* those daemon restarts and re-wedging the process
it had just replaced -- the precise ordering trap f60c3651b's own message warns
about.  Add a --no-fppd-restart flag (setupAudio(bool)) and pass it from
settings.php, which owns that sequence.  Every other caller keeps the internal
restart, including the recovery re-run, which inherits the caller's choice.

Verified: the runs that genuinely restarted the stack log "PipeWire was
restarted under a running fppd; restarting fppd so it reconnects" and bounce it
(pid changes, audio works after); three consecutive settled runs report "audio
config unchanged since boot; skipping restart" and leave the pid untouched.

fix(audio): compare the cards the probe considered, not the adapters it wrote

The "ALSA sink adapters already match present cards; skipping probe" fast path
existed to keep a boot from re-running the per-card ALSA probe -- aplay, amixer
and arecord plus a 2s hw-params dump each, all via popen, the slowest part of
audio setup -- when nothing about the hardware had changed.  On a Pi with a
display attached it had never once been taken.

The check compared the adapters the conf declares against the cards considered:

    existingAdapterCids == adapterCandidateCids

Those cannot agree whenever the probe drops a candidate as unusable.  A
connected-but-IEC958-only vc4hdmi0 is a candidate -- cardIsDeadHDMI() is false,
the display is plugged in -- but gets no adapter ("skipping card 3 (vc4hdmi0) --
no standard PCM format"), so the sets differed permanently and the conf was
regenerated every boot.  Silently, too: of the checks that reject a cached conf,
the three that print a reason were all passing, and the one actually rejecting
it printed nothing, so there was no trace of why the probe kept running.  This
is the ordinary state of any Pi with a monitor attached.

Record the candidate set as "# cards: a b c" and compare that instead.  It asks
the question that actually matters -- the hardware on offer is unchanged, so the
probe would reach the same conclusions, skips included.  A card that was merely
busy at probe time gets its skip cached too, which the no-sinks recovery at the
end of runAudioSetup() already exists to catch, and a probe-rule change is what
the generation tag is for.  Add the missing log line so it cannot fail silently
again.

Generation bumped for the extra marker; existing installs re-probe once.

Verified on a Pi with HDMI-A-1 connected and two USB cards: the conf now records
"# cards: icusbaudio7d s3 vc4hdmi0" including the card that got no adapter, and
three consecutive setupAudio runs report "skipping probe", "groups config
unchanged after regeneration" and "audio config unchanged since boot; skipping
restart", leaving the fppd pid untouched.  Before, each run re-probed.

Also here: drop the dead reloadOther on AudioOutput.  1c563dcf7 removed
AudioMixerDevice from the settings page but left AudioOutput reloading it, so
every AudioOutput change fired a request for the options of a setting that is no
longer rendered, shelling out to amixer for a result nothing reads.

or no card, and applied no correction -- which is Simple mode's default on any
board with no other sound card, i.e. most of them.  Replayed against this box's

  Simple mode, Pi on HDMI audio, another card also present
      before: card 0 (a Sound Blaster -- wrong card entirely)
      after:  card 3 (vc4hdmi0)

  Simple mode, HDMI the only card, so the 95 conf declares nothing
      before: -1, meaning no correction at all
      after:  card 3 (vc4hdmi0)

colon, so sysdefault: paths parse exactly like hw: ones.

returned 0 silently, so a box running uncorrected looked identical to one
running correctly -- and uncorrected means the sequence leads the sound by the

once per media, naming the reason (no matching adapter, no playback substream,
unreadable rate, implausible queue depth).  Deliberately not a UI warning: on a
board with no usable sink it would fire on every track forever, and this is a
tuning shortfall rather than a fault demanding immediate action.

fix(aes67): resample the send stream, which the graph no longer delivers at 48k

AES67 mandates 48 kHz L24 on the wire, and the send pipeline pinned
audio/x-raw,format=S24BE,rate=48000 straight after a lone audioconvert.  That
worked for as long as the PipeWire graph also ran at 48000, which 90-fpp.conf
made true by default.

c0d35f97f and 529b25f36 changed the graph clock to follow the output card, so it
now sits at whatever that card is configured for -- 44100 with the default
AudioFormat.  pipewiresrc cannot satisfy a caps filter asking for a rate the
graph does not run at AND a format PipeWire does not carry natively (S24BE, the
big-endian packing L24 needs).  It does not fail cleanly: it never negotiates,
so gst_element_set_state() blocks and eventually returns FAILURE, which is the
"AES67: audio send stream failed to start" warning (id 44).

Measured against the live 44100 graph, with a producer connected:

  audioconvert ! S24BE@48000                                   hangs
  audioconvert ! S24BE@44100                                   works (no rate change)
  audioresample ! audioconvert ! S24BE@48000                   hangs
  audioconvert ! audioresample ! audioconvert ! S24BE@48000    works

audioresample advertises S24BE, so the middle case is not a caps gap, but the
conversion still only negotiates when it is split: reach a format the resampler
will work in, resample, then pack to S24BE.  Costs nothing on a graph already at
48000, where the resampler passes through.

The receive pipeline needs no equivalent: it pins no rate after rtpL24depay, so
pipewiresink negotiates whatever the graph runs and PipeWire resamples, exactly
as the media pipeline's sink already does.

Verified on hardware: with this and the group config naming the send node, the
pipeline goes from a 30 s block ending in FAILURE to
"AES67 Stream 1 started -> 239.69.0.1:5004 (2ch, 4ms ptime)" in 44 ms, warning
44 clears, and tcpdump shows L24 multicast on the wire both during playback and
while idle.

fix(aes67): rebuild the audio graph when a sender instance is enabled or renamed

Enabling an AES67 send from the UI left it failing with "AES67: audio send
stream failed to start" (warning 44), and nothing pointed at the cause.

A group member targets a network sender by a node name derived from the
instance -- aes67_<slug of instance name>_send -- and
GeneratePipeWireGroupsConfig() drops a member whose instance is disabled,
recording "# WARNING: Could not find PipeWire sinks for: aes67_1 (AES67 instance
not found or disabled)" in the generated conf.  ApplyAES67Instances() then only
signalled fppd, never rebuilding the groups, so the two were left disagreeing:

  21:52:50  97-fpp-audio-groups.conf generated -- instance still disabled,
            member dropped
  21:53:17  instance enabled, apply signals fppd
            -> send pipeline starts against a graph with nothing feeding it

The send pipeline uses node.autoconnect=false, so with no filter chain connected
it cannot preroll; gst_element_set_state() blocks for 30s and returns FAILURE.
Confirmed directly: the same pipeline with no peer hangs even at the graph's own
rate, so this is the wiring, not the format negotiation fixed in 6fb644252.

Nothing about that is discoverable from the UI.  The user enabled a stream and
was told it failed to start; the stale thing was a different page's config, and
re-applying the audio groups by hand is the only thing that fixes it.  So do it
for them: regenerate, and if the graph really changed, apply it and bring fppd
back so the sender starts against the new wiring.

Generation is pure, so the comparison is cheap and the restart is only paid when
the wiring actually changes.  Editing an already-wired instance's bitrate, ptime
or multicast address produces an identical group config and still takes the old
signal-only path, restarting nothing.

Opus RTP has the identical coupling (opusrtp_*_send) and the same failure, so it
shares the helper.

Verified end to end on hardware, disabling and re-enabling a send instance:
disable+apply removes the group and rebuilds; enable+apply rebuilds with
fpp_group_aes67_stream_1 and node.target = "aes67_aes67_stream_1_send", the
pipeline reports "started -> 239.69.0.1:5004 (2ch, 4ms ptime)" in 44ms, warning
44 stays clear, and tcpdump shows L24 multicast on the wire.

fix(audio): one way to restart the audio stack, and skip applies that change nothing

Three related problems, all of which made applying audio settings more
disruptive than it needed to be.

1. Four paths restarted PipeWire and left fppd wedged

fppd cannot survive the daemons restarting under it; f60c3651b established that
and fixed two call sites.  Four were missed -- ApplyPipeWireAudioGroups()'s main
path and all three restarts in ApplyPipeWireInputGroups() -- so pressing Apply on
the audio groups or input groups page restarted the stack and left fppd holding a
dead connection.  Verified what that costs by reproducing it: with fppd left
alone across a daemon restart, playback is completely silent, the card never
opens and hw_ptr never advances.  fppd's own preroll watchdog does eventually
notice and self-restart, but only after three wedges of 15s each.

Collapse every stack restart onto one helper, RestartPipeWireStack(), which
restarts the daemons in dependency order, waits for both sockets, and brings fppd
back.  Restarting fppd is not a separate concern the caller may forget; it is
part of what restarting the stack means, so it lives inside the helper.

2. Three different ways to restart fppd

`systemctl restart fppd` (settings.php, resetConfig.php, FPPINIT_Audio.cpp),
SendCommand('restart') (RestartPipeWireServices), and RestartFPPDResumingPlaylist()
(the wedge watchdog).  Standardise on the graceful one -- SendCommand('restart')
in PHP, `fpp -r` from C++ and shell.  It asks fppd to re-exec itself, which is an
equally fresh process image and is what actually clears the cached gst-pipewire
connection, and unlike systemctl it resumes a playlist that was running and does
not spend the unit's start limit.  It is also already the reactive recovery, so
proactive and reactive now agree.

settings.php no longer hand-rolls the sequence at all: setupAudio already decides
whether the config changed, restarts the daemons only if it did, and restarts
fppd afterwards.  It was repeating all of that unconditionally and restarting
fppd twice on the runs that had changed.  One owner, one decision -- which also
retires the --no-fppd-restart flag added in bf6b45ed8.

3. The generated config was not deterministic, so every apply looked like a change

GeneratePipeWireGroupsConfig() decided whether to emit a custom ALSA adapter from
whether that node currently existed in the graph.  But an fpp_alsa_* node exists
precisely because FPP declared it, and one of the two places it can be declared is
the conf being generated.  So it oscillated: adapter present -> judged unnecessary
-> dropped -> next restart removes it -> judged necessary -> re-added.  In the half
of the cycle where it was dropped, its member targeted a node that did not exist,
which is a silent output.  Decide from 95-fpp-alsa-sink.conf instead, which is
unaffected by what this function writes.

A second oscillation had the same shape: hw: vs sysdefault: (and the format) is
chosen from the card's capability list, which is only readable while the card is
free.  During playback /proc reports the format the device is RUNNING, never the
IEC958-only capability that made sysdefault: necessary, so it flipped back to hw:
-- and back again on the next idle apply.  Carry the running graph's own choice
forward when the card is busy rather than re-deriving it from a device that
cannot answer.

With generation stable, compare before doing anything: an apply whose config is
byte-identical to what PipeWire already loaded needs no restart at all.  The
comparison happens before playback is stopped, so a no-op apply costs nothing.
Volumes are still restored, since those apply live.

Verified on hardware, advanced mode with 3 USB cards, an IEC958 HDMI card and an
AES67 sender:

  apply during a running show, config unchanged
      before: "Audio groups applied, PipeWire restarted, playback resumed",
              card closed, show stopped
      after:  "Audio groups already match the running graph; nothing to restart",
              card still RUNNING, audio advanced 0.53s straight through it
  apply with the on-disk conf deliberately altered
      restarts, then the next apply settles to no-op
  two consecutive generations, and generation vs on-disk
      byte-identical, both idle and during playback

fix(fseq): never read a frame into an UncompressedFrameData whose malloc failed

UncompressedFrameData's constructor does `m_data = (uint8_t*)malloc(sz)` and
does not check the result. readFrame() tests m_data for null, but none of the
five getFrame() implementations that fill the buffer do: they go straight to
`read(&data->m_data[sz], toRead)` or `memcpy(data->m_data, ...)`. When the
allocation fails, the read path becomes fread(NULL, 1, N, fp), which faults
inside glibc's own buffer copy - a memcpy crash with no FPP frame below it,
which is exactly the shape that makes these reports hard to bucket.

This is reachable, not theoretical. A channel range whose start lies past the
end of the sequence turns m_dataBlockSize into a ~4GB request; the range guard
in V1FSEQFile::prepareRead keeps master out of that particular hole, but the
allocation can still fail for its own reasons on a 512MB controller, and four
of the five call sites are in the V2 handlers, which compute the size their
own way.

Add one guard used by all five sites: log the size that could not be allocated
and hand the frame back untouched. Returning the object rather than nullptr
matches the existing early-exit paths in these functions, and readFrame()
already reports false for a null buffer, so callers see a frame that did not
load instead of a daemon that died.

Verified with a standalone harness that builds FSEQFile.cpp on its own and runs
it under a capped address space so malloc genuinely fails. The control fails
first: the same harness against a tree without the range guard segfaults inside
fread with buf=0x0, and with this change it logs the failed allocation and
returns a frame that readFrame() rejects.

fix(BBShiftString): a zero length frame ate a ring block and skewed every later one

Reloading the channel output config left every string shifted one byte, for
the life of the output: a solid blue draw came out green, and the port number
test lit its first pixel yellow instead of white.  Only a full fppd restart
cleared it.

SendData() gated the start command on pruData alone while sendData() gated the
frame on outputStringLen.  A freshly Init()ed output has outputStringLen 0
until its first PrepData(), and PrepareChannelData() and SendChannelData() are
separate walks of the output list - Init() of a replacement deliberately runs
outside outputThreadLock - so on a config reload the new output can reach
SendData() first.  The command then came out as 0x10000: zero length, but the
custom-length flag makes it nonzero, so the pump issued it as a real frame with
nothing behind it.

WORD_LOOP reads its block before testing the count, so that zero length frame
still consumed one 64 byte ring block the ARM never wrote.  From then on the
firmware's frame boundary sat one block ahead of the pump's.  Both sides kept
moving the same number of blocks per frame, so the ring still reached empty
every frame and the drained() gate added in 7f8d8f634 never saw it - that gate
is necessary but not sufficient, since a whole frame offset by N drains just as
cleanly as one offset by 0.

On the wire the strip took the stray byte, then met the 300us reset delay in
the middle of the frame instead of at the end, latched, and read the rest one
byte over.

Do not issue a command for a port with no frame to send, and refuse a zero
length frame in the firmware rather than absorb it.

Measured on a 16 port cape with 50 pixels per port, decoding the ring back to
per-port bytes and sampling the PRU program counter: before, after a reload the
core idled in WAITDATA for the whole inter-frame gap, 74 of 121 frames carried
a 310us stall in the reset delay loop at block 1, and the frame span was
1.74ms.  After, it idles in _LOOP, no in-frame stalls, 1.43ms - and it stays
that way across six consecutive reloads.

feat(BBShiftString): publish the frame start so a ring misalignment heals itself

The command word tells the firmware how many blocks to render but not where
the frame begins - it just reads on from wherever it stopped - so the two
sides' idea of a frame boundary was only ever established once, at startup,
and never re-checked.  Anything that disturbed it stayed disturbed: both sides
go on moving the same number of blocks per frame, so the ring still empties
every frame and the drain gate cannot tell a frame offset by a whole number of
blocks from one that is not offset at all.  Every skew found so far has had to
be diagnosed and fixed at its source, and the output stayed wrong until a
restart.

State the boundary instead of remembering it.  The pump writes the ring
address the frame starts at immediately before the command that acts on it -
nothing of the frame has been written yet, so the write position is its first
byte - and the firmware takes its read position from that.  On the AM62x that
data RAM word was already loaded with the command and otherwise unused, so it
costs one compare and one move per frame.

The firmware zeroes the word once it has used it.  That pairing is the part
that matters: acting on a start that did not arrive with this command means
jumping to a stale position, which on a first attempt at this walked the read
pointer backwards into already consumed data and deadlocked.  A command with
no start now leaves the position alone.

The reverse failure - the firmware never renders a frame it was handed - had
no recovery at all and left the ring permanently non-empty, so output stopped
until a restart.  Give the pump a 250ms watchdog on the firmware's frame
counter that re-seats onto the read pointer and carries on.  seekToConsumer()
republishes the write position unconditionally; returning early when the local
offset already agreed left a stale published value uncorrected, which is the
same wedge one level down.

Both paths log, and the firmware counts the corrections, so this stops being
silent.

Verified on a 16 port cape with 50 pixels per port, by decoding the ring back
to per-port bytes and sampling the PRU program counter.  30s idle and six
config reloads: no corrections, 40.5fps, 1.43ms frame span.  Six injected one
block skews: six corrections, and the output never left 40.5fps/1.43ms - each
cost one frame instead of lasting for the life of the output.  An injected
lost frame reported exactly the seven unread blocks and recovered.  The
injection reproduces the pre-fix fault on demand, so the healing result could
have come back red.

AM62x only; the AM33XX firmware preprocesses byte identical to before.
