fix(pru): memcpyToPRU's block loop was dead and overran short destinations

memcpy_ldnp() opened with

    int sz = sztotal - sztotal & 64;

which parses as (sztotal - sztotal) & 64, i.e. always zero.  Two consequences.
Every copy fell through to the byte loop, so the ldnp/stnp path the function
exists for - the optimized memcpy faults on the uncacheable PRU mappings - has
never actually run.  And the asm block is a do-while, so it always executed one
iteration and stored 64 bytes at the destination regardless of the length
asked for, writing past the end of anything shorter.

Mask the low bits instead, skip the block loop when there is nothing for it,
and only take it when both operands are 16 byte aligned, since an unaligned
vector access to an uncacheable mapping faults.  Head and tail go through the
byte loop as before.  Exactly sztotal bytes are written and no more.

Callers are unaffected.  Every existing call is either a whole number of 64
byte units or at least 64 bytes long, and for any length of 64 or more the old
and new code write the same bytes over the same range - the stray store just
repeated the first block.  Only shorter copies change, and there the bytes that
are no longer written were uninitialized stack.

The BBShiftPanel comments describing the copy as spilling into the next 64 byte
unit no longer hold; the padding they explain is kept, and now writes that slot
outright rather than relying on the overrun to do it.

Verified two ways.  A/B harness over 66816 combinations of length 0-260 and
source/destination alignment: the old code wrote past the end in 16368 of them,
the new code in none, and neither ever got the copied bytes wrong.  Removing
the new byte loop and re-running the aligned, block sized cases still copies
correctly, which is what shows the ldnp path is now the one doing the work
rather than the test passing on the fallback.  On hardware, the BBShiftString
command table lands in PRU data RAM byte identical to before.

BBShiftPanel and BBB48String are compile and equivalence checked only, not run
on panels or a 48 string cape.

fix(build): pin the PCH's own CFLAGS so fppinit's filter can't reach it

Target-specific variables are inherited by a target's prerequisites, and
$(PCH_FILE) is a prerequisite of every %.o.  makefiles/fppinit.mk sets

    boot/FPPINIT*.o: CFLAGS := $(filter-out -fpch-preprocess -g1,$(CFLAGS))

on its four objects, so whichever object pulls the shared fpp-pch.h.gch in is
what decides the flags it gets built with -- and since fppinit.mk prepends
fppinit to TARGETS, that is always an FPPINIT object.  The .gch therefore ends
up built without -fpch-preprocess and -g1; the ':=' additionally snapshots
CFLAGS before fpp_so.mk appends the pkg-config output, so it loses -pthread and
the gstreamer/libdrm includes as well.

gcc then rejects the PCH for every translation unit and re-parses the whole of
fpp-pch.h in each one -- slower than having no PCH at all, while still paying to
build a ~148MB image nothing reads.  Nothing reports it: the diagnostic is
suppressed unless -Winvalid-pch is on, and the stated reason varies by platform
("created with 'none' debug info, but used with 'dwarf-2'", or "`_REENTRANT' is
defined" where -pthread is dropped too), which makes it look like two bugs.

Pin the .gch's own CFLAGS -- a target's own value takes precedence over one
inherited from a dependent -- and enable -Winvalid-pch so a future mismatch is
one warning per TU instead of a silent slowdown.  The FPPINIT objects still
compile without the PCH, as intended.

Measured on a 4-core aarch64 board, full tree, 204 objects, ccache disabled,
each arm run twice with the order reversed:

    make -j4     before 311.5s     -DNOPCH 259.5s     after 178.1s
    make -j1     before 695.7s     -DNOPCH 593.7s     after 418.6s

Single-core boards are hit harder; an 8-TU serial sample went 382s -> 158s on
32-bit armhf and 642s -> 153s on aarch64.

Regressed in feecf1837.

perf(build): resolve pkg-config once at parse time, not once per recipe

CFLAGS is a recursively-expanded variable, so "CFLAGS += $(shell pkg-config
...)" appends the shell call itself rather than its result, and make re-runs it
every time CFLAGS is expanded -- which is once per compile recipe.  Three
helpers were wired up that way (gstreamer, libdrm, and GraphicsMagick++-config
on generic-Linux builds), so a build forked them several hundred times to
recompute a string that never changes.

Capture each into a simply-expanded variable and append that instead.  The
resulting compile lines are unchanged token for token; only the number of forks
differs.

    pkg-config invocations per build     406 -> 3
    make -n over a full build, 1-core armhf     11.5s -> 0.9s
    make -n over a full build, 4-core aarch64    0.8s -> 0.2s

The cost is paid on every make invocation, so it is proportionally largest on
no-op and incremental builds.

fix(bb64): validate and repair the PocketBeagle2 EEPROM before flashing eMMC

Some industrial boards leave the factory with the identity EEPROM only partly
programmed.  u-boot's SPL applies the 1GB DDRSS timings only when the EEPROM
identifies the board as the industrial variant, so those boards come up as the
512MB base board -- and flashing one produced a finished-looking unit that was
wrong in a way nothing downstream would notice.

The eMMC is the tell: only the industrial has it populated, and mmcblk0 is the
only target this profile ever flashes.  So flash_storage.sh's bb64 preflight,
previously a no-op, now checks the EEPROM and repairs it where it can, before
anything is written.  A preflight die already runs under the same EXIT trap as
every other phase, so an abort ends with all user LEDs blinking rather than
with a board that looks done.

The detect/repair/verify logic moves out of BB64-AutoFlash.sh into a shared
check_pb2_eeprom.sh so the boot-time flasher and the interactive one cannot
drift.  BB64-AutoFlash.sh's fail() moves above its first use: the EEPROM check
is now the first thing that can fail, and sh only resolves a function once it
has read the definition.

An EEPROM that cannot be repaired now stops the flash instead of warning and
continuing.  There is no EEPROM part on this board -- an MSPM0L1105 emulates a
24c32 at 0x50 -- so when its firmware was never flashed, 0x50 does not ACK,
at24's probe read fails, and the driver never binds.  Nothing can be written to
a silent device, so the only honest answer is to refuse.  The same MSPM0 also
emulates the ADC at 0x20, which separates three faults that need different
people to look at them: neither bound (MSPM0 not running), ADC bound but 0x50
silent (MSPM0 running, firmware fault), and no i2c client at all (device tree,
not the board).  Its own address at 0x48 is useless for this -- it does not ACK
there even on a healthy board.

Also fixed, all of which reported success on boards that were not repaired:

- The repair is now re-read and re-verified.  A sysfs write to a write
  protected or wedged part looks exactly like a successful dd.
- A read that fails with EIO yielded an empty header, which read as "blank" and
  sent the board down the repair path to abort later complaining about the
  write.  Short reads are now rejected up front.
- A base-board ID programmed on hardware with eMMC now aborts.  The fix scripts
  merge only over 0xFF bytes, so they cannot correct an EEPROM that is fully
  but wrongly programmed; running one would have changed nothing and said it
  worked.
- [ $OLDNUMHEX != ... ] was unquoted, so an empty read was a syntax error
  rather than a branch.

The two sysfs paths in the fix scripts and the four in the checker are
overridable so the failure modes can be exercised against fixtures; nothing in
FPP sets them.  Verified on a PocketBeagle2 Industrial: fixtures byte-identical
to real PB2I and PB20 dumps, and the driver-unbind controls reproduce the real
sysfs shape for each MSPM0 fault.

perf(audio): only charge a USB card the drift headroom when it can actually drift

api.alsa.headroom was 4096 frames for every USB card, which is 93 ms of pure
output latency at 44.1 kHz.  The headroom exists so that a USB card *following*
another card's clock gives the adaptive resampler room to absorb the drift
between two independent oscillators; without it the resampler hard-resyncs,
audible as crackle and pitch wobble.

A card that is the only sink in its audio group has nothing to follow.  PipeWire
makes it the graph driver -- pw-top shows it as the one node with a non-zero
quantum -- so the graph clock is that card's own oscillator and there is no drift
to absorb.  For that case the 4096 frames buy nothing at all, and the single USB
card is by far the common configuration.

Decide it from group membership instead: alone in its group, 1024; sharing a
group with another sink, 4096 as before; not USB, 256 as before.  Both config
generators get the same rule -- the boot-time one in FPPINIT_Audio.cpp reads the
active groups JSON, and the PHP has the groups in hand already.

Measured through fppd/GStreamer by the card's own queue depth
(/proc/asound/cardN/pcm0p/sub0/status), 44.1 kHz, single USB card:

  Pi 5, full-speed dongle        156.0 ms -> 86.3 ms
  single-core AM335x, dongle     155.2 ms -> 85.1 ms

Sustained playback held zero xruns on the sink node at every value tried, on
both boards, including 42 s at 3x CPU overcommit on the single-core one.  1024 is
the knee rather than the floor: 512 saves only 13 ms more and 256 only 3 ms
beyond that, because PipeWire's own minimum buffer fill dominates below 1024, so
further cuts only thin the scheduling margin.

Two things this needs to stay honest:

  * 95-fpp-alsa-sink.conf is written once per boot and the group editor
    deliberately does not touch it, so moving a second card into a USB card's
    group would leave the sole-sink value live until the next reboot -- the
    unsafe direction.  SyncBootAdapterUsbHeadroom() rewrites those lines on
    apply and marks the graph changed so the restart picks them up.
  * group membership moves without the set of present cards moving, which the
    existing cards tag cannot see, so the conf records the decision itself and
    the boot-time validity check compares it.  Generation bumped to 7 so
    existing installs re-probe once.

GStreamerOut's position correction needs no change: it reads the queue depth
live and scales by the card's real rate, so it simply reports a smaller number
(verified at 77 ms with the new headroom against 131-162 ms with the old).  Its
comment quoted the old USB figure as a per-platform constant, so say there that
the number moves with the headroom.

fix(media): say why a video-only file will not play instead of blaming a missing plug-in

Playing a file with no audio track on an item whose video output is disabled --
or whose display is unplugged, which drops FPP into the same fallback -- produced
three messages, each pointing somewhere the problem was not:

  GStreamer sync error (src=decodebin0): Your GStreamer installation is missing a plug-in.
  GStreamer sync error (src=qtdemux0): Internal data stream error.
  GStreamer: pipeline never reached PLAYING within 15000ms — A PipeWire restart
             under a running fppd does this; fppd must be restarted to reconnect.

Nothing was missing, the stream was not corrupt, and PipeWire was uninvolved.  The
audio-only fallback pins decodebin to caps="audio/x-raw", so a file with no audio
gives it nothing to expose and the autoplug failure surfaces as a missing plug-in.
Reported as #2839, where it cost the reporter a hunt for absent packages.

Only that fallback is affected.  The video pipeline links its pads by hand and
OnNoMorePads already tears down the unconnected audio chain for video-only media,
so with a display attached these files play silently and correctly -- confirmed on
a Pi with an HDMI display, where the same file plays clean with the video output
set and fails the moment it is disabled.

So name the fallback's decodebin and watch pad-added.  GStreamer itself then
answers whether the file yielded decodable audio: no probe, no TagLib guess (its
zero-channel answer cannot distinguish "no audio track" from "container I cannot
parse"), and nothing added to the normal start path.  The demuxer's follow-on
error is folded into the same event rather than logged as a second, unrelated
failure, and the raw GStreamer wording is kept at debug level.

A missing audio pad is not on its own evidence about the file, which the first
version of this got wrong: stop PipeWire under a running fppd, play a plain WAV,
and pwsink errors before decodebin ever gets that far -- reporting a backend
outage as "this file has no audio" is a worse lie than the one being fixed.  The
error has to come from inside the decode chain too, so the source is walked up
GST_OBJECT_PARENT to the named decodebin before the file is blamed.

Separately, the preroll check reported GST_STATE_CHANGE_FAILURE and a genuine
timeout identically.  An element that errors returns FAILURE at once, so the
message claimed a 15-second wait it never made and named a PipeWire restart that
never happened -- for any failure at all.  Split the two: FAILURE points at the
error the bus handler has already logged, and only a real timeout keeps the
stale-connection advice.  Both paths verified on a single-core AM335x board,
which is slow enough to lose the race to the bus handler and take that branch.

The entry still ends rather than holding its duration, so a playlist advances
early past such an item; making it consume the full duration means synthesising
playback timing and is left alone here.

initializer, so scheduler info reported a 1970 date next to a correct
numeric currentTime.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(scheduler): produce one string for the missing playlist/sequence warning

The two sites that raise and clear warning 23 built its text
independently, and the copy in AddScheduledItems used = where the
original used +=, mangling the message to " 'name' does not exist".
Warnings are removed by exact text match, so the differing strings also
meant one site's warning could never be cleared by the other — a
missing-playlist warning could stick after the file reappeared. One
helper now feeds all four add/remove call sites.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(scheduler): never start or stop the player while holding the schedule lock

A playlist entry can run an FPP Command inline while Playlist::Start
holds m_playlistMutex, and several of those commands call back into the
scheduler and take m_scheduleLock — so m_playlistMutex -> m_scheduleLock
is the established order. Scheduler code that called Player start/stop
while holding m_scheduleLock took the same two locks in the opposite
order and could deadlock the daemon against a command thread. Both
mutexes are recursive, which does not help across threads.

Decisions are now made under the lock and carried out by value:
doScheduledPlaylist and StartNextScheduledItemNow collect PlayerActions
that run after the lock is released, and CheckScheduledItems becomes a
decide-then-act rescan loop that stops scanning at the first action so
each item is still judged against the player's real state. doCountdown
had the same inversion through synchronously-run presets and now
collects them for after the lock drops. The read-only player getters do
not take m_playlistMutex and stay under the lock; the ordering rule is
documented at the m_scheduleLock declaration.

Behavioral deltas, both safer: an item is marked ran before its start
action executes (so a re-entrant check cannot start it twice), and
countdown presets fire after the lock is released.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(playlist): make the inserted-playlist switchover safe

Three interlocking fixes to how Process() hands control to an inserted
playlist:

- Drain the condemned-playlist cleanup lists only from the outermost
  Process() frame on this thread. Process() re-enters itself via
  'return pl->Process()' after a switch while the outer frame still
  holds its own m_playlistMutex — and that outer instance may already
  be on the cleanup list, so the nested drain deleted an object whose
  locked mutex was still on the stack (unlock-after-free on unwind).

- Don't Start() the new playlist a second time: SwitchToInsertedPlaylist
  already starts it via PlayImpl. The extra Start() replayed the first
  entry — double-counting playOnce entries (which then FinishPlay'd
  themselves) and firing duplicate start events.

- Condemn the old playlist only after the replacement is confirmed
  playing. It was condemned up front, so a failed insert could leave a
  condemned instance as the active global playlist — deleted by the
  next tick's drain and then dereferenced. On failure the instance is
  now condemned only when the failing child's SetIdle() has already
  handed the global to the parent (otherwise it stays live and valid).

Also fixes the switchover log line, which printed an empty name because
the field was cleared just before it was logged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(playlist): route current-entry access through one bounds-checked accessor

m_sectionPosition legitimately parks at exactly the section size while
the playlist is between items, and m_currentSection is null before a
load — but PrevItem, RestartItem, PlayImpl's jump-to-index fast path,
and GetCurrentPosInMS all indexed the section unguarded, so a prev/
restart/start command landing in that window threw std::out_of_range
out of an API or MQTT thread and aborted fppd (the same crash class
previously fixed one site at a time in NextItem and GetCurrentStatus).

CurrentEntry() now gives the guard a single home: the formerly
unguarded sites treat a null entry the way their guarded siblings
always have, and the already-guarded sites go through the accessor so
the invariant can't drift again. Resume() turned out to be unguarded
too and now resumes only a real entry while still leaving the paused
state, so a paused playlist with no current entry can't stick.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(status): copy media playback fields under mediaOutputLock

The status producer read the raw mediaOutput pointer with no lock while
CloseMediaOutput() deletes the object under mediaOutputLock at every
media transition — a use-after-free on the filename string. It was an
occasional per-request race for HTTP polls; the websocket status push
now drives this build once per second from three thread contexts on any
remote-mode box with a page open, so fix it at the producer. The
writers hold the lock only briefly (teardown happens after unlocking),
so the status path cannot stall behind a media stop.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(status): stop status producers before shutdown frees their sources

Two coordinated ordering fixes for the shutdown crash window where a
warning change or notify timeout built a status payload from freed
objects:

- fppd now stops the warning notify thread BEFORE deleting the
  scheduler and sequence, not after. The notify thread's listeners run
  arbitrary code, and the status listener builds a full status payload
  from exactly those objects.

- ~APIServer tears down the status websocket (new idempotent
  StatusWebSocketShutdown()) as its first act, before drogon's quit():
  it removes the warning listener while WarningHolder still holds its
  listener lock semantics (so no notify pass can be in flight after it
  returns) and clears the tracked connections, which drogon's quit()
  does not reliably release through close callbacks. A g_shutdown flag,
  checked under the same mutex by the broadcast paths and by
  handleNewConnection, closes the window where a connection arriving
  mid-teardown could repopulate the set or build a payload against
  dying producers.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(channeloutput): make the threaded-output worker handoff race-free

Three interlocking fixes to ThreadedChannelOutput:

- Init no longer hangs when the worker thread cannot be created. The
  catch block used to fall into 'while (!m_threadIsRunning)' — a flag
  only the never-started thread could set — wedging startup or a config
  reload forever. StartOutputThread now reports failure, the wait is
  bounded by m_runThread, and Init() fails the output so the loader
  rejects it with its normal warning instead of hanging.

- The frame handoff had a lost-wakeup: SendData raised m_dataWaiting
  and notified without holding m_sendLock, against a predicate-less
  wait, so a notify landing between the worker's check and its wait was
  dropped. With 12 of 14 subclasses using an untimed wait, the frame sat
  until the next one arrived. The flags are now owned by m_sendLock and
  both waits take a predicate. (UDMX/USBDMX previously masked this with
  their 250ms timeout and now send on the notify.)

- A pending frame is flushed before the worker honors a stop. The old
  loop checked m_runThread before m_dataWaiting, so the final blanking
  frame — which StopOutputThread follows immediately — was dropped
  deterministically and the lights stayed lit. SendOutputBuffer also
  claims the frame before copying it out; clearing after the copy would
  wipe the flag of a frame that landed mid-send, which is fatal for a
  blanking frame with no successor.

m_bufLock now guards exactly the buffer contents: the worker no longer
takes it to read flags, and it is no longer held across join() — with
the exit flush that hold would deadlock every double-buffered output.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(channeloutput): publish output ranges as immutable snapshots

ComputeOutputRanges() swapped the two range vectors with no lock while
other threads iterated live references handed out by GetOutputRanges()
-- the RT output thread's blanking loop, sequence open, MultiSync, and
the channel tester -- and GetOutputRanges() itself lazily seeded the
default into both vectors unsynchronized. A config reload during
playback could invalidate iterators mid-loop and feed torn range pairs
into memset lengths.

The lists are now immutable vectors published through AtomicSharedPtr
(deliberately mutex-backed with priority inheritance -- see
AtomicSharedPtr.h for why std::atomic<shared_ptr>'s spinlock must not
be used near the RT output thread). GetOutputRangesSnapshot() hands out
shared_ptr snapshots that are never null and never empty (seeded with
the {0,8} default at static init, so the lazy mutation is gone);
ComputeOutputRanges() builds locally and publishes with store().
In-tree callers hold one snapshot per iteration.

GetOutputRanges(bool) keeps its exact original signature as a
plugin-compatibility shim: external plugins call it, and since the
return type is not part of the name mangling, changing it would let an
already-compiled plugin silently misread the return value instead of
failing to link. The shim returns a thread-local copy of the snapshot
(one per precise-flavor), so a plugin's reference stays stable until
the same thread calls again -- plugins get the same race fix instead of
keeping the old exposure.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(channeloutput): make the Fold processor safe for non-RGB node sizes

The constructor divided by the raw UI selector instead of the node size
it selects, and the UI's default option is selector 0 ('By Channel') --
an integer divide-by-zero that SIGFPEs fppd at config load on x86 and
32-bit ARM (aarch64 silently yields 0, still UB). ProcessData also
hardcoded a 3-byte source stride and copy width, so only RGB nodes were
folded correctly: By Channel read three times past the scratch buffer
with overlapping writes, and RGBW misread every node after the first
and never wrote the W byte.

The selector is now translated to a node size once, with a warning and
a By Channel fallback for unknown values, and the fold's index math
uses the node size throughout. The RGB case is byte-identical to the
old behavior (differentially verified across buffer sizes under ASan).
The per-frame scratch allocation is also hoisted to a member sized at
construction. Log messages in the touched lines had mismatched format
arguments and over-reported the channel range; fixed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(channeloutput): clamp model-based processors to the model's real span

ProcessModelConfig compared the channel count alone against the model
size, ignoring the start offset -- a processor starting mid-model could
run past the model's end into whichever channels follow, while the log
reassured that using fewer channels 'may be intentional'. And when the
clamp did fire, the off-by-one dropped the model's last channel.

The check now tests the actual span (offset + count - 1 against the
model's channel count) and clamps to the remaining channels from the
offset, floored at zero for a start entirely past the model. Affects
every model-based processor (Brightness, SetValue, Remap, Clamp, Scale,
Hold, OverrideZero). The overrun path now warns that it is clamping.

fix(channeloutput): zero HoldValue's history so dark channels don't get heap garbage

The held-values buffer was allocated uninitialized, and a channel value
of zero means 'substitute the held value' -- so every covered channel
that started dark output random heap bytes until it first went nonzero,
visibly lighting random pixels at startup. Also fixes the %S wide-string

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(channeloutput): refuse channel ranges that would corrupt the range math

Range lengths are computed as max - min + 1 in unsigned arithmetic, so
a bogus range from an output's GetRequiredChannelRanges underflows to a
~4GB length that eventually reaches the blanking memset. The callers
pass ints, so a negative max isn't even inverted by the time it arrives
-- it shows up as a near-UINT32_MAX value -- which is why the guard also
bounds max against the sequence buffer size. Belt-and-suspenders behind
the per-output fixes: a range this wrong is dropped with an error
rather than clamped, since it never worked anyway.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(channeloutput): fail serial outputs loudly when the port cannot be opened

setupSerialPort() ignored SerialOpen()'s result and returned true with
fd == -1, and SerialOpen's open() failure was the one path in the
function that neither logged nor warned -- exactly the path an
unplugged or absent device takes. Every serial output (DMX-Pro,
Pixelnet, Renard, Relay, Generic Serial, LOR) therefore reported Init
success and then wrote to fd -1 silently every frame: dark props with
nothing in the log or UI. (DMX-Open alone failed by accident, via an
EBADF from its RTS reset with a misleading message.)

The open() failure now logs and raises the same warning id the
function's other failure paths use -- which also finally surfaces
failures for the bridge input caller, which ignores the return value --
and setupSerialPort() checks the fd, warns which output is affected,
and returns false, making every caller's existing failure guard live.
Also frees Generic Serial's packet buffer in its destructor: an output
whose Init() fails is deleted without Close(), a path that could not be
reached before this change.

fix(channeloutput): stop ModelPixelStrings tearing and overrunning its frame buffer

PrepData (output thread) rewrote the model image in place while the
worker thread was handing the same allocation to the overlay model --
torn frames. The base class's double buffer cannot help: the contended
buffer is the model-shaped image, filled through an absolute channel
map the private per-output copy cannot satisfy. PrepData now fills a
second buffer and swaps under a lock the worker also holds while it
hands the frame to the model.

Also fixed while verifying the data flow: the buffer is zeroed (rows
with no string were shipped to the model as uninitialized heap), it is
sized for the model's bytes-per-pixel (setData reads width*height*bpp,
which over-read the allocation by a full plane on RGBW models), string
count is validated against the model height (extra strings wrote past
the buffer), a use-after-free in the too-long-string error log, and a
leaked string on Init failure. Note: PrepData still lays pixels at an
RGB stride, so RGBW overlay models get structurally wrong data -- that
predates this change and needs a design decision, but it no longer

fix(channeloutput): confine zigzag to its own virtual string and fix node-width swaps

Three related map-construction bugs:

- The zigzag fold iterated from the start of the whole port instead of
  the virtual string it belongs to, so a zigzag setting on one virtual
  string re-flipped segments owned by every other string on the port,
  and lead-in/null bytes ahead of it shifted every fold boundary. The
  fold is now anchored at the string's first pixel and stops at its
  last, the same anchoring the reverse path already used. Single-string
  configurations are byte-identical (differentially verified across

  fourth, so RGBW segment ends could read one past the map with mixed

  already did. Nodes now swap exactly channelsPerNode() channels, and
  the fold guard requires the whole last node inside the string.

- The smart receiver count from a hand-edited differentialType was
  unbounded past the 6 receivers the label table and per-receiver state
  arrays hold -- a stack out-of-bounds write. Clamped with a warning,
  and the arrays are sized from one shared constant so they cannot
  drift apart.

fix(channeloutput): give X11PanelMatrix a coherent buffer contract

The output double-buffers, so RawSendData receives a private copy of
just its own channels -- yet it offset that buffer by the absolute
start channel (an out-of-bounds read for any start past 1) and ran the
submatrix overlay on it, whose source channels and enable flag are
absolute sequence addresses that do not even exist in the relative
copy (the enable-flag read was out of bounds even at start channel 1).

The submatrix overlay now runs in PrepData on the absolute sequence
buffer -- where Matrix's math is correct, and where BBBMatrix and

pointers are also null-initialized; the destructor deleted them even

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(status): stop the restart banner flickering off on every status push

Saving a setting that needs an fppd restart raised the banner for a fraction
of a second, then hid it again for 10-25 seconds before it finally stuck.

restartFlag/rebootFlag only ever come from PHP: fppd's own status payload has
never carried them, so api/system/status is their sole producer. Before the
status WebSocket landed, LoadSystemStatus() replaced lastStatusJSON wholesale
from that one response and then fired the change callbacks, so RefreshHeaderBar
copying the flags back out of the cache was reading data it had just written.

Pushing status over the WebSocket broke that invariant without updating the
consumer. lastStatusJSON became a merged cache with two writers on very
different clocks -- fppd's push (~1/s) and the PHP augmentation poll (30s in
WebSocket mode) -- and RefreshHeaderBar kept re-copying the flags on every
push. So a field refreshed every 30 seconds was re-asserted once a second:
set the flag, banner appears, next push re-applies the stale 0, banner hides
until the slow poll catches up. The WebSocket change also widened that window
from 5s to 30s, which is why it went from invisible to obvious.

Take the copy out of RefreshHeaderBar and apply the flags from the response
that actually delivered them. An epoch counter, bumped whenever the page sets
a flag locally, additionally discards a status response that was already in
flight at that moment: it read the settings file before the write landed, so
its value is older than what the page already knows.

Verified with headless Chrome against a live player, sampling the banner every
250ms for 14s after the flag is set: before, hidden in 53 of 55 samples with
settings.restartFlag clobbered back to 0 from t=1.1s; after, hidden in 0 of 55.
The harness asserts the banner became visible at least once, since "never
shown" is indistinguishable from the failure being tested for.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat(multisync): apply sync destination changes without restarting fppd

Ticking a per-remote Unicast checkbox on the MultiSync page, or toggling any
of the send-method checkboxes, flagged fppd as needing a restart. It never
had to: fppd already re-reads the settings file whenever the web UI writes it
(FileMonitor in fppd.cpp), and settings.cpp already has a listener mechanism
for reacting to individual keys. The only thing missing was rebuilding the
destination list those settings feed, which OpenControlSockets() did once at
startup and never again.

Split that parsing out into ReloadSyncDestinations() and register it against
MultiSyncRemotes, MultiSyncExtraRemotes and the three send-method settings.
Hostnames are resolved into a local vector first, since getaddrinfo() is an
unbounded lookup and the send path takes m_socketLock on the output thread
every frame; the sockaddr and mmsghdr vectors are then swapped in together
under that lock, because each mmsghdr points at its own element of the
sockaddr vector and the pair must never be observed half-updated. The rebuild
holds the same lock UpdateUnicastDestinations() uses, so the "all known
remotes" list can't read the static list for its dedupe set mid-swap. The
three send-method flags become atomic: the output thread reads them without
holding anything. Listeners are unregistered in ShutdownSync(), which is
idempotent because the destructor calls it again at static-destruction time;
that also acts as a barrier, since unregistering takes the listener list's
write lock that the firing loop holds while a callback runs.

Two bugs found in the parsing while moving it:

- Hostnames have never worked. A 2020 refactor rewrote "does this contain a
  letter" as `find_if(...) == s.end()`, which is the opposite test, so
  hostnames took the inet_addr() path, came back INADDR_NONE, and were then
  installed as a destination of 255.255.255.255 -- every entry that wasn't
  already a dotted quad silently broadcast its sync packets. An unparseable
  address is now rejected and logged instead of becoming that destination.
- Clearing the remote list stored a literal pair of quote characters, since
  the page PUTs the value as a JSON string. That parsed as a hostname and
  cost a full DNS timeout (~4s) on every load. Tokens are unquoted first.

Verified on a single-core ARM player. Sync destinations, with tcpdump running
across a settings change mid-playback and no restart: packets to the first
loopback address stop, the reload logs, packets to the second start, all
within 250ms and all under one fppd pid -- the new destination starts and the
old one stops. Hostname handling: a remote entered as "localhost" now sends to
127.0.0.1 rather than the broadcast address, and a malformed dotted quad
yields zero destinations instead of one bad one. In headless Chrome, clicking
a per-remote Unicast checkbox raises no restart banner in 60 samples over 15s
(one flash before this change) and the checkbox survives every table re-render.

Fixes #2834

perf(channeloutput): batch LOR and USB relay serial writes

LOR issued one 6-byte write() per changed channel -- a fade across
hundreds of channels was hundreds of syscalls per frame. Commands now
accumulate and flush in chunks sized under the tty's queue (the fd is
non-blocking, so a single worst-case 23KB write would silently drop its
tail), with boundaries always between commands and the flush always
ahead of the trailing heartbeat. Bytes on the wire are identical.

The CH340 relay path wrote 4 bytes per relay every frame -- 1280 B/s of
mostly-identical state through a port that carries 960 B/s. Relays
latch, so only changed relays are sent now (the first frame always
transmits everything, via an 'unknown' initial state, so a genuinely
all-off opening frame still establishes startup state), batched into
one write. The low-rate bitstream path keeps its per-frame refresh and
just gains the batching.

build: give shared objects an $ORIGIN RUNPATH so plugins can dlopen their deps

A dlopen()ed plugin resolves its own dependencies through its own
RUNPATH, not the executable's -- so a channel output plugin that links
another (GenericUDP needs UDPOutput) only loaded if something else had
already pulled its dependency into the process. That held whenever an
E1.31/DDP config loaded first, and failed with a bare null dlerror for
a config using only the dependent output. Linux g++ links only; macOS
resolves these at build time.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(channeloutput): validate the Brightness processor's config

gamma and brightness were read with no validation at all. A blank UI
field arrives as JSON null, and a config predating the gamma field has
no key -- both read back as 0, and pow(x, 0) is 1, so a zero gamma
built a table that drove every input at the full brightness value:
dark channels lit at 100%. A missing brightness went the other way and
blacked the range out.

Missing or null values now fall back to the UI defaults (100 / 1.0)
and out-of-range values clamp, each with a warning naming the
processor. Valid configs build a byte-identical table -- the loop is
untouched.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(playlist): own playlists through shared_ptr so readers can't race deletion

The current playlist was a plain global deleted by the main loop's
cleanup drain while HTTP, MQTT, and command threads dereferenced it
with no synchronization -- a status poll racing an inserted-playlist
finish was a cross-thread use-after-free.

Player now owns every playlist it creates: the current one is published
through a mutex-backed atomic shared_ptr (AtomicSharedPtr, same
rationale as the output-range snapshots), a registry holds every
instance still reachable through the parent chain, and every Player
method pins one snapshot for the duration of its call. The internal
lifecycle -- the cleanup lists, the drain depth gate, the raw parent
chain, the idle walk -- is structurally unchanged; the drain now drops
the owning reference instead of deleting, so an instance a reader still
holds lives until that reader is done. Destruction stays main-thread
only: the shared_ptr deleter parks the pointer and the drain deletes at
the same point in the frame it always did (~Playlist parks its entries
on a main-thread-only list, so it must never run on a reader thread).

The 'extern Playlist* playlist' global becomes a source-compatible
arrow-proxy: plugin code like playlist->GetCurrentPosInMS(...) compiles
unchanged, and the proxy's temporary handle pins a snapshot for the
full expression, making the old plugin idiom lifetime-safe rather than
merely still-compiling. ABI is deliberately not preserved -- plugins
recompile against these headers at update. Nothing in-tree uses the
facade; all internal access goes through the owner.

Player::Process() deliberately re-snapshots before delegating: its stop
handling can unwind an inserted playlist and hand the player back to
the parent, and the tick must process whichever playlist is current
after that, as the raw global read always did.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(playlist): synchronize the cleanup lists and the status flag

Running the ownership fix under ThreadSanitizer surfaced two
pre-existing races the old use-after-free noise had drowned out:

- The condemned-playlist and parked-entry lists are reached from
  command threads as well as the main loop -- a stop on an HTTP thread
  condemns instances in SetIdle and a Load parks replaced entries --
  while the main loop drained both unsynchronized. Every access now
  holds one lock; deletes still run outside it (entry destructors park
  further entries, so the entry drain swaps the list out and loops
  until a pass drains nothing). The lock is held across the whole
  condemned pass so SetIdle's condemned-parent walk never observes a
  half-drained list.

- m_status was volatile, which never made the unlocked cross-thread
  getter reads well-defined; it is now atomic.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(www): harden the status WebSocket client

Five interlocking fixes to the /fppdws consumer plus a hidden-tab
behavior change:

- Handlers are bound to the socket generation that installed them, and
  a replaced socket's handlers are detached. A wedged socket the
  watchdog abandons can deliver its close event a TCP timeout later --
  that late event tore down the NEW connection's state and cleared its
  watchdog, which only onopen re-arms, leaving the page showing frozen
  status forever while claiming to be WebSocket-fed.

- The page only flips into WebSocket-fed mode on a successfully parsed
  status snapshot, not on any received frame; a garbage first frame no
  longer switches the poll to augmentation-only with no status base.

- Snapshots rebuild the status object instead of Object.assign-merging
  into it. fppd emits several keys only conditionally (breadcrumbs
  while a nested playlist runs, media fields while playing), so merging
  left their last values in place forever -- a stale '(Main -> ...)'
  label long after the nested playlist ended. The PHP augmentation keys
  (enumerated from finalizeStatusJson) are carried across; everything
  fppd-owned is replaced.

- Status-change callbacks each run in their own try/catch, and
  RefreshHeaderBar tolerates a payload without advancedView -- one
  consumer dereferencing a key only one status source carries could
  previously kill the whole render chain for the tick.

- A full poll response that raced a WebSocket connection no longer
  clobbers the fresher pushed status and its warnings.

- Hidden tabs keep the socket but skip the per-second DOM work, buffer
  the newest snapshot, and catch up in one pass on return to visible;
  the WS down/up transition polls no longer resurrect polling in a
  hidden tab.

Verified with behavioral harnesses run against the extracted function
bodies (35 assertions; the pre-fix baseline fails them with the exact
reported symptoms, including the HostDescription TypeError and the
dead-watchdog sequence).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(build): give plugins the same CFLAGS the core builds its PCH with

External plugins include only makefiles/common/setup.mk and
makefiles/platform/*.mk, but the gstreamer and libdrm detection lived in
fpp_so.mk, which only the core reads. Two consequences:

  * gstreamer's pkg-config --cflags ends in -pthread, so the core (and
    therefore fpp-pch.h.gch) compiles with _REENTRANT defined and every
    plugin without it. gcc then refuses the PCH -- "not used because
    `_REENTRANT' not defined" -- and re-parses the whole header in each
    plugin TU.

  * Headers in mediaoutput/ gate class members on
    __has_include(<gst/gst.h>), and framebuffer/KMSFrameBuffer.h on
    __has_include(<xf86drm.h>). A plugin compiled without those -I paths
    sees a different layout for those classes than libfpp.so was built
    with. That one has no diagnostic at all; the PCH warning was just the
    visible face of it.

Move both detections into setup.mk so core and plugin CFLAGS are identical
by construction; the link flags stay in fpp_so.mk, since only the core
links them.

Also list the makefile fragments as prerequisites of fpp-pch.h.gch, the
same way every %.o rule already does. Otherwise a CFLAGS edit rebuilds
every object but leaves the .gch alone, and the two disagree on macro
state for the rest of that tree's life.

The flags now land before the platform -D's rather than after, so the
first build after this is a full ccache miss. Content is unchanged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(sequence): copy m_seqFilename under a lock for cross-thread readers

m_seqFilename is a public std::string reassigned by the sequence
open/close paths and read from other threads -- the status producer
(now polled at 1Hz by the websocket push from three thread contexts),
MultiSync, OutputMonitor, and the output thread's per-frame sync
packet. A reallocating assignment can hand a concurrent reader a freed
buffer.

A dedicated innermost mutex now guards the string: the three writes
take it (they already held m_sequenceLock), and a GetSeqFilenameCopy()
accessor copies under it. Every cross-thread reader goes through the
accessor, including two internal reads that were also racing --
StartSequence and SendSequenceData/CloseSequenceFile run without
m_sequenceLock. The member stays public with its name for plugin
source compatibility. The crash signal handler keeps reading it raw and
says why: taking a lock there could self-deadlock the report against a
thread the signal interrupted mid-write.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(status): build each websocket snapshot under the lock, drop the dead version map

Two changes to the status push:

The snapshot JSON was built outside g_mutex on three thread contexts
(the drogon timer, the warning-notify thread, and IO threads via
handleNewConnection), so a slower thread could win the lock after a
faster one and publish an older payload as the newest state -- a
just-added warning could blink away for a second. The build now happens
inside g_mutex; only the sends stay outside it (target list copied under
the lock, sent after). g_mutex is file-static and taken only from those
entry points, none of which hold any lock buildStatusJson reaches, so
the nesting is one-directional.

The envelope's per-key version map is removed. The client never read
it, per-connection version bumps made the numbers non-comparable
between clients anyway, and each snapshot is already complete for the
keys it carries -- a reconnecting client re-syncs with the full status
poll it has to do regardless. The wire format is now
{type:snapshot, data:{...}}, and the format comment is rewritten to
match.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(www): build plugin header indicators through the DOM, not string concatenation

RefreshHeaderBar concatenated six plugin-supplied fields straight into
markup, including an inline onclick built from indicator.link and
data-plugin from indicator.pluginName -- a plugin value could break out
of the attribute and run script in the authenticated FPP UI. The block
is now built with DOM construction: the link is validated (http/https
only, javascript:/data: rejected) and held in a click closure, the
color and icon and animation names are pattern-checked and applied via
.css()/.addClass(), and the text fields go through .attr(), which
cannot break out. Malformed values fall back to the generic defaults
with a console warning naming the plugin. Rendered output is unchanged
for well-formed data (the two duplicated inline styles already live in
.pluginIndicator). The render cache is keyed off the raw values now,
since the link lives only in the closure.

Other unescaped header fields from different sources (media filenames,
sensor labels, interface names) are the same class of bug and left as
follow-ups.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(schedule): survive invalid values in settings and schedule.json

Both files are hand- and API-editable, and the scheduler reads them from
the Scheduler constructor on the fppd startup path, where nothing above
catches an exception. Six ways a bad value took the daemon down or hung
it, each reproduced on hardware against a fixture before the fix:

Latitude/Longitude went through std::stod(), so a value like "N38.9"
threw out of the constructor and put fppd in a boot loop. They are parsed
with strtod() and an end-pointer check now, falling back to the default
coordinates. Warning 48 covers unset and unparseable alike, so its add
and its remove pair on one string.

A negative "repeat" divides and scales to a negative interval, which
walks startTime backwards in both occurrence-expansion loops; they never
reach endTime and append pairs until the process dies of bad_alloc. It is
clamped at load, and both loops now require a positive interval.

The holiday day-of-week calculation indexed its month table above the
branch that assigns the month, so every easter and lunar holiday read
t[-1]. It is computed only in the branch that uses it, and the month
coming from JSON is range-checked.

A start or end time string with fewer than three colon-separated parts
indexed split()'s vector out of bounds. Both readers share
ParseTimeString(), which takes HH:MM as well as HH:MM:SS and reports
anything shorter.

pushStartEndTimes built std::pair<int, int> temporaries out of time_t,
narrowing every occurrence through a 32-bit int on the way into a
pair<time_t, time_t>. Past 2038 that wraps negative and the schedule
serves no items at all -- with the clock set to 2039 the API returned
zero occurrences for an entry that yields 32.

"Extend Schedule" called std::stoi() on its arguments, so an unset %VAR%
or a typo threw on the detached scheduler thread, which is std::terminate
by definition; it parses defensively and returns an error result. The
detached command thread also gets a catch-all, so a throwing command from
anywhere -- including one this commit does not touch -- is a logged error
rather than the end of the show.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(playlist): bound what a URL step sends and what a branch step accepts

PlaylistEntryURL passed a hardcoded 4096 to CURLOPT_POSTFIELDSIZE
regardless of the body it was sending. curl copies exactly that many
bytes, so a body shorter than 4096 shipped the adjacent heap to the
remote host and a longer one was truncated. Captured against a local
listener, a four-byte body went out as Content-Length 4096 carrying
4092 bytes of live process memory, heap and stack pointers included. It
now sends the body's own length.

PlaylistEntryBranch read two settings without checking them. A time of
"8:00" rather than "08:00:00" indexed split()'s vector out of bounds --
with libstdc++ assertions on, that aborts inside Init() on the thread
handling the API request that started the playlist. It goes through the
shared ParseTimeString() now, which accepts HH:MM. An iteration count of
0 reaches a modulo by zero in the Loop test; the editor enforces a
minimum of 1 but hand-written and API-supplied JSON does not, so it is
clamped at load. Note that on arm64 the modulo does not trap -- it
quietly yields 0 and takes the wrong branch -- so this reads as a
scheduling oddity on the SBCs and as a SIGFPE elsewhere.

Both branch cases raise warning 62, new here for a playlist entry
setting FPP cannot use.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(build): derive the PCH's header prerequisites with -MMD

The fpp-pch.h.gch rule was the one compile in the tree that did not get
$(DEPFLAGS), so it generated no dependency file and relied on a
hand-written list of headers instead. That list named only what
fpp-pch.h included when it was written, and only one level deep, so it
had drifted: fpp-json.h and Events.h are included directly and were both
absent, as was common_mini.h one level under common.h. Editing any of
them left make reporting the .gch up to date, and every translation unit
then compiled against the stale declarations baked into it -- adding a
function to common_mini.h produced "not declared in this scope" for its
callers until the .gch was deleted by hand.

gcc does emit a dependency file for a header compile; it just names it
after the -o argument with the suffix replaced, so it lands as
fpp-pch.h.d and $(DEPFILES) -- built from the object list -- never
matches it. It gets its own -include, and clean removes it.

The makefile fragments stay listed explicitly: they decide the flags
rather than the contents, and -MMD cannot see them. Verified in both
directions -- touching common_mini.h or Events.h now rebuilds the .gch,
touching an unrelated header does not.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(framebuffer): stop the draw loop before any derived teardown

FrameBuffer::~FrameBuffer() was the only place the draw/sync loop was
stopped and joined, and it runs last.  Every subclass destructor body had
already executed by then, so across the whole of ~KMSFrameBuffer() -- which
disables the plane and, on the last framebuffer, closes the DRM card fds and
deletes the CardInfo objects -- the loop thread was still live in
FBDrawNormal(), writing into the mapped dumb buffer and then making a virtual
SyncDisplay() call on an object whose vtable was already demoted to the base.
Saving a channel-output config drives this: the FileMonitor reload calls
FBMatrixOutput::Close(), and the loop thread faults in that window while the
main thread sits in the join().

Add a protected, idempotent StopDrawLoop() and make it the first statement of
every subclass destructor, so the thread is dead before any derived state goes
away.  It also flips m_runLoop under m_bufferLock; the old bare notify_all()
could be lost between DrawLoop()'s predicate check and its wait(), leaving the
join() to hang forever.

Same read turned up a second defect: ~FrameBuffer() invoked the virtual
DestroyFrameBuffer(), which from a base destructor can only ever reach
FrameBuffer::DestroyFrameBuffer().  KMSFrameBuffer's, IOCTLFrameBuffer's and
SocketFrameBuffer's overrides therefore never ran on delete, leaking the dumb
buffers and permanently holding the connector/CRTC/plane reservations across a
reload (and leaving the tty in graphics mode on the fbdev path).  Each subclass
now calls its own DestroyFrameBuffer() from its destructor, where the call
resolves, and the overrides are made idempotent so the init-failure path that
already calls them cannot double-free.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(scheduler): synchronize the ran-items prune and the reload flag

ScheduleProc pruned m_ranItems (the map of items already run) without
holding m_scheduleLock, while SetItemRan mutates the same map under the
lock from HTTP, MQTT, and detached command threads -- concurrent map
mutation is undefined behavior, the kind that surfaces as an unrelated
crash after a midnight rollover or a clock step. The prune now holds the
lock. m_loadSchedule, written lock-free from ScheduleProc,
ReloadScheduleFile, and SetTimeDelta on different threads, is now atomic.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(playlist): don't let a transient file read replace a playing show

FileHasBeenModified ignored stat()'s return value, so a momentarily
absent playlist file -- the brief window a non-atomic UI save
(write-temp-then-rename) opens -- left attr uninitialized and compared
stack garbage against the stored mtime, fabricating a spurious
"modified". The reload that followed loaded an empty root (the file was
gone) over the running playlist, Cleanup()ing it and silently stopping
the show even as the file reappeared milliseconds later.

Two guards: FileHasBeenModified returns "not modified" when stat fails,
and -- the invariant fix -- ReloadPlaylist refuses to install a failed
load. That needed a real failure signal: LoadJsonFromFile normalizes
every failure to an empty object, indistinguishable from a validly
empty playlist, so LoadJSON now returns a null root on failure while a
real parse (even of an empty playlist) returns an object. ReloadPlaylist
bails on null and keeps the running playlist; a genuine reload to an
empty file still works.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(playlist): derive the status string from the enum so paused isn't reported as playing

Pause() moved only the m_status enum; the m_currentState string mirror
that GetInfo/GetMqttStatusJSON/GetCurrentStatus and the "status" event
report had no paused value, so a paused playlist announced "playing" to
MQTT and status consumers.

The string mirror is deleted. A single PlaylistStatusToString(m_status)
is now the one place the enum becomes a string, so the two can't drift:
it returns the exact camelCase values the code always used, plus
"paused" (which www/multisync.php and the status_name path already
expect) and "stoppingNow" (a state the old mirror never named, and that
no reader can observe -- SetIdle overwrites it within the same lock
hold). The == "idle" guards become direct enum comparisons. Behavior is
unchanged for every non-paused state; only paused now reports correctly.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(settings): store fan trip temperatures with a decimal so F round-trips

Fan temperatures are stored in C because that is what the kernel wants,
but a whole degree C cannot name every whole degree F: 85F rounds to
29C, which reads back as 84F. 60 of the 136 F values in the settable
range drift a degree that way, so a value entered in F frequently -- but
not always -- came back changed after a page reload.

The saved value now carries one decimal place. A tenth of a degree C is
0.18F, so the worst-case storage error is 0.09F and every whole degree F
survives the round trip; a value entered in C is still a whole number.

Two consumers assumed an integer and had to be fixed with it:

- applyThermalSettings() read the setting with getRawSettingInt(), whose
  hand-rolled digit loop does not stop at a decimal point and turns
  "29.4" into 2884. The kernel accepts the resulting 2884000-millidegree
  trip write, so the fan would simply have stopped turning on after the
  next boot. It now reads the raw string and parses a float.

- SetGPIOFanProperties() built millidegrees for the gpio-fan overlay by
  appending "000" to the setting; it now multiplies.

Displaying in C also sets step="any" on the input, since a value holding
a tenth is invalid against the default step of 1. Existing whole-degree
values stay valid and stable -- they just aren't exact until re-entered.

Fixes #2840

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
fix(channeltester): improve error message construction for test start argument validation

fix(playlist): stop PlaylistEntryImage leaking its buffer and garbling one-off sizes

The image buffer (new unsigned char[width*height*3], ~1.4MB for the
default size) was never freed -- the destructor joined the prep thread
and restored the model but never delete[]'d it, so every image entry
leaked one buffer per playlist load. Freed in the destructor now, after
the thread join so no prep write races the free.

The scale guard also used && where the re-read guard uses ||, so an
image matching exactly one of the model's two dimensions was never
scaled: its RGB blob came out the wrong size and the length-guarded
copy truncated it into a garbled render. Both guards are || now -- an
image is scaled when it differs in either dimension, and one matching
both is still (correctly) left alone.

The thread pointer and the volatile bool flags also gained default
member initializers: they were only assigned on Init()'s success path,
so an Init that failed early left them indeterminate -- which the next
commit's destructor would then act on.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(playlist): delete a playlist entry whose Init() failed

LoadPlaylistEntry (and PlaylistEntryDynamic::ReadFromString) returned
NULL on Init failure without deleting the entry it had just new'd --

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

refactor(schedule): one day-index-to-mask and odd/even helper for scheduler and calendar

The 14-case dayIndex->mask switch and the FPP-epoch odd/even parity
test each existed in two places -- the live scheduler
(AddScheduledItems) and the calendar preview (OccursOnDate) -- exactly
the kind of duplication that lets the two disagree about which days an
entry runs. Both are now ScheduleEntry::DayIndexToMask() and
IsOddEvenMatch(), byte-for-byte the same mappings (default returns the

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(scheduler): confine the Saturday crossover to Saturday, and don't drop missed commands

Two scheduling bugs:

The Sunday-morning crossover push -- which schedules yesterday
(Saturday) 22:00->02:00 so a show crossing midnight into Sunday still
runs -- fired for EVERY enabled entry, with no day check, so a
Monday-only 22:00->02:00 entry got a Saturday occurrence and played
early Sunday. It now fires only for entries that actually run on
Saturday (day mask), and skips odd/even entries, whose crossover the
parity block above already handles with Saturday's own parity.

Scheduled FPP commands were dropped unless the scheduler ticked on their
exact second: a slow midnight reload in the same pass, an NTP step, or a
stalled loop pushed the clock past a 00:00:00 command and it was marked
ran without executing -- silently. A command now fires when its second
falls in the (last-checked, now] window, capped at 60 seconds late so a
large forward clock step logs and skips stale commands rather than
replaying a batch. Double-firing is prevented by the window's lower
bound (advanced once per pass, past a reload that resets the ran flags)
plus the existing ran flag within a pass. Playlists need no window --
they already tolerate a late start via their end time.

cleanup(schedule): remove the dead CSV schedule-entry parser

schedule format and has had no callers anywhere in the tree since the

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(playlist): run URL playlist steps asynchronously through CurlManager

A URL playlist step hand-rolled a curl handle and did a blocking
curl_easy_perform on the main loop -- up to a 30s freeze of playback,
media, and the scheduler if the target host was slow -- even though the
step discards the response and finishes the instant the request is
sent. It now dispatches the request through CurlManager (async, pumped
by the main loop) and finishes immediately; the completion callback only
logs, and warns on a non-2xx, capturing the URL by value so it never
touches the (possibly already destroyed) entry.

This also retires the last of the hand-rolled curl setup here in favor
of the shared client, which brings the FPP User-Agent and consistent
timeouts, and drops the POSTFIELDSIZE handling entirely (CurlManager
copies the body via COPYPOSTFIELDS).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat(curl): let CurlManager share cookies across a request group

Adds an optional cookie 'session' to the async add/addGet and sync
doGet paths: requests tagged with the same session token share an
in-memory cookie jar (a per-token CURLSH with CURL_LOCK_DATA_COOKIE),
so an ordered sequence of requests keeps its server-side session (PHP
PHPSESSID etc.) the way a single reused easy handle did. The share
carries lock/unlock callbacks over its own mutex, since CurlManager is
driven from more than one processCurls() site and a share crossing
threads must be locked.

releaseCookieSession() ends a session; it refuses to free a share curl
still reports in use (that would free the mutex curl holds -- a UAF) and
leaks with a loud log instead, which the caller avoids by cancelling the
session's requests first. Existing callers are unaffected: the session
argument defaults to empty (no share), exactly today's behavior.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(playlist): fetch dynamic plugin items asynchronously

A plugin-backed dynamic playlist ran three blocking curl requests per
item transition (prepNextItem, loadNextItem, startedNextItem, 5s
timeout each) on the main loop, freezing playback, media, and the
scheduler for up to ~15s when the plugin host was slow.

The prep->load chain now runs asynchronously through CurlManager during
the entry's Prep() window: Prep fires prepNextItem, its completion
chains loadNextItem, and the loaded item JSON is buffered so
StartPlaying consumes it with no blocking in the normal ahead-of-time
prep case. A per-instance cookie session (also the CurlManager owner
tag) keeps the prep->load pair on one server session, the way the old
reused handle did. startedNextItem becomes async fire-and-forget. When
prep hasn't completed by StartPlaying (inline prep, cold start), a
bounded pump waits up to 15s -- no worse than the old fully synchronous
path, and a dead host now fails on the 2s connect timeout instead of
hanging.

Lifecycle: the load callback touches this entry, so the destructor
cancels the entry's in-flight requests (CurlManager destroys their
callbacks without invoking them) before releasing the cookie session;

fix(multisync): bound control-packet parsing against remote-supplied lengths

The receive buffers are reused across recvmmsg batches, so any parse that
walks past a packet's own extraDataLen reads stale bytes from earlier

  hand stale garbage to CommandManager as a command.  Parse against the

  name made the length run one past the datagram and left a negative data
  length for plugins, which take it as size_t.  Use strnlen against
  extraDataLen and reject unterminated names.

  so one empty datagram in a batch misaligned the dedup indexes and read
  past the vector.  Keep one entry per message (null for invalid ones)

refactor: drive async Result polling from Timers instead of main-loop ticks

RecurringTasks::tick() and IfCommand::tick() were called unconditionally
every fppd main-loop iteration just to poll in-flight async Command::Results.
Replace both with a self-re-arming one-shot timer (100ms / 50ms) that is
armed when work is parked and re-armed only while any remains, removing the
per-iteration calls and the fppd.cpp coupling entirely.

One-shot rather than periodic is deliberate: a periodic timer would have to
stop itself from inside its own callback, and stopPeriodicTimer() deletes
the TimerInfo - including the std::function currently executing. One-shots
are removed from the timer list before the callback runs and deleted after
it returns, so re-adding under the same name from within the callback is
safe. Every push of pending work is followed by an arm on the same thread,
so a poll can never be missed; a racing arm at worst fires once and finds
nothing to do.

IfCommand::tick is removed from the public header; RecurringTasks::tick
becomes the private pollPending().

fix(outputmonitor): don't let the smart-receiver callback outlive its owner

SetOutput() copied srCallback out from under gpioLock and invoked the copy
after releasing it.  The callback is installed by FalconV5Support and captures
its raw 'this', so the copy carries no ownership: a string-config reload
destroying that object between the copy and the call left the dispatch writing
into freed memory.  The destructor's unregister could not prevent it -- it can
only clear the member, never a copy already on another thread's stack.  The
window is reachable because "Set Port Status" arrives on the API, MQTT, GPIO,
and scheduler threads while the reload runs elsewhere.

Invoke the callback through the member under a dedicated mutex that
setSmartReceiverEventCallback() also takes.  The unregister then blocks behind
any in-flight call and no call can start after it returns, so no copy escapes.
Kept separate from gpioLock so dispatch still happens with the port state
unlocked and can't re-enter into a self-deadlock.

The state the callback publishes had the same problem one level down: the
port, receiver index, and command string were three unsynchronized fields
written from the command thread and read by the packet generator on the output
thread.  As well as pairing a new port with a stale command, assigning and
comparing the std::string concurrently is a torn read of a heap pointer.
Replace them with a single lock-free atomic word, snapshotted once per pass and
cleared with a compare_exchange so a request arriving mid-pass isn't dropped.
static_asserts pin the two properties that relies on: no padding (the exchange
compares the object representation) and lock-freedom, which is what keeps the
32-bit build off a libatomic lock.

Builds clean for 32-bit and 64-bit BeagleBone platforms; the padding assert was
confirmed to fail when deliberately broken.

fix(channeloutput): don't run OUTPUTS_DISABLED presets in a state that wedges the output thread

The output thread's exit path cleared ThreadIsRunning and then called
StoppingOutput() while holding both outputThreadLock and the non-recursive
outputThreadStatusLock. StoppingOutput() fires the OUTPUTS_DISABLED command
presets on that same thread, so any preset command that reaches
StartChannelOutputThread() (starting an effect, enabling an overlay model,
starting a playlist) self-deadlocked on outputThreadStatusLock - and even
without that, it spawned a replacement thread that blocked on the held
outputThreadLock while the preset spun forever waiting for it to come up.
The wedged command also pins whatever locks it holds (the overlay commands
hold modelsLock), so every /api/overlays and /api/models request then hangs
while /api/fppd/status keeps answering 200 - fppd looks healthy but the UI
is dead until a restart.

Fire StoppingOutput() with ThreadIsRunning still set, ThreadIsExiting set,
and statusLock released, keeping outputThreadLock held so a replacement
thread's StartingOutput() cannot interleave with the disable. A preset that
restarts output now queues its replacement on outputThreadLock and its
startup wait returns immediately. Also cap the previously unbounded
startup spin at 5 seconds, mirroring StopChannelOutputThread().

Reproduced on real hardware with an OUTPUTS_DISABLED preset running
"Overlay Model State ... Enabled": stock build wedges with two replacement
threads parked on outputThreadLock; fixed build hands off cleanly on every
idle-out.

fix(sequence): fire sequence presets from the main loop, not under the sequence locks

Sequence::CloseSequenceFile() and StartSequence() triggered the
SEQUENCE_STOPPED/SEQUENCE_STARTED command presets while holding
m_sequenceLock (often recursively, from CloseIfOpen, the filename overload,
or ReadSequenceData on the channel output thread). A preset that starts or
stops a playlist takes m_playlistMutex - the reverse of the playlist
thread's m_playlistMutex -> m_sequenceLock order when opening a sequence -
so an HTTP "Start Playlist" command racing a MultiSync-driven sequence stop
(or a second HTTP thread's "Stop Now") deadlocked the two threads. Same
class of inversion af22a8f5e fixed for the scheduler lock.

Firing after unlock inside those functions is not enough, because callers
hold m_sequenceLock recursively across them. Instead, queue the preset into
a small FIFO drained by a one-shot Timers entry on the main loop with no
sequence locks held. Ordering stays deterministic (STOPPED before STARTED
across a transition), and the shared timer name is safe because the drain
empties the whole queue.

The FSEQ frame-triggered presets in SendSequenceData() go through the same
queue, which also stops the channel output thread from running arbitrary
commands while it holds outputThreadLock for the frame. Presets now execute
a few milliseconds after the triggering event, on the main loop - the same
thread that already runs presets arriving via MultiSync.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(overlays): never block on modelsLock from under a model's effectLock

The effect update threads can reach PixelOverlayModelSub::setState() while
holding the model's effectLock (an effect stopping calls setState on its
model), and an unresolved submodel parent then made foundParent() block on
modelsLock via getModel(). Every HTTP and command path takes those locks
the other way - modelsLock for the lookup, then effectLock to inspect or
replace the running effect - so the two directions deadlock. Same shape as
37c8f92a8, one lock over, and worse: the effectLock side can run on the
channel output thread via updateRunningEffects(), wedging output as well as
the API. An unresolved parent is reachable at runtime because deleting a
model resets every child's cached parent to null.

Add PixelOverlayManager::tryGetModel(), a try_lock lookup, and use it for
parent resolution. Paths that already hold modelsLock (all the manager and
command paths) still resolve exactly as before - the recursive try_lock
always succeeds. A contended effect-side resolve now returns unresolved and
retries on the next setState instead of blocking, which leaves
modelsLock -> effectLock as the only ordering in the subsystem, so the
cycle can no longer close.

fix(bridge): reload safety, packet length validation, and receive-path efficiency

Correctness:
- DMX serial inputs now live in their own list of shared_ptr entries instead
  of being interleaved into the UDP universe vector. A ci-universes.json
  reload used to rebuild that vector from index 0, destroying the DMX entries
  while their epoll callbacks kept writing through captured (now stale)
  indices - bridge data landed at the wrong channels and the serial port
  leaked. The callbacks now capture the entry itself, so neither reload path
  can invalidate the other's state.
- The universe lists are rebuilt locally and swapped in under a new structure
  lock, which the HTTP-thread stats readers (GetE131UniverseBytesReceived,
  ResetBytesReceived) also take. A stats poll during a config reload could
  previously iterate the vector mid-rebuild. The packet path shares the
  main-loop thread with every mutation and stays lock-free.
- All three protocols now validate against the actual received datagram
  length (the receive buffers are reused, so bytes past msg_len are stale
  data from earlier packets). E1.31 clamps the stored data to
  min(configured size, received bytes, DMP property count) instead of always
  copying the configured size, and counts truncated packets as errors;
  ArtDMX clamps its length field to received bytes; DDP requires its header,
  bounds its length field, and no longer honors a push flag read from a
  malformed packet.

Performance:
- The universe-number cache now caches misses too. The sync-address check
  runs a lookup on every data packet, and the advertised sync universe is
  normally not a configured input, so every packet paid a full scan of the
  universe list - at several hundred universes that dominated per-packet
  cost.
- Bridge range bookkeeping is committed once per recvmmsg drain instead of
  once per packet (SetBridgeData split into WriteBridgeData +
  CommitBridgeRanges), and ProcessSequenceData now snapshots/prunes the
  ranges under the lock but runs the merge memcpys after releasing it, so
  the receive path is never blocked on the merge.
- hasBridgeData() is a relaxed atomic instead of a mutex (called several
  times per frame from two threads), and the per-frame merge scratch is a
  reused vector instead of a fresh std::map.

Stats:
- Per-universe suppressedPackets (from the BridgeSourcePriority feature) is
  now reported by /api/fppd/e131stats, cleared on reset, and shown as a
  column in the UI stats table when nonzero.
- The ArtNet unconfigured-universe byte counter reuses the clamped ArtDMX
  length instead of re-parsing with the E1.31 12-bit mask.

Verified end-to-end on real hardware: E1.31/DDP/ArtNet packets in, byte-
identical E1.31 loopback output captured and compared, including short /
truncated / lying-length packets per protocol, two-source priority
suppression and takeover, and 80 config reloads under a concurrent stats
hammer and packet load.

fix(audio): stop postNetwork waiting 15s on boards with no audio hardware

Two stacked boot-time waits fired on a board with no audio at all:

- AudioOutput gets canonicalized to the synthetic snd-dummy card's ID
  ("Dummy") when no real card exists, and the next boot then waited the
  full 10 seconds for a card named Dummy to register -- which can never
  happen, because snd-dummy is only modprobed after that wait. Treat
  "Dummy" as an explicit selection: load snd-dummy immediately so every
  wait is already satisfied, and skip the hardware-bind wait since the
  user asked for no real audio.

- deviceTreeDeclaresSoundCard() only checked that a sound node exists.
  Some device trees (e.g. AM62x boards) ship the simple-audio-card node
  with status "disabled" until an audio cape overlay enables it; a
  disabled node can never bind, so it burned the 5-second bind wait on
  every capeless board. Honor the status property (absent means enabled
  per the DT spec).

Also keep the preloaded Dummy card out of the noRealSoundcard
computation so the PipeWire skip-probe fast paths still fire, and skip
the later "No Soundcard Detected" modprobe when Dummy is already
registered. Verified on a capeless PocketBeagle2: the postNetwork audio
path drops from ~15s to ~1s, and a board with real cape audio (DT
status "okay") still gets the bind wait.

fix(boot): drop the redundant auto-bootDelay network poll

In auto bootDelay mode, handleBootDelay() polled up to 5 seconds for an
NTP-capable interface before postNetwork's concurrent audio/network
threads even started -- serial dead time on every boot, and a flat 5s
loss on a box with no network at all (which then paid the link-wait
timeout again anyway).

The poll was load-bearing when it was added: waitForInterfacesUp() then
bailed out instantly if no interface had link yet, so a fast-booting
board could skip the IP/NTP wait before its NIC came up. Since the June
rework, waitForInterfacesUp() itself waits up to half its timeout for
link before deciding anything, and handleTimeSyncWait() re-checks for
an NTP-capable interface after that wait -- so the pre-poll's verdict
was computed and then discarded. Verified on a Pi 5 booting with the
network not yet up: the in-function link wait catches it (3s) and the
time-sync path proceeds normally.

Also give announceIPAddresses() a bounded wait for an address: the boot
IP wait can time out with the DHCP lease landing moments later, and the
announce service previously assumed the address was already there and
silently skipped announcing. It runs off fppd's critical path, so
waiting there is free.
