fix(ui): show a settings child listed under more than one parent value

The generated Update<setting>Children() emitted one independent if/else per
parent value, so a child appearing under two values (Compile Hosts, under both
'distcc' and 'nocc') was marked hidden by whichever branch did not match:

    if (val == 'distcc') { ...show... }
    else { hide; hiddenChildren.DistccHosts = 1; }
    if (val == 'nocc')   { if (mode == 0 || hiddenChildren.DistccHosts != 1) show }
    else { hide; hiddenChildren.DistccHosts = 1; }

On page load UpdateChildSettingsVisibility() runs a hide pass then a show pass,
and the show pass is gated on that flag, so the row never came back.  On the
onChange path (mode 0) the gate is skipped and the last emitted block won, which
is why one value appeared to work when the dropdown was changed but neither
survived a reload.

Replace the three copies of the emitter (checkbox, select, text) with one shared
PrintSettingChildrenFunction() that builds the show set for the current value
first and only hides children that are not in it.  Cross-parent behaviour is
unchanged: a child claimed by two parents is still hidden if either hides it.
Also index hiddenChildren with brackets and escape dots in the row selector so a
plugin setting with a dotted child name cannot break the generated code.

Verified by rendering every setting that declares children through the real
generators, before and after, and simulating both passes: 115 child/value combos
on the load path and 115 on the onChange path differ only for the affected
setting, and 8 cross-parent combos are identical.

refactor(pixeloverlay): remove unused colorOrder parameter and update related logic for channel handling

Add a "nocc + mdns" distributed compile mode

nocc gained mDNS discovery, so it can now match what "distcc + zeroconf" does:
pick a mode in Settings -> Developer and the board finds its compile helpers on
the LAN instead of being handed a host list.

setup_nocc_host.sh turns advertising on when it sets a box up as a helper. The
nocc package ships with it off -- a server that answers anything on the network
should be a decision rather than a default -- and running that script IS the
decision, since it is what makes the box a helper in the first place. NOCC_MDNS=0
opts out, and re-running with it takes advertising back off.

That script now always restarts nocc-server rather than using "enable --now".
On a host where the helper was already running, --now is a no-op, so the options
it had just edited (the port, and now the mDNS flag) would sit in the env file
while the running server kept serving with its old ones. The nocc package has
the same trap on upgrade, which is why an upgraded helper needs an explicit
restart to actually be running the new binary.

DiscoverNoccHosts asks nocc itself ("nocc-daemon -print-discovered-servers")
instead of browsing with avahi-browse the way the distcc path does. A helper
with more than one interface announces more than one address: a raw browse lists
it twice, which hands that machine a double share of the build (nocc shards
files across the server list by index), and it may pick the address on a subnet
the board cannot reach. Both helpers here announce on two subnets, so that is
the normal case. nocc already resolves each helper to one routable address.

Verified on real boards: a 32-bit client discovered both helpers, sized -j from
them, and compiled through them, producing a correct 32-bit object with no local
fallback. A client whose nocc predates the flag falls back to a local build with
a clear message rather than misparsing anything.

AES67: PTP media clock, stable SAP identity, and sender diagnostics

Drive the send pipeline from PTP time so the RTP timestamps mean what the
SDP has been claiming with "a=mediaclk:direct=0".  The clock source is
chosen so it is correct in both PTP roles: the NIC's PHC where hardware
timestamping is available (ptp4l disciplines it as a follower and
distributes it as grandmaster), CLOCK_REALTIME otherwise (ptp4l's own
clock on the software-timestamping path).  Deliberately not CLOCK_TAI,
which is only maintained by phc2sys as a follower and read equal to
CLOCK_REALTIME on a measured grandmaster; and not GstPtpClock, which
would put a second PTP client on the domain beside ptp4l.  The PHC is
resolved via ETHTOOL_GET_TS_INFO rather than assuming /dev/ptp0.

Stop minting a new SAP session on every restart.  The msg id hash is
derived from the SDP text (RFC 2974 requires it to change when the
payload changes), so seeding the o= version from the wall clock made
every rebuild a new session and left receivers listing a phantom stream
per restart until their timeout.  The version now tracks the announced
content and is persisted, so unchanged config re-announces byte-identical
SDP.

Report the rate pipewiresrc actually negotiated per stream instead of the
graph's default.clock.rate: per-card and per-group rates sit in between,
so the graph clock can read 44100 while a stream is fed a clean 48000.
Surfaced on the AES67 page next to the PTP state, warning only when a
stream is really being resampled.

UI: relabel the clock role Auto/Master/Slave, note it is unrelated to
FPP's Master/Remote player mode, and put PTP state, grandmaster, domain,
offset and source rate under the control that sets them.

Add ptpMediaClock and sourcePacing config switches so the send path can
be bisected against real receiver hardware without a rebuild.

Known not fixed:

  - Packet pacing.  The sender still emits one graph quantum of RTP
    back-to-back (~83% of packets) then idles.  udpsink sync=true starves
    the live pipewiresrc and cost 36% of the audio; a packet-sized
    node.latency request distorts, most likely because 192/48000 is a
    fractional quantum on a 44100 graph; forcing the graph quantum below
    256 broke the pipeline outright.

  - Timestamp anchor.  perfect-rtptime=true keeps increments exact but
    counts samples, so dropped buffers push the RTP timeline permanently
    behind PTP (-180ms measured).  perfect-rtptime=false tracks PTP but
    wobbles +/-1 sample per packet, which is audibly distorted.  Neither
    satisfies AES67; re-anchoring the payloader to PTP is still to do.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

AES67: split the send stream into packet-sized buffers before payloading

The payloader was being forced to choose between two wrong behaviours,
because pipewiresrc hands it whatever the graph quantum produced with
timestamps that do not land on packet boundaries:

  perfect-rtptime=false  followed those timestamps, so RTP increments
                         wobbled +/-1 sample on every packet.  Audibly
                         distorted on a receiver that places samples by
                         timestamp, while looking clean in every packet
                         level measurement -- sequence unbroken, no
                         gaps, payload statistically normal music.

  perfect-rtptime=true   counted samples instead, so increments were
                         exact but every dropped buffer pushed the RTP
                         timeline permanently behind PTP.  Measured at
                         -180ms, which breaks the a=mediaclk:direct=0 we
                         advertise just as thoroughly.

audiobuffersplit re-blocks the audio into exactly one ptime per buffer on
a sample-aligned timeline, which removes the choice: the payloader can
follow the running time -- so the RTP timeline stays anchored to PTP --
and still step exactly one packet each time.

Measured during playback, 4ms ptime: 250 pkt/s, no sequence breaks, RTP
timestamp increments exactly 192 for 100.00% of packets, and the RTP
timeline sitting +7ms from PTP (sender latency) instead of drifting off
it.  Confirmed clean by ear on an AES67 receiver.

Still outstanding: packets leave one graph quantum at a time rather than
evenly paced, and the sample clock is the sound card rather than PTP, so
the offset walks slowly (~80ppm measured against a free-running PHC).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(GStreamerOut): use-after-free in the decodebin pad-added callback

Start() hands an owning pipeline ref to a detached set_state(PLAYING)
thread precisely so that thread can outlive the GStreamerOutput, but
pad-added/no-more-pads were still connected with a bare `this`.  On a
fast stop, Close() nulls m_audioChain/m_videoChain and drops our
pipeline ref, ~GStreamerOutput frees the object, and the still-live
decodebin then fires OnPadAdded on freed memory -- crashing in
gst_element_get_static_pad() on a dangling m_audioChain, which is a
stale pointer rather than a null one so no defensive check would have
caught it.  Field reports show the callback landing after the
~MediaOutputBase / post-close breadcrumbs, with set_state returning
ASYNC in between.

Fix it at the owner rather than guarding the deref: each Start()
allocates a CallbackGuard holding a mutex and a self pointer, and every
closure owns its own shared_ptr to it, released by a GClosureNotify when
the connection dies with the decoder.  The guard takes no GstObject
refs, so there is no refcount cycle keeping the pipeline alive.  Close()
clears `self` under the guard lock as its first statement, which both
blocks until any in-flight callback returns and turns every later one
into a no-op.  Allocating a fresh guard per Start() means a connection
left on an older pipeline can never reach a restarted output.

fix(uuid): reject duplicated and truncated hardware serials

get_uuid emitted the first value each method produced, with almost no
validation, so a bad value became the system identity instead of falling
through to the next method. Every branch is now a candidate that must pass
uuid_valid() -- non-empty, no whitespace, at least 6 characters, not all
zeros or all f's, and not a known shared vendor default -- and a candidate
that fails is discarded rather than emitted.

Two specific failures this closes:

- The dmidecode branch took a single awk field, which reduced
  "Serial Number: Not Specified" to the word "Not" and passed every check.
  It now takes the whole value after the colon, so a multi-word placeholder
  stays multi-word and is rejected, falling back to the DMI UUID.

- BeagleBoard-family serials are <4-digit date code><board code><sequence>.
  A serial truncated by the flashing tool keeps a valid-looking prefix and
  loses its tail, and the duplicates that creates are shared by hundreds of
  unrelated hosts. A per-family shape check rejects them: a real sequence is
  at least four characters, and exactly five digits in the GPB family. This
  catches truncations at any length rather than only the values already
  known to be duplicated.

In a container every source in the chain describes something other than the
instance -- /proc/cpuinfo, the device tree and dmidecode are the host's, and
/etc/machine-id comes from an image layer, so every container started from
that image is born with the same one. Containers now skip the whole
host-hardware chain and use a generated UUID kept in the media directory,
which is the only thing that survives the container being recreated.

machine-id also now rejects the literal "uninitialized" that images ship and
that the file briefly contains after an upgrade.

The generated UUID is mirrored to the media directory and recovered from
there, so it survives upgrade paths that hand control to an older
upgradeOS-part2.sh.

addMultiSyncUUID() wrote "Failed" or "Not Set" into a peer's identity field
when it could not be probed. Every install emits the same token, so those
peers all merge into one identity. It now derives a locally stable, globally
unique substitute from a hash of this host's UUID and the peer address, which
keeps the peer distinguishable within its own show, cannot collide with
another install, and leaks no address. Peer-supplied UUIDs are validated with
the same rules. Also drops a dead validateAndAdd() call that passed an
undefined $mapping by reference.

Adds a uuidSource field naming which method produced the UUID, so identity
quality can be weighted or excluded without reverse-engineering the prefix.

fix(upgradeOS): preserve the generated system UUID across an OS upgrade

/etc/fpp/fpp_uuid holds the randomly generated system identity used when a
board has no usable hardware serial. It is created on the device and never
ships in an image, so the root filesystem rsync -- which runs with
--delete-during and had no exclude for it -- simply deleted it, and the board
generated a new identity on the next boot. The device silently became a brand
new install on every OS upgrade.

Saved and restored around the rsync, alongside the ssh host keys, hostname
and machine-id that are already preserved there. Guarded on existence,
because most boards derive their identity from a serial and never create it.

fix(bb64): assign repaired PocketBeagle2 boards a unit number the factory cannot issue

The EEPROM repair wrote a fixed template and randomized only the low four
digits of the unit number, so every repaired board shared the same twelve
leading characters and drew from 10000 values. That is the same failure shape
as a truncated serial: a shared prefix with too small a tail. Worse, those
values sit inside the range the factory issues, so a repaired board could
collide with a real one rather than merely with another repair.

Boards are manufactured in batches of under 10000 per day, so a factory unit
number never exceeds 9999 and the leading digit of the six-digit field is
always 0. That leaves 2-9 free as a marker. A unit number we assign now uses
one of those as its leading digit plus five random digits, which makes the
assigned range disjoint from the factory range -- a repaired board cannot
collide with a real one at all, rather than being unlikely to -- gives
8 x 10^5 values, and makes a repaired board identifiable from its serial.

The unit number is applied outside the merge. The merge only replaces bytes
that are still 0xFF, which is right for every other field but wrong here: a
board with the field partly programmed would keep its "00" lead and take only
our low digits, landing back inside the factory range unmarked. The field has
to be decided as a whole. A fully programmed unit number is still left
exactly as it is, so a factory serial is never overwritten.

check_pb2_eeprom.sh now tests all six digits rather than the low four, so a
board with the high digits still blank is no longer reported as healthy.

Also corrects two comments: the base template's readable column disagreed
with the hex it annotates -- a leftover from the real board dump the template
was built from -- and the industrial script carried the base script's note
about an impossible date while its own template date may well be a real one.
That is safe now because of the marker, which holds whatever date the
template carries.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat(bb64): check the PocketBeagle2 identity EEPROM at boot

Some PocketBeagle2 boards leave the factory with the identity EEPROM blank or
half-written, which makes u-boot bring the industrial variant up as the 512MB
base board and costs the board its hardware-derived system UUID. Until now
that was only ever noticed by the flashing paths, so a board that reached FPP
any other way kept an unusable identity indefinitely.

The detection is done in C++ and the repair script is forked only when it is
needed. Running the script unconditionally is not viable at boot: on a healthy
base board its "programmed as the base variant but has eMMC" cross-check waits
out the full eMMC timeout, about 10 seconds, every boot. That check exists to
stop a misidentified board being flashed, which is not what is happening here
-- by boot time u-boot has already sized the RAM -- so reading the two fields
that decide whether anything needs doing costs a healthy board one 56-byte
read instead. Measured on hardware: 0.27s versus 10.39s.

When the EEPROM is absent entirely, nothing can be repaired, so this logs and
returns rather than paying the script's diagnostic wait; the flashing path
still reports why in full.

A repair here only takes effect after a reboot, since u-boot read the old
contents at power-on, so it says so rather than setting the reboot flag on a
running player.

Both paths are overridable for testing under the same names the repair
scripts already honour, so a fixture run stays a fixture run through the fork.

fix(stats): repair three collectors that have been emitting nothing

All three confirmed against a live device's payload rather than by reading:

- stats_generate() echoed into the HTTP response body on a collector failure,
  using an undefined variable for the name. echo inside an API request writes
  straight into the response, so one failing collector put a bare string ahead
  of the JSON and broke parsing for every caller. It now logs, names the
  collector correctly, initialises $obj so a total failure yields an empty
  object rather than an undefined-variable warning, and catches Throwable so a
  TypeError in one collector costs that collector instead of the payload.

- stats_network() tested isset($rc[...]['config']) -- the array being built --
  instead of the source, so the interface block could never be true and has
  emitted nothing since it was written.

  Fixing the condition alone would have been worse than leaving it: the
  unset() list it carried strips PSK and SSID but not BACKUPPSK or BACKUPSSID,
  so switching it on as-written would have started uploading a wifi passphrase
  and network name. Replaced with an allowlist of non-identifying keys. A
  denylist fails open every time a key is added to the interface config; an
  allowlist fails closed, which is the only safe default for a payload that
  leaves the device.

  that depth, so enabled, threaded and type have never been emitted for

feat(stats): collect destination class, output shape, and sequence timing

Adds the fields the payload most obviously lacked, all aggregate or
classified rather than raw.

Destination class on network output rows. "How many channels go to each brand
of controller" was unanswerable, because the universe collector aggregated
rows into counts and discarded each row's address. FPP already holds the other
half of that join in memory -- the multisync table maps address to device type
-- so the classification is derivable in-process. Each active row is now
tagged with the CLASS of device at its destination; the address itself is
never emitted, an unresolvable one is "unknown", and a row with no address is
"multicast". That yields channels-per-brand, protocol-per-brand, and how many
outputs point at hardware FPP cannot identify at all.

The same collector now walks every channelOutputs entry rather than only the
first. A second universe-output block, and every row it carried, was invisible
-- in testing that undercounted a four-row config by more than half. It also
reports a priority histogram, which shows how many installs layer inputs.

Sequence and playlist shape. Only a count and a byte total were reported,
which says nothing about whether the fleet has moved to 20ms timing or how
large a typical sequence has become. Step time, channel count, fseq version
and compression now come from the fseq header via the existing meta endpoint,
so no sequence content is read and no name is kept. Playlist lengths are
bucketed from the playlist directory. The per-sequence header reads are capped
and the cap is reported, because a truncated sample that looks complete is
worse than no sample.

Install age, carefully. The identity file's birth time gives a real install
date, but only for the minority of installs that generate one, so it is
reported with its source rather than inferred. The root filesystem's birth
time is reported separately and explicitly NOT as an install date: for a
prebuilt image that is the date the image was built, identical for everyone
who flashed it, so conflating the two would misreport the age of the fleet.
Both are rounded to the month, since day precision plus a timezone is a
re-identification handle.

Peer records keep five fields the mapping table already had on the wire and
dropped: model, local, multiSyncCapable, channelOutputsEnabled and
channelInputsEnabled. Address, hostname and HostDescription stay excluded.

Pixel string protocols were built as a set, so a cape with sixteen ws2811
ports looked identical to one with a single port in use; they are now counts.
Port population is reported as buckets rather than per-port, which shows how
fully people fill their ports without becoming a per-install fingerprint, and
virtual strings per port are counted, which is what a smart receiver or a
differential split looks like from here. Other outputs gained per-type counts
and channel totals, so one DMX universe no longer looks like twelve.

feat(multisync): collect remote system and cape details in fppd

The multisync page needs a fair amount of slow-changing detail about every
discovered remote -- OS version, host description, background color, git
branch/commit, whether channel inputs/outputs are enabled, and what cape is
installed.  None of it fits in (or belongs in) the UDP ping packet, so the
browser used to go collect it itself: at least one HTTP request per remote per
page load, plus a second pair of requests per remote to work out channel I/O.
That is why the table visibly reflowed as the answers trickled in.

fppd already knows every remote, so collect it there instead.  A sweep from
PeriodicPing() fetches /api/system/info and then /api/cape from each full FPP
remote over the async CurlManager, caches the result on the MultiSyncSystem,
and GetSystems() hands it to the UI as "systemInfo" and "capeInfo".  The page
now renders platform, OS version, host description, row color, git details,
channel I/O icons and the cape on the first paint, and checkRemoteChannelIO()
returns without issuing its per-remote universe fetches.

Details worth noting:

- Nothing is ever fetched straight off an event.  A record that is due but not
  yet scheduled gets a random time inside a window that grows with the size of
  the known system list, and is only read once that time arrives.  Every peer
  sees the same discovery traffic, so without this a hundred-instance show
  would converge on whichever box just appeared -- the box least able to serve
  it, and on a slow single-core controller that is a real stall.  Budgeting
  about a second of window per known system holds the arrival rate at any one
  target near two requests a second no matter how large the show is, while a
  small setup still refreshes within a few seconds.
- A remote is re-read every 30 minutes, 5 after a failure, and is marked due
  again both when its version string changes (an upgrade rewrites most of what
  was cached) and when it announces itself with a discover ping.  That ping is
  what an instance sends as its fppd starts, which is exactly when channel
  inputs and outputs, host description and background colour change.  It
  cannot cascade: a discover ping is only ever answered with plain pings, and
  the discovery ping xLights sends carries no address so it is never treated
  as an instance at all.
- At most 4 fetches are in flight, and that cap gates only what is sent.  The
  scheduling pass has to keep running even while the cap is reached, or a
  large fleet would never get its times assigned.
- A device with more than one NIC has one entry per address; it is queued once
  and the answer is fanned out to its siblings by uuid.  The callbacks capture
  the address by value and re-find the entries, because the systems list is a
  vector that discovery push_back()s into.
- A fetch that completes after its remote was marked due again leaves it due
  rather than locking it in for another 30 minutes: the remote restarted while
  the request was in flight, so what came back may already be stale.
- Instances routinely discover themselves as a "remote" over loopback and over
  an address that is not one of their own interface addresses.  Those entries
  are skipped rather than probed.
- /api/cape answers 404 when nothing is installed; that is cached as an answer
  rather than treated as a failure.
- The cape's serial number is deliberately not carried.  It is a per-board
  hardware identifier with no use in the UI, and this record goes to every peer
  that asks for the systems list.

Measured on real hardware: with a peer's own fppd restart as t=0, refreshed
detail arrived at +3.1s, +13.1s, +16.3s and +20.2s across four trials against a
27 second window, versus never moving in a 40 second control where the peer's
setting was changed without a restart.

Nothing new reaches the usage statistics upload: its multisync collector copies
an explicit allowlist of fields.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat(stats): report per-peer platform and cape from the multisync record

fppd now caches a subset of each remote's /api/system/info and /api/cape on
the peer record, so the stats payload can finally say what other devices in a
show actually are. Cape identity per peer was the single biggest gap in the
hardware picture: capeInfo was collected only for the uploading device, so a
cape in someone else's yard was just "BeagleBone Black" unless that specific
box happened to opt in itself. On a 20-peer test show this resolved 13 peers
to real cape hardware that were previously unidentifiable.

Both are copied through allowlists rather than denylists. The peer record
carries the remote's IP list and its background colour today, and will carry
whatever gets added to it next; an allowlist is the only form that stays safe
when the source grows. Platform, variant, sub-platform, OS version, OS
release, kernel and branch are kept. IPs, HostDescription and backgroundColor
are excluded as addresses and user-entered content, UpgradeSource because it
can name a private mirror, and the git hashes because the version string
already carries that. From the cape: id, name, version, designer and vendor
name, but not the description, and not the vendor's url, email or image.

A cape can opt out of hardware detail in the statistics, and that flag has to
be the flag of the cape being described rather than the flag of the host doing
the reporting -- otherwise a peer-side collector quietly overrides a choice
made on another device. The flag was not on the peer record, so MultiSync now
carries it: parsed from the remote's /api/cape, and emitted only when a cape
opts out, so the common case costs no bytes. Only a signed cape can carry it
at all, since CapeUtils strips it from an unsigned one.

An opted-out cape is still reported as present with no identifying detail, so
it keeps counting toward how many devices have a cape without being named.
The serial number is not carried on the peer record in the first place.

fix(stats): uuidSource reported the UUID instead of the branch that produced it

getSystemUUIDSource() cached the answer to `get_uuid --source` and then trusted
that cache forever. A get_uuid predating the flag ignores it and prints the
UUID, so any upgrade that lands the www files and the scripts at different
moments writes an identity into the source cache. It never corrects itself,
and the field silently becomes a duplicate of uuid -- worthless in exactly the
window it exists for, since monitoring identity quality after a rollout is the
whole point of it.

Both identity caches are now validated on read rather than trusted: the source
against the set of tokens the script can actually emit, the UUID against
isValidSystemUUID(). That also means a UUID this version rejects, such as a
duplicated or truncated serial cached by an older script, no longer stays live
until the next reboot.

A value that fails validation is never written back, so a box heals as soon as
its scripts catch up instead of being stuck for the rest of the boot. Until
then the source reads "unknown", which is deliberately not in the accepted set
for the same reason.

The cache cannot be repaired in place in any case. /tmp is sticky and the
kernel runs with fs.protected_regular set, so whichever user creates one of
these files owns it and no other user -- root included -- can reopen it for
writing. The web path runs as fpp while fppd and the boot scripts run as root,
so which got there first decides who may refresh it afterwards. The write is
now best-effort and its failure is not an error, with an in-process memo so
that a cache nobody can rewrite costs one exec per request rather than one per
call -- the peer identity helper calls this once per discovered peer.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(multisync): stop reporting loopback as a discovered system

Every instance listed 127.0.0.1 among its discovered systems.  It is not a
discoverable thing -- it is the box finding itself.  Avahi resolves this host's
own _fppd._udp advertisement to the loopback address, mDNS hands that straight
back to MultiSync, and the HTTP probe that follows identifies it as a perfectly
good FPP instance, so it was recorded as a peer like any other.  A channel
output or an HTTP discovery subnet aimed at localhost produces the same entry
by a different route.

The result is useless to everything downstream.  No peer can reach it.  The
multisync page already dropped the row rather than render a link no browser can
follow, and the detail collector already skipped it rather than fetch from
itself, so the address existed only to be filtered out again at each consumer.

Reject it at UpdateSystem() instead, which is the single point every discovery
path funnels through and the only place the remote list grows -- so no route
can reintroduce it.  Local entries are unaffected: they come from
FillInInterfaces(), which already skips "lo".

MDNSManager now ignores a loopback resolve before spending a ping and a
detached HTTP probe on it, and the consumer-side filter in the detail sweep
drops its loopback half, keeping only the link-local case that is still real.

This does not touch the host's own address on a non-loopback interface, which
is a genuine address other instances can reach.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat(multisync): fall back to a device's MAC when it reports no UUID

Nothing but a full FPP instance ever had an identity in the systems list.  The
ping packet has no UUID field, so ProcessPingPacket() has none to pass on, and
NetworkController fills one in only for FPP.  Every third-party controller
therefore arrived with an empty UUID, leaving the UI to key its row on the
hostname -- which collides the moment two controllers ship with the same
default name, and moves out from under the row whenever someone renames one.

The MAC is the stable identity such a device does have, and for anything on a
directly attached subnet the kernel already knows it.  Where nothing better is
available, record "MAC:" plus the hardware address.  Reading the ARP table also
means a routed host simply has no entry, so we can never mistake a gateway's
MAC for the device behind it.

The lookup runs only while a system still has no identity at all, so it costs
one small read per device rather than one per ping.

A real UUID always wins.  The prefix marks the value as a stand-in: one arriving
later replaces it, and a stand-in can never overwrite a real UUID.

The web side must not treat it as a real identity either.  isValidSystemUUID()
now rejects the prefix, which keeps the statistics collector doing exactly what
it did before this existed -- ask the controller for its own identity, and fall
back to a salted local hash.  Without that it would have seen a "valid" UUID,
skipped the identity request, and reported a hardware address upstream where it
had previously reported a hash.  That regression was real and observed, not
theoretical.

feat(multisync): detect Experience controllers over HTTP

These controllers do answer MultiSync pings, so on a shared subnet FPP already
knew the exact model.  Two things the ping cannot do, though: it carries no UUID
field, and it does not cross a subnet boundary -- which is precisely the case
seeding discovery from the configured output addresses exists to cover.  A unit
reachable only that way showed up as an unknown device with its address for a
name.

The family (the Genius pixel, PRO, long range and pixel link range, plus the
rebadged units sold under other brands) serves one web app whose title carries
the retail brand, so the title is not something to match on.  The app's own
component markers are, but the HTML only decides whether it is worth asking:
nothing is accepted until the state endpoint answers with the fields this
firmware defines, so a stray HTML match cannot misidentify another device.

The identity endpoint is the only place these report something stable and their
own.  It is turned into the same string the statistics collector has always
built from it, so a controller is not identified two different ways depending
on which part of FPP is asking -- and being a real identity, it replaces the
MAC-derived stand-in.

The generic family type is used rather than a table mapping each retail model
code to its own type id: that would be guesswork for models that cannot be
tested and would rot as the range grows.  The exact model name reported by the
device is the part a user reads, and where a ping does reach the controller it
supplies the precise type anyway -- update() will not let an HTTP result
overwrite information learned through the sync protocol.

Verified against real hardware: identity resolved, and the precise model type
from the ping survived the HTTP update rather than being flattened to the
generic one.

fix(multisync): parse the 2.x Experience firmware version, and log the result

reported a name followed by "v1.3.1-2"; the 2.x line reports a bare "2.2.0-0".
Only the prefixed form was matched, so a 2.x controller discovered over HTTP

still requiring the dot so a model number cannot be taken for one.

absence was not just an inconsistency: it made the detector invisible in the
logs, and while chasing the version problem the missing output read as "the

with the model name taken from the device and the precise type still coming from

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat(multisync): read an Experience controller's MAC over HTTP

The MAC-derived identity came from the kernel's ARP table, which only answers
for a host on a directly attached subnet.  That leaves out the case discovery
seeded from the configured output addresses exists to reach: a controller on
another subnet, which is discovered fine but had no identity at all.  These
controllers report their own interfaces, so ask them.

The 1.x firmware carries the addresses in the state document already fetched,
so that costs nothing.  The 2.x firmware moved them to their own endpoint,
which is only requested when the first place came up empty -- and for 2.x this
is the only identity available at all, since it dropped the endpoint that used
to serve a real one.

Both lines report every interface, so prefer the one answering on the address
being probed.  A controller reached over wifi would otherwise be given its
wired address here and its wifi address by the ARP path, and change identity
depending on how it was found.

For the same reason the normalisation is now shared: the ARP table spells a MAC
in lowercase with colons, these report uppercase, and the two must reduce to
one string or a device silently re-keys itself.  Every path that derives an
identity from a hardware address goes through the one function.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(stats): keep a peer's MAC-derived identity instead of a per-reporter hash

A peer with no identity of its own fell back to localPeerIdentity(), which is
salted with the reporting host's own UUID.  That is deliberately
uncorrelatable: two players describing the same controller emit two unrelated
values, so the same device counts twice and the shape of a show's network
cannot be recovered at all.

A MAC-derived stand-in is the same value for a given device no matter which
player reports it, which is exactly what deduplication and network graphs need.
Prefer it.

The ordering still asks the controller for a real identity first -- that is why
isValidSystemUUID() goes on rejecting the stand-in, and it is what recovers a
proper identity from the controllers that do serve one.  Only when that fails
does the stand-in get used, and only when there is no stand-in either does the
per-reporter hash remain as the last resort.

Verified against a controller whose firmware serves no identity of its own: the
reported value went from a per-reporter hash to the shared MAC-derived one, and
across the whole payload every peer now carries either a real identity or a

fix(overlays): use-after-free iterating a model's child list

PixelOverlayModel::children was a plain std::list read by the channel
output thread (flushChildren(), doOverlay(), the FB subclass) and mutated
by setChildState() from an HTTP/command thread or an effect update thread.
The two sides are covered by different locks -- readers arrive from
doOverlays() under activeModelsLock, writers from
PixelOverlayModelSub::setState() under modelsLock or the model's own
effectLock -- so there was no exclusion at all. A concurrent erase() freed
the node the output thread was standing on, and it then read that node's
garbage width/height and scattered through channelMap with a wild index.

Guarding the list with a lock either side already holds would close a
cycle with the existing modelsLock -> activeModelsLock and
modelsLock -> effectLock orders, which is the shape that has deadlocked
this path before. So the list is copy-on-write instead, published through
AtomicSharedPtr: a reader takes a snapshot and iterates something nobody
can mutate or free, and needs no lock at all. childrenWriteLock serializes
only the read-copy-publish -- writers really are concurrent, so without it
an update can be lost -- and is a leaf, held across nothing but the copy
and the store, released before modelStateChanged() takes activeModelsLock.

AtomicSharedPtr here is the mutex + PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT implementation,
so the real-time output thread can load a snapshot without the spinlock
livelock the native atomic<shared_ptr> would reintroduce.

Verified with ThreadSanitizer on a 4-core Pi 5, hammering four 8x8
submodels of a 20x20 parent with concurrent state changes while a sequence
played: 11 flushChildren/setChildState data races and 4 heap-use-after-
frees before, zero after, with no deadlock and the API still responsive.
The one remaining setChildState-adjacent report is a pre-existing race in
CalculateNewChannelOutputDelay that is present identically both ways.

fix(framebuffer): keep the page index inside the pages that were allocated

Only m_pageBuffers[0 .. m_pages-1] are ever assigned, but two paths could
put m_cPage outside that range, leaving the draw path with a null pointer
and faulting on the first pixel write:

 - IOCTLFrameBuffer started autoSync on page 1 unconditionally. With a
   single page m_pageBuffers[1] is never assigned, so FBCopyData()'s
   "ob = m_pageBuffers[m_cPage]" was null. Derive the start page from
   m_pages instead.
 - The page count came straight from config with no bounds check, while
   m_pageBuffers holds a fixed three. NextPage() walks m_cPage modulo
   m_pages, so a larger count hands out an index with no buffer behind it.
   Clamp at the single place the value enters.

Both are latent today -- nothing in the tree enables autoSync and no UI
writes a page count -- so this enforces the invariant rather than fixing an
observed crash. Named the array bound MAX_PAGES so the two stay tied.

fix(multisync): keep one identity per device across its addresses

A box with more than one address gets one entry per address, and a real UUID
only ever reaches the entry that was probed for it -- UpdateSystem() matches on
the address.  Before MAC-derived identities existed the others were simply left
empty, and the UI merged them onto one row by borrowing the device's UUID
through its hostname.  Filling those entries with a stand-in took that away:
two addresses of one box now held two different non-empty identities, so the UI
drew the device twice and the statistics counted it twice, defeating the
deduplication the identity is for.

Reconcile after every update instead: once any entry for a device knows a real
UUID, the entries still on a stand-in adopt it.  Guarded the way the UI guards
its own hostname fallback -- a hostname claimed by more than one real UUID is
not identifying a device, so nothing is touched.  A real UUID is never replaced
by another; this only fills in for entries that have no identity of their own.

Verified on a network where a box was being listed twice: eight devices report
more than one address, and none of them now disagree with themselves.

fix(gpio): reclaim Pi header pins the kernel claims under strict pinmux

Kernel 6.18 turns on strict pinmux mode in both pinctrl-rp1 and pinctrl-bcm2835
(raspberrypi/linux#5870), so a header pin that a peripheral node claims in the
device tree -- i2c1 on P1-3/5, spi0 on P1-19/21/23, uart0 on P1-8/10, i2s on
P1-12/35/38/40 -- is now reported to gpiolib as in use by the kernel, and every
gpiod request against it fails with EINVAL. Re-muxing the pad with "pinctrl set"
no longer helps: that writes FUNCSEL behind the pinctrl driver's back and leaves
the kernel's claim in place. Through the 6.12 kernels those drivers were
non-strict, so the old approach worked; boards that wire buttons straight to
those pins come up dead on the newer kernel.

Before configuring a pin for GPIO use, look up the device holding the mux claim
in debugfs and unbind its driver so the pin is released properly. Skip HOGs and
pins already muxed as the gpio function, which stay requestable under strict
mode via .function_is_gpio. Unbinding a controller runs its children's remove
paths, which can wedge in the kernel and take the whole bus with it, so refuse
when the owner has a child device bound to a driver other than spidev and warn
with that driver named instead.

On a non-strict kernel the debugfs line carries no "device " prefix, so the
lookup finds nothing and none of this engages -- which is correct, since a
non-strict controller hands the pin over without help.

fix(strings): reject a cape pinout written for the other string driver

A cape's pinout file targets exactly one pixel string driver and the two
forms are not interchangeable: a BBB48String pinout names a header pin per
output ("P8-08"), a BBShiftString pinout gives a shift register stage
(pru/pin/index).  Capes whose eeprom predates the shift driver carry no
"driver" key at all, which the UI reads as BBB48String -- so an early
revision of a cape whose later revisions shift their strings out still wants
BBB48String, and an uploader that picks the driver from the controller model
rather than from the cape will configure BBShiftString for it.

BBShiftString then read the header pin name through asInt() and threw, and
all the user saw was "Could not initialize output type BBShiftString. (Value
is not convertible to Int.)".  The reverse case was quieter and worse:
BBB48String read a shift stage through asString(), looked up a pin named "7",
matched nothing, and left every port silently unconfigured.

Check the shape once in each driver, before either walks the outputs, and
name the driver the cape actually wants -- taken from its own "driver" key,
so a third driver would report itself rather than always saying BBB48String.
Both drivers also bounds check the config's outputs against the count the
cape declares: a bare operator[] past the end read as pru 0 / pin 0 / stage 0
and collided with a real port.

Extends the BBShiftString check added in f993d3f7c, replacing it rather than
sitting alongside it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

AES67: stop running phc2sys — it corrupts the system clock against real grandmasters

phc2sys existed to copy PTP time onto the system clock so the pipeline
could track PTP through it.  Nothing needs that since the media clock
reads the PTP source directly (the PHC with hardware timestamping,
CLOCK_REALTIME with software).

Meanwhile it actively breaks the host.  PTP's timescale is whatever the
grandmaster distributes, and Dante/Brooklyn devices commonly distribute
an arbitrary epoch rather than wall time -- one measured at ~4411
seconds, i.e. time since that device booted.  "phc2sys -a -r" faithfully
slaved CLOCK_REALTIME to it and dragged the Pi's clock back to 1970,
taking the scheduler, logs and everything else on wall time with it
(reported on #2848).

A site that wants PTP-disciplined system time should run phc2sys from
systemd with an offset chosen for its grandmaster.  An audio stream
should not impose it.

fix(flash): zero the inode tables at mkfs instead of on the customer's first boot

mkfs.ext4 defaults to lazy_itable_init=1, which leaves the inode tables
unzeroed and hands the work to the kernel's ext4lazyinit thread on first
mount.  A freshly flashed player therefore sits at the init page writing
2-4MB/s for several minutes with the drive light going constantly.  It is
a kernel thread, so nothing in top or in any process's /proc/<pid>/io
accounts for it -- measured on a 250GB root, ~1.35GB written over ~8
minutes on an otherwise idle box, then a hard stop.

Flashing is already a watch-the-progress operation, so do the zeroing
there, where it is expected, and hand over a filesystem that is finished.
Route all four ext4 creates through one helper so the Pi, BeagleBone and
BB64 profiles cannot drift apart on this.  lazy_journal_init is already 0
by default; state it so a future mke2fs.conf cannot quietly turn it on.

Verified by the presence of the ext4lazyinit thread 30s after mounting a
64GB filesystem: present with the default, absent with the flag.  Note a
loop device over a sparse file cannot test this -- mke2fs offloads the
zeroing to BLKZEROOUT, which is a punch-hole there, so both variants look
identical; -E nodiscard is required to get a control that can fail.

AES67: correct media clock drift with libsamplerate

Adds driftResample (default OFF), which reconciles the sound card's
crystal with the NIC's PHC -- the ~56ppm difference that drains both the
receiver's buffer and sinkPacing's queue.  libsamplerate is used rather
than a hand-rolled resampler: src_process() takes a ratio per block,
interpolates it across the block so there is no zipper, and keeps a
fractional read pointer across calls.  It is detected the same way
gstreamer and libdrm already are, and the code is gated on the same
header, so builds without it are unaffected.

The control law leads with a direct measurement rather than a servo,
because all three previous attempts here oscillated: the card's true rate
is (input frames / PHC seconds), which is two crystals and therefore
near-constant, so the ratio that cancels it needs no gain.  A weak
proportional term only trims residual offset.

Two failure modes were found by measurement and are handled explicitly:

  - A gap is not drift.  Chasing a 200ms startup deficit pinned the trim
    at its clamp and audibly pitched the stream for minutes.  Offsets over
    50ms are now absorbed by re-anchoring to PTP, which is the property
    audiorate lacked.
  - The learned trim must survive an absorbed gap.  Resetting it turned a
    burst of gaps into a death spiral: trim collapsed to 0, the pacing
    queue drained for want of correction, the drain starved the source
    into more gaps, and those absorbed away every chance to re-learn.

Results with sinkPacing: 4.000ms cadence, 1.00 packets per burst, 250.1
packets/s, uniform 1152-byte payloads, queue stable at 56-80ms, residual
drift ~2.5ppm against 56ppm uncorrected.  The resampler is transparent --
power spectra against the source differ by 0.09 dB stdev, ON versus OFF.

It stays default OFF because that state holds for only 9-11 minutes before
the send rate falls to ~155/s.  That degradation is not this code: the same
onset appears with audiorate, sinkPacing alone collapses at ~15 minutes,
and the media file is 220 minutes long with no restart.  Something starves
the AES67 branch after ten-odd minutes and finding it is the next step.

AES67: fix the send rate collapsing partway through playback

This is the "sounds fine, then goes fragmented" fault from #2848, and it
is upstream of everything else in this file: pipewiresrc negotiated
min-buffers=2 with always-copy off, so a buffer only returned to
PipeWire's pool once every downstream reference was dropped.  Anything
holding one cost the next cycle, and PipeWire skipped it without
recording an xrun.

Measured at the pipewiresrc pad on a 25 minute playback, delivery held at
nominal for ~13 minutes, then stepped to exactly 3/4, then to 3/5, and
stayed there -- a scheduling ratio, not a rate error.  With
always-copy=true and a 16 buffer pool it is flat for 26 minutes.

Everything else was eliminated by measurement first, because the symptom
looks like half a dozen more likely things:

  - Not our pipeline: byte counters at pipewiresrc and udpsink hold a
    constant 1.010 ratio throughout, so nothing downstream loses a sample.
    There is simply less audio arriving.
  - Not xruns, leaks, CPU or heat: the AES67 node logs zero xruns across
    the whole run, RSS moves 248KB in 24 minutes, threads and fds are
    constant, CPU falls slightly and the SoC cools by 6C.
  - Not per-node resampling: it degrades identically when the source is
    taken at the graph's own rate, and pw-record's own 48k-from-44.1k
    stream is unaffected.
  - Not the graph: recording the sound card's monitor gives 99.9% of
    realtime while AES67 is at 52%.  That last one also explains why the
    sound card always sounded fine while AES67 fell apart -- the physical
    sinks were never the ones starving.

localised this, and nativeSourceRate (default on), which takes audio at
the graph rate and converts in GStreamer rather than asking PipeWire to
deliver 48kHz from a 44.1kHz graph.  nativeSourceRate did not fix the
collapse and is kept because it is the configuration this was validated
in, and it avoids a conversion we are equipped to do ourselves.

AES67: rework the drift control loop

The loop worked but converged badly: the trim swung from -9.5 to +180ppm
before decaying, and was still crawling towards its answer 26 minutes into
a run.  Two changes fix it.

The rate estimate is now a sliding 60s window rather than a cumulative
average since the anchor.  The cumulative form was itself an integrator,
so together with the phase feedback -- which integrates too -- the loop had
two in series, which is what rang.  It also grew steadily less responsive
as a run went on, which is what made the tail so slow.

The phase feedback is proportional-only and clamped.  The plant is already
an integrator (a rate error accumulates into offset), so proportional
gives first-order decay with nothing to ring; the previous second
integration was removed rather than damped with a derivative term.

The gain came from measurement rather than theory, and the first value was
an order of magnitude short: at 3000 ppm per second of offset the loop
settled with a standing 23ms error it would not remove, which I initially
and wrongly took for a dead feedback path.  At 30000 the error sits within
+/-0.1ms.  A 10x probe settled that in one run after three explanations
for the standing offset had each been wrong.

Measured over 25 minutes, against the committed version:

  settling            still moving at 26m  ~60s
  trim range          -9.5 .. +180 ppm     +49.6 .. +59.5 ppm
  residual offset     +23 ms standing      +/-0.1 ms
  tracks card rate    no                   yes (trim sits on feedforward)

AES67: unbreak sink pacing at short ptime, and the harness without numpy

Both from hardware testing on #2848 (Yamaha MRX7-D, PTP follower, 48kHz
graph, 1ms ptime).

The pacing queue's 64-buffer cap is a ptime trap.  It is 256ms of audio at
4ms ptime, which is where it was chosen, but only 64ms at 1ms -- and the
queue has to hold the sink latency plus a whole graph quantum's burst,
about 61 buffers at 1ms.  The cap therefore sat right on top of normal
steady state: the tester saw "queue 64 buffers / 64ms" repeating with the
sender apparently running and no audio at all from the MRX7-D, and
removing sinkPacing restored audio immediately.  The queue is now bounded
by time alone, which is what was intended and is ptime-independent.

This also corrects a prediction made in the tester notes.  sinkPacing was
described there as likely to make no difference on hardware that places
samples by RTP timestamp; on the MRX7-D it silenced the stream outright.

scripts/aes67_verify now runs without numpy, which is not present on a
stock FPP image -- the tester could not run it at all in the failed state,
which is exactly when its output is worth having.  The transport half
(rate, loss, payload, pacing, media clock) is plain arithmetic and is now
implemented as such; only the content checks need numpy and they are
skipped with a note when it is absent.  Verified both paths report the
same transport figures on the same stream.

AES67: detect and recover from sustained under-delivery

The send path can settle into a state where it keeps streaming but at
89-95% of nominal, with periodic RTP timestamp gaps, and it never recovers
on its own -- a restart of fppd is the only cure.  Reproduced twice: after
~79 minutes of playback and ~25 minutes with the source then quiet, the
rate steps to about 235/s and stays there.  Resuming playback does not
clear it, which is what makes it user-visible: a show started after a quiet
afternoon plays broken.

The existing watchdog cannot see this.  It looks for bytes-served failing
to advance, and throughout this failure bytes keep climbing -- there is
simply less audio in them.  So it now also measures throughput against what
the instance should emit (AUDIO_RATE * 3 * channels bytes/sec, which is
ptime-independent) and rebuilds after three consecutive low readings.

The trigger is 95% deliberately.  The first version used 85%, which sat
below every degradation actually measured (89%, 90%, 94%) and so could
never have fired -- a watchdog that looks like protection and provides none.
A healthy stream measures 100.0% consistently, so 95% still leaves real
margin, and three consecutive checks is ~90s of sustained under-delivery,
far longer than the dip a track change produces.

Verified end to end on a real failure rather than a synthetic one:

  105m  235.2/s VARIES          degradation begins
  110m  235.1/s VARIES          5 warnings logged
  111m  90% for 3 checks        rebuild triggered
  115m  250.1/s uniform         recovered
  145m  250.1/s uniform         still clean 30 minutes later

This is recovery, not a cure.  The cause -- why the capture node degrades
after a long playback goes quiet -- is still unknown, and the correlation
with idle is not yet separable from cumulative pipeline uptime: a 31 minute
idle after only 25 seconds of playback stays clean, so idle alone is not
sufficient.

AES67: sink pacing sent every packet after its own playout deadline

Reported on #2848: with pacing enabled the transport looked ideal -- 1.000ms
median spacing, zero loss, exact RTP timestamp increments, a Dante
subscription that went from flickering red to solid green, and valid stereo
L24 confirmed by decoding the payload -- and the Yamaha MRX7-D produced
silence.  The tester's own read was right: the packets were being
transmitted too late relative to the presentation time they declared.

A receiver plays a packet at (RTP timestamp + link offset), and link offset
on that hardware is 1-5ms.  We were putting packets on the wire 23.7ms after
the timestamp they carried, so a conformant receiver discarded all of them
while every check we had still passed.

Two attempts missed before the measurement landed, both worth recording:

  - Advancing the payloader's timestamp-offset changed nothing.
  - Shifting the buffer PTS changed nothing either -- and the reading was
    identical to four decimal places, -23.73 both times, which is what gave
    it away: a PTS shift moves the RTP timestamp and the render time
    together, so it cannot alter the difference between them.

The -23.7ms is GStreamer's own latency compensation; sinks render at PTS
plus the pipeline latency, which here is one graph quantum.  So the fix has
to move the timestamp without moving the wire time: shift the PTS ahead of
the payloader, then cancel the shift again with ts-offset on the sink.
Measured +16.27ms of lead afterwards (p10 +16.01, p90 +16.54), which is the
40ms shift less the quantum, and pacing is unaffected at 4.00ms median.

Adds the check that would have caught this immediately.  aes67_verify now
reads the NIC's PTP clock and reports how far each RTP timestamp leads its
actual transmission, so "subscribed, green and silent" is a number rather
than a mystery.  It needs no numpy.

Note sinkPacingMs must exceed the pipeline latency or the lead goes negative
again; the new check makes that visible rather than silent.

Merge aes67-drift-loop: drift loop rework, under-delivery recovery, presentation-time fix

AES67: derive the pacing timestamp lead from the real pipeline latency

The presentation lead is (shift - pipeline latency), and the latency is one
graph quantum: 21.3ms at 1024/48000 but 42.7ms at 2048.  A fixed 40ms shift
is therefore comfortably positive on one graph and negative on another, and
negative means a conformant receiver discards every packet and plays silence
-- exactly the failure just fixed.  That made sinkPacing unsafe to ever
default on, whatever the bench said.

The shift now comes from querying the pipeline and keeping a 16ms margin
above its latency, taking whichever is larger of that and the configured
value.  The probe reads it from an atomic so it can be corrected after the
fact, and that cell is reused per instance rather than reallocated: the
watchdog rebuilds pipelines, and a probe on the old one can still be in
flight when the new one is built, so freeing would be a use-after-free and
reallocating would leak on every rebuild.

The query has to happen in the watchdog, not at startup.  Asked immediately
after set_state(PLAYING) it returns 0, because the state change is
asynchronous and the pipeline has not prerolled -- which silently left the
shift at its default and defeated the whole change.  It logged "pipeline
latency 0.0ms" and looked like it had worked.

Measured after: latency 24.0ms, shift 40ms, lead +16.27ms (p10 +16.00, p90
+16.56).  A 2048 quantum would now compute 48+16=64ms and land at the same
+16ms rather than at -8ms.

AES67: find the periodic under-delivery -- the source pool drains at 54ppm

The stream degrades on a metronome: every ~118 minutes the send rate falls to
90% of nominal and stays there until the watchdog rebuilds.  This is the cause.

pipewiresrc receives into sourceMinBuffers slots while the pipeline consumes
against PTP.  The PipeWire graph clock free-runs ~54ppm slow of the NIC's PHC
here, so the pool loses that difference steadily and empties after (N-1) quanta
of accumulated slip.  From then on the source skips exactly one graph cycle
every N buffers, indefinitely.

Confirmed by changing N and predicting the result in advance:

  min-buffers  onset buffer   onset    gap spacing   implied drift
  16           273985         97.4m    every 16      54.7 ppm
   8           128604         45.7m    every  8      54.4 ppm

against 54.2ppm measured independently with phc_ctl.  Onset ratio 2.130 vs
15/7 = 2.143 predicted.  All three predictions -- onset halves, spacing tracks
min-buffers, implied drift unchanged -- held.

What made this findable was forcing the graph to 48000: the onset moved to 98
minutes from 108, which is 10% off in wall time but the same buffer count.  The
trigger counts graph cycles, not seconds.  That also rules out the 44100 graph
rate as a cause, so the 44.1 default stays as it is -- measured here it costs
3.1% of a core against 3.8% at 48000, because 44.1 media then plays natively.

sourceMinBuffers is therefore a reservoir, not a fix.  It was added to cure a
13-minute collapse and did, but it only sets how long the stream survives.  A
reporter whose clock drifts ~17ppm sees the same failure at 5h18m, with the
same signature: pacing collapses to bursts once the queue starves, and the
drift loop saturates at its +300ppm clamp trying to correct a starving source.

Instrumentation: every source PTS discontinuity is now logged with its size and
the buffer index it happened at.  The absorb path only reported gaps over 50ms,
which aggregated three single-quantum drops into one 64ms line and biased every
onset measurement late.

Also corrects the note from 3557a3026.  "Uptime-driven" was fitted to runs that
happened to contain no restarts; the cadence continues straight through an fppd
restart, which is what ruled uptime out.

The gap instrumentation lived inside DriftResampleProbe, so it only existed
when ptpMediaClock and driftResample were both on.  Those are exactly the flags
a diagnostic needs to turn off, which made the obvious next experiment -- is the
PTP pipeline clock what drains the source pool? -- impossible to run: turning

to be abandoned for that reason.

  always-copy=false   reservoir 7.00 quanta   gap every 8 buffers
  always-copy=true    reservoir 7.98 quanta   gap every 9 buffers

AES67: PipeWire can drive the capture node from PTP, but not on its own

Investigating whether the pool drain can be fixed on the producer side, where
it belongs, rather than by servoing the sink.  It can, in principle: PipeWire
has supported this case since 1.1 and ships pipewire-aes67.conf doing exactly
it.  A support.node.driver clocked from the NIC's PHC drives any node joining
its node.group, and the upstream comment on aes67.driver-group describes the
intent precisely -- "force rate matching on the AES67 node rather than other
nodes".

Adds sourcePtpGroup (default OFF) which puts pipewiresrc's node in that group,
plus 98-fpp-ptp-driver.conf creating the driver.  Verified working as far as
scheduling goes: the node reports node.group=pipewire.ptp0 and driver-id
pointing at PTP0-Driver instead of the sound card.

It is default OFF because that alone stalls the stream.  Measured: delivery
went to +0 bytes within two minutes and the watchdog rebuilt.  Scheduling the
node from PTP splits it into its own driver domain, and the link back to the
card-driven graph then has no way to bridge the two -- PipeWire 1.2's async
scheduling (node.async, spa_io_async_buffers, one quantum of latency, minimum
two buffers) is the missing half.  Whether an async link also rate-adapts
between clock domains is not documented, and it has to: the graph genuinely
produces 47997.4 samples per PTP second, so 54ppm of real audio has to be
manufactured somewhere no matter how the scheduling is arranged.

Note for whoever picks this up: setting stream-properties in the
gst_parse_launch string does not work here.  The later g_object_set replaces
the structure wholesale, so the property has to be added to that structure.
It is set silently either way, which cost a test cycle to spot.

AES67: fix the source pool drain by scheduling the capture node from PTP

The pool drains because pipewiresrc is filled at the sound card's rate and
emptied against PTP.  Correcting downstream cannot refill it.  This corrects it
on the producer side: the capture node joins a PTP-clocked driver group and
PipeWire rate-matches the card into that domain, upstream of the pool.

Needs four things together, and it took a while to find that out:

  1. a support.node.driver clocked from the NIC's PHC (clock.interface)
  2. node.group on the capture node, to join that domain
  3. node.async, so the cross-domain link can exchange buffers a cycle apart
  4. phc2sys, or pipewire segfaults

Measured on a 44100 graph, min-buffers=8, against an unfixed onset at buffer
145407:

  before   card 47997.4/s  (-54.0 ppm)   gap burst every 9 buffers from 145407
  after    card 48000.0/s  (+0.1 ppm)    no burst by buffer 2,300,000 (19 hours)

driftResample now measures ~0 and has nothing to correct, so it becomes a
safety net rather than the mechanism, and sinkPacing's queue stops draining.

On (4): pipewire crashed five times before this was understood, and the crash
was misread twice.  The "+0 bytes stall" attributed to node.group needing async
was a segfault seven seconds in; async only made it survive longer.  The
measurements taken of the native module-rtp-sink were also taken while the
daemon was crash-looping, so the conclusion recorded then -- that it does not
lock its media clock -- is not supported and needs redoing.

The trigger is the PHC drifting in RATE against MONOTONIC, not the size of the
offset.  node-driver.c runs a DLL tracking the two and hard-resyncs whenever
error exceeds resync.ms; at 54ppm that fires every ~28s until something breaks.
Verified by holding a constant 37s offset with no rate difference: no crash in
7 minutes, where a drifting offset crashed within 7s-3.5min.  So a conformant
TAI grandmaster 37s off UTC is not itself a problem.

Default OFF.  It needs a driver node placed deliberately (not shipped -- with
priority.driver 100000 it takes over the whole graph the moment anything joins
its group, moving the sound cards onto PTP too), and follower mode is not yet
validated: a software-timestamped grandmaster is not enough to lock FPP's
hardware-timestamped ptp4l, so that needs real PTP hardware.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

AES67: step a large PTP offset instead of slewing it out

linuxptp defaults step_threshold to 0, so ptp4l steps only on its very first
correction (first_step_threshold, 20us) and slews everything after.  Initial
lock is therefore fine and followers do converge on real hardware -- reported
working against a Yamaha MRX7-D at 117ns offset.  What is not fine is a
grandmaster changeover or a GM time jump after that point: the resulting offset
is slewed out at the servo's frequency limit, which for anything past a second
takes hours, with the stream nominally locked but wrong throughout.

The published AES67 profile sets this for the same reason.  Harmless in
grandmaster mode, where there is nothing to step towards.

Not related to the pool drain, and not the reason a follower failed to lock on
the bench -- that was meanPathDelay never resolving against a software-
timestamped grandmaster, which is a limitation of the test rig rather than of
FPP.

Status: report media playing outside a playlist instead of "idle"

"Play Media" runs on a stream slot rather than through the player, so
status_name read "idle" while audio was audibly playing.  The slot data was
already in the status JSON under streamSlots; nothing looked at it.  That cost
real debugging time more than once -- a box gets declared silent on the
strength of this field while a track is running.

status_name now reports "playing media", or "playing background" when only
slots 2-5 are active, and current_song names the file.

The numeric status deliberately stays FPP_STATUS_IDLE.  Player::GetStatus()
reports the playlist, and changing it would break things badly: the scheduler
gates on it in eight places, and both Player::StopNow() and Scheduler spin on
`while (GetStatus() != FPP_STATUS_IDLE)`.  Those loops stop the playlist, not a
slot, so reporting slot activity as player activity would never terminate.
Only the display fields move.

Audited the consumers before changing the string.  Two compare against 'idle'
and both are display-only, but both needed updating or they would have
regressed: the header badge in fpp.js matches on exact strings and would have
gone blank, and multisync.php builds a remote's "Syncing: <files>" panel inside
its idle branch, which a syncing remote would have skipped.  Nothing keys on
'idle' to decide whether it is safe to act.

Background is keyed on slot > 1 rather than StreamSlot::isBackground, because
nothing sets that flag -- it is only ever assigned false -- so testing it alone
gives a branch that can never fire.  Slots 2-5 are already what
StopBackgroundSlots() and ProcessBackgroundSlots() mean by background.  The
flag is still honoured for when it gets populated.

Positions are published only when non-zero.  Nothing drives slot 1's Process()
when media starts outside a playlist -- both StreamSlotManager loops begin at
slot 2, since slot 1 is normally the playlist's own media and the playlist
pumps it -- so setMediaElapsed() never runs and elapsed/remaining stay 0 for
the whole track.  Omitting them beats publishing a frozen 0 as a real position.
Tracking that properly is a separate fix.

Stats: report unique UDP targets and whether each was discovered

The usage payload described universe outputs only as row and universe
counts, so it could not distinguish twelve rows aimed at one controller
from twelve controllers, and said nothing about whether a configured
destination was ever seen by discovery.  An install pushing data at an
address that answers nothing looked identical to a healthy one.

Add a per-destination roll-up under output_e131.targets: unique unicast
destinations, a rows-per-target histogram, and the row/universe/channel
totals split by whether the destination appears in the multisync system
list.  Destinations are classified only by the form of the address
(ipv4 / hostname / broadcast / multicast); no address or hostname is
ever emitted.

Supporting fixes:

- The peer lookup was keyed on address only, so a row configured by
  hostname read as an unknown destination.  Key on address, hostname and
  hostname.local, case-insensitively.  This also corrects destType,
  which had the same undercount.

- Collapse targets on the peer uuid rather than the configured string,
  so one controller named by address on one row and by hostname on
  another counts once, and a multi-homed host (announced once per
  address) does not count several times.

- Broadcast and multicast literals feed an unknown number of devices and
  can never be discovered, so they are reported separately rather than
  counted as one target each.  This matches the existing treatment of an
  empty address.

Channel counts for DDP and Twinkly rows were wrong in both universe
collectors.  fppd reads channelCount alone for those types, but the row
still carries a universeCount that the UI disables and then saves
anyway, so multiplying by it produced a span that was zero, correct, or
inflated depending on what happened to be left in the disabled field --
an error that differs per install and so cannot be corrected for in
aggregate.  Derive the span through a shared helper that ignores
universeCount for those types, and report zero universes for them.
Both collectors now emit countsVersion so a consumer can tell a
corrected payload from an older one.

Field accesses in both collectors are guarded; an undefined-index
warning would otherwise land in the HTTP response body ahead of the
JSON, the same failure mode the collector try/catch already guards.

fix(oled): restore panel geometry so flipped 128x32 displays aren't blank

The drawing routines clip and mirror against the file-static _width and
_height, but nothing has assigned them since the H-flip work: that commit
repurposed rotation 1 from a 90 degree rotate to a plain horizontal mirror
and, along with the now-unneeded SWAP() cases in drawPixel(), removed the
switch in setRotation() that was the only place the configured panel
geometry ever reached the drawing code. Both fell back to their 128x64
initializers.

On a 128x32 panel that makes rotation 2 mirror about row 63 instead of
row 31, so every pixel lands in GDDRAM pages 4-7. With the multiplex
ratio set to 31 those pages are never scanned out and the display just
stays dark - the non-flipped variant is unaffected, which is why only
the flipped option looked broken. A 128x128 SSD1327 has the opposite
problem: everything below row 63 is clipped away and transfer() ships
half a frame.

Set both from LED_DISPLAY_WIDTH/HEIGHT at the top of display_Init_seq(),
which runs after the driver constructor establishes the geometry and
before any drawing. Deliberately not restored inside setRotation(): the
old width/height swap there belongs to the 90 degree rotation that no
longer exists, and reinstating it would break the horizontal flip.

Verified against a harness that stubs the i2c layer and counts lit bytes
per GDDRAM page. Only the 128x32 rotation-2 case changes (all 39 lit
bytes move from off-screen pages back on-screen); 128x32 normal and
H-flipped and all three 128x64 orientations are byte-for-byte unchanged.
A 128x32 panel now also transfers 512 bytes per refresh instead of 1024,
and a 128x128 SSD1327 transfers all 8192 instead of 4096.

fix(sensors): stop a failed ADS7828 read from smashing the caller's stack

I2CUtils::readI2CBlockData() returns -1 on any failed transfer, while
isOk() only reports that the bus device was opened -- so a chip that
stops acknowledging sails past the guard and returns -1. The read loop
accumulated that return blindly:

    int c = readI2CBlockData(cmd, (uint8_t*)b2, samples * 2 - 2);
    while (c < (samples * 2))
        c += readI2CBlockData(cmd, (uint8_t*)&b2[c / 2], samples * 2 - c);

With c negative, &b2[c / 2] indexes before the 8-byte stack buffer and
the requested count is larger than the buffer, and c only falls further
each pass, so the loop never terminates and walks off b2 in both
directions. Reports show the overrun writing sample bytes over the low
bytes of a pointer spilled next to the buffer, which the caller then
reloads: SIGBUS/BUS_ADRALN on a doubleword load through an address whose
low bits are ADC data.

Treat any non-positive return as a hard failure. The successful path
issues the same two transfers as before.

A failed transfer is nearly always transient -- one NAK on a marginal
bus -- and getValue() re-reads on the next status poll a second later,
so hold the last good reading per channel rather than reporting 0 and
blipping the displayed value down and back up.

Also bounds-check the channel in getValue() and enable() -- both index
an 8-entry array with a value straight out of the cape's JSON -- and
give SensorSourceSensor::channel a default, since a config entry with no
"channel" member left it uninitialized.

at the one reported call site: add JsonInt()/JsonString() next to the

cases a bare accessor would throw on, and use them across every

BBShiftString: drop frames the PRU can't take yet; warn when the sequence rate exceeds string capacity

pumpFrameData() only snapshots pendingFrame once the firmware is ready for
another frame.  A frame staged before that point is overwritten and never
rendered.  When the sequence frame rate exceeds what the configured string
length can clock out, that surplus of never-rendered frames is what
eventually leaves the PRU ring misaligned (#2855) - the receiver picture
corrupts and telemetry freezes until fppd restarts.

SendData() now declines the frame while the previous one is still pending:
frame dropping at the source, at whatever rate the hardware sustains.
Configurations inside their budget are untouched - nothing is pending when
the next frame arrives, so nothing is declined.  pumpedSeq becomes atomic
so the output thread can read it against pendingSeq without a data race.

A persistent UI warning (WarningHolder id 61, hysteresis on at >=10%
dropped / off below 2%) surfaces the over-rate condition, measured from
what actually happened rather than computed from protocol timing.

Evidence on a K32-Max (PB2, FPP v10.0, FalconV5 SRx1 on 4 ports):
stock locks up in minutes at 100fps/700px; with the gate, ~6 hours clean
across repeated soaks.  Declined fraction tracks 1 - achieved/offered at
three tested rates (0% @40fps, 31.2% @66.7, 55.8% @100).

Fixes #2855

fix(BBShiftString): harden the back-pressure gate

Follow-ups to the gate added for #2855.

- Include a PRU in the gate only when the pump actually services it
  (pru && ring.attached()) rather than on maxStringLen.  A PRU whose ring
  never attached would climb pendingSeq against a pumpedSeq nothing
  advances, declining every frame forever - including the other PRU's,
  turning a half-dead output into a fully dead one.
- Move the counters off function statics onto the output.  They now reset
  with the rest of the frame state in StartPRU(), and the frame rate
  warning is retracted in Close() and in the destructor, so an output that
  is reconfigured or removed cannot leave it stranded in the UI.
- Only log at warning level when frames were actually declined; a healthy
  output was printing a 0.0% warning line every window.
- Report on a 60 second wall clock window instead of a 6000 frame one, so
  the hysteresis reacts at the same speed whatever the sequence rate.
- Publish pumpedSeq only after the pump's copy of pendingFrame is known
  good, not before it.  The gate reads pumpedSeq == pendingSeq as its
  licence to restage, so the old ordering invited the output thread to
  rewrite pendingFrame while the pump was still copying it.
- Drop the falconV5Support condition.  The gate is a no-op whenever the
  hardware keeps up, and what it protects does not depend on a receiver:
  pendingFrame is written in two phases (byte counts in sendData(), the
  command word after), and only a frame the pump has already taken may be
  restaged, so the pump can never pair one phase of one frame with the
  other phase of the next.  Without a receiver the torn fields happen to
  be identical today, which is a property of the current values rather
  than an invariant.
- Wrap the block in #ifndef PLATFORM_BBB.  AM335x has no ring and no pump
  and never bumps pendingSeq, so this was already dead code there.

Also worth recording: the gate stops curV5ConfigPacket advancing on
frames that are never streamed.  Over budget, better than half of a smart
receiver's config and dynamic packets were being marked consumed and
never sent, which is a mechanism for the frozen receiver telemetry
reported in #2855.  The same packet cursor bug remains on AM335x, where
dropped frames are the expected behaviour.

BBShiftString: warn about an over-budget frame rate as soon as it applies, not after a minute of drops

The measured warning added for #2855 needs a 60-second window of declined
frames before it appears. The predictive half can fire immediately: Init()
computes the sustainable ceiling from the longest configured string (10us per
byte at 800KHz plus ~1700us of measured per-frame overhead) and logs it, and
SendData() re-checks whenever the published refresh rate changes - warning 63
names both numbers. Checking on rate change rather than in StartingOutput()
matters for playlists mixing frame rates: the output thread keeps running
across sequence transitions, so a rate that rises mid-playlist would never be
flagged by a start-time check (found in live testing; a stale warning also
survived into a compliant sequence). A 1% grace band keeps a config that is a
