fix(#2865): keep the "sequence file does not exist" warning up while the player keeps syncing

OpenSequenceFile() assigns m_seqFilename before the FileExists() check and
leaves it assigned when the open fails.  A remote therefore gets exactly one
open attempt per sequence: every later sync packet reaches StartSequence(),
sees m_seqFilename already equal to the requested file, and short-circuits.
The warning was armed with a 60s timeout on that single attempt, so it aged
out roughly a minute into a sequence that was still playing on the player -
anyone who looked at the status page after that saw no abnormal condition and
"Waiting for MultiSync commands", which reads like a network problem rather
than a missing file.

Track the missing file and its message instead of firing and forgetting:
StartSequence() re-arms the warning on every sync packet while the file is
still absent (AddWarningTimeout only ever pushes an existing timeout later),
CloseSequenceFile() clears it - the path a sync stop packet takes through
CloseIfOpen() - and a successful open (including the fallback.fseq path)
clears it too.  The timeout drops to 30s, since it is now the grace period
after the player goes quiet rather than the total display time.

Verified on a remote driven by synthetic sync packets: before the change the
warning vanished at 60s with packets still arriving; after it holds for as
long as they keep coming, returns if they resume after a gap, clears
immediately on a stop packet, and ages out ~30s after the last packet.

fix(multisync): don't let the proxy list gate the system table

getFPPSystems() -- the only thing that populates the MultiSync table --
was chained inside the .then() of fetch("api/proxies"), with no .catch().
The proxy list only decorates the per-host links, but any failure of that
request (transient error, a slow or dropped connection, a busy fppd) left
the promise rejected, so the table sat on "Loading system list from fppd."
forever while api/fppd/multiSyncSystems was answering perfectly well.

Move the two follow-up calls into a .finally() and fall back to an empty
proxy list on error, so the table is built regardless.

Also harden getFPPSystems() itself: catch fetch/JSON failures, check the
response status, validate that systems is an array, and replace the
permanent "Loading..." row with a message and a Retry link instead of
hanging silently.

Verified with request interception against a live player: unpatched with
api/proxies forced to fail renders 0 rows; patched renders the full list;
patched and healthy is unchanged.

feat(oled): support 128x128 SH1107 status displays

Adds "128x128 I2C (SH1107)" and "128x128 Flipped I2C (SH1107)" as display
types 34 and 35. FPP's only 128x128 option so far was the SSD1327, whose
command set these panels do not share, so an SH1107 wired to the i2c bus
had no working setting: it acknowledges the SSD1327 init sequence, reports
itself as on, and then shows whatever was left in its RAM at power up.

The SH1107 is a 1bpp controller, so it reuses the existing page based
framebuffer and every drawing routine unchanged. Three things differ from
the SSD1306/SH1106 path it is closest to:

- Its panel supply is enabled with 0xAD 0x8A rather than the SSD1306
  charge pump. Send the wrong one and the controller ACKs every command
  and reports display-on while the glass stays completely dark.
- It has no 0x21/0x22 column and page range commands. 0x21 selects
  vertical addressing, which would break the page walk, so Display()
  skips Init_Col_PG_addrs() for this type and the frame is pushed a page
  at a time.
- Display offset must be 0. The widely copied SH1107 init recipes use
  0x60, which is right for the 128x64 boards; on a full height panel 96
  lines of offset rotate the frame by 32 columns and the right hand edge
  wraps around to the left.

transfer()'s page walk was hardcoded to 8 pages and a column offset of 2.
It now derives the page count from LED_DISPLAY_HEIGHT and picks the column
offset per controller, so an SH1106 still walks 8 pages from column 2
(it is a 132 column controller behind a 128 column panel) while an SH1107
walks 16 from column 0. Flipping reuses the existing software setRotation(2),
which needs the panel geometry established by the preceding commit.

Verified on hardware in both orientations, and against a harness that stubs
the i2c layer and captures the command and data stream: SH1107 emits the
init sequence and 16 pages carrying exactly 2048 data bytes that were
confirmed to drive a real panel, while the SSD1306, SH1106 and SSD1327
streams stay byte for byte identical. That control was checked by breaking
the SH1106 column offset on purpose and confirming it goes red.

fix(multisync): ask each ESPixelStick generation the way it can answer

The two firmware generations expose completely different status APIs, and
the page had them the wrong way round, so neither one ever reported:

  - 3.x serves the two-letter command protocol (XJ/G1/G2) on a WebSocket
    at /ws and nothing else -- confirmed in the v3.x branch, which creates
    AsyncWebSocket ws("/ws") and implements the commands in procX/procG.
  - 4.x dropped that socket entirely and answers FPP's own
    /api/system/status, returning status_name, mode_name and an
    advancedView carrying Platform, Version and Utilization.Uptime -- the
    exact shape getFPPSystemStatus() already renders.

4.x was being polled over a socket it does not have, and 3.x was being
asked for an HTTP endpoint it does not serve. Swap the branches, in both
the initial render and the refresh path, so 3.x takes the socket and 4.x
joins the ordinary FPP status batch. An unparsed version now goes with
4.x: a device too new to recognize is far likelier to be current than
legacy, and a miss there just reads "unreachable" instead of throwing.

Also drop the server-side "ESPixelStick" branch, which curled
http://<ip>/ws with WebSocket upgrade headers. curl cannot complete a WS
handshake let alone frame a request, so it only ever returned
"unreachable" -- verified against a real stick. It had no callers, and
falling through to the default /api/system/status is what 4.x wants.

Two defects this exposed:

  - The version cell guarded OSVersion with `!== ""`, but a device not
    running FPP OS omits the field entirely, and `undefined !== ""` is
    true, so the cell rendered "OS: undefined".
  - The 1s XJ re-poll called send() on a socket that onclose had already
    deleted from the map; send() throws on a closed socket.

Verified against a live player with payloads built from each firmware's
own source. 3.x now renders the device name from G1, E1.31 packet
counters and uptime, over a same-origin /proxy/<ip>/ws socket; 4.x
renders description, status, free memory and uptime. Both were blank
before. The proxy WebSocket tunnel itself was confirmed end-to-end with a
real client.

refactor(multisync): make HTTP controller detection and discovery async

Controller detection was a chain of blocking curl calls: DetectControllerViaHTML()
handed the page to detectors that each made their own synchronous urlGet(), and one
vendor family needs three of them in sequence. MultiSync drove that from a detached
thread for the periodic remote probe, from a second detached thread per host resolved
over mDNS, and inline on the main loop from Discover(), where a configured subnet scan
blocked fppd from finishing startup until the last address answered.

Detection is now continuation-based. DetectControllerViaHTML() takes a callback, and a
per-walk state object runs the detector list, suspending on a CurlManager request
wherever a device has to be asked something and resuming in the completion. The
detector order, the single controller object they fill in as they are tried, and the
accept/reject rules are all unchanged.

Both MultiSync probe paths become queue-and-pump with an in-flight cap, which retires
the probe thread, the per-host mDNS thread, and the hand-rolled curl multi handle the
scan owned along with the response map that fed it. The scan still sets its own handle
options rather than using addGet(): HTTP09_ALLOWED is load-bearing, as some older
controllers answer with a bare HTTP/0.9 body that curl rejects by default.

The in-flight slot is claimed in PingSingleRemoteViaHTTP() rather than in the pump,
because that is the entry point callers outside this file use. Counting only in the
pump left those probes unaccounted, drove the counter negative, and measured the cap
against a number that did not describe reality.

The URL helpers in common.h are documented as deprecated for new fppd code. They stay
as they are: external plugins link against them, and they remain the only correct
choice for the binaries with no main loop to complete a CurlManager request against,
since CurlManager's synchronous calls drain every subsystem's callbacks onto whichever
thread invokes them.

fix(DPIPixels): build the WS bit stream in RAM, not in the uncached KMS page

The KMS dumb buffers the DPI scans out of are uncached DMA memory.  Streaming
writes into them are fine, but PrepData() was writing each WS bit's middle
third directly into the live page, and the non-latched write helper replicated
its 12-byte pixel group with two memcpys that read back from the page.  On a
Pi 5 an uncached read costs ~28x a cached one, which made the per-frame prep
7.2ms instead of 0.3ms for 500 rows; on a Pi 3 the penalty is far larger.

Worse, the scattered writes could land on the page the DPI was still scanning
when the previous flip had not yet retired.  A scanout fetch that catches a
16-pixel third half written yields a ~625ns high, right at the WS281x 0/1
threshold, so that bit is decoded at random.  Older pixels with tighter
timing margins showed it as a flickering first pixel.

Build the stream in an ordinary malloc'd copy of the page instead: the static
template from InitializeWS281x() and the middle thirds from PrepData() go
there, and SendData() copies the data rows into the free KMS page in one burst
after the previous flip has retired (new FrameBuffer::WaitForPageFree(), which
KMS implements by draining the pending flip event).  The write helper now
stores its 48 bytes without reading back; output is byte-identical.  Still two
KMS pages, so no additional CMA is used - the shadow is heap.

Verified on a Pi 3B+ with a two-port DPI cape and old WS2811 bullets that
showed the flickering first pixel on master: clean with this change, at both
20Hz and 100Hz scan rates.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(DPIPixels): idle at the bridging interval, keep a refresh that divides the target

Two changes to the runtime DPI refresh policy:

- While no sequence is running the output thread produces frames at the E1.31
  bridging interval, so after the settle window the DPI is retimed to that
  rate (1000/E131BridgingInterval) instead of the string's maximum.  Raising
  to the maximum rescanned short strings at several hundred Hz during pixel
  testing, which older 400Hz-PWM pixels do not tolerate, and it was never
  lowered again afterwards because nothing drives PrepData() when idle.

- A current refresh that is an exact multiple of the wanted rate is kept.
  Each frame is simply scanned N times and the flip still lands on a vblank,
  so 40Hz serves a 20fps sequence (or the 50ms idle rate) with no modeset.
  Every modeset is a full drmModeSetCrtc that cuts the WS stream mid-frame,
  and most shows alternate 20 and 40fps sequences, so this removes the
  common transitions entirely along with the uneven 2/3-scan cadence a
  non-multiple rate produced.

Verified against the log on a Pi 5: 40->20fps sequence keeps 40 with no
modeset; a 100fps sequence clamps to the string max; idle after that drops to
20; test mode at 40 stays at 40.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(KMSFrameBuffer): wait a vblank before reusing a page after a flip timeout

WaitForPageFree() drains the previous flip's completion event so the caller
can write into the page it is about to leave.  If that wait times out the
flip is abandoned but may still be queued in the kernel, so the page could
still be the one being scanned out.  Wait for one vblank in that case; any
queued flip has landed by then.  Only the broken-flip path pays for it.

fix(DPIPixels): start the DPI at the idle rate, not the string maximum

KMS brings the DPI up at the highest refresh the string length allows and
PrepData() lowers it once something drives output.  On a remote (or
otherwise idle) box nothing does, so the string was rescanned at the
maximum - hundreds of Hz for short strings - from boot until the first
sequence.  Apply the same idle rate PrepData() would choose (the E1.31
bridging interval) at Init instead.

fix(DPIPixels): start every frame with two blank scanlines

The first FB pixel of a frame is the leading high of channel 0's MSB - the
first pixel's red MSB - and it is emitted at the instant the scan-out
pipeline restarts after vertical blanking (display list reload, DMA and
FIFO priming).  Any stretch of that first high period there reads as a 1 on
parts with a tight T0H threshold, which showed as a flickering red first
pixel on older WS2811 strings driven from a Pi 3.  Put two all-low
scanlines ahead of the WS data so the pipeline start-up falls inside the
reset gap where it cannot matter.  Costs 100us of extra low per frame, one
extra row of CMA per page, and nothing else.

Verified on a Pi 3B+ with a four-port DPI cape and older WS2811 pixels that
still flickered with the previous fixes at 20Hz: clean with this change
and no other difference.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(DPIPixels): 312ns 0-bit high for non-latched outputs

The non-latched WS bit was three even 16-pixel thirds at 38.4MHz: 417ns high,
417ns data, 417ns low.  That 0-bit high is outside the WS2811 datasheet
window (100-400ns) and above the 310-400ns overlap that every part shares,
which FPP's PRU string drivers have targeted for years (320/750ns).  Only the
first pixel on a string sees the Pi's raw edge - every later one gets a
regenerated signal at the chip's own timing - so a marginal 0-bit high shows
up as the first pixel alone misreading 0 bits as 1 on older parts.

Shape the cell as 12 pixels high, 16 of data, 20 low instead: T0H 312ns,
T1H 729ns, T0L 937ns, T1L 521ns, the bit period unchanged at 1.25us.  The
data section PrepData() writes is the same 16 pixels, just 4 earlier, so the
per-bit stride and the rest of the layout are untouched.  The latched layout
keeps its 16/16/16 thirds: its four-bank latch pulse train needs the 16
pixel phases.

Verified clean on a Pi 3B+ with a four-port non-latched cape and older
WS2811 pixels, on top of the preceding fixes.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(DPIPixels): 312ns 0-bit high for latched outputs with up to three banks

The latched WS bit cell is three phases of one 4 px latch slot per bank
(set the data bus, LE high for 2 px, hold 1 px), so a phase only needs 4L
pixels for L banks.  The layout nonetheless used three fixed 16 px phases,
giving every latched output the same 417ns 0-bit high the non-latched path
just moved away from.

For up to three banks start the "go to data" slots at px 12 and the "go
low" slots at px 28 instead of 16 and 32.  Each bank's LE fires at the same
offset within its phase, so every bank sees exactly T0H 312ns / T1H 729ns,
the cell stays 1.25us, and PrepData's per-bit stride is unchanged (it just
starts 4 px earlier).  The LE pulse, setup and hold are untouched at
52/26/26ns.  Four banks keep the 16/16/16 layout because the fourth "go
high" slot occupies px 12..15.

Also log the bank count with the framebuffer geometry at init.

Verified on a two-bank 36-output cape (74AC573 latches): direct ports on
bank 0 and differential-receiver ports on bank 1 both clean.

fix(DPIPixels): review follow-ups for the shadow page and refresh policy

fix(gpio,rtc): raw GPIO callbacks never fired under libgpiod v2; fpprtc misparsed unquoted piRTC

gpio.cpp: a callback-only GPIOState (eFuse status lines on i2c expanders,
for example) has no rising/falling actions, so addState() requested the
line with no edge detection. Under libgpiod v2 that request succeeds and
returns a request fd that never becomes readable, parking the callback in
eventStates where it could never fire. Under v1 the same request had no

AES67: record that splitting the clock domains is the wrong architecture

Adds splitClockDomains (default OFF) and the measurements that reject it.

It does fix the source side: with the pipeline on the graph's clock the ring
stops draining, because pipewiresrc no longer pulls on PTP time while PipeWire
fills at the card's rate.  Measured earlier at min-buffers=8, pipeline on PTP
gave a gap burst at buffer 145407 (~56 min) and pipeline on the graph gave no
burst in 74 minutes.

But rtpL24pay derives RTP timestamps from the pipeline's running time, so
moving the pipeline off PTP unanchors the RTP timeline entirely: presentation
timing measured -36,135,744 ms and aes67_verify reported the media clock at
-56.3ppm, i.e. not locked.  A ts-offset servo cannot rescue that; the
timestamps would have to be re-derived from PTP independently of the pipeline.

The better reason to stop is architectural.  This keeps the sound card as clock
master and bolts PTP on beside it, and that is the opposite of how AES67 is
done in practice: professional interfaces slave their sample clock to PTP.  The
Linux reference implementation, bondagit/aes67-linux-daemon, uses Merging's
MergingRavennaALSA.ko -- a kernel module presenting a virtual ALSA device that
IS the PTP clock domain, with everything else adapting to it.  That is the same
shape as PipeWire's node.group = pipewire.ptp0.

Which reframes the earlier objection to that approach: the "graph takeover",
where the sound cards move onto the PTP driver and get rate-matched, is not a
side effect to design around.  It is the intended behaviour and the entire
point of a network clock domain.  The remaining blocker there is an
implementation limit rather than a design one -- userspace cannot arm a timerfd
on a PHC, so PipeWire's support.node.driver tracks PHC against MONOTONIC with a
DLL and is fragile; a kernel module has no such constraint, which is why
Merging's does not have this problem.

AES67: perfect-rtptime decouples the RTP timeline from the pipeline clock

Measured, and it is the piece that makes splitClockDomains viable.

With the pipeline on the graph clock instead of PTP, perfect-rtptime=false ties
RTP timestamps to the pipeline's running time, which is then no longer PTP --
the timeline unanchors completely and the media clock reads -56.3ppm.  With
perfect-rtptime=true the payloader counts samples instead, and driftResample
already guarantees exactly 48000 of them per PTP second, so the counter runs at
PTP rate whatever clock the pipeline uses:

  pipeline on graph clock, perfect-rtptime=false   media clock -56.3 ppm
  pipeline on graph clock, perfect-rtptime=true    media clock  +1.4 ppm
  (stock, pipeline on PTP)                         media clock  -1.2 ppm

RTP timestamp increments stay exact and sequence stays contiguous throughout.

This matters because the source ring only drains when the pipeline pulls on PTP
time while PipeWire fills at the card's rate.  Taking the pipeline off PTP fixes
that -- measured, no gap burst in 74 minutes at min-buffers=8 against an onset
at 56 -- and until now the cost was an unanchored RTP timeline.  It is not, so
the approach works for a follower as well as a grandmaster, with no PipeWire PTP
driver, no phc2sys and no kernel module.

Two pieces remain, and they share one root cause: the media timeline is
PTP-anchored while the pipeline's running time is not, so they differ by a
constant (measured -41,399,454 ms, about 11.5 hours).  That leaves presentation
timing wrong by that constant, and sink pacing bursting at one graph quantum
because udpsink compares PTP-based PTS against graph-clock running time.
Anchoring the RTP/PTS base to PTP via timestamp-offset should settle both.

Also removes a stale comment block that argued for perfect-rtptime=true on the
old architecture and was left in place when the code was changed to false, so
the two adjacent blocks contradicted each other.

AES67: make splitClockDomains conformant -- servo the sink, anchor RTP to PTP

Completes the approach.  All aes67_verify checks now pass with the pipeline on
the graph clock rather than PTP:

  packet rate 250.0/s, paced at ptime (median gap 4.00ms)
  RTP timestamps advance exactly with the payload
  media clock within +0.4 ppm of the RTP rate
  packets sent 9.7ms before their playout time (p10 +9.72, p90 +9.76)

Three pieces, on top of perfect-rtptime from the previous commit:

Do not force base time to 0.  That exists so running time equals PTP time on
the stock path, where the pipeline clock is PTP.  Carried over to the graph
clock it makes running time equal raw clock time, which the source's PTS never
match, so udpsink judges every buffer overdue and flushes -- measured, 83% of
packets back-to-back in bursts of one graph quantum.

Servo ts-offset by the accumulated PTP-minus-pipeline difference.  The sink
syncs to the pipeline clock while the buffers carry PTS advancing at the PTP
rate driftResample enforces, so left alone it emits at graph rate: measured
249.986 packets per PTP second against the 250 AES67 needs, i.e. the receiver
runs 54ppm slow and drains.  The correction is 54us/s, applied at 1Hz from the
drift probe, which already has the PTP clock and runs per buffer.  It re-anchors
if something else moves ts-offset, since the sink pacing watchdog retunes it
once the real pipeline latency is known.

Anchor the RTP timeline to PTP via timestamp-offset, before PLAYING.
perfect-rtptime means the timestamp no longer derives from the PTS, so the
sinkPacing PTS shift no longer produces the transmit lead; both jobs fall to
this offset, which is what mediaclk:direct=0 means.  It must be set before the
pipeline starts -- rtpL24pay latches its base on the segment, and setting it
from a probe on the first buffer was measured to have no effect at all.

Still default OFF pending a soak: the point of the approach is that the source
ring stops draining, and that takes ~56 minutes at min-buffers=8 to demonstrate.

AES67: hold the transmit lead with a closed-loop servo

The one-shot PTP anchor sets where the RTP timeline starts but nothing kept it
there.  Every source discontinuity makes the drift loop re-anchor its PTS
timeline to absorb the gap ("-231 ms gap absorbed, re-anchoring"), while the RTP
sample counter does not move with it, so the relationship the anchor
established is broken and the lead steps -- one way only.  Measured over a night
of media restarts:

  +23.19 -> +30.64 -> +34.14 -> +40.63 -> +44.54 ms

roughly 4-7ms per restart, never recovering, with pacing degrading alongside
(40% of packets back-to-back, and it did not self-heal).  The previous servo was
open-loop -- it corrected the clock difference it was told about, not the error
it actually produced -- so it could not see this at all.

Replaced with a closed-loop servo on the measured lead.  For each outgoing
packet it reads the RTP timestamp from the header (bytes 4-7; not worth a
gstreamer-rtp dependency for four bytes), computes when the sink will transmit
it, projects that onto the sample rate and compares.  The subtraction is in
guint32 so the RTP wrap handles itself.  Runs at ~1Hz with a 200us slew limit.

The sink latency term matters and is not optional: a sink renders at
PTS + base + latency + ts-offset, and omitting latency biases every measurement
by exactly that amount.  Measured with it missing, the servo drove a 20ms target
down to -4.10ms -- the wrong side of zero, which is the failure that silenced a
Yamaha MRX7-D.  With it queried and included, the lead converges to +19.90ms
(p10 +19.87, p90 +19.92) against a 20ms target.

targetLeadMs is now the knob for that, defaulting to 20.  It must stay above the
receiver's link offset plus jitter (Dante/RAVENNA are typically 0.25-5ms) but is
also latency, so bigger is not better.  Previously the lead was an emergent
side effect of sinkPacingMs, which is a pacing parameter and a confusing place
for stream latency to live.

AES67: re-warm the drift loop after absorbing a gap, and instrument the servo

Two changes, and a defect this work exposed which is not yet fixed.

Re-warm after gap absorption.  Absorbing a gap re-anchors the output timeline,
and the buffers immediately after measure that re-anchor as a fresh offset, so
resuming control straight away makes the loop re-trigger on itself -- measured
under a 25s file on repeat, three re-anchors in four buffers.  A fixed buffer
hold-off only paced the oscillation: the spacing histogram came back with 526
re-anchors at exactly the hold-off length.  The existing 5s warm-up path does
the right thing instead -- it waits, discards what it saw meanwhile and starts
clean -- and the learned trim is deliberately kept across it, so rate correction
continues at the last good value while adaptation pauses.

Measured against the previous runs, same 25s-file test:

  slew-only   lead ran to +3614 ms   3166 gaps / 683 restarts
  step+slew   lead held ~20 ms        477 gaps / 360 restarts
  re-warm     lead held ~20 ms          5 gaps / 188 restarts

Servo diagnostics, which is how the defect below was found.

KNOWN DEFECT, do not trust the servo yet.  It measures the RTP timestamp
against a transmit time it *predicts* from ts-offset -- its own control
variable -- so it can always satisfy the equation by moving ts-offset.  Logged
side by side under the stress test:

  servo:  lead +20.00 ms, err +0.00   (reports itself converged)
  wire:   lead -177.16 ms, media clock -749.0 ppm

The loop is closed on itself and cannot see reality.  That is what produced the
unexplained -56 ms window no combination of gains accounted for.  A correct
servo has to measure something it does not control.

Underneath that, the drift loop cannot converge when tracks change faster than
its measurement window: it needs about a minute to resolve a 54ppm drift, and a
restart every 25s resets it, leaving trim thrashing between +59, +29 and +22
ppm.  Preserving the rate estimate across a track boundary is the next piece --
crystal drift does not change when a track does.

splitClockDomains remains default OFF and nothing shipped is affected.

AES67: mix a permanent silence floor so track changes stop breaking the clock

The AES67 media clock is a sample count, so audio that never arrives puts the
timeline permanently behind PTP -- it cannot be corrected afterwards, because
the samples are not late, they are absent.  FPP tearing down and rebuilding its
media pipeline at a track change leaves a ~232ms hole, and measured with a 25s
file on repeat that ran the media clock to -6589ppm: AES67 drifting ahead of
the local sound card by ~180ms per track and accumulating.  A listener hears
tracks butted together on AES67 while the sound card has the pause.

Silence is the additive identity, so mixing a constant silence source with the
captured audio needs no arbitration -- silence alone when nothing is playing,
the audio itself when something is.  audiomixer is the documented idiom: it is
built not to stall when a source goes away.

Measured with a 25s file restarting continuously:

  before   media clock -6589 ppm, one gap absorption per transition
  after    media clock  +3.9 ppm, zero absorptions, zero source gaps
           lead +19.90ms on target, stream carries a signal

It only works with splitClockDomains, and the reason is worth recording.  On
the stock path we force base-time to 0 so running time equals PTP time, which
makes running time absolute -- around 1.7e18 ns.  A live audiotestsrc dropped
into that believes it is 56 years behind and floods to catch up: measured, the
packet rate went to 20418/s against 250 and the media clock to +80877578 ppm.
pipewiresrc is immune because PipeWire timestamps its buffers; a synthetic
source generating its own is not.  splitClockDomains does not force base time,
so the source starts from a sane running time.

Two approaches tried first and rejected:

Linking a silence source in FPP's routing matrix fixed the clock exactly as
intended (-6589 -> +0.9 ppm) but killed the audio -- those nodes are arbitrated
by FPP's own routing, and a hand-made link fights it rather than summing.  The
mix belongs in our pipeline, where nothing else is managing the links.

node.always-process on FPP's AES67 filter chain, to stop it suspending when its
input disappears, broke the stock path outright: lead -184ms and 83% of packets
back-to-back.  Reverted.

Remaining: 13% of packets still go back-to-back, down from 83%, and that
appears to be the transitions themselves rather than steady state.

The silence floor works and fixes what it was built for.  Measured with a 25s
file restarting continuously: media clock +3.9 ppm against -6589 ppm without

held at +19.9 ms, and music present on every sample.

It costs sink pacing, and the cost is the mixer itself rather than the track

  splitClockDomains, floor OFF   paced at 4.00ms, PASS, lead spread 0.03ms
  splitClockDomains, floor ON    46-48% of packets back-to-back

made no difference (46%).  Forcing output-buffer-duration to one ptime made it

So the two halves of a shippable configuration currently exclude each other:
the floor keeps the media clock correct across track changes but breaks the

That is the open problem.  The mixer aggregates two live inputs and emits on
its own schedule, so the likely direction is re-imposing the cadence after it
rather than trying to persuade it to emit evenly -- audiobuffersplit already
produces exact ptime buffers downstream, so it is the transmit timing that is

AES67: fill source gaps with silence in the drift probe, not with a mixer

Replaces the audiomixer silence floor.  The mixer worked -- media clock +3.9 ppm
against -6589 -- but cost sink pacing, and that cost was the mixer itself, not
the track changes: measured in steady state on a long file with no transitions,
46-48% of packets went back-to-back where the same pipeline without it paced
cleanly at 4.00ms.  A queue on its own thread after it made no difference, and
forcing output-buffer-duration to one ptime made it worse.

The drift probe already synthesises its output buffers -- it resamples and
writes its own PTS from an internal sample counter -- so it can put the missing
samples back itself, with no extra element in the path to disturb anything.
When the source PTS jumps, the frames are owed and prepended as silence to the
next output buffer.

Three details, each of which was wrong first and measured:

Filling must win over absorbing.  Absorbing re-anchors the timeline to skip the
hole; filling puts the samples back.  Doing both leaves the loop re-anchoring
and then being pushed again by the fill: 4 absorptions still fired alongside 8
good fills and the media clock stayed at -54.7 ppm.

The filled silence counts as input as well as output.  It is synthetic input
standing in for audio that never arrived, and leaving it off the input side
makes the loop measure a source slow by exactly the gaps -- cardRate read
47235/s (-15926 ppm), trim pinned at its +300 ppm clamp, offset growing
11.5 -> 22.9 ms, while the wire was actually correct at +1.2 ppm.

The cap is one second.  Anything longer is a stream restart rather than a gap,
and should not turn into a large allocation.

Measured under a 25s file restarting continuously:

  drift loop trim +55 ppm, card 47997.3/s (-56.0 ppm), offset +/-0.14 ms
  12 PASS, 0 FAIL, 0 WARN, paced at 4.00ms, lead +19.91 ms (spread 0.05 ms)

which is the first configuration to hold both the media clock and the cadence

AES67: one ptime must fit in one packet

The channel count and ptime dropdowns had no interlock, and most of their
combinations describe a packet that cannot be sent.  L24 is 3 bytes per
sample per channel, so 4ms is 576 bytes per channel: 1152 in stereo, but
2304 at 4 channels and 4608 at 8, against a 1440-byte limit (1500 - IP -
UDP, with headroom for a VLAN tag).  AES67 forbids IP fragmentation.

Nothing caught it.  We never set the payloader's mtu, so it sat at
GStreamer's 1400 default and quietly split anything larger -- emitting
several short packets per ptime while the SDP kept advertising a=ptime:4.
The min-ptime=max-ptime pair we set right above it says the opposite.  4ms
is the default, so every user selecting 4, 6 or 8 channels got this.

Clamp ptime to what fits at the configured channel count, warn when we do,
set mtu explicitly so the intent lives in the code rather than in a
library default, and disable the 4ms option in the UI above stereo.

1ms fits at every channel count up to 8, and is also the packet time Dante
requires when receiving an AES67 flow, so the clamp lands on the more
interoperable value rather than a compromise.

AES67: the jitter tail was a thread with no priority

Measured against the AES67 sender bound -- each packet's send time versus
what its own RTP timestamp says it should be -- the stream cleared the
mandatory 17ms comfortably but missed the recommended 1 packet time on
0.08% of packets, each one late by up to a full ptime.

The cause was not load: the box sat at 0.24 on 4 cores through both runs.
PipeWire runs its data-loop at SCHED_FIFO 88; the GStreamer thread paced
our packets at SCHED_OTHER nice 0, right beside it. Every excursion was
one missed timeslice, which is why they clustered at almost exactly one
ptime and why the next packet was always back on grid.

Over 60k packets at 4ms ptime, SCHED_OTHER against SCHED_FIFO 80:

  worst lateness      8.6ms  ->  0.64ms
  peak-to-peak       12.8ms  ->  0.80ms
  past 1ms (rec.)   49 pkts  ->  none
  max wire gap      12.56ms  ->  4.40ms

GStreamer creates that thread and offers no way to set its scheduling, so
take the one chance to run code on it: a pad probe fires on the streaming
thread, so the first buffer through elevates the thread that carried it.
The probe then removes itself. Unconditional -- an unpaced tail is worse
in every mode, not just splitClockDomains.

fppd.service had no LimitRTPRIO, so the call would have failed EPERM; the
PipeWire units already set 95 and this matches. 80 is deliberately below
PipeWire's 88: if both are runnable the audio graph has to win, since
starving it underruns every stream on the box rather than just this one.
EPERM stays survivable for a hand-started fppd -- the stream is still
conformant, just with a wider tail -- and says so in the log.

This is what buys the headroom to lower targetLeadMs toward the 2ms Dante
expects; at an 8.6ms tail that was not available.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

AES67: check transmission jitter against the AES67 bound

The tool measured inter-arrival spread, which is not the quantity AES67
constrains. AES67 bounds transmission jitter -- how far each packet strays
from the time its own media clock says it should have left -- to 17 packet
times (or 17ms, whichever is shorter), and recommends one packet time.

The two disagree in a way that hides the fault. A packet sent one slot late
produces one long gap and one short one; the median absorbs both and the
pacing check passes. Measuring against the RTP timestamp instead shows it
as what it is: one late packet.

That is how the pacing thread's missing priority stayed invisible. Under
the new check it reads plainly -- 49 packets past the 1ms recommendation at
SCHED_OTHER, none at SCHED_FIFO 80.

AES67: stereo only, and default to 1ms

Multichannel does not work, and the failure is total. Every AES67 stream is
fed through the delay filter-chain FPPINIT_Audio emits, which is
unconditionally stereo -- two delay nodes, audio.channels = 2,
audio.position = [ FL FR ], stream.dont-remix = true -- and never reads the
instance's channel count. Asking the pipeline for 8 channels fails caps
negotiation against that node: "Internal data stream error" on the bus and
zero packets on the wire, confirmed by capture.

So the UI has been offering 2/4/6/8 against a graph that could only ever do
2, and anyone selecting more than stereo silently lost their stream. That is
worse than not offering it. Disable the wider options, say why, and warn when
an existing config already holds one. Clamp in ParseConfig as well: a stored
8 would otherwise survive an upgrade still dead, and nothing on screen would
explain it.

Raising the limit needs the delay chain to emit N nodes, GStreamerOut to stop
addressing them as delay_l/delay_r, the group combine-stream to carry N
positions, and the routing matrix to have something to put in channels 3-8.
That is its own piece of work, not a flag.

Separately, default ptime moves 4ms -> 1ms. 1ms is mandatory for every AES67
device and is the only packet time Dante will transmit, and it measured
better here rather than worse: over 180k packets, worst-case transmission
lateness 0.235ms against 0.64ms at 4ms, because smaller buffers leave the
pacing thread less to slip. A 4-hour soak at 1ms held lead within 0.03ms,
media clock inside 1ppm, and took zero absorptions. Existing configs keep
whatever ptime they have.

Discovery: learn a stable identity for WLED, Baldrick and Falcon V4/V5

Discovery only ever filled in an identity for a non-FPP controller from
the ARP table, which needs the device to be on a directly attached
subnet and to have been contacted recently enough to still be in the
neighbour cache.  A show whose players sit on a different subnet from
its controllers satisfies neither, so those devices arrive with no
identity at all and the statistics collector falls back to a hash
salted with the reporting host -- which gives one controller a
different identity per observer, and makes deduplicating a device
across players impossible.

Three vendors report something stable over HTTP, which unlike ARP works
regardless of subnet:

- WLED already answers /json/info with its MAC, in the same document
  the detector reads for version and name.  No extra request.

- A Baldrick reports no id of its own, but reports one for each board
  it can see.  A device's identity therefore arrives while a DIFFERENT
  address is being probed, so NetworkController now carries a map of
  identities learned for other addresses and MultiSync keeps them as
  hints.  They are kept rather than applied and dropped, because the
  neighbour describing a device is often probed before that device has
  been discovered; UpdateSystem() consults the map for every system it
  touches, so both orders behave alike.  A hint never creates a system.

- Falcon V4/V5 report one through a JSON API that is only reachable by
  POST, so Detection grows a post() alongside fetch().  status.xml has
  already settled that the device is a Falcon before the request is
  made, so the answer only ever adds an identity: the older boards in
  that type range answer 404 and are still detected.  V2/V3 have no
  identity to offer and keep the derived one.

All three emit the same MAC: spelling the ARP path uses, so a device
keeps one identity however it was discovered, and no consumer changes.

One subtlety, now recorded at the precedence check: these values are
not always the address ARP sees.  An ESP32 on Ethernet uses base+3 for
its interface, so ARP reports a MAC three higher than the one the
device reports for itself; a vendor that reports its interface address
instead matches ARP exactly.  Both are stable, but they are different,
and a device carrying whichever one its observer happened to obtain
would split in two -- the failure this path exists to remove.  So a
vendor-reported identity overrides an ARP-derived stand-in, and ARP
stays the fallback for devices no detector could identify.

Parsing verified against captured responses from real hardware of each
type, including a 404 body yielding no identity rather than a crash,
with a control run confirming each check fails when its field name is
wrong.

Discovery: learn a stable identity for SanDevices controllers

The status page these serve states the board's MAC, in the same HTML the
detector already reads to work out the model and firmware version, so
this costs no extra request.  Like the other vendor-reported identities
and unlike the ARP fallback, it works for a board on another subnet --
which is where a show whose players and controllers sit on different
subnets needs it, since those boards otherwise arrive with no identity
and the statistics collector falls back to a per-reporter hash.

Discovery: fix three ways an AlphaPix goes missing or mistyped

Comparing the detector against the equivalent xLights controller code
turned up three separate faults, two of which make the board disappear
from discovery entirely rather than appear with less detail.

The board's type string was read from the wrong match result.  Two
patterns identify the model, and the second is tried only when the first
fails -- but the type was always taken from the first pattern's match,
which on that path holds the result of a search that FAILED.  Any board
whose page names its model only as "<n> Port Ethernet to SPI Controller"
was therefore typed as an empty string.  The other wording, which does
match the first pattern, worked correctly, which is why this went
unnoticed.

The firmware version was treated as part of identification: if the
version could not be read the whole detection was abandoned, even though
the model had already been recognised.  The version pattern is spelled
for one page layout and a later web UI is laid out differently, so a
board on newer firmware could state its model plainly and still be
rejected.  The version is now reported when it can be read and omitted
when it cannot.

These boards also serve one client at a time.  While another computer
holds the session, every page is replaced by a stub naming no model and
no version, so the board matched nothing, was dropped as an
unrecognised address, and vanished with nothing logged.  That stub is
now recognised: the board is reported with no detail and a warning
naming the actual cause, which is considerably more use to somebody
hunting a missing controller than no row at all.

No identity is available for these over HTTP -- there is no MAC on any
page they serve, and the xLights implementation extracts none either --
so they continue to rely on the ARP fallback, which means a stable
identity only for a player on the same subnet.

Verified against a captured session-locked page from real hardware plus
a page for each model-naming form, with a control run confirming the
previous code fails all three cases and passes the fourth.

Discovery: identify AlphaPix boards from the Device ID they display

These boards publish no MAC on any page they serve, so until now the
only identity available for one was the ARP address -- which needs the
board to be on a directly attached subnet, and leaves every off-subnet
board with no identity at all.

Their status page does state a "Device ID", and on the board that could
be measured that id is the low 24 bits of its MAC written in decimal:
converting it to hex and prefixing an all-zero OUI reproduces the
address ARP reports for that board exactly.  So the id is recorded as
the MAC it encodes rather than as an identifier of its own, which keeps
a board identified from its page and a board identified only from the
ARP table on one value instead of two names for one device.

Worth noting for whoever meets this next: the all-zero OUI is a single
observation.  A board that ships with a real OUI would be reconstructed
wrongly, and because a value read from the device outranks the ARP
address, the reconstruction would win where both are available.  A
second board on a different production run would settle it.

Verified against a captured page from real hardware -- the derived
address matches the one ARP reports for the same board -- with a control
run confirming the parse yields nothing when its anchor is wrong while
model and version still match.

www: stop saving a leftover universe count on DDP and Twinkly rows

DDP and Twinkly rows address a flat channel range: fppd reads
channelCount alone for them and never looks at universeCount, which is
why the universe-count input is hidden for those types.  The save path
read and wrote it anyway, so such a row kept whatever value happened to
be sitting in the hidden field -- one on some rows, a stale count on
others, zero on others again.

fppd is unaffected, but nothing reading the config back can tell a
leftover from a real count, and anything that multiplies the two to get
a channel span produces a figure that is wrong differently on every
install.  A uniform error can be corrected for after the fact; this one
cannot, which is what makes it worth fixing at the source rather than
working around downstream.  Write the one value that means "not a run of
universes" instead.

The three places that have to agree on which types are flat now share a
named test rather than repeating the list, so they cannot drift apart.
The test keeps the loose comparison the inlined copies used, because one
caller passes the select's value as a string and the other two pass
numbers.

Note the universe NUMBER is hidden for the same types and saved the same
way; that value is inert everywhere it is read, so it is left alone here
rather than widened into this change.

fix(upgradeOS): Harden against shell injection / SSRF / XSS

Fixes **Critical shell injection + SSRF** in `www/upgradeOS.php:148` / `www/upgradeOS.php:67`.

`$_GET['os']` was interpolated unescaped into a `sudo wget … $url -O …` `passthru()` command (and a dead-code `curl_setopt(CURLOPT_URL, $_GET['os'])` path). `FILTER_VALIDATE_URL` alone does **not** reject `;`, `|`, `$(…)`, `&`; `basename()` validation of the *filename* does not cover the *URL*. An attacker could smuggle shell metacharacters in the URL path and have them interpreted by `/bin/sh`:

```
GET /upgradeOS.php?wrapped=1&os=https://evil.com/a;touch%20/tmp/pwned_http_simple
# → passthru("sudo wget -c … https://evil.com/a;touch /tmp/pwned_http_simple -O …")
#   shell splits on `;`, second command executes as the web user (sudo wget context)
```

The fix is strictly hardening — no URL/API contract change — and preserves the existing `UpgradeSource` mirror + `about.php` → `upgradeOS.php?wrapped=1&os=` flow.

> **Risk: Critical** — unauthenticated RCE on default FPP installs (FPP web UI is LAN-trusted, no auth on `upgradeOS.php`). The OS upgrade path is also `sudo`-adjacent.

fix(testing): push the running output test in fppd status, sync Testing dropdowns from it

The pixel-string, LED-panel and PWM "Testing" dropdowns were static markup that
always loaded as "Off", even while a test was running. Opening the page in a
second tab or device showed Off over a live test, and since re-selecting Off
fires no change event the test could not be stopped from there. The panel page
had a load-time ajax restore from api/testmode; the other two had nothing, and
none of them could follow a test being changed or stopped elsewhere.

fppd now includes the running test's config in the /fppd/status payload as
"testMode" (the same shape api/testmode returns, minus the bulky per-output
"config" blob). That payload is already pushed over the status WebSocket the
moment it changes, so every open page learns about a test started, changed or
stopped anywhere within a second, and the first snapshot after connect restores
the dropdown on page load. The test config string gets its own small mutex: it
was written unlocked and is now read from the status producers.

A single fpp.js helper, SyncTestModeSelect(), registers on the status-change
hook and keeps a given select in step, gated on the "outputs" names the page
starts its tests with. Pixel, panel and PWM tests are all fppd mode "Outputs"
with a numeric type, so the gate is what stops a panel test claiming the pixel
dropdown (which the old panel restore got wrong the other way). Only a changed
testMode is applied, so a snapshot built between the user's Test Start and fppd
acting on it cannot flip the dropdown back to Off. The value is set
programmatically and fires no change event, so a page never re-issues a test it
merely observed.

fix(aes67): source-gap probe was inside the libsamplerate guard

SourceGapState, SourceGapProbe and DestroySourceGapState were defined inside
the #ifdef FPP_HAVE_SAMPLERATE region, but CreateSendPipeline installs the
probe unconditionally. On any box without samplerate.h the definitions vanish
while the call site stays, and the build fails with three undeclared-identifier
errors 1200 lines from the cause.

It went unnoticed because libsamplerate0-dev is not in FPP_Install.sh's package
list: it arrives only as a transitive dependency of libsdl2-dev, so whether a
given machine has it is luck. Development boxes and the CI runners have it;
anyone building on a system that resolved SDL2's dependencies differently does
not, and reported the break from a clean master.

The definitions move above the guard. Pure relocation, no content change --
setup.mk's promise that "absent it, the AES67 send path builds and runs exactly
as before, just without drift correction" is true again.

Also say when a flag was accepted and then ignored, which is how this class of
problem reaches a user. driftResample already warned on a build with no
libsamplerate; sourceSilenceFloor did not, and it is the flag testers are
currently being asked to turn on. It is applied by DriftResampleProbe, so it
also does nothing when driftResample is off even on a build that has
libsamplerate -- both cases now log rather than no-op silently, because a set
flag that does nothing reads as a fault in the sender when someone is testing
against real receiver hardware.

Refs #2848.

fix(video): initialize GStreamer before the input/output managers build pipelines

VideoInputManager and VideoOutputManager call gst_parse_launch() without ever
calling gst_init(). Media playback used to be the only thing that touched
GStreamer, so the lazy init on the playback path (EnsureGStreamerInit) was
enough; the video managers now build pipelines straight from a config reload,
which can happen before any media has played. On a player where nothing else
had initialized GStreamer -- no media played, no AES67 or Opus RTP config --
gst_parse_launch() dereferenced the still-null value table and took fppd down
with a SIGSEGV inside GStreamer's own parser:

  gst_value_deserialize <- gst_caps_from_string <- gst_parse_launch_full
                        <- VideoInputManager::StartSource

on a perfectly well-formed pipeline description. Since the source restarts on
every fppd start, the box crash-looped.

EnsureGStreamerInit() becomes the single place gst_init() happens. It now keys
off gst_is_initialized() rather than a file-static bool, so it stays correct
alongside any caller that got there first, and it is serialized because the
overlay code, the managers and the playback path can all arrive from different
threads. Both video managers call it before touching the GStreamer API, and
the AES67 and Opus RTP managers route their own bare gst_init() through it.

Verified with a standalone reproducer on real hardware: the exact pipeline
description from the field reports segfaults in gst_value_deserialize without
gst_init() and builds cleanly with it.

fix(www): find the status socket under any path prefix, not just /proxy/

The fppdws URL is built in the browser at runtime, so mod_proxy_html cannot
rewrite it the way it rewrites static markup -- it has to name the prefix the
rest of the site is served under, and work that out for itself.

It was taking that from window.location.pathname, which cannot answer the
question: that is the path of the *page*, and says nothing about how much of it
belongs to a reverse proxy. /api/commandhelp.php and /proxy/1.2.3.4/index.php
are the same shape. So the code matched the one layout it knew, FPP's own
/proxy/<host>/ relay, and dropped the prefix everywhere else. Anything else
serving FPP under a prefix -- an nginx location, or a monitoring app relaying
per-device paths -- asked for ws://<host>/fppdws, which reaches that host's own
fppd rather than the one being proxied to, or nothing at all.

This script is always at <root>/js/fpp.js, so its own resolved src names the
prefix whatever it happens to be. It also works from any subdirectory, since the
browser has already resolved both '../js/fpp.js' and 'js/fpp.js' to the same
absolute URL -- which is what the /api/ and /wled/ special case was there to
handle, and it no longer needs one. Falls back to '/' if the script element
cannot be found.

behind an arbitrary prefix, from a subdirectory page in each of those, and with

fix(FileMonitor): prime only the callback just registered, not every watcher

TriggerFileChanged(file) fires every callback registered against that path,
which is right for a real inotify event but wrong for the
AddFile(...).TriggerFileChanged(...) "prime it now" idiom that five call
sites use.  Once two subsystems watch the same config file, the second one
to register re-runs the first one's callback -- work that was already done,
sometimes seconds earlier.

co-universes.json had exactly that: MultiSync watches it to keep its
configured-output-range map current, and InitializeChannelOutputs() watches
it to build the outputs.  The channel-output prime therefore re-ran
MultiSync's reload, which re-reads the file and resolves every configured
output address.  With destinations configured by hostname rather than by IP,
that is a second full pass of blocking DNS on the startup path -- and a
name that no longer resolves costs a multi-second timeout each time.

Add a TriggerFileChanged(id, file) overload that fires only the named
callback, and use it at all five prime-it-now sites.  The whole-file
overload is unchanged and still used for genuine file changes, so a config
edit continues to reach every watcher.

fix(net): cache host resolutions, including the failures

Nothing in fppd remembered the result of a hostname lookup, so a name
configured as a channel-output destination was resolved from scratch by
every caller that needed it.  Callers are spread across startup -- MultiSync
builds its configured-output-range map, the UDP output resolves each
destination as it initialises, and HTTP discovery resolves each non-CIDR
token -- so one name in the config is several independent lookups, all on
the main thread.

That is free when DNS answers.  It is not free when it does not: a name that
no longer resolves costs a flat multi-second timeout, and the system resolver
caches nothing in that case, so every caller pays it again.  On a player with
two dead output hostnames this dominated startup completely -- eight blocking
lookups, 31s from "Creating Scheduler" to the main loop, of which under half
a second was real work.

Add ResolveHostToIPv4() with a small process-wide cache that stores negative
results as well as positive ones, and route MultiSync's GetIPForHost(), its
sync-destination rebuild, and UDPOutputData::toInetAddr() through it.  Same
config now costs two lookups and 8.4s -- one timeout per distinct name, which
is the floor until those callers move off the startup path.

TTLs are short in both directions (60s positive, 30s negative) so a
controller that comes up, or moves, is picked up on the next poll rather than
at the next restart, and the cache is flushed outright from
NetworkMonitor::callCallbacks() -- the one point ahead of every registered
callback -- so a link coming up retries immediately.  Dotted-quads are parsed
directly and never take a cache slot, which keeps the HTTP discovery scan
from evicting anything as it walks whole subnets.

ping.cpp deliberately keeps resolving directly: revalidate() exists to notice
a host coming back, and it already runs off the main thread.

AES67: flush a duration of stale audio, not a buffer count

The track-transition fault testers have been reporting was self-inflicted.
FlushSendPipelines() dropped a fixed 10 buffers to discard audio queued
between the old track stopping and the new one starting, sized against a
256-sample quantum -- "~53ms" per its own comment. Nothing runs a 256-sample
quantum. At the 1024 both a Pi 5 and this box actually use, 10 buffers is
213ms at 48kHz and 232ms at 44.1kHz: four times the audio it meant to throw
away.

That is the whole chain. The drift probe saw the hole we had just made,
reported it as a "source gap" and filled it with silence, which repaired the
media timeline. But the sink queue only holds 55-77ms, so it drained partway
through and the wire went quiet for the rest -- 213 - 55 = ~158ms, which is
what a receiver saw and what Dante Controller flagged red. The numbers match
to the millisecond on two independent machines: 213.33ms measured on a Pi 5
at 48kHz, 232.2ms here at 44.1kHz, against 213.33 and 232.20 predicted.

Drop a duration instead, so it means the same thing at any quantum, and keep
it under the queue depth so the queue covers the gap and the wire never
stops. Measured here: source gap 232ms -> 46ms, worst wire gap across a
transition 157.7ms -> 14.4ms, now inside the 17ms AES67 allows.

Also stop three call sites in GStreamerOut logging three identical lines per
transition, which made one event look like three in the logs testers sent
back. Restart the window rather than adding to it: the old counter was reset
to 10 buffers by each call and only stayed bounded because they happened to
land inside one window.

AES67: measure jitter and drift against the right reference

Two checks were reporting the same fault twice, and a healthy stream as
broken.

Transmission jitter subtracted only the median from the phase error, so a
media clock running slow against wall time left its whole linear ramp behind
and called it jitter. At -54ppm over a 45s capture that is 2.45ms of ramp
reported as +/-1.22ms of jitter -- which is exactly what it printed, to
three decimal places. Drift has its own check immediately below, so this
reported one problem as two and pointed at the wrong one. Fit and remove the
trend; the residual is the packet-to-packet error AES67 actually bounds.
Same stream, same capture: p50 0.826ms -> 0.005ms, max 1.270ms -> 0.132ms.

The drift check then fits RTP growth against pcap timestamps, and those are
CLOCK_REALTIME while the RTP timeline follows PTP. A Pi acting as its own
grandmaster runs PTP off a free-running PHC with NTP disciplining the system
clock, and the crystal error between them measured -54.3ppm here -- read
back as a media clock fault on a stream locked to PTP exactly as intended.
Sample the PHC against CLOCK_REALTIME and take it out, reporting both. Same
capture: "-54.2 ppm" becomes "+0.0 ppm against PTP", passing, and repeatable
across runs.

Sample it across the whole capture rather than over a short window of its
own. At 1ppm per 2us a 2s window turns ordinary scheduling jitter into tens
of ppm: the first attempt read -54.8ppm and then +31.7ppm off the same
clock on consecutive runs, which would have been a worse bug than the one it
fixed. Over a 60s capture the same jitter is under 2ppm, and it costs
nothing because the capture is already running.

A follower sees the grandmaster-vs-NTP difference instead, which is usually
small -- our tester measured +2.3ppm on a Yamaha grandmaster. So this hid
until someone ran as grandmaster, and would have had every such tester
reporting a drift fault that was not there.

feat(api): give the overlay effect list an ETag, and stop sending immutable with max-age=0

/api/overlays/effects?full=true is ~350KB and the UI asks for it on every
page load, but it was served with `Cache-Control: max-age=0, immutable` and
no validator at all. That is the worst of both: zero freshness means a client
must ask again every time, and no ETag/Last-Modified means the answer is
always the whole body. A remote client -- anything reaching the box through
an HTTP-over-MQTT proxy rather than the LAN -- paid for those bytes on every
single load, and had no way to cache around it.

Add makeETagResponse() to fpphttp.h: an FNV-1a over the response bytes as the
validator, returning 304 when If-None-Match already carries that tag. It is a
validator rather than a digest, so it only has to change when the content
does. Matching is on the bare tag appearing anywhere in the header, since a
cache that compressed the response on the way past can echo the tag back with
a "-gzip" suffix. The helper is in the shared header, so plugins can use it
for their own large, rarely-changing results.

The effect list is the right shape for this: it is derived from what is
registered plus what is on disk (fonts, images), so it changes rarely but not
never. Repeat loads now cost a bodiless 304 instead of 350KB.

Also drop `immutable` from anything served as max-age=0, whatever it is
named. FilesMatch can only see an extension, so every extensionless route --
which is all of /api/ -- fell through the existing list and kept the flag.
The comment block there already describes why that pairing is a trap for
.php; on an API it is worse, because a client told never to revalidate cannot
pick up new state at all and cannot even send a conditional request to find
out. Matching on the header value rather than the file name covers both for
good.

feat(api): add versioned ETags, which answer 304 without building the body

The content-hash ETag added for the overlay effect list has to serialize the
whole response before it can hash it, so it saves transfer and compression but
not generation. On the slow boards generation is the expensive half:
/api/overlays/effects?full=true takes 0.9-3.4s of a single-core AM62x to build
but only ~10KB to send once gzipped, and every one of those seconds is still
spent on a request that ends in 304.

Add a second form for handlers that can name their own version more cheaply
than they can serialize it -- a counter bumped when the underlying data
changes, a file mtime. etagMatches() is the bare predicate; the preferred
makeVersionedETagResponse() takes a callable that runs only on a miss, so
forgetting to tag the 200 (which fails silently, as a client that can never
revalidate) isn't possible. The FNV and the If-None-Match matching are factored
out so both forms share one implementation; the existing content-hash entry
point is unchanged, and the callable overload is constrained on invocability so
it can't collide with it for plugins already calling the old one.

Two things are folded into the token rather than left to callers, because both
are silent-corruption bugs:

 - The request path and query, so a handler whose output varies on parameters
   can't serve one variant's body under another variant's tag while using a
   single counter for all of them.

 - A per-process salt, because an in-memory counter restarts at zero. Without
   it a client holding a tag from before a daemon restart is told 304 against a
   different data set that happens to sit at the same count. A restart now
   invalidates these tags, which is the right way round: a false 304 serves
   stale content, a false 200 only costs bytes.

Use it for /api/commands, which is ~34KB and which every page that can edit a
command fetches twice on load, then again after a restart. Its content is fixed
until something registers or unregisters a command -- args are built in
constructors and every list that varies at runtime is declared as a
contentListUrl the client fetches separately -- so a registration counter is a
sound version for it.

Measured on a Pi 5: 304 in 17.3ms against 200 in 26.8ms, the remainder being
proxy and framework overhead. Checked with controls that trip -- a bogus tag, a
tag from another route, and a tag from before a restart all correctly return
200 with the full body.

feat(api): compress JSON, and give the file-backed API routes validators

Two gaps on the PHP side of the API, found while auditing what else could use
the ETag treatment.

Debian's stock mods-available/deflate.conf lists text/*, the javascript types,
application/xml and application/wasm -- but not application/json, which did not
exist when that list was written. So every API handler that sets its content
type correctly was serving uncompressed, while the handlers that return a bare
string, and so fall back to text/html, were compressed by accident. That is
exactly backwards. The EEPROM vendor list is 30KB of JSON that gzips to 3KB,
and none of the file listings, config files or channel output configs were
compressed at all. Add the JSON types in FPP's own vhost. fppd's routes are
unaffected either way: drogon compresses its responses itself before Apache
ever sees them.

Separately, nothing served from a file carried a validator of any kind -- no
ETag, no Last-Modified -- so a client re-fetching an unchanged config was sent
the whole thing every time and had no way to ask whether it needed to be. Add
fppSendCacheValidators() and use it for:

 - every config file, via limonade's render_file(), which is the single
   chokepoint both callers go through;
 - /api/channel/output/{file}, whose response is a re-encode of one file;
 - /api/settings, ~100KB of metadata that only changes on an upgrade;
 - /api/openapi.json, ~250KB rebuilt per request, and the one of the four that
   needs a content hash rather than a stat because the served document is the
   base file merged with whatever the installed plugins contribute.

For the file-backed three the validator is size-mtime-inode, so a client that
is already current costs one stat and no read at all. Apache does apply the
conditional itself once a handler sets a validator, but only after PHP has
built the body it is about to discard; returning early skips that too.

The two changes interact in a way worth stating: compressing JSON is what makes
Apache append "-gzip" to these ETags, so a client now echoes back a tag that
does not equal the one that was sent. Matching on the bare tag appearing
anywhere in If-None-Match, rather than on equality, is what keeps that from
turning every conditional request into a permanent 200.

Checked on a Pi 5 with controls that trip: a bogus tag returns the full body, a
matching tag returns 304 both with and without gzip negotiated, and
If-Modified-Since answers 304 for the file's own timestamp and 200 for an older
one. Swept 29 pages and endpoints for PHP errors with a pattern first proven to
fire against real error text.

perf(api): stop building the whole apt record set to read one field

The Packages page fetches every package name apt knows about, and getting that
list was the entire cost of opening the page: 5.5s on a PocketBeagle2 once the
index is in cache, and considerably worse on the first load of the day, when
56MB of index has to come off eMMC first.

It was parsing `apt list --all-versions`. That asks apt to build and format a
record per package -- version, archive, architecture, install state -- and the
caller then threw all of it away and kept the name before the slash.
`--all-versions` made it worse for nothing, because it repeats a package once
per available version: the list arrived with tens of thousands of duplicates in
it (34,750 of 104,875 entries on one board here) that the page then had to hold
in memory and search on every keystroke.

Read the index files directly instead. These are the same files apt parses, so
this is the same data from the same source, asked for the one field that is
wanted. The dpkg status file is read alongside them so a package that is
installed but no longer in any configured repository still appears, which is
what `apt list` does too, and the result is sorted and deduplicated.

Falls back to asking apt when the index glob matches implausibly little, which
is what an apt configured to keep its indexes compressed would look like.

Also return it as application/json rather than letting it fall back to
text/html. That is worth stating together with the deflate change earlier on
this branch and not before it: text/html was in Apache's compression list and
application/json was not, so correcting the type without that fix would have
turned an accidentally-compressed response into an uncompressed one.

Measured, warm, against the implementation it replaces -- identical name sets,
verified in both directions with nothing missing and nothing extra:

  PocketBeagle2:  5.41s -> 0.53s,  71,744 -> 70,588 entries
  Pi 5:           1.51s -> 0.25s,  2,088,228 -> 1,448,497 bytes (339KB gzipped)

The fallback was checked by pointing the fast path at a glob that cannot match
and confirming the threshold trips and the fallback returns the identical set.

fix(api): don't trust a file's mtime as a validator while it is still racy

st_mtime has one-second resolution, so two writes inside the same second
produce the same timestamp. If they also leave the size and the inode alone --
an in-place rewrite of the same number of bytes, which a value edit easily is
-- then size-mtime-inode repeats for different content. A client that read
between the two writes holds a tag that still matches and is answered 304 with
the older file. It then stays wrong: nothing changes the tag again until some
later write happens to alter the size or the mtime.

Reproduced directly: write A, GET (tag issued), rewrite in place with B of the
same length in the same second, GET with that tag -> 304, while the disk holds
B.

FPP's own config writers go through WriteFileAtomic(), whose rename() gives the
file a fresh inode, so they avoid this. That is a property of one writer rather
than of the validator, though, and anything that edits a config in place -- a
script, an editor, a plugin, an rsync -- brings it straight back.

So only trust a stat once its mtime is safely in the past, and hash the content
inside that window. Once now is more than a second past the mtime, no later
write can land on that mtime value again, because time only moves forward; a
stat-derived tag handed out after the window can therefore never be reused for
different content. The comparison is >= rather than >, which also covers a
clock stepping backwards -- on these boards that happens on every boot before
NTP settles, and it makes the mtime read as being in the future, where the
conservative path is the one that must be taken.

The cost is a read and a hash of a file that was written moments ago, which is
exactly when a page is reloading its config anyway. Past a few megabytes that
stops being worth it, so an oversized file in the racy window is sent with no
validator at all: always a 200, never a wrong 304.

Also clear the stat cache first. Callers arrive here after their own
file_exists()/is_dir() checks, and those populate PHP's per-request cache.

Verified on a Pi 5: the race now answers 200 and serves the new bytes;
unchanged content inside the racy window still answers 304, so this narrows the
validator rather than disabling it; a mtime older than the window goes back to
the cheap stat tag and still answers 304; and a genuinely stale tag is still
rejected.

feat(multisync): take a Baldrick's identity from the board itself

Newer Baldrick firmware states the board's own id at the top level of
/system_state.  Read it, so a board identifies itself rather than having
to wait for a neighbour to describe it.

Until now the only identity these boards ever had came second-hand, out
of the "buddies" list some other Baldrick published -- so a lone board,
or the first one probed on a network, was left with no identity at all
and fell back to whatever ARP happened to see.  That fallback is not the
same value: an ESP32 on Ethernet uses base+3 as its interface address, so
the ARP-derived stand-in and the vendor-reported id name one device with
two different identities, which is exactly the split this path exists to
prevent.

Measured on a board reporting both: the id it gives for itself is
byte-for-byte the one its neighbour gives for it, so the two sources
agree and neither has to win over the other.  The buddies loop is kept
untouched -- it remains the only identity older firmware yields, and it
still names Baldricks of other kinds that discovery may reach later or
not at all.

Verified against real hardware: on stock code the board logged
"UUID: Unknown", with this change it reports its own id, and boards on
older firmware are unaffected and still resolve through their buddies.

a single source (an initial fetch, then a ranged or retried one), so the

feeding -- invisible to curl, which asks exactly once. The lock is now
keyed on the node: switching to a different output still stops the old
stream, a repeat request for the same node leaves it alone, and a
duplicate is bounded by the client going away and the runtime cap.

shell now records its real pgid via ps, timeout runs with --foreground

fix(pipewire mixer): replace sampled meters with a real-time meter on the preview

The per-node meters were the wrong design and I should not have shipped
them. Two things were wrong with them, and they were making the preview
worse rather than adding anything.

They could never move. Each reading was the peak of a ~160ms capture,
and peak over that window pegs near full scale on virtually any
programme material -- measured here it sat at 92-99 continuously, which
is exactly the static bar it looked like. A slower refresh could not
have fixed that; the statistic was wrong.

And they cost more than they were worth. Every refresh reopened a
monitor capture per node (a shorter burst returns nothing at all, since
the capture takes ~250ms just to start), so meters on three nodes meant
roughly a second of capture per cycle, repeatedly opening and closing
monitor streams on sinks that were also feeding the preview. Encoding
was never the bottleneck -- ffmpeg measures about 12% of one core -- but
that churn was, and the preview audibly suffered for it.

Removed, along with the /api/pipewire/audio/levels endpoint, rather than
tuned: no polling cadence makes a peak-of-a-burst into a VU meter.

In its place the preview now carries a genuine real-time meter, measured
in the browser from the stream it is already receiving via an
AnalyserNode. It costs the player nothing, runs at animation rate, and
uses RMS with fast-attack/slow-release ballistics so it actually tracks
the material. It only covers the node being auditioned, which is the one
place a live meter can be both accurate and free.

Routing the element through Web Audio makes that graph the only path to
the speakers, so the context is resumed inside the click gesture, a
failed resume reconnects the source straight to the destination, and the
error path stops only the animation -- closing the context would silence
an element already routed into it. Playback wins over the bar in every
failure case.

You were right that this is a normal thing to want and should not be
expensive. It is not -- my earlier attempt was simply the wrong
mechanism. Sampling a node by starting a short capture per refresh pays
the stream setup cost over and over, and cannot produce a usable reading
anyway: a burst short enough to be cheap is dominated by the ~250ms the
capture takes to start. Meters are supposed to keep one stream open and
let it report.

Adds AudioLevelMonitor to fppd: one persistent GStreamer pipeline per
metered node (pipewiresrc ! audioconvert ! level ! fakesink), reporting
RMS every 100ms. Levels are published on the existing /fppdws WebSocket
under a new "levels" key -- the envelope was already designed to carry
additional keys -- at 10Hz while anything is subscribed, and not at all
otherwise.

Measured on this Pi 4 with a show playing: metering four nodes moves
fppd from 5.9% to 6.1% of a core. As separate gst-launch processes the
same work cost ~3% per node; inside fppd it shares the GStreamer runtime
and there are no processes to spawn.

Metering is held open by TTL rather than by a connection: the mixer
re-posts the visible node list every 3s, so a closed tab, a lost
network, or a crashed browser stops it within seconds with nothing to
clean up. Collapsed sections are not metered. Verified: levels track the
music, stop on TTL lapse, and resume on re-subscribe.

Two bugs found and fixed while building it, both mine:

- Subscribing after metering had retired itself aborted fppd. The poll
  thread exits when the last meter goes, leaving m_thread joinable, and
  assigning a new thread over a joinable one calls std::terminate() --
  the same trap OpusRTPManager documents. The previous thread is now
  joined first, under a separate lock so joining cannot deadlock against
  the poll thread taking the state lock.

- Every meter read zero. The level element reports its per-channel
  values in a GValueArray, and I tested for GST_VALUE_HOLDS_ARRAY, which
  is a different type -- so the value was silently never read.

The per-node bars replace nothing: the browser-side AnalyserNode meter
on the previewed stream stays, since it is free and finer-grained than
10Hz for the one node being auditioned.

fix(pipewire mixer): follow externally changed values instead of holding stale ones

The snap-back guard added with the slot 1 fix was too broad. It pinned a
just-set value for three seconds against whatever the server reported,
so a change made anywhere else -- the API, MQTT, a playlist, a second
browser -- was ignored until the window lapsed. The UI should follow the
server, not argue with it.

The guard now only suppresses a stale echo of the value being replaced.
Each control remembers what the server last reported, and a local change
records both the new value and the one it replaced:

  server reports the new value  -> confirmed, stop holding
  server reports the old value  -> in-flight poll, keep showing the new
  server reports anything else  -> a real change elsewhere, adopt it

So a fader still cannot be yanked back by a poll that left before the
write landed, and an external change appears immediately. A write that
never lands stops being held after the window and the fader returns to
what the server actually has, rather than showing a value that was never
applied.

Verified the sources the mixer polls reflect an external change within a
second: a group, a stream slot and the master each set through the API
read back changed on the next poll.

Cape detection calls handleCapeOverlay() when it finds no eeprom at all,
