AES67: bound the stale-audio flush instead of overshooting it

Two defects, both found by a tester's measurements on a Pi 5 at 48kHz.

The probe tested "is there budget left" and subtracted afterwards, so it
always overshot by up to one quantum. Buffers are whole graph quanta, so a
50ms budget at the 21.333ms quantum took three buffers and cut 64.00ms --
exactly what the tester logged. Only drop a buffer that fits in what
remains: 42.67ms there, 46.44ms at 44.1kHz, never more than asked.

Three call sites in GStreamerOut fire at one track change, and each re-armed
the budget. A later call landing mid-sequence extended the drop, which is
why transitions alternated between three and four quanta (64.00ms and
85.33ms) for a single 50ms request. Ignore a call while a flush is already
running, so one track change discards one budget's worth however many code
paths announce it.

That matters because the gap has to stay under the sink queue's depth for
the queue to cover it. The tester's queue floor was 55ms, so 64ms was
marginal and 85.33ms was not covered at all -- his residual 30.59ms wire gap
is 85.33 - 55.

Worth recording for whoever revisits this: setting the budget to zero
removes the source gap entirely (16 transitions here, not one gap logged),
because pipewiresrc is a live source and holds no stale audio to discard.
The drop may be vestigial. Not taken yet -- it needs an audible check at a
track boundary that this box cannot currently do.

AES67: stop discarding audio at track boundaries

The flush was there to drop "stale audio queued between the old track
stopping and the new one starting". pipewiresrc is a live source: it
delivers the graph in real time and holds no backlog. There was nothing
stale to discard, so the drop only cut a hole in a stream that was already
continuous -- and everything downstream was machinery built to survive that
hole. The drift probe reported it as a source gap, the silence fill patched
the timeline over it, and the sink queue had to stay deep enough to cover it
or a receiver heard the wire stop.

Same box, same audio, across track transitions:

  flush   source gaps        worst wire gap   worst tx jitter
  213ms   213-232ms              157.7ms          156.7ms
   50ms    23.2ms                  6.13ms           5.18ms
    0ms    none, 54 transitions    1.14ms           0.172ms

At zero a transition is indistinguishable from steady state, and clears the
1ms AES67 recommends rather than merely the 17ms it requires. It is also the
only setting where AES67 carries exactly what the sound card carries, so an
artefact at a boundary is FPP's own audio and not something this path
invented.

The mechanism stays, set to zero, in case some source does turn out to need
it. Verified with real audio: signal present, channels distinct, no stalled
or repeated frames, media clock +0.0 ppm against PTP.

AES67: multichannel needed a channel mask, not a rewrite

Anything above stereo produced "Internal data stream error" and not one
packet, which read as multichannel being unimplemented and got it clamped to
2 with a scoped-out plan to wire it up across the PipeWire graph, the delay
control path and the routing matrix.

None of that was needed. Running the pipeline standalone gave the real
error: not-negotiated (-4), with audioconvert warning "Upstream caps contain
no channel mask". Above stereo GStreamer needs an explicit channel-mask in
the caps or negotiation fails; mono and stereo carry an implicit layout,
which is exactly why 2ch worked and nothing above it did. The PipeWire side
was already channel-aware -- the delay chain emits one delay node per
channel with the right positions at any width, and the 8ch chain for a USB
card sits in the same generated config as the 2ch one for AES67.

So: name the layout in both caps filters and lift the clamp to 8.

Verified end to end at 8 channels, 1ms ptime, with an 8-channel source file:
uniform 1152-byte payload (8 x 48 x 3, as predicted), 1000 packets/s,
sequence contiguous, all eight channels carrying audio at equal level, media
clock within 0.1 ppm of PTP, transmission jitter inside the 1ms AES67
recommends, no dropouts.

The stream's channel count and its output group's are separate settings and
both need setting -- the group builds the delay chain feeding the stream. A
mismatch is not fatal: the stream still runs at the stream's width and the
channels the group does not cover carry silence. The UI says so.

AES67: multichannel needs the buffer copy and a 48kHz graph

Above stereo the stream paced badly -- at 8 channels 32-50% of packets went
back-to-back and 90% missed the 1ms AES67 recommends, while the presentation
lead collapsed from 20ms to 2ms. It degraded with channel count rather than
switching on: 2ch and 4ch clean, 6ch 7% back-to-back, 8ch 32-50%.

Not CPU (fppd at 10% of one core, load 0.8 of 4), not the drift resampler
(same with it off), and not GStreamer: the same downstream pipeline fed by
audiotestsrc paces 8 channels perfectly, 0.4% back-to-back. Two things
together caused it.

Zero-copy. always-copy=false hands out PipeWire's own buffers, and one only
returns to the pool once everything downstream has dropped its reference.
audiobuffersplit fans a graph quantum into ~21 one-millisecond buffers, and
past stereo it holds them long enough that the source misses cycles. The
buffers then reach udpsink already past their PTS, and sync=true cannot pace
what is already late -- it sends back-to-back to catch up, which is exactly
the burst pattern. A deeper pool does not substitute: sourceMinBuffers=64 on
its own still left 64% back-to-back. Enable the copy above stereo, keeping
the zero-copy path stereo runs on, which is what every soak and all the
hardware testing to date actually used.

Graph clock. At 44.1kHz PipeWire resamples every quantum into the 48kHz
AES67 node, and above stereo that delays delivery the same way. 8 channels,
same box, same audio:

  graph    copy    result
  44.1k    off     32-50% back-to-back
  48k      off     88% past the 1ms recommendation
  44.1k    on      74% back-to-back
  48k      on      clean, jitter 0.154ms max, full 20ms lead

Both are needed. The copy is automatic now; the graph rate is not ours to
set -- it follows the selected playback card's achieved rate -- so warn
instead, naming the rate found and what to do about it.

Stereo is untouched: still always-copy=false, verified after the change at
jitter 0.171ms max and +0.1 ppm against PTP.

BBShiftString: the receiver enable pin gates the whole differential bus

On a cape that wires the receiver enable line to PRU1, that pin has to be
configured whenever the cape has it.  It is not a Falcon-receiver feature
and not a smart-receiver feature: left unmuxed, nothing behind it gets
data at all, dumb strings included.

3fef60504 (the V4/V5 receiver split) narrowed the condition to hasV5SR,
so any cape configured with v1/v2/Standard or send-only V4 receivers lost
the pin entirely and went dark on every differential port.  Restore the
original condition and hang it off one member so the Init() and Close()
sides cannot drift apart again.

Configuring the pin also commits us to actually running PRU1 - the
firmware parks the pin in its disabled state, so a halted PRU1 would hold
the bus off - so the maxStringLen bump that guarantees PRU1 starts moves
to the same condition.  Previously it was gated on hasV5SR too, which
happened to be consistent only because the pin was as well; a config with
receivers whose ports all land on PRU0 would have muxed the pad to a PRU
that never started.

Verified on a listener-capable 16-port cape with a differential receiver
in auto mode: with every differentialType set to v2 the pad read "reset"
and all four receiver ports were dark while the direct ports lit; with
the fix the pad reads pru1out and all four light.  Re-checked with the V5
configuration restored.

Only show gpiochip/line numbers where they're stable

The chip/line behind a header pin only means something on the Pi's 40-pin
header, where it maps to a fixed set of SoC lines.  Everywhere else -- the
BeagleBone family, and anything behind an i2c GPIO expander on any platform --
the chip index comes out of an asynchronous boot-time probe and can differ from
one boot to the next, so the number in the UI is noise the user can't act on.

Put the rule in one place per language: GPIOPlatformHasStablePinNumbers() and
GPIOPinLabel() in common.php, fppPinHasGpioNumbers() in fpp.js fed by a flag
menuHead.inc emits from the PHP side.  The GPIO input page already did this
locally and now uses the shared predicate; the GPIO dropdowns in the options
API and the "Other" channel outputs now go through GPIOPinLabel().

Also fixes the pixel-string port tooltip, which read "GPIOundefined on port
P1-22" off-Pi: the pin info carries no gpio key there, and the guard tested
only for null.  Note P1- is a PocketBeagle header name too, so the platform
check is what actually covers that case, not the pin prefix.

Publish statistics when the configuration changed, not on every restart

Every fppd start published. PublishStatsBackground() guards on a static
lastPublish initialised to now-minus-the-interval, so the rule was per-process
and a restart always reset it: 91% of the stored corpus is restart records, the
median device has 24 a year and the 90th percentile 99. That is a timestamped
power-on log per household -- start of season, nightly restarts, the evening a
show came down -- and it answers no question the project asks.

Suppressing the boot-time publish outright would be worse in the other
direction. A cape swap, an output reconfiguration or an upgrade would go
unreported for a week while the stored record for that device said something
untrue, and those are exactly the events the statistics exist to observe.

So the trigger is content, not time. On start the route hashes the parts of the
payload that describe how the device is configured and publishes only if that
signature has moved since the last publish, or if the interval has elapsed. A
rebooted-but-unchanged box sends nothing; a box that actually changed reports
immediately, which is better than both the old behaviour and simply going quiet.
The decision lives in the route rather than in fppd because that is the side that
can see the payload; fppd's counter now only decides how often it asks.

The signature covers an allowlist of configuration fields, not everything minus
a denylist, and that asymmetry is the point. The payload carries CPU load,
uptime, sensor temperatures, Wi-Fi signal, free memory and peer lastSeen
timestamps, all of which move on their own; include any of them and the
signature differs on every boot, publish-on-every-restart returns, and nothing
reports an error. A denylist that misses a new volatile field fails open and
silently restores that. An allowlist that misses a new configuration field fails
closed and delays its first report by at most one interval.

Peer data is deliberately out of the signature: the peer set churns as other
devices boot, and at the start of a season every box on a show would watch it
move. Sequence and media counts are out for the same reason -- real, but frequent
enough to be noise. The periodic publish picks both up.

The interval drops from 10 days to 7. Weekly is a round number; 10 was not.

Also gates the route on statsPublish. It is unauthenticated and CSRF-free by
design, so without that a cross-origin form POST from any page the user visits
would upload the payload after they had opted out -- the check previously existed
only in fppd, which does not run the route.

Verified on hardware: first call publishes and records the signature, four
successive restart-reason calls with nothing changed are all skipped, and
changing one setting publishes again immediately.

Keep the weekly check-in when nothing changes, and stop it drifting

Publishing on configuration change alone would have lost the signal that says a
device is still there. A box that never changes and a box that was switched off
for good look identical unless the unchanged one still reports in, so the
interval is a floor rather than a ceiling: publish when the signature moves, and
publish anyway once the interval has elapsed.

That part was already right, but the cadence around it was not. fppd's in-process
guard was set to the same interval as the publish rule, and that guard resets on
every restart. A box rebooting shortly before the interval elapsed would be told
"not yet", spend its guard on that answer, and not ask again for a full interval
-- pushing the periodic publish out to nearly double it. Boxes that restart on a
cycle just under the interval would have sat there indefinitely, which is exactly
the population where liveness data matters most.

So the two cadences are now deliberately different: fppd asks daily, and the
route decides. Asking far more often than the publish interval bounds the error
at one day instead of one interval. The ask counter is also cut from 60480 ticks
to 3600 -- doPing runs about once a second when idle, so the old value was
roughly 17 hours and would itself have become the limiting factor against a
24-hour guard.

Verified on hardware: a fresh publish records the signature; an unchanged repeat
is skipped and reports how long until the next periodic one; backdating the
stored timestamp past the interval with the signature untouched publishes again;
and the following call is skipped, so the timer re-arms.

A cape may set a default; it may not override a choice or switch on telemetry

Three mechanisms let a cape EEPROM decide privacy settings for the person using
the device. The blunt fix -- forbid EEPROMs from touching those keys at all --
throws away something legitimate: a vendor knows their hardware, and "this board
has no serial to send" is a reasonable thing for a cape to say. The defect was
never that a cape has an opinion. It was that the opinion overwrote a decision
the user had already made, and that it could switch transmission on.

So two rules replace the special cases:

  Never override a set value. If the settings file already holds the key, an
  EEPROM does not touch it, whatever the key and whatever the region. This also
  disposes of the FetchVendorLogos removal by construction: removing a key
  restores the shipped default, which is a write like any other and is judged
  the same way.

  Telemetry ratchets one way. Where nothing is set, a cape may set a telemetry
  key only to a value that transmits nothing, unless the region permits a
  transmitting default.

Which regions those are lives in etc/jurisdictions.json, read by this and by the
web side, so the policy is stated once rather than re-listed per consumer -- the
same reason settings.json carries the pii/password declarations. Prior opt-in is
true for the EU/EEA and the UK, whose regimes actually require asking before
transmitting, and false elsewhere: CCPA is opt-out for sale and sharing rather
than opt-in for telemetry, PIPEDA accepts implied consent for non-sensitive data,
and applying EU mechanics to users those rules do not cover protects nobody while
making FPP worse for them.

A device that has never been asked infers from its time zone, which every device
already has, so a European box stays strict while the rest of the fleet does not
wait for a prompt. The inference is never written back and a real answer always
wins. Longest prefix wins, so Europe/London reads as UK rather than EU.

"Transmits more" is declared beside each setting rather than inferred: option
order and numeric value both get it wrong, since ShareCrashData "-1" (create no
report) transmits less than "0" (keep it locally) and statsPublish's options are
an unordered map. FetchVendorLogos is deliberately unranked -- with the serial
off the image URL it is a remote image on a page the user opened, not telemetry,
so a cape may set it either way.

The ratchet compares against zero rather than against the shipped default. That
looked like the natural anchor and is wrong: ShareCrashData ships at the
maximum-disclosure value, so anchoring there would have let a cape switch on full
crash reporting under EU rules simply because the baseline was already maximal.
A ratchet against a bad baseline inherits the badness. Caught by the test below,
which is the only reason it is not in this commit.

The branch that switched statistics on for an unsigned EEPROM is gone. It fired
precisely when the cape was least trusted, wrote a transmitting value nobody had
chosen, and stripped the cape's own opt-out while doing it.

Verified on a Pi: seven cases covering declared EU and US, unset inferring from a
European and an American time zone, unset with no time zone at all, and an
already-set value under both regimes. CapeUtils does not build on macOS -- the
objects there are two years stale -- so a clean host build proves nothing about
this file.

copyFiles: keep the capability, constrain provenance and one target

An EEPROM can copy files into place, and the capability is deliberately broad --
a cape may legitimately need to write outside the media directory, for instance
an apt source so a hardware driver can be installed. That stays. What was missing

Four rules, and the shape matters more than the list. The risk is which file is
read and which is written, not whether a path happens to be absolute:

  No ".." in either path. Nothing legitimate needs it, and it is what makes the
  media-relative form mean anything -- "../../etc/x" walked straight out of it.

  An unsigned EEPROM may read only from /opt/fpp/, FPP's own install tree, which
  holds no secrets. A signed one may read anywhere. This keeps the shipped
  asoundrc pattern working, which names an absolute path under /opt/fpp and would
  have broken under a blanket "no absolute sources" rule.

  Writing outside the media directory requires a valid signature. Adding a
  package source installs arbitrary code as root, so it is exactly the capability
  that wants provenance. No cape ships that today, signed or otherwise.

  The settings file is never a target, signed or not. Overwriting it wholesale
  bypasses every rule that governs defaultSettings -- never-override, the
  telemetry ratchet, the jurisdiction check -- and does it silently. A cape that
  wants to set a setting has defaultSettings, which is governed.

A signed cape may still read the settings file as a source. That is deliberate
rather than overlooked: a signed cape can already write an apt source and install
what it likes, so refusing this one read would not change what it can do.

removeSettings requires a signature; defaultSettings does not

The two are not equivalent and were being treated as one.

defaultSettings only writes a key that is absent, and never-override plus the
telemetry ratchet already constrain it, so the worst an unsigned EEPROM achieves
is choosing a default nobody had chosen. That is what a default is, and the user
remains free to set the key and keep it. No signature needed.

removeSettings deletes a value the user may have set deliberately and restores
FPP's shipped one -- a change nobody asked for, and for a telemetry key
potentially a more-transmitting one. That wants provenance, so it now requires a
valid signature and is ignored with a log line otherwise.

Also restores what -force-defaults means, which the never-override rule had
silently taken away. Never-override exists to stop the CAPE deciding for the
user; it was never meant to stop the user deciding. -force-defaults is what the
"reset to defaults" action in the firmware-upgrade UI passes, so an overwrite
there is precisely what was asked for. Making the rule absolute had left that
flag doing nothing for exactly the keys it exists to reset. The telemetry ratchet
still applies either way: asking to reset defaults is not a jurisdiction
changing.

An existing line is now replaced rather than appended, so a forced reset cannot
leave two lines for one key.

fppcapedetect: ask what a cape's defaults would do, without doing any of it

Cape detection runs from fppinit, before anyone has been asked where they are, so
a cape's telemetry defaults are held rather than applied -- a permissive default
is only allowed once a jurisdiction is known. By the time the setup wizard has
that answer, detection has already run and the cape's opportunity has passed.

Re-running detection for real would fix that and break something else: it writes
to the settings file, and the setup page's whole shape depends on nothing being
persisted until the user finishes it. It would also leave the browser holding a
stale settings object against its own in-flight edits.

So the re-run reports instead of acting:

  fppcapedetect -settings-only -regime=<code> -dry-run

The jurisdiction goes in, the settings that would be applied come out, and
nothing is written -- no settings, no boot config, no file copies, no CSP. The
wizard merges the result into its pending edits and saves everything at the end,
in the order it already uses.

The evaluation calls the same predicate a real run calls, so this cannot drift
from what would actually happen. Anything the user has already set is absent from
the result for the same reason it would be skipped for real, which is also why a
non-privacy default applied at boot does not come back: it is set. Refusals are
returned alongside with the reason, so the caller can say why rather than
presenting an unexplained gap.

Output is compact single-line JSON printed last. Detection writes progress to
stdout throughout, so a pretty-printed object would be interleaved with it and
unparseable; one line lets the caller take the last non-empty line.

Writing that predicate down made an existing wart obvious, so it is fixed here
too. A cape's defaultSettings block lists what it wants, not what it wants
changed, so on a box that has been running a while most entries name a value the
settings file already holds -- and every one of those was logging "cape may not
set X=Y: the user has already set it". That reads like a conflict and is not one.
The predicate now has three outcomes rather than two: a differing value is still
refused and still says so, reworded to "the user has set it to something else"; an
identical value is skipped silently, since there is nothing to change and
rewriting a value with itself would only dirty the settings file. The dry run
reports that case as neither a proposal nor a refusal, which is the shape the
caller wants -- no gap to fill and nothing to explain for a setting already where
the cape wanted it.

Verified on a Pi. The regime reaches the decision (priorOptIn true for EU, false
for US), and with one of the cape's own defaults deliberately unset it moves from
the refused list into the proposed settings -- which is what proves the settings
file is being read and the predicate consulted, rather than an empty object being
returned for the wrong reason. Two settings whose values already matched the
cape's proposal log nothing and appear nowhere in the output, and changing one of
them to a different value brings the refusal straight back. Both runs left the
settings file and cape-info byte-identical.

Split initial setup into a four-step wizard, with location first

The setup page asked everything at once, which made the privacy questions
impossible to ask well. A device cannot know which rules cover its user, so the
page had to either apply the strictest regime to everybody or apply none of
them. Applying EU mechanics to a user the EU does not reach is not more
correct, just cruder: it makes FPP worse for them and protects nobody.

So the page becomes four steps, and the first one establishes where the player
is. Once that is answered the later steps can adapt to it:

  1  Location  holiday list, time zone, coordinates, WiFi regulatory domain
               and legal jurisdiction
  2  Device    fppMode, HostName, HostDescription, InstalledCape, uiLevel
  3  Privacy   presented according to step 1
  4  Security  UI and OS passwords, plus SSH keys at an advanced UI level

Nothing is written until Finalize. The page already routed every tracked
control's onChange into a pending map instead of saving, so steps are pure
show/hide and Back costs nothing.

WHERE THE PLAYER IS

The jurisdiction starts unanswered and step 1 will not advance until it has an
answer, the same way the password choices work. Seeding it from the time zone
was the obvious alternative and is weaker: once a box is pre-selected there is
no way to tell somebody who read it and agreed from somebody who never saw it,
and this is the one field whose entire purpose is to record what the user
declared. It costs one click, and the Lookup buttons fill it in for anyone who
would rather not think about it. A jurisdiction already in the settings file is
an answer given earlier and stands, so setup re-run after an update does not
ask again. The timezone inference is untouched in CapeUtils, where it still
decides for cape detection at boot -- before anybody has been asked anything.

The list is geographic and carries no recommendation -- steering the answer
would be worse than not asking it. The mapping and the one behaviour that
depends on it live in etc/jurisdictions.json, already read by cape detection
and now by www/jurisdiction.inc, so the two halves cannot drift; a new region
stays a data change.

Both "Lookup" buttons already asked a geoip service where this player is and
threw away everything but the one field they were named after. They now fill in
the rest of the location too. That mapping also lives with the data: each
etc/locale/<name>.json declares the countries it covers, and so does each
jurisdiction. api/geoip resolves them server-side and returns an `fpp` object
alongside the response it passed through before, so the browser applies fields
rather than reimplementing the mapping. The EU list is the 27 member states
plus Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway -- EEA rather than EU, reached by the
GDPR, and absent from the `in_eu` flag providers return, which is why the list
is written down instead of delegated. Geoip resolves the public IP, so it
reports where a player reaches the internet rather than where it is: fine for a
seed the user is shown and can correct, and it is not used any other way.

The holiday list keeps its key but loses its old label. "Locale" promised
language, number formats, date formats, currency and collation, none of which
FPP touches; all it does is choose which named holidays the scheduler knows
about. Next to the new jurisdiction field the two looked like the same question
asked twice, when one picks holidays and the other picks which privacy rules
are assumed.

PRIVACY, ADAPTED TO THE ANSWER

Where a regime requires consent before a device transmits, step 3 starts with
no answer selected for the sharing settings and will not continue until each
has one. Everywhere else they are pre-filled and moving on accepts what is
shown -- values the user can see, not defaults nobody was shown. Either way
every privacy key is written on Finalize, touched or not: only the pending map
is saved, so a step whose defaults were accepted wholesale previously wrote
nothing at all and left no record of the answer.

Between step 1 and step 2 the cape is asked again what its defaults would do.
Detection runs from fppinit before anyone has been asked where they are, so a
telemetry default was held; the answer may now permit it. GET /api/cape/defaults
is the dry run, so nothing is written, and the result merges into the pending
edits at gap-filling precedence -- what the user chose always wins, even if
they chose it on an earlier step and came back.

THE REST

Nothing here reboots: a box must not restart out from under someone still
setting it up. But a change that needs one still needs it afterwards, so the
reboot flag is raised with the rest of the save and FPP's own banner asks on
the page the user lands on -- the same mechanism restore-from-backup uses.
Which settings need it is read from settings.json rather than listed in the
page. HostName also moves to the end of the save order, beside the passwords,
so rewriting /etc/hosts cannot happen while later settings are still saving.
Validation moves to the step that owns the field, so a typo is caught where it
was made instead of three steps later.

SSH keys are a config file rather than a setting, so they are laid out and
pre-filled exactly like the same field on the System settings page. Because the
box shows what is already installed, the test at Finalize is whether the value
CHANGED: an unchanged box writes nothing, and an empty one is an instruction to
remove keys only when there were keys to remove.

The two password choices stay as they are, and stay uniform everywhere.
Preselecting "no UI password" is fine -- nothing is shipping a shared secret.
Preselecting the default OS password is not: UK PSTI and California SB-327 both
target universal default passwords, and the forced choice is the compliant
shape rather than arbitrary friction. That is also the one place where the US
is the stricter jurisdiction, so branching it by region would age badly in the
opposite direction to everything else here.

TESTING IT

The country behind the Lookup buttons comes from the caller's public IP,
resolved server-side, so the interesting cases are unreachable from wherever
you are sitting and the browser's location sensor is not involved at any point.
The mapping is the half FPP owns and needs no network, so it gets a
table-driven harness over the cases a plausible wrong implementation fails:
the EEA states, the Crown Dependencies, Switzerland (European, not EEA, and
must not be assumed strict), a country with a jurisdiction but no holiday list,
one with neither, and the empty and unknown inputs. End to end,
GET /api/geoip?country=XX substitutes just the country, and setting
fppGeoIPTestCountry makes the real buttons use it.

VERIFIED

In a browser against a Pi with a signed cape, each check run until it failed as
well as until it passed: navigation and every validation gate; the jurisdiction
starting unanswered, blocking Next with a prompt, being satisfied either by
picking one or by pressing Lookup, and -- the control -- not being asked at all
on a box that already recorded one; the jurisdiction reaching the server
decision and flipping priorOptIn; a first-boot box blocking
on step 3 under EU and pre-filling under US; an already-answered box keeping
its answers under both; the dry run returning proposals and refusals, and
neither once the box already matches; hostname and password validation; the SSH
field appearing only above Basic; the lookups filling what they can determine
and leaving alone what they cannot, in four countries. Removing two EEA states
from the jurisdiction file fails exactly the two harness cases covering them
and flips Iceland from requiring prior opt-in to not, so the harness can go red
for the right reason.

Finishing setup was driven for real, both ways: with the regulatory domain
changed it writes rebootFlag=1 and the banner is showing when the browser lands
on index.php; with only a non-reboot setting pending the flag stays 0 and no
banner appears. In both runs the only lines added to the settings file were the
expected ones, no password field was written, and the installed SSH keys were
untouched. Note the password-ENABLING paths were not exercised, since enabling
the UI password locks the browser out by design.

THREE BUGS THIS FOUND

Deciding whether a setting had already been answered went wrong twice.
`!settings[key]` discarded ShareCrashData's "keep locally, do not send", which
is the string "0" and falsy in JavaScript -- the strict path threw away an
explicit and deliberately restrictive answer. Its replacement had to come from
the server: the browser's settings object omits anything not marked
exposedAsJSToPages, PHP's merges defaults in so isset() is true for everything,
and the rendered control shows the shipped default for a setting nobody ever
set. ReadSettingFromFile() asks what cape detection asks -- is the key literally
in the settings file.

Separately, both Lookup buttons wrote the response's value into their field
unconditionally, so a partial or rate-limited answer -- which happened during
this testing -- wrote `undefined` and wiped a good time zone or coordinate.
Absent now means leave the control alone.

Fill in the location from the browser when the player has no internet

The geoip lookup runs on the device, so it fails on a player with no route out
-- an ordinary show-network layout, and one where the laptop looking at the UI
is perfectly online. Both Lookup buttons reported failure and left the fields at
their shipped defaults, which for latitude and longitude means the scheduler
computes sunrise and sunset for Falcon, Colorado.

Those two fields are the reason this matters more than it looks. They exist to
schedule shows at sunset, so "roughly right" has a budget measured in minutes.

WHAT THE BROWSER CAN DO

Three approaches, and only one survives contact:

  - navigator.geolocation is unusable. It is a secure-context feature, FPP is
    served over plain HTTP on a LAN address, and Chrome answers "Only secure
    origins are allowed". Measured, not assumed.
  - Deriving coordinates from the browser's time zone works offline and is not
    accurate enough on its own. tzdata's zone.tab gives the zone's reference
    city, and against real places inside those zones that is Minot ND 80
    minutes of sunset error, Houston 64, Seattle 63, Miami 63, Inverness 58. A
    show told to start at sunset would start an hour off, and the field would
    look answered.
  - Letting the browser ask the geolocation service directly is accurate, and
    was blocked only by our own connect-src. Not by CORS: ipapi.co does send
    Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, contrary to a comment here that has been
    corrected. It was a decision, not an obstacle.

So the decision is taken, narrowly. scripts/ManageApacheContentPolicy.sh emits a
LocationMatch over the three pages that draw the buttons, adding ipapi.co to
connect-src there and nowhere else; the global policy stays exactly as it was
just tightened to. settings-localization.php holds the buttons but is loaded
INTO settings.php, and a fetch is governed by the policy of the document that
issued it, so settings.php is the one that carries the allowance.

Only the geolocation service sees anything new, only on a button press, and only
on pages whose purpose is establishing where the player is. What it sees is the
administrator's address rather than the player's -- which is the point, since
the player's is unroutable, and why this path exists at all.

LAYERED, WITH THE GUESS ADMITTED

The device's own lookup is still tried first and still preferred. When it fails
the browser asks directly. When that fails too -- an isolated bench, or an
extension blocking it -- the browser falls back to what it knows without asking
anyone:

  Intl.DateTimeFormat().resolvedOptions().timeZone       -> America/New_York
  new Intl.Locale(navigator.language).maximize().region  -> US

No permission prompt, no network, no third party. The country goes back to the
device, which runs the same mapping against the same data files -- the browser
supplies values, never the rules -- and nolookup=1 skips the timeout the caller
has already waited out once (23ms rather than 210ms). Coordinates come from
zone.tab at that point, and a real lookup always wins over them.

That last case does not fill the fields quietly. The dialog says the estimate
can move sunset by an hour, and a standing warning sits beside the coordinates
until either field is edited, because dismissing a dialog is not the same as
having fixed the value. It matters most on the Settings page, where a value is
saved the moment it is set.

VERIFIED

On a Pi with the player's own lookup blocked at the browser, so every layer ran

Browser also blocked: the time zone's coordinates, warning raised, cleared by
editing a field. Both checked on the wizard and on the Settings page, where the

The scoping is proven by fetching from each page rather than by reading the
header: allowed on initialSetup.php, settings.php and settings-localization.php;
refused with a CSP violation logged on index.php, status.php and playlists.php.

fills the location half and says the region was left to choose, rather than
claiming a location it did not establish. The online path is unchanged, and the

Fix RTSP video input crash when the camera also offers audio (#2924)

rtspsrc/decodebin only have a single sink pad between them, so when an
RTSP source's SDP describes both a video and an audio track, decodebin
links to whichever pad it sees first. If it picks audio, the video pad
is left unlinked, and rtspsrc (running over TCP) treats that as a fatal
"Internal data stream error ... reason not-linked" and tears down the
whole pipeline within milliseconds - surfacing to users as "No frames"
in the video input preview, intermittently, depending on pad-connect
timing.

Name the rtspsrc element and connect its select-stream signal to reject
any non-video media before SETUP, so decodebin only ever receives the
video track. FPP does not extract audio from rtspsrc sources today, so
this removes no current capability.

Co-authored-by: Pat D <patd@kulplights.com>
Co-authored-by: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Take only the first video track from an RTSP SDP, and say when there is none

The select-stream filter added in #2924 accepts every media the SDP labels
as video. Cameras that advertise two video media in one SDP -- some offer
H.264 and MJPEG as alternatives -- therefore still get two src pads from
rtspsrc while decodebin has only one sink pad to link them to, and the
second pad is left dangling: exactly the "Internal data stream error ...
reason not-linked" teardown that filter exists to prevent.

Give the filter per-pipeline state so it accepts the first video media and
refuses the rest. The state is owned by the signal closure rather than by
SourceInfo, because the pipeline outlives StartSource() and a Reload can
reallocate m_sources while it is still running -- the same hazard the run
thread's copied-by-value locals already guard against.

A stream carrying no video track at all was the other way to reach an empty
pipeline, and it surfaced only as "No frames" in the preview with nothing in
the log pointing at the cause. Report it from no-more-pads instead.

Main and sub substreams are normally separate RTSP URLs, so the multi-video
SDP is the uncommon case rather than the routine one; this is a defensive
guard, not a fix for a reported failure.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Honour audioEnabled for RTSP cameras, not just YouTube

SourceInfo::audioEnabled, its UI checkbox and its audioPipeWireNodeName have
existed since audio extraction was added, but only the YouTube urisrc path
ever read them. RTSP was fixed video-only in C++, so a camera with a mic --
a doorbell, an intercom, a PA feed -- had no way to reach the mix bus, even
though it is a far more natural audio source for a player than YouTube is.

Build the RTSP pipeline with two branches when audio is enabled: video to
intervideosink as before, audio to a pipewiresink published as its own
Audio/Source node. Both branches live in ONE GstPipeline so they share a
clock and base_time, which is why StartSourceWithAudio() combines its own
branches that way rather than running two pipelines that drift apart.

rtspsrc's pads are left unlinked in the parse description and routed by
media type in pad-added: gst_parse_launch drops its delayed-link handler
after the first pad it manages to link, so it can satisfy one branch and
would leave the other dangling. select-stream now keeps the first audio
media too when audio is wanted, and still refuses everything beyond one
stream per branch.

A camera may advertise no audio at all, leaving that branch with nothing
flowing, so its sink takes async=FALSE and stays out of preroll where an
empty audio branch could otherwise stall the video branch reaching PLAYING.
The YouTube path resolves a real audio URL before building its pipeline and
keeps the default.

The pipewiresink Audio/Source setup and its throughput probe are factored
into ConfigureAudioSourceSink() rather than duplicated, and the UI's audio
block into BuildAudioExtractionBlock() alongside the other Build* helpers.

Verified: builds clean, and the generated two-branch description parses with
both decodebin sinks unlinked as the pad routing expects. Not yet run
against a real RTSP camera carrying audio.

faults, one per half of that sentence.

for a brand-new config uses the same constant.

Privacy step: one row per disclosure, with what it sends behind each one

The privacy step listed settings. A setting name does not tell anyone what
leaves their player or who receives it, which is the only thing that makes the
choice meaningful. It is now a table of disclosures: what is shared, who it goes
to, Allow or Deny, and a help icon carrying the full account of what that row
actually sends. Based on a mockup by Daryl, with the corrections below.

ROWS ARE NOT SETTINGS

They do not line up one to one, and the differences are the interesting part.

ShareCrashData is a single ordered value, so its three rows are a ladder:
"include configuration and logs" necessarily includes "your settings", which
necessarily includes the stack. Drawn as three independent Allow/Deny pairs the
mockup could express states that do not exist. Allowing a row now allows its
parents, and denying a row denies and locks its descendants, so an impossible
combination cannot be clicked into being rather than merely rejected afterwards.
The four reachable states map to 0, 1, 2 and 3.

Denying the crash rows writes 0, keep locally, not -1. A report is written to
the crashes folder either way, which is what the help text promises, and -1 is
deliberately not reachable from this page.

The cape serial row sits under the logo row because that is how it behaves: the
serial rides on the logo request, so denying the logo denies it too.

statsPublish ships as "Banner", which is neither Allow nor Deny -- it is a
prompt to decide later. The table has no third state, so under a permissive
jurisdiction it resolves to Allow, the shipped intent. Leaving it blank would
have been worse than either answer: the step would pass validation with nothing
selected and write no value at all, which is the "Finish writes nothing" hole
this whole exercise exists to close.

Allow all and Deny all sit in the footer of the columns they act on, centred on
the same axis as the radios above them, so each reads as the whole-column
version of that control rather than as a page action.

DEFAULTS BY JURISDICTION

Where prior opt-in is required every row starts unanswered and the step will not
advance until each is answered -- except "send crash reports", which starts
allowed. Sending a stack trace rests on legitimate interests (GDPR Art 6(1)(f))
rather than consent; the tiers that do need consent are the two below it, and
they start blank. Everywhere else the normal defaults are pre-filled and moving
on accepts what is shown.

A row already answered in the settings file keeps its answer under either
regime. A cape's proposed default is explicitly NOT treated as an answer: it is
the vendor's suggestion, so under a prior-opt-in regime the row is still asked.

THE TEXT ITSELF

Lives in www/privacyDisclosures.inc rather than inline, because it is what FPP
stands behind about where a user's data goes, it has to be reviewable on its
own, and the Settings privacy tab will want the same words.

Every factual claim was checked against the code that implements it, and the
draft was wrong in six places:

  - "about once every 10 days, and each time FPP starts" -- it is 7 days plus
    publish-on-change, and has been since those landed.
  - "Kept up to 400 days, then deleted" -- nothing enforces that. There is no
    fixed deletion date and older records are archived, so it now says so.
  - The device ID is hardware-derived on Pi and BeagleBone, but get_uuid falls
    through to machine-id and then to a generated value, and the images ship
    machine-id as "uninitialized" so a fresh card makes its own. "Same after a
    reinstall" is true of most players, not all, and the text now says which.
  - Peers were described as contributing "their type and version only -- not
    their addresses, names or serial numbers". Both halves were wrong, the
    second materially: each peer contributes its device ID, and that is the
    whole point, since it is what lets a ten-player show be counted once rather
    than ten times. The allowlists in stats.php also carry model, platform, OS,
    kernel, cape model, player mode, channel ranges and the output/input flags
    -- considerably more than two fields. What is genuinely withheld for peers
    now gets its own line.
  - "Other FPP and Falcon devices" understated the reach: MultiSync's system
    types name AlphaPix, Baldrick, DIYLEDExpress, ESPixelStick, the
    Experience/Genius family, HinksPix, SanDevices, WLED and xSchedule too, so
    a reader with a mixed network was told only part of it was described.
  - Cape vendors were "companies in the USA and Australia, outside the EU/UK".
    True of today's vendor set only; the geography is gone.

The cape logo row also listed a cost with no reason anyone would say yes, which
reads as a warning rather than a choice. There is a real one: the volunteers in
the FPP support Zoom room can see which cape is installed the moment somebody
shares their screen, instead of spending the first few minutes of the session
working out what hardware is in front of them.

The AI paragraph is new and states measured behaviour rather than a guess. The
daily narrative step is granted the source tree and the reports directory, which
holds no raw uploads, so it receives a derived summary -- and that summary
carries the device ID and roughly a kilobyte of log tail for 221 of 228 records
in a sample day. The log ring ships only at level 3, and FPP's own comment says
logs carry host names and LAN addresses, so the text names that level
specifically. The ad-hoc case, where a developer opens a whole report the same
way, is stated too.

The geoip paragraph needed updating for the same reason as the code did: when
the player has no internet the browser does the lookup, so the address disclosed
is the browser's.

Verified on a Pi, each check run until it failed as well as passed. The ladder
walks up and down correctly, locks and greys blocked rows, hides the e-mail
field until crash reports are allowed, and produces exactly 0, 1, 2 and 3 for
the four reachable combinations. On a fresh box the permissive regime pre-fills
every row and writes all five keys including statsPublish=Enabled, while the
prior-opt-in regime blanks everything except the crash row and refuses to
advance, naming the five outstanding rows. With the keys already in the settings
file both regimes keep the recorded answers. All seven help icons open their
disclosure, and the two footer buttons measure 0px from their column centres. No
console errors on any path, and the settings file was restored byte-identical
after the fresh-box runs.

installs with no dialog. It is deliberately worded as a statement about how
plugins work rather than a warning about any particular one; a scary box on the
official path would be friction the project has chosen not to have, and would
train people to click through the boxes that do matter.

Cape Info: stop contacting the signing API, and stop executing its code — C-18

Opening Cape Info to see which cape you have contacted api.falconplayer.com
twice, on every view, whether or not the page had any use for the answer.

The server side ran a curl to that host before anything about the cape had been
read. The browser side loaded a <script> from it and checked for a global the
script defined. Both fed one thing: whether the online signing UI can be offered.
That UI is drawn only when $printSigningUI is set, which happens only for a cape
on a licensed output driver that is unsigned or signed with the 'fp' key -- so
on every other player, both requests fired for markup that is never rendered.
$offlineMode is read only from inside `if ($printSigningUI)` blocks, so nothing
else ever wanted the answer.

The curl now runs only when the signing UI is going to be drawn, which meant
moving it below the cape parsing that decides that. The browser test runs only
when the signing UI is drawn AND the device itself could not reach the API --
the case it exists for, and an ordinary one: a show network with no route out,
administered from a laptop that has one. We are keeping that capability, which
is why the review's "remove the <script>" is not what landed; deleting it would
push users who can sign normally onto the offline path.

What the browser test does not need is to run somebody else's code in an admin
UI that has no authentication by default. A reachability test is a yes/no: a
no-cors fetch resolves when the host answered and rejects when it did not, which
is the same answer without executing anything. That also moves the host from
script-src to connect-src, where it already was, so
ManageApacheContentPolicy.sh drops its only script-src entry and the generated
policy is now 'self' 'unsafe-inline' 'unsafe-eval' with no third-party host at
all.

Verified on a Pi whose cape needs no signing. The browser makes no request to
that host and the page carries no remote <script> tags, while still rendering
the cape. For the server side, with the signing host pointed at a black-holed
address the page renders in 0.08s; forcing the curl to run unconditionally makes
the same page take 5.10s, which is the connect timeout -- so the gate is what is
doing the work rather than a lucky fast lookup.

That control needed a second attempt worth recording: opcache revalidates every
two seconds, and the first run's three requests all completed inside that

Give a cape its own serial when flashing a blank EEPROM

A downloadable vendor image is one file written to every cape of that model, so
the serial it was built with is a sample rather than any unit's identity. Every
Kulp Lights and Wired Watts image carries one -- the K4-PB image ships
200824211045 -- and the two generic images in capes/other/ show the same shape.
Copying it verbatim onto a blank EEPROM gives every cape flashed from that image
the same serial, which defeats the one thing a serial is for: telling two capes
apart, deduplicating them, and letting a vendor recognise a unit.

So a blank EEPROM now gets its own. This is the only place it can happen: the
upgrade path below preserves whatever serial the cape already had, and a blank
EEPROM has none to preserve.

'FPP-' + 12 hex fills the 16-byte field exactly. The prefix says plainly that
FPP generated this rather than a vendor assigning it, so a vendor receiving one
knows there is no order record behind it, and it cannot be confused with
FPP-INTERNAL, which is compared by equality wherever it is used. 48 random bits
puts the chance of a collision across hundreds of thousands of capes in the
thousandths of a percent, against a certainty today.

FPP-INTERNAL is the one exception and is left alone: it marks a virtual EEPROM,
FPP's own generic image for a Pi header, which is not a cape and has no per-unit
identity to record -- and cape-info.php keys its licensing display off that
exact value.

A SIGNED image is deliberately NOT an exception, though it looks like it should
be, and treating it as one would have made this change a no-op: the real vendor
images are signed AND carry a sample serial. The signature is computed from the
byte after the signature section to the terminator -- DoSignatureVerify captures
ftell() on entry, after the caller has read that section -- so the 58-byte
header holding the serial is outside it. The upgrade path already relies on
this, rewriting the cape name and version at offsets 6-41 and still expecting
the signature to verify. Nor does this disturb a cape signed and bound to
hardware: for those the serial comes from the signed section 96 record, which
overrides the header.

The vendor's 'cs' checksum authenticates THEIR serial, so it cannot travel with
a different one -- the pair would fail the vendor's check and look like
tampering rather than what it is. It is blanked in place, keeping the record's
length so nothing downstream of it moves. FPP cannot compute a replacement that
means anything: this script is open source, so anything it could generate anyone
could generate, and a checksum that proves nothing is worse than none. The
'FPP-' prefix carries that information honestly instead.

Verified on a Pi against the real Kulp Lights K4-PB image. Two writes of the
same image produce different serials (FPP-1BFDD8BCB7D9, FPP-21BEABE810F9); the
FPP-INTERNAL image comes through untouched. The signature claim is proved rather
than asserted: the signed range is (186, 2278) before and after, the serial at
offset 42 and the cs record both sit below it, and the 2092 signed bytes are
bit-identical by SHA -- same bytes into the same hash, same verification result.
Sixteen bytes differ in the whole file.

Add an RTSP video output that carries audio alongside the video

FPP's existing RTP video output sends video alone to a fixed address and
leaves the receiver to find a hand-written SDP file before it can decode
anything. That is the wart this replaces: an RTSP mount is a URL you paste
into VLC, ffplay, OBS or a video wall, and the server describes its own
streams. Audio comes along nearly free once something is muxing, so the
mount carries it too.

This is the one place FPP deliberately recombines the two media planes it
otherwise keeps apart, and it does so only at the edge. Video still travels
over intervideo channels and audio still travels over the PipeWire graph,
because show control is audio-clocked and the audio graph has to be a
many-to-many mixer while video is one-to-many frame fanout. Nothing upstream
of the RTSP mount changes; the planes meet only where the wire format
demands one container, and because both branches live in one GstRTSPMedia
they share a clock, so lip sync costs nothing extra.

The audio node lives in an always-running bridge pipeline
(pipewiresrc -> interaudiosink) rather than inside the RTSP media, because a
GstRTSPMedia only exists while a client is connected and a PipeWire node
that came and went with client connections could not be wired up in the mix
bus UI ahead of time. The bridge honours the same requireGroupSource guard
OpusRTPManager documents: with nothing linked into it a pipewiresrc cannot
preroll, and starting it anyway burns 30 seconds before failing. A mount
whose audio is still waiting serves video normally.

Factories are shared, so one encoder serves every client rather than one per
connection, which a Pi could not afford.

RTSP streams belong to Video Output Groups, not their own source picker

The RTSP page asked for a video source per mount, which duplicated the job a
Video Output Group already does. A group owns one source and fans it out to
its members, and the PHP layer flattens that into the consumer list by copying
the group's source down onto each member -- which is exactly how the existing
RTP network output works, carrying only address/port/encoding and inheriting
its source.

Standing outside that model cost three things. The source was configured in
two unrelated screens and could drift. One source could not reach an HDMI
display and an RTSP client from a single group. And stream slots were
unreachable altogether: a group aimed at a playback slot has no videoSource at
all, so there was no way to serve what fppd is actually playing over RTSP --
only named input sources.

So RTSP becomes a member type alongside hdmi/overlay/rtp, carrying just the
mount path, size, encoding, bitrate and audio flag. The generator emits
type "rtsp" consumers with the group's source filled in, and
RTSPOutputManager reads its mounts from that list. A member on a stream-slot
group resolves to the slot's intervideo channel, which exists whether or not
anything is playing -- intervideosrc holds the mount up on black in between,
which is what a client watching should see.

The server itself stays a separate manager: its mounts share one port and
GMainLoop, and a GstRTSPMedia only exists while a client is connected, none of
which fits ConsumerInfo's one-pipeline-per-consumer lifecycle. Only where the
source comes from changed. The RTSP page correspondingly shrinks to what has
no home in a group -- enable, port, status -- and lists what is being served
read-only, pointing at the groups page to change it.

Applying groups now signals the RTSP server too, since its streams are group
members.

Verified on this device against a live fppd: an RTSP member on a named-source
group serves 1280x720@30 H.264 plus Opus from the same source its group puts
on HDMI, and an RTSP member on a stream-slot group -- previously impossible --
resolves to the slot channel and serves 640x360@15.

Pin rpi-swap to plain zram so boot cannot hang on the /var/swap loop

Raspberry Pi OS Trixie's rpi-swap defaults to "zram+file", which attaches
/var/swap to a loop device and hands it to zram0 as a writeback target. It is
never swapped on, so it adds no usable swap -- DiskBackedSwapKB already ignores
it for that reason. It does put rpi-setup-loop@var-swap.service on the boot
critical path, and sysinit.target is ordered after swap.target, so that one unit
gates the whole boot.

Its ExecStartPost waits for udev's /dev/disk/by-backingfile/var-swap symlink
with an inotify loop that arms the watch after testing for the symlink. Lose
that race and it blocks on an event that never comes; Type=oneshot defaults
TimeoutStartSec to infinity, so the boot stops dead with no console and no ssh
until the board is power cycled. Being a race, the next boot usually works,
which makes it look sporadic.

Pinning the mechanism to plain zram drops the loop unit and the writeback timer
and leaves zram itself untouched -- same generator, same sizing, same
dev-zram0.swap. rpi-swap removes a leftover /var/swap itself under this
mechanism, off the boot path.

Publish statistics when the user turns them on, after a two minute grace period

Turning statistics on during setup published nothing for up to 24 hours. The
main loop asks at most once a day, and the ask was spent unconditionally -- so a
box that booted with statistics off burned its one ask of the day on a branch
that contacts nobody, and the wizard's save does not restart fppd, so the static
that tracks it never reset. Only a reboot got the first upload out. Not the
seven day publish interval, which is the route's cadence and would have allowed
it; the daily ask was the blocker.

Now enabling it is the trigger. fppd registers a listener on statsPublish and,
when it goes to Enabled, waits two minutes and publishes.

The delay is a grace period rather than a delay: the setting is read AGAIN when
the timer fires, so somebody who ticked the wrong box, or was looking around the
wizard, can put it back and nothing is sent. A generation counter means toggling
repeatedly leaves exactly one timer that acts rather than one upload per toggle.
Both ways of ending in no upload log at LogInfo -- "nothing was sent and nothing
was said" is indistinguishable from the timer never having been scheduled, for
somebody reading the log and for a test trying to prove the cancel ran.

The ask budget is also no longer spent on a call that cannot publish. That
branch is now reached on every idle tick instead of daily, so its message needed
its own limiter or it would become a per-second log.

Clicking a tab in settings scrolled the page in Safari, far enough that the tab
strip went off the top and took the start of the pane with it -- the "Notes"
heading on Logging, for instance. Long-standing.

Two things in the shared tab wiring move the page on every tab click, on every
page, and they fight:

  window.location.hash = event.target.dataset.bsTarget;   // scrolls DOWN
  ...
  scrollToTop();                                          // scrolls to 0

pushes a history entry. scrollToTop() then tries to go to 0. Which one you end

assignment, so the bug looked browser-specific while the cause was not.

The url still records the tab, via replaceState, which does not scroll and does
not push. Neither does anything else now: selecting a tab leaves the page where
it was.

lands at 0 every time and adds 8 history entries; with this, the page holds its
position (moving only where the incoming pane is genuinely too short to hold it,
which is the browser clamping to the new maximum, one step and no bounce) and
adds 4, one per click. Deep links (#settings-logs, #settings-privacy,
#settings-av) still select the right tab on a real reload, and backup,
channeloutputs, networkconfig, testing, troubleshooting and filemanager all
still switch tabs and update their hash.

This replaces the scroll-pinning workaround that was here before, which could
not have worked: the earlier version restored the position after the event, and
the version after that re-pinned from inside a scroll handler. Both were

Do not let a backup with an unexpected name take out the whole listing

A .json in the backups directory whose name carries no timestamp -- one copied
in by hand, or renamed -- was fatal:

  Uncaught Error: Call to a member function format() on false
    in www/api/controllers/backups.php:622

The timestamp is read off the end of the filename, after the last underscore.
When that is not 14 digits createFromFormat() returns false, and ->format() on
false is an Error, so the request dies. ffd9d0b43 anticipated this and skips
anything that is not a .json, which covers the blob subdirectory but not a .json
that simply is not named the way we name them.

Blast radius is bigger than the listing it kills. /api/backups/configuration/list
feeds pruneOrRemoveAgedBackupFiles(), which json_decodes it and calls count() on
the result -- null in PHP 8 -- so one such file also stops the automatic
settings-change backups from pruning.

Now the name is required to be exactly the 14 digits we write, rather than
letting createFromFormat() have a lenient go at whatever is there and hand back
some other date, and a file that does not have them falls back to its own mtime.
That keeps it listed and restorable rather than hidden, which is what someone who
copied a backup in by hand would want.

Verified against the failing case: with two such files present, stock returns the
fatal and the Backups page renders nothing; with this, the endpoint returns all
71 entries, count() on the decoded list works (which is what the pruning needs),
and both files appear in the download and restore tables with their mtime as the
date, their real comments, and working actions. Names that do carry a timestamp
still parse from the name, unchanged.

Record the consent, not just the setting it produced

"statsPublish = Enabled" is a value. Article 7(1) asks the controller to
demonstrate consent, and the ICO reads that as five things: who, when, what they
consented to, how they gave it, and what they were shown at the time. A value in
the settings file answers none of them, and the two keys we had -- one global
date and a version -- answered one and a half.

This records the act. One JSON setting, 'privacyConsent' (WriteSettingToFile
already writes JSON objects unquoted and reads them back byte-identical; 'locale'
and 'cape-info' rely on it), holding the disclosure version, a hash of the text,
the device id, and per choice the value, the date and where it was given.

Per choice is the part that is easy to get wrong. One global timestamp updated on
any change would say, of somebody who allowed statistics in March and changed
their crash level in September, that they consented to statistics in September --
not a weaker record than none but a false one, and it is the timestamp we upload
with the statistics. Measured: stamping the other three in September left the
March statistics date untouched.

The five, and where each now comes from:

  When   - per choice, from the browser's clock. A player on first boot may have
           no NTP and can be years out; the machine setting it up is usually right.
  What   - the value consented to, stored beside the stamp, so the record reads
           "shown version N (hash H), on DATE, via VIA, chose VALUE" without
           having to trust the live setting still to be that value.
  How    - 'wizard' or 'settings', and nothing else is accepted. Settings are
           writable over the API and from the command line, so this is what
           separates a choice from a value that arrived with nobody looking at a
           disclosure. It is why recording is a separate call rather than a side
           effect of PUT /api/settings/<key>: only a page that actually showed
           somebody the table gets to say it did.
  Shown  - the version decides who gets re-prompted, but rewording deliberately
           does not bump it, so the version alone cannot say which words were on
           the screen. A hash of privacyDisclosures() AND privacyTableRows() can.
           Both, because the row labels and the "goes to" column are what most
           people read and all some of them read; hashing only the bodies would
           have let the visible half be rewritten unnoticed.
  Who    - there are no accounts, and the record sits on the owner's own device,
           which is most of the answer. The device id covers the rest: without it
           a settings backup restored onto a second player carries the first
           player's consent and its owner is never asked anything. That case now
           reports 'other-device' and sends them through the privacy step.

Changing your mind is recorded too. The Privacy settings page previously saved
values and never touched the record, so a later grant kept an old date and a
withdrawal left no trace at all -- and under Article 7(3) withdrawing is as much
an act as consenting. It now stamps what changed, and only what changed.

The statistics upload carries the statistics stamp, so the record exists
somewhere we can produce it rather than only on an SD card we do not hold. Only
that stamp: the crash and vendor-logo choices authorise other transmissions to
other people, and shipping them here would be the same mistake in the opposite
direction. It joins the significant subset, so re-consenting republishes.

Verified end to end on hardware. The wizard writes all four with via 'wizard' and
no drift; denying statistics on the settings page rewrites that one stamp with
via 'settings' and leaves the other three at their wizard dates; a POST claiming
via 'curl' is refused; a record with a foreign uuid or an older version reports
'other-device' / 'stale-version' and MissingSetupSettings() returns privacyConsent
for both; and /settings.php on a box with no record redirects into the wizard. The
text hash moves when a word changes in either file and returns when it is put
back -- the first version of that control was vacuous, because the sentence I
edited lives in privacyTable.inc, which is what showed the hash was covering only
half of what the user reads.

privacyConsentVersion and privacyConsentDate are superseded and no longer read.
There is no migration: they only exist on boxes that ran the unreleased wizard, and
synthesising a record for them would have to invent the "how", which is the one
field worth having. Those boxes run the privacy step once more.

fix(upgrade): re-deploy the systemd units on a version upgrade

etc/systemd/*.service is copied into /lib/systemd/system exactly once, by
FPP_Install.sh at install time. Nothing refreshes it afterwards, so a unit
change has only ever reached freshly flashed images: a version upgrade updates
the copy under /opt/fpp and leaves the unit systemd actually reads frozen at
whatever the image shipped with.

The two paths that look like they cover this do not. FPPINIT_Audio refreshes
fpp-pipewire.service, fpp-wireplumber.service and fpp-pipewire-pulse.service on
boot -- those three only, and only under the PipeWire backend. install_pipewire.sh
re-copies fppd.service as well, but nothing invokes it; it is a manual recovery
step.

What made it visible: fppd.service gained LimitRTPRIO=95 so the AES67 packet
pacing thread can go SCHED_FIFO. It is a ceiling, not a request, so without it
sched_setscheduler fails EPERM and the sender pushes packets up to a full ptime
late every few thousand -- the exact jitter tail the limit was added to remove.
On an upgraded box the limit never arrived.

Only units already present in /lib/systemd/system are refreshed, and only when
the content differs. A unit missing there means the platform's install never
wanted it (fppoled and fpprtc are Pi/BBB-only, the PipeWire units are written by
install_pipewire.sh), so introducing one would leave a file nothing enabled.
daemon-reload and the reboot flag are skipped entirely when nothing changed, so
this is a silent no-op on a current system. Copying a unit does not start, stop,
enable or disable anything, and a changed resource limit applies at the
service's next start -- hence the reboot flag rather than an in-band restart,
same reasoning as upgrade 138.

Verified on a Pi 5 whose tree had been advanced by branch update: the installed
unit was missing LimitRTPRIO while its /opt/fpp copy had it, and after the run
systemctl show reported LimitRTPRIO=95. Re-running copied nothing.

fix(overlays): use-after-free when an overlay model is removed mid-effect

A PixelOverlayModel could be freed while another thread was still running an
effect on it, or while a channel output still held a pointer to it. Three
crash buckets on 10.0 are this, all crash-looping, all with a channel output
reload or a playlist edit immediately before the fault:
PixelOverlayModel::setData, PixelOverlayModelFB::setData and
FBMatrixOutput::PrepData.

Two independent holes.

1. The effect scheduler. doOverlayModelEffects() snapshotted the due batch,
   erased the map entry, then dropped threadLock for the whole batch, and
   doOverlays()'s afterOverlayModels drain did the same. removePeriodicUpdate()
   only edits those lists, so a model removed part way through a batch was
   still run afterwards -- by which point removeAutoOverlayModel() had freed
   it.

   Draining one model at a time under the lock makes removal authoritative for
   anything not yet started. For the update already running, waiting for it to
   finish is not enough on its own: the in-flight thread erases its own record
   and then requeues the model while still holding threadLock, so a waiter --
   which cannot wake until that lock is released -- would see an empty registry
   and a model freshly put back, and delete it anyway. Each in-flight entry now
   carries a removed flag that removal stamps, and the update reports
   EFFECT_DONE for a stamped entry so its caller never requeues.

   The wait is split out as removePeriodicUpdateAndWait() and used only by the
   one caller that actually deletes the model. It must never be reached from
   the hot path: setRunningEffect() calls in holding the model's effectLock,
   and an in-flight entry is registered before updateRunningEffects() acquires
   that same lock, so waiting there deadlocks the lock holder against a thread
   that needs it -- silently, since the daemon stays up. Verified by building
   both ways: with the hot path waiting, a scrolling text effect wedges the
   daemon within ~50 effect changes; with the split it does not.

   The stamp also fixes a pre-existing duplicate. setRunningEffect() removes
   and re-adds the model, and the in-flight caller then requeued it again on
   return, ticking that model at twice its configured period until the next
   removal.

2. FBMatrix. It cached a bare model pointer from Init() and never tracked it,
   while the other two consumers of a model pointer both register a model
   listener for exactly this reason. It now registers one, nulls the pointer
   under a lock that PrepData()/SendData() also take so "removed" and "not in
   use" are the same instant, and unregisters in Close() plus the destructor --
   Init() can fail after registering, and a failed output is deleted without a
   Close().

fix(overlays): segfault from an effect command with too few arguments

ApplyEffectOverlayCommand::run builds the effect's argument vector from
args.begin() + 3, so a command naming a valid model and a valid effect but no
effect arguments hands the effect an empty vector. Every effect indexes that
vector positionally with no bounds check of its own, so the first read walks
off the end: a single well-formed HTTP request is enough to segfault fppd, and
it restarts into the same fault on the next request.

Validate once in applyEffect(), the sole point that dispatches to any effect,
rather than bounds-checking every effect body. The effect's own declared
argument list is the authority, and trailing arguments marked optional may
still be omitted. A short command is now refused with an error result and a
log line instead of taking the daemon down.

Found while building a test harness for the overlay lifetime fixes; reproduced
against an unmodified build.

fix(VideoOutputManager): std::terminate from a SAP announcer start/stop race

StartSAPAnnouncer() tested m_sapRunning and then assigned m_sapThread as two
separate steps, with nothing serializing the pair. m_mutex does not cover it,
deliberately: SAPAnnounceLoop() takes m_mutex and StopSAPAnnouncer() joins that
thread, so every call site sits outside the lock. That left the atomic as the
only guard, and an atomic flag cannot make a test-then-set atomic.

The callers are genuinely concurrent. StartConsumers()/StopConsumers() run on
the detached start thread inside each media output's Start(), so two stream
slots starting together reach StartSAPAnnouncer() on two unsynchronized
threads.

Three failures followed:

  * Two Starts both pass the flag check and both assign m_sapThread. Assigning
    over a joinable std::thread is an unconditional std::terminate(), which
    takes the daemon down with SIGABRT -- no exception, no recovery.
  * Start racing Stop: Stop clears the flag and finds the thread not yet
    assigned, so it returns without joining; Start then assigns it. The loop
    exits immediately on the cleared flag but the object stays joinable
    forever, so the next Start terminates.
  * joinable()/join() in Stop concurrent with the assignment in Start is a
    data race on the thread object itself.

Add a dedicated m_sapLock covering the announcer's lifecycle. It is separate
from m_mutex on purpose and is never taken by SAPAnnounceLoop(), so no cycle is
introduced; the existing "call these with m_mutex not held" contract is now
stated at the declarations rather than only at the call sites.

Also drop Stop's early-out on the flag, which is what let a leftover joinable
thread survive to the next Start, and join any leftover thread before assigning
so the invariant holds at the assignment itself.

Verified by building both ways with the precondition forced and the window
widened: the previous code aborts with "terminate called without an active
exception" within seconds of concurrent start/stop traffic, while the fixed
code completes 160 interleaved calls with the daemon still healthy.

feat(filemanager): Upload and Delete for locally-kept crash reports

fppd writes a crash report every time it crashes but only uploads it when
ShareCrashData is 1 or higher. At "Keep locally, do not send" it still writes
one -- at level 3, the fullest bundle -- so the operator can submit it by hand,
which the setting's own tip already promises. Until now "by hand" meant
downloading the zip and mailing it to a developer, so most of those reports were
never seen. This makes it one button on the File Manager's Crash Reports tab.

Two routes to the same endpoint, because the player and the operator's browser
are not always on the same side of a working internet connection:

  * The player posts it itself, via POST /api/crashes/upload/<file>, to the same
    endpoint and form field the crash handler uses.
  * If the player reports it could not reach the server, the page fetches the
    zip from the player and posts it from the browser instead. That is the
    ordinary show network: players on an isolated switch, laptop on Wi-Fi with a
    route out.

A report is only deleted after an upload is confirmed. The API deliberately
does not delete on success -- the caller does, once told the upload landed --
and anything that cannot be confirmed is reported as "sent, unconfirmed" and
kept. Deleting the only copy of a crash report on a maybe is how the evidence is
lost.

The browser route sends exactly once. A FormData post is a CORS simple request,
so the bytes reach the server whether or not the response can be read; retrying
after an unreadable answer would upload the same report twice. Reading the
answer at all depends on the upload endpoint returning
Access-Control-Allow-Origin, which it now does (a server-side change, since
players live on unguessable LAN addresses the allowance has to be a wildcard).
Without it the client could not tell a delivered report from a dead network.

The upload endpoint reduces the caller-supplied name to a basename, requires it
to match the fpp-*.zip shape fppd generates, and confirms the resolved path is
really inside the crashes directory, so this cannot be turned into "upload any
file on the player to the internet".

The confirmation dialog says what a locally-kept report contains -- the crash
stack and fault registers, the player's settings, its configuration files and
logs -- and that passwords, passphrases and location were already removed when
the report was written.

crashes.falconplayer.com is added to the CSP connect-src for the browser route,
in ManageApacheContentPolicy.sh: etc/apache2.csp is generated from it, so the
generated file is not the place to put it.

fix(oled): drop the cached cape image when the EEPROM no longer has one

fppoled keeps a copy of cape-image.xbm on the root fs so the cape logo can
be displayed before cape detection has run: its ExecStartPre "clear" pass
snapshots media/tmp into /var/tmp, and OLEDPage::readCapeImage() falls back
to that copy whenever media/tmp has no image.

The snapshot only ever wrote the copy, never removed it, so the fallback
became permanent the moment detection stopped producing an image.  On the
first boot after an EEPROM goes blank or its header stops matching, "clear"
runs before detection, promotes the outgoing cape's image into /var/tmp,
and detection then wipes media/tmp -- from then on nothing writes or clears
/var/tmp and the OLED shows the logo of a cape that is no longer installed,
across every later boot.

Keep the copy in step with its source at both places that know the answer:
"clear" removes it when there is nothing to snapshot, and a detect run that
regenerated media/tmp reconciles it afterwards so the display corrects
itself without waiting for a reboot.  A -ro detect run is excluded: it
copies nothing out of its scratch directory, so its "no image" says nothing
about the hardware.
