feat(capes): board specific device tree overlay variants from the EEPROM

The firmware resolves a device tree overlay all or nothing. A fragment
referencing a symbol the board does not have discards the ENTIRE overlay,
not just that fragment, and the only evidence is a dterror in
/proc/device-tree/chosen/user-warnings -- long after cape detection has
already reported the cape as found. An overlay carrying a fragment that
disables a node present on only one Pi generation is therefore fine on
that board and fatal everywhere else, taking the cape's codec, RTC and
i2s down with it while everything in FPP still looks healthy.

A cape may now ship tmp/fpp-cape-overlay-rpi-<filter>.dtb alongside the
base overlay, where <filter> is a config.txt conditional filter (pi5,
pi4, pi02, cm4, ...). Each is installed as
overlays/fpp-cape-overlay-<filter>.dtbo and applied after the base
overlay on matching boards only, so the board specific fragments move out
of the base and the base resolves everywhere.

Removal is the harder half: a variant that a cape stops shipping, or that
belonged to a previously installed cape, must lose both its .dtbo and its
config.txt lines or the firmware fails to resolve an overlay that is no
longer on disk. Rather than editing lines, the whole marked block is
rewritten from the variants actually present, and orphaned .dtbo files
are unlinked. The block always closes with [all] so a later append does
not land inside somebody's filter. Filter names arrive from an EEPROM and
are written verbatim into config.txt and a path under /boot, so they are
allowlisted. A cape whose overlay is entirely board specific may ship
variants and no base.

Two existing bugs fall out of the new naming:

- The base overlay line was located with a substring search, and
  "dtoverlay=fpp-cape-overlay" is a substring of
  "dtoverlay=fpp-cape-overlay-pi5". A config.txt carrying only a variant
  line looked like it already had the base overlay, so the base line was
  never written and the cape came up with its board specific fragments
  and nothing else. Replaced with a line exact match, which the append
  handling in processBootConfig needed just as much.

- That base line was appended at end of file with no section header,
  inheriting whatever filter the file happened to end in. It now emits
  [all] first.

fix(capes): do not rewrite config.txt when a cape ships no overlay variants

The variant block writer normalised trailing newlines before deciding
whether anything had changed. On a cape with no variants and a config.txt
ending in a blank line -- which is the shape of a stock file -- that
counted as a change, so the file was rewritten for a cosmetic whitespace

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

Add a Pi 5 setting to disable the built-in RTC

The Pi 5's own RTC registers around 0.35s, where an i2c RTC on a cape is not
up until ~2.5s, and whatever holds rtc0 is what the kernel sets the system
clock from (CONFIG_RTC_HCTOSYS_DEVICE is "rtc0").  With no cell on the Pi's
RTC header it comes up unset, so the clock is set from it early in boot and
stays wrong until fpprtc runs seconds later.  On a cold start that is a
successful set of 1970 rather than a visible failure, which is worse: anything
that sanity checks the clock sees a plausible value.

A cape can fix the ordering with a pi5 overlay variant that aliases the Pi's
RTC out of rtc0, but the Pi's RTC is then still present reading 1970.  Where
there is known to be no battery, turning it off is better.  Whether a cell is
fitted is a fact about the installation rather than about the board, so it is
a setting: DisablePiRTC, on the Localization page under Real Time Clock, Pi 5
only, off by default.  A cape that ships in an enclosure where the header
cannot be reached can preselect it through defaultSettings, which fppinit
honours on the boot that cape is first detected on.

"dtparam=rtc=off" is a stock firmware override -- the rtc entry in the Pi 5
DTB's __overrides__ maps to the rpi_rtc node's status -- so this needs no
overlay of FPP's own, just the line, under a [pi5] filter so an SD card moved
to an earlier Pi does not draw an "Unknown dtparam" warning.

The block is written IN PLACE rather than stripped and re-appended at EOF, and
is created ahead of CapeUtils' cape-overlay-variant block.  That block IS
managed by strip-and-append, and two writers that both append at EOF leapfrog:
each boot one lands after the other, both see a changed config.txt, and both
ask for a reboot.  This runs in fppinit's "start" action, before networking
comes up, so that loop is a board that never reaches the network to be fixed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(capes): restore the default overlay by what is installed, not what resolved

The decision to put the shipped default overlay back was gated on reading
/proc/device-tree/chosen/overlays/fpp-cape-overlay.  That node exists only
when an overlay actually resolved at boot, which makes it the wrong thing to
ask.  A stale overlay left by a previous cape that cannot resolve on this
board -- a fragment referencing a Pi 5 only symbol, running on a Pi 4 -- is
discarded by the firmware, creates no such node, and so was indistinguishable
from "no cape overlay is applied at all".  The restore was skipped, the broken
overlay stayed installed, and it repeated every boot: the one state that
cannot recover on its own was the one state never repaired.

It is also wrong in the ordinary case, because that node describes the overlay
that BOOTED while the installed file is what governs the next boot; the two
differ for the whole window between detection and reboot.

Compare the installed overlay against the shipped default instead, which is
exactly the pair restoreDefaultCapeOverlay() copies, so the check and the
action agree and re-running is a no-op.  The same comparison replaces the
open coded read-and-memcmp on the base overlay path.

Nothing reads the firmware's user-warnings, so there is no other route by
which a failed resolution could have been noticed.

fix(wifi): Pi Zero W / Pi 3B could not join Wi-Fi on PMF-capable routers (#2953)

The user entered a correct SSID and password, wlan0 associated and then
dropped in a loop, never got an address, and the player fell back to
its hotspot - indistinguishable from a wrong password.

FPPINIT_Network.cpp wrote `ieee80211w=1` (PMF optional) into every
wpa_supplicant network block. wpa_supplicant honours a per-network
ieee80211w blindly, so on the BCM43430 (Pi Zero W / Pi 3B, brcmfmac fw
7.45.98, no MFP support, no BIP cipher advertised) it negotiated PMF
with any MFP-capable AP - most Wi-Fi 6 / mesh routers by default - and
the kernel then rejected the IGTK ("key setting validation failed" /
"WPA: Failed to configure IGTK to the driver"), tearing down the
association. No FPP setting could turn it off.

Emit a single global `pmf=1` instead. wpas_get_ssid_pmf() applies a
driver-capability guard to the global default that it does not apply
to the per-network option: with no BIP cipher PMF is skipped; on boards
that advertise one (BCM43455, rtw88, ...) PMF is negotiated exactly as
before, including against PMF-required and WPA3-only APs. This mirrors
NetworkManager on stock Raspberry Pi OS, which is why the same hardware
works there.

Tested (UniFi, wpa_supplicant 2:2.10-24): Pi Zero W reproduces the loop
on stock and connects with the patch via both `fppinit setupNetwork`
and a cold boot; Pi 3B+, Pi 4, Pi 5 and Pi 2 + Archer T4U v3 (rtw88)
still negotiate pmf=1 on MFP-capable, pmf=2 on PMF-required, and SAE

fix(wifi): the WPA3 checkbox never connected to most WPA3 routers

Ticking WPA3 against a router in WPA2/WPA3 mixed mode - the common
consumer setting - left the player scanning forever, on every board.

The generated config used `sae_pwe=1`, which means hash-to-element
only. Many APs (including UniFi) don't advertise H2E in their RSNXE,
and wpa_supplicant then rejects every BSS at selection time ("skip -
SAE H2E required, but not supported by the AP") before it would ever
fall back to WPA-PSK. Use `sae_pwe=2` (H2E when the AP offers it,
hunting-and-pecking otherwise); an H2E downgrade is still detected in
4-way message 3. Also emit `sae_pwe` when only the backup network is
WPA3 - it's a global option and was previously gated on the primary.

Zero W (no SAE in firmware) falls back to WPA2-PSK instead of failing.

fix(plugins): say which phase of a plugin upgrade failed

mqtt: fix swapped retain/qos arguments in MosquittoClient::Publish() (#2954)

Publish(subTopic, msg, retain, qos) called PublishRaw(topic, msg, qos, retain),
whose signature is (topic, msg, retain, qos).  The swap dates from 9c37023ed
(2021), which reversed the parameter names in the signatures without touching
the body of Publish().

Since every caller passes qos=1, the effect on the wire was that every message
was retained (retain received the int 1) and the "non-retained" topics went
out at QoS 0 (qos received the bool false).  The topic list in the two-arg
overloads (version/branch/warnings/ready) therefore never affected retention,
only QoS.

Fix the argument order and make the two-arg overloads retain unconditionally,
which preserves what is stored on the broker today.  Consumers such as Home
Assistant and the fpp-HomeAssistant plugin rely on state topics being retained
to recover current state on (re)connect, and the plugin's empty-payload clears
of its cached ha/.../config topics only work because they are retained.
Changing the default would leave stale retained values on every user's broker,
since a non-retained publish never replaces a retained one.

Net change: the formerly QoS 0 topics (status, playlist/*, fppd_status,
playlist_details, port_status, command/*, gpio/*) are now QoS 1 as every
caller requested.  No topic gains or loses retention.  PublishRaw()'s
signature is unchanged so existing plugin binaries keep working; the MQTT
command and MQTTOutput call it directly and were never affected.

Also correct the help page: "status" has always been retained.

The logo needed FetchVendorLogos, and put the serial on only if SendVendorSerial was also set; the Cape Info link put the serial on whenever SendVendorSerial was set, logo or no logo. The privacy text promises "denying the logo denies this too", which was true of the image and false of the link: a user who denied logos, allowed the serial, and clicked the vendor link sent it. CapeVendorUrls() in common.php is now the only place the two URLs are made. Nothing is built unless FetchVendorLogos is 1; sn, id and cs go on both URLs only when SendVendorSerial is 1 as well; hideExternalURLs blanks the link. The header asks for the header_cape_image variant, Cape Info for vendor.image, as before. Only http(s) URLs are accepted -- a javascript: or data: URL from an EEPROM previously went straight into an href. Every value in these blocks comes from the EEPROM and none of it was escaped. fix(backups): restoring your own older backup no longer turns off web authentication

The provenance check added in 8c2af486b withheld the login credentials from any
backup it could not prove was this player's own. Every backup written before
88f194700 fails that proof: parse_ini_string() stripped the quotes out of the
privacyConsent record, so it no longer decodes and the backup counted as another
device's. Rebuilding a player from one of its own earlier backups -- including
every automatic backup on every upgraded box -- came up with password,
passwordEnable, osPassword and emailtoemail dropped, which is web authentication
off.

Provenance is now three-way. 'own' restores everything, as before. 'foreign'
(a record naming a different real device) withholds the privacy answers, the
identity and the credentials, as before. 'unknown' (no record, or one naming
nobody) withholds only the privacy answers and identity; the credentials and
mail destination are carried, as every release before the check did. A
quote-stripped record still has its uuid read out of it, so a same-box backup
from an earlier release is recognised as 'own' outright.

Verified on a player against three synthetic backups (stripped-own,
stripped-foreign, no record) and a control run of the previous code, which
restored nothing from the stripped-own file.

fix(plugins): Reinstall can re-clone a plugin whose installed copy can no longer fetch

Since the disclosure check became the gate for every reinstall, a plugin whose
update check failed was left installed and untouched. That was right for an
offline player, but the same failure comes from a clone whose origin alone has
gone -- the --single-branch branch renamed or deleted, or the repository moved
-- where a fresh clone from the plugin list's URL works. Such a plugin was
stuck: Reinstall All skipped it, a direct Reinstall refused, and after an FPP OS
upgrade it stayed on the reinstall list with fppd's non-dismissible warning up
for good.

The update check now tells the two apart. The page posts the listing's srcURL
with the check; when the clone's own fetch fails, the server fetches the
reinstall target from that URL into the same origin/<branch> ref the
reinstall-side privacy diff reads. If that works the check succeeds with
originUnreachable set (updatesAvailable 0, since nothing about the checked-out
branch could be learned), the page says an Update cannot run and Reinstall is
the fix, and a Reinstall proceeds through the usual disclosure review. If the
listing URL is unreachable too, the check fails as before and nothing is
uninstalled.

Verified on a player: healthy origin unchanged with and without the body; origin
pointed at a nonexistent repository fails without the body and succeeds with
originUnreachable when the listing URL is posted; a bogus listing URL fails.

fix(BBShiftString): a V4 chain gets its config packet in every packet frame

The FalconV5 packet phase is clocked out on every pin of the cape at
once, so a send-only (V4) chain is on the bus for every packet frame the
V5 chains need: number, fuse and query frames, not just its own config
frames.  Its slot in those frames was the zero-filled buffer, which the
receiver sees as a framed 57 byte packet with a token it does not know
(neither the V4 0xAA nor the V5 0xBB).  A V4 receiver next to a V5 chain
took that for a chain break plus pixel data and showed garbage on the
tail of its strings (#2948).

Fill the slot with the chain's V4 config packet instead.  The protocol
sends that packet regularly after data frames anyway, and a V4 chain
alone already tolerates it every 12th packet slot.  The encoded packet is
cached per chain at setup and stamped into every static and dynamic
packet frame.

The two packet number frame needs one more thing: a V4 receiver has had
its config packet by the second packet and must see its line go low, not
a second packet.  The command table is indexed by data byte position and
never reloads inside the packet phase, so the last 32 bytes of the table
become a fixed slot holding the end-of-frame masks with send-only chain
heads cleared, and the firmware reloads the masks from there before the
second packet.  Written on every configuration, so the reload changes
nothing on a cape without V4 chains.  The offset is shared with the

fix(BBShiftString): read FalconV5 replies only when complete; budget the query frames

Two problems behind #2959 (phantom eFuse trips and unwarned frame drops
with long strings behind V5 receivers at 40fps).

The listener firmware bumped its byte count in PRU data RAM after every
32 byte store, and the ARM read that count at the top of every SendData,
before the back-pressure gate.  Once the string data plus the packet
phase and listen window exceed the frame period, the next frame tick
lands inside the window and the ARM decodes a partial reply, which on
the reporter's rig set fuse flags for all four ports of the receiver on
every query.  The listener now keeps the length in a register for the
whole window and publishes it, followed by a capture counter, only when
the string PRU closes the window.  The ARM processes a capture only when
that counter changes and never writes the length back, so a read that
lands mid-window sees the previous, complete capture or nothing.

The frame time used for the sustainable-rate warning was string bytes
plus a flat 1700us.  A query frame adds about 2.9ms on every pin (packet
lead-in, 57 bytes of 10 cells at 1130ns, listener lead-in and a window
of 500us plus 1.7ms when the receiver answers), and queries go out on
most frames once the receivers are being polled.  The FalconV5 support
now reports the share of frames that carry a query (each mux cycles
through its receivers and idles one frame) and that share of the query
cost is added to the frame time, so a configuration whose string data
fits but whose queries do not is warned about instead of quietly dropping
frames under the 10% hysteresis.

Verified on an AM62x 16 port cape with eight V5 chains and no receivers
attached: the capture counter advances once per listen window with the
published length stable across reads; the budget line reports queries on
89% of frames.  AM335x listener firmware assembled on a BeagleBone.  Not
yet run against a receiver, so the "reply now decodes complete" half is
by construction, and the reporter's rig is the test for it.

fix(BBShiftString): a listen window that opens mid-read no longer splices two receiver replies

The phantom eFuse trips in #2959 survived the counter-gated read: the
capture the ARM decoded was complete, but it was two replies spliced
together.  Reproduced on an AM62x 16 port cape with one SRx1 v5 at 768
pixels per port and a 25ms period, and traced by copying each published
capture three times back to back: the copies differed in hundreds of
bytes while the capture count stayed the same.  The listener was writing
the next window's samples over the buffer the ARM was reading.

That happens whenever a frame tick lands inside the following listen
window with the previous capture still unread, which a frame period the
frame only just fits produces regularly (the two packet number frame
overruns it, and the phase then drifts through the window).  The ARM's
copy then carries the new reply's head and the old reply's tail.  Each
reply is scrambled with its own random key offset, so unscrambling the
splice with the header's offset yields garbage past the seam that still
parses: a 12 port receiver with ports 5-12 blown, on a 4 port receiver.
Nothing was wrong with the receiver, the wire, or the decoder; the same
receiver at a 26ms or 50ms period, or throttled below the frame time,
was clean.

Two changes.  The listener now raises a busy flag from the moment a
window opens until the capture is published, and the ARM checks the
flag and the count on both sides of its copy, dropping a copy that
either check says was overwritten under it.  And the copy is no longer
tied to the frame tick: the capture is staged into a buffer by
stageListenerData(), which the AM62x pump thread polls every few hundred
microseconds so the reply is taken well before the next window can open,
and the output thread decodes the staged copy on its next frame.
Platforms without a pump thread stage at frame time as before.  The
byte decoder also gets a zeroed tail on its sample buffer, since it
walks up to a byte cell past the capture while finishing the last byte
and could read past the array on a full length capture.

Measured on the same cape, 60 seconds each, against the unfixed build's
52 to 144 trips per run:

  768px @ 25ms period: 0 trips, 0 captures dropped, telemetry live
  585px @ 20ms period: 0 trips, 3 of ~2400 captures dropped
  768px @ 50ms period: 0 trips, 0 dropped (control, clean before too)

With the busy check alone about half the captures at the tight periods
were dropped as torn; the prompt staging is what recovers them.  AM335x
listener firmware assembled on a BeagleBone.

fix(upgrade): stop the version upgrade building a "vv10.1" git ref

The Upgrade button on the release-notes dialog sent upgrade_FPP a doubly
prefixed ref, so the branch switch never happened.

ViewReleaseNotes() normalized the version to the git form ("10.1" ->
"v10.1") before handing it to UpgradeFPPVersion(), which then prepended
"v" again, unconditionally, for both the dialog title and the
upgradefpp.php URL. Normalize once instead, at the single point that
builds the git ref: UpgradeFPPVersion() now accepts either form and
strips any leading "v"s, and ViewReleaseNotes() passes the version
through as-is.

The failure was also silent, which is why it looked like it worked.
upgrade_FPP discarded runGitLocked's exit status, so a ref that could not
be checked out rebuilt the tree in place and still reported "Upgrade
complete". It now records the failed switch, prints the branch it is
actually on and exits non-zero. It deliberately does not bail out at the
point of failure -- cleanCompiledBinaries has already removed the
binaries by then, so the rebuild still has to run or the device is left
with no fppd. upgradefpp.php reads that exit status and reports "Upgrade
FAILED" rather than an unconditional "Upgrade complete. Please reboot."

fix(build-image-bbb): stop the stock bone kernel from hijacking the image

The 10.1 BBB image shipped booting 6.18.52-bone54 instead of our
PRU-patched 7.1.6-fpp17, so no PRU-driven cape could start (#2966).

The FPP kernel was installed correctly as the last chroot step, but the
apt calls *in that same step* undid it. FPP_Install.sh's "apt-get upgrade"
had kept bbb.io-kernel-6.18-bone back, because a plain upgrade never
installs new packages. The later "apt-get remove --autoremove
bbb.io-kernel-tasks" is allowed to install, so it resolved that pending
upgrade, pulled in linux-image-6.18.52-bone54, and its postinst ran
zz-uenv_txt and repointed /boot/uEnv.txt at itself. The cleanup loop
could not catch it either: OLD_KERNELS was snapshotted before dpkg -i,
so the kernel apt installed afterwards was invisible to it and survived.

The window is open whenever debian.beagle.cc is newer than the rcn-ee
base image, which is most of the time -- the nightlies pass only because
rcn-ee happened to have caught up. Four changes so it cannot recur:

  * Pin linux-image/headers-*-bone* and bbb.io-kernel/headers-* to
    priority -1, before any apt call. This ships in the image too: an
    on-device "apt upgrade" hits the identical trap.
  * Take the kernel version from the .deb rather than guessing it by
    sorting /lib/modules.
  * Purge non-FPP kernels by re-scanning /lib/modules after all apt
    activity instead of from a pre-dpkg snapshot, and clear their
    vmlinuz/System.map/config out of /boot as well.
  * Write /boot/uEnv.txt ourselves, last, then fail the build -- both in
    the chroot and again from the host once it exits -- if the image
    would boot anything other than the FPP kernel.

Verified against the shipped 10.1 artifact: uEnv.txt says
uname_r=6.18.52-bone54, and both kernels are present in /boot and
/usr/lib/modules. The stock kernel has CONFIG_PRU_REMOTEPROC=m behind a
wkup_m3 dependency where ours has =y, which is the deferred-probe delay
and "Cannot get wkup_m3_ipc handle" spam reported in #2966.

fix(upgrade): repoint BBB uEnv.txt at FPP's PRU-patched kernel (144)

The 10.1 BBB images shipped booting the stock 6.18.52-bone54 instead of
FPP's PRU-patched 7.1.6-fpp17, so BBB48String could not start the PRU and
every PRU-driven cape went dark (#2966). The build-side fix stops it
recurring; this repoints the devices already flashed.

Both kernels are present on an affected device, so the repair is only a
uEnv.txt edit -- nothing is downloaded and no package is touched.

Which kernel to boot is read off the device rather than hardcoded: the
newest installed vmlinuz-7.1*, so a device still on 7.1.6-fpp15 or -fpp16
is repointed at its own kernel rather than one it does not have. A
candidate is only accepted when its modules and its DTB tree are both
present -- pointing u-boot at an incomplete kernel would leave the device
unbootable, which is much worse than dark pixels. A device still on an
older FPP kernel series (6.18.x-fppNN) has no vmlinuz-7.1* and is left
alone.

Gated to "BeagleBone Black": BeagleBone 64 runs the stock bone kernel by
design and the Pis have no uEnv.txt. Idempotent, and sets rebootFlag
rather than rebooting under the upgrade's own output stream.

fix(BBShiftString): keep a V4 chain head off the listener lead-in

e87369eea gave a send-only (V4) chain its config packet in every packet
frame and dropped its line only for the second packet of a two packet
frame.  With a V4 receiver beside a V5 chain that still garbled the chain
head's port, idle or playing (#2964).  In a query frame the head took its
config packet and then saw the listener lead-in, 15.5us low and 19.5us
high, which is the V4 protocol's own cue for "a packet follows" (the
receiver switches to serial receive on that low/high), followed by the
bus turnaround, where nothing drives the pair and the receivers bias it
to idle high, and then the next frame's pixel data.  A V4 receiver alone
never meets that: its config frames end in the frame's low reset.  And
no mask can help during the turnaround itself, since the cape is not
driving.

So the send-only chain heads now sit low for the whole packet phase of a
frame that opens a listen window, as ports 2-4 of every chain already do
(the mute from #2949, but only in those frames), and take their config
packet in the packet frames that end in the low reset: the config slots
and the number and fuse frames.  There the line still drops right after
the packet, so a two packet frame never repeats it.  Both use the mask
set the ARM parks at the tail of the command table; the firmware loads
it at the start of the packet phase when the listen flag is set and
after the first packet on every path.  V5 chain heads are on in that set
and are untouched.

Verified on an AM62x 16 port cape with a V5 receiver on one chain: the
receiver reports through the query frames as before, no eFuse events,
at 50 and at 768 pixels per port at 40fps.  AM335x firmware assembled
for both PRUs.  Not tested against the V4 receiver in the report; that
rig is the test.

Remove the managed gpio-fan line when the GPIOFan setting goes away

A cape that drives its fan from its own board specific overlay drops GPIOFan
through removeSettings.  Nothing then cleaned up after it: handle_boot_actions
only applied the setting when the key was present, so on a board that already
had one the "dtoverlay=gpio-fan" line stayed in config.txt forever, and the
cape's fan and that line both declared a cooling device on the same pin.

Absent is now distinguished from "0".  "0" still means a fan is fitted and
switched off, and leaves the line commented out; absent means no fan here is
ours to manage, and takes the line out.  ReadSettingFromFile returns false only
for a missing key, so the two cannot be confused.  The boot path calls this
unconditionally, since the case that needs cleaning is precisely the one where
the key is gone.

Any line-anchored dtoverlay=gpio-fan counts as ours, commented or not, which is
already how the rewrite below treats them -- it claims every one it finds and
forces it to gpiopin=14.  An indented or otherwise non-anchored line is left
alone by both.

(cherry picked from commit d7c5278232c5bf5acb6984dc9bf9d76f2bbad8fe)

Stop showing the fan trip temperature twice

GPIOFanTemperature was listed in the System Settings group in its own right,
not only as GPIOFan's child, so it rendered as a standalone row -- and rendered
even where the cape had removed and hidden GPIOFan itself, since hiding a
setting says nothing about a sibling that merely looks like its child.

Meanwhile PrintFanThermalSettings() emits a Fan Temperatures section for every
thermal zone with a fan cooling device bound to it, which includes the single
trip case this setting was meant to cover.  The result was the same trip
offered twice, under the same label, in two places.

The dynamic section is the better of the two and is now the only one: it covers
a cape's own fan and the Pi 5 active cooler as well as this setting's overlay,
and it writes sysfs immediately where GPIOFanTemperature only rewrote config.txt
and waited for a reboot.  So GPIOFanTemperature stops being rendered -- dropped
from the group listing and from GPIOFan's children.

The definition stays: SetGPIOFanProperties() still reads it for the temp= it
writes into the overlay line, and an already stored value still seeds that.
What it no longer is, is a second editor for a trip point the Fan Temperatures
section already owns.

One consequence worth naming: enabling GPIOFan on a board with no fan yet means
no thermal zone, so no Fan Temperatures section until the reboot that applies
the overlay.  GPIOFan is declared "reboot": 1, so that is a reboot the user is
already being asked for, and the device tree default of 70C applies until then.

(cherry picked from commit c8280e537b18c1af64392bfd346ee9e435a056cf)

Let a cape that hides GPIOFan own the fan outright

A cape declaring its own fan in its device tree hides GPIOFan and asks for it
to be removed.  The removal is refused far more often than it is granted:
settingIsSet() only asks whether the key is present, so a value written by an
EARLIER eeprom's defaultSettings is indistinguishable from one the user chose,
and removeSettings declines rather than overrule a choice nobody actually made.

That refusal lands on exactly the wrong population.  Every board that ran the
previous eeprom already has GPIOFan set, so those are the boards that keep
writing dtoverlay=gpio-fan while the cape's overlay declares a fan of its own --
two cooling devices and two active trip points on one pin.

So stop reading the value alone.  Hiding the setting is the cape saying it owns
that hardware, and it is unambiguous in a way the stored value is not: FPP
writes no overlay line and removes any it wrote before, whatever is stored.  The
value keeps its old meaning where the cape is silent -- "0" is a fan fitted and
switched off, and still only comments the line out.

(cherry picked from commit 0354d3c83131776b4298d252fa19f76d1543909e)

Let a cape retire a setting it has taken over, except a privacy one

removeSettings was routed through the rule that guards defaultSettings, which
refuses when the key already holds a different value.  A removal's precondition
is that the key IS set, so that rule refused every removal that could have done
anything: the only key removeSettings could clear was one whose value was the
empty string.  The mechanism could not work, and its single observable effect
was a "cape may not remove setting X: the user has set it to something else"
line on every boot, which reads like a cape misbehaving rather than a feature
that never functioned.

The signature already required of removeSettings, and not of defaultSettings, is
what authorizes a removal -- that asymmetry exists precisely because a removal
discards a value somebody may have chosen.

What a cape still may not retire is a setting that governs what the device
discloses.  Removing one restores FPP's shipped default and those defaults
transmit, so a cape could raise disclosure just by deleting the answer.  Whether
it happens to raise it on a given box is not the test; that is not a cape's
question to decide.  Those settings are exactly the ones declaring a
transmitRank, which is the same list the defaultSettings ratchet consults, so
the two rules read from one source.

Enable uart0 on a Pi 5 without letting it claim GPIO14 and GPIO15

A Pi 5 needs uart0 turned on explicitly or there is no /dev/ttyAMA0 at all, and
"dtparam=uart0=on" enables the device AND muxes both header pins onto it at
boot.  Kernel 6.18 enabled strict pinmux for pinctrl-rp1, which makes that claim
final: gpiod requests against either pin fail, the runtime "pinctrl set" FPP
uses is reasserted by the pinctrl driver, and the pin cannot be reclaimed by
unbinding its owner the way an i2c or spi pin can -- the PL011 driver publishes
no unbind attribute at all, so there is nothing to unbind.

A cape with a button or a pixel string on one of those pins loses it, quietly:
the request fails and the input is left registered against a -1 descriptor,
which reads as permanently asserted rather than as absent.  A cape putting its
test button on GPIO15 therefore behaves as though that button were held down
(issue #2965).

Every other board FPP supports leaves the UART unmuxed and claims the pin at
runtime only when a serial output is actually configured -- which is what allows
DMX out of GPIO14 while GPIO15 stays an ordinary GPIO, and is how the BeagleBone
capes have always worked.  fpp-uart0-nopins enables uart0 pointing at an empty
pin group, so a Pi 5 does the same: the device probes, /dev/ttyAMA0 appears, and
no header pin is claimed until something asks for it.

upgrade/145 carries existing installs across.  It compiles the overlay to a temp
file and checks it before installing anything or touching config.txt, because a
dtoverlay line naming a missing or empty .dtbo costs the board its UART and
gains nothing, and it replaces only a line-anchored dtparam so a commented or
indented copy is left alone.
